title: Ranking Member Angie Craig Slams Trump Administration Effort to Kick an Additional 6.3 Million Americans off SNAP
text:
Today, House Agriculture Committee Ranking Member Angie Craig (MN-02) released the following statement in response to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s proposed rule to eliminate broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE). BBCE gives states the option to allow someone who has already qualified for Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) or similar state benefits to qualify for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), since their eligibility requirements are similar.

“This move by the Trump administration to take food assistance away from millions more elderly Americans and children is heartless and cruel,” said Ranking Member Craig. “The proposed rule would make it harder to meet basic needs and roll back efforts to streamline federal programs. SNAP is a highly effective and efficient program when it is allowed to work as designed. Unfortunately, the Trump administration and the outgoing Republican majority in Congress have undermined the program’s integrity at every turn, harming millions of vulnerable Americans in the process. If Congressional Republicans want to be responsive to the needs of American citizens, they can start by joining Democrats in loud and unified opposition to the Trump administration’s latest attack on hungry Americans.”

According to the Trump administration’s regulatory impact analysis of the proposed rule:

6.3 million individuals in 3.2 million households will lose their SNAP benefits entirely.

The 3.2 million families impacted make up 17 percent of SNAP households.

SNAP benefits will be cut by $50.82 billion.

Federal spending on benefits will be cut by $44.65 billion over 5 years (FY2027-FY2031), and state spending on benefits will be cut by $6.17 billion.

SNAP administrative expenses will increase by $1.24 billion.

Federal spending on administrative expenses will increase by $309.5 million over five years.

State spending on administrative costs will increase by $928.5 million.

Increased burden on participants is estimated to be approximately $71.7 million over five years.

Because SNAP participation is often used to streamline eligibility for basic needs programs, the proposed rule's effects reach beyond the program.

1.78 million children would no longer be categorically eligible for school meals. Of those children:

97 percent would likely remain eligible but need to go through an onerous paperwork process to maintain eligibility.

93,000 children would be shifted from free to reduced-price school meals.

28,000 children would lose free school meals entirely and have to pay full price.

42,000 children will no longer receive Summer EBT (“Sun Bucks”) beginning in the summer of 2029.

An estimated 13,000 of these children would lose benefits they qualify for due to administrative burden (i.e., not applying for SEBT, even though they remain eligible).

5,500 women, infants and children would be kicked off the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children (WIC).

The number of states opting in to broad-based categorical eligibility has increased steadily each year because of its positive impacts on participants and program administration. Currently, 46 states, Republican and Democratic alike, opt to use BBCE.

title: Meeks, Amo, Kamlager-Dove Demand Answers from Trump Administration Over Advanced AI Chip Exports Amid Reports of Chinese Intelligence Ties
text:
Washington, DC — Today, House Foreign Affairs Ranking Member Gregory W. Meeks (D-NY), Vice Ranking Member Gabe Amo (D-RI), and Ranking Member of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-CA), demanded answers from Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick over the Trump Administration’s approval of advanced AI chip exports, including to companies with concerning links to China and amid alarming reports of potential Chinese intelligence ties to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

In a letter to Secretary Lutnick, Meeks, Amo and Kamlager-Dove pressed the Department to explain what it knew about the reported connections between Huang and potential Chinese intelligence operatives, when senior officials were informed, and why it continued to permit exports despite the national security risks.

The Members wrote in a letter to the Secretary:

“We call on the Department of Commerce to immediately halt exports of advanced artificial intelligence chips to the People’s Republic of China (PRC) amid recent reporting about PRC intelligence activities and of potential PRC access to these critical national security technologies. You cannot claim to be protecting American leadership in artificial intelligence while allowing our most advanced technology to reach a strategic competitor. National security must come before corporate sales targets.

“As we previously warned, allowing China to obtain advanced U.S. AI chips puts our national security at risk. These chips power the computing capabilities that will shape the future of artificial intelligence, military modernization, and economic competition. Once these capabilities reach the PRC government or entities acting on its behalf, the consequences could be nearly impossible to reverse.

“Considering these alarming reports, the American people must have transparency into what your Department knew, when it knew it, and why it continued to permit these exports.

“We hope that the Department did not ignore warnings about a suspected PRC intelligence operation while allowing advanced American technology to flow through companies under scrutiny. If Commerce was not briefed, we need to know why. If it was briefed, we need to know how it responded. And if the Department knowingly permitted these exports despite credible national-security concerns, the American people deserve an explanation.”

The full letter can be found here.

title: Ranking Member Takano: It is Time to Pass Major Richard Star Act
text:
WASHINGTON–Today, House Committee on Veterans’ Affairs Ranking Member Mark Takano (CA-39) held a press conference to demand the passage of the Major Richard Star Act by Veterans Day. The Major Richard Star Act legislation will end the “wounded veteran tax,” or the offset that keeps 59,000 medically retired veterans from receiving their full Department of Defense retirement pay and their full Department of Veterans Affairs disability pay.

“Veterans, we have heard your call for action, and we are ready to help deliver relief. For 59,000 combat-injured veterans, relief has been long overdue, but House Democrats have worked tirelessly to change that. We are closer than ever; now is the moment to finish the job. We refuse to settle for half-measures when it comes to our nation’s combat-injured veterans, and I urge my colleagues in the Senate to act swiftly so we can deliver this critical support before Veterans Day," said Ranking Member Takano.

“Combat-wounded veterans who were forced to medically retire are being shortchanged by the VA,” said Congressman Raul Ruiz (CA-25), one of the original authors of the bill. “For every dollar in VA disability compensation these veterans receive, a dollar is taken out of their retirement pay. Our veterans deserve respect, they do NOT deserve to be treated like a burdensome, expendable line item in a budget. That is why I am proud to co-author the Major Richard Star Act, which ends this unfair offset. Our veterans stood up for us. Now we must stand up for them. I urge Speaker Johnson to bring it up for a vote and my colleagues on both sides of the aisle to vote yes.”

“Combat-injured veterans are still waiting for Congress to right this wrong, and they have waited long enough,” said Corey Geisler, VFW’s Commander-in-Chief, who served in the U.S. Army and is a veteran of Operation Iraqi Freedom. "We want the full Star Act: no cuts, no caps, no gimmicks. Honor the contract.”

Veterans and family members spoke as well, including retired Air Force veteran Naomi Mathis and Army infantry veteran Scott Craig. A number of Veteran Service Organizations participated in the event, including Veterans of Foreign Wars, Disabled American Veterans, Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America, Jewish War Veterans, Marine Corps League, Reserve Organization of America, as well as veterans and family members impacted by this legislation.

The Major Richard Star Act is supported by the above organizations as well as Wounded Warrior Project, Veterans Justice Alliance, American Legion, Military Officers Association of America, Vietnam Veterans of America, National Guard Association of the United States, Blue Star Families, Fleet Reserve Association, Elizabeth Dole Foundation, Team Rubicon, Blinded Veterans Association, Non Commissioned Officers Association, Military Family Association, Air Force Sergeants Association, Association of the U.S. Army, U.S. Army Warrant Officers Association, Tragedy Assistance Program for Survivors, National Defense Committee, Mission Roll Call, and a number of other Veterans Service and Advocacy Organizations.

The full recording of the press conference can be found here.

title: Chairman Guthrie Applauds House Passage of Six Bills to Advance American Nuclear Energy

committee.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – This week, Congressman Brett Guthrie (KY-02), Chairman of the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, applauded House passage of six bills that will unleash reliable nuclear energy and cut red tape that stands in the way of lowering prices for American families.

The bills include H.R. 3978, the Nuclear REFUEL Act; H.R. 9612, the American Enrichment Deployment Act; H.R. 5549, the Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act; H.R. 9613, the Nuclear Advisory Committee Reform Act; H.R. 9614, the NRC Staff Pay Alignment Act; and H.R. 9084, the Department of Energy Nuclear Transparency Act. Building on the work of the ADVANCE Act, these bills continue improving the NRC’s licensing process and reporting by the Department of Energy, helping to maintain positive momentum for U.S. nuclear deployment.

“Nuclear energy provides safe, reliable, and affordable power to communities across the United States. Throughout this Congress, our Committee has worked to strengthen the American nuclear industry to help meet the needs of families and businesses. The passage of these six bipartisan bills will continue that work by improving the Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s licensing processes, supporting a resilient nuclear supply chain, and upholding the NRC’s unwavering commitment to safety,” said Chairman Guthrie. “Thank you to all of my colleagues who worked tirelessly to support these critical pieces of legislation.”

BACKGROUND:

H.R. 3978, the Nuclear REFUEL (Recycling Efficient Fuels Utilizing Expedited Licensing) Act (Reps. Latta and Peters): Amends the definition of a production facility in the Atomic Energy Act (AEA) to exclude facilities that reprocess spent nuclear fuel in a manner that does not isolate plutonium. In effect, this clarifies that these spent fuel reprocessing facilities may be licensed under the same one-step regulatory process as other fuel cycle facilities, rather than a longer, two-step process more appropriate for facilities that produce special nuclear material in quantities significant for national security.

H.R. 9612, the American Enrichment Deployment Act (Reps. Fry and Schrier): Amends the AEA to update the process for licensing of uranium enrichment facilities to align with the licensing requirements for all other fuel cycle facilities. It does so by removing enrichment-specific requirements for environmental review and adjudicatory hearings, and by clarifying that construction of a facility may be allowed prior to licensing under the same terms and conditions applicable to other fuel cycle facilities.

H.R. 5549, the Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act (Reps. Griffith and Schrier): Removes the need for the NRC to expend resources on unnecessary hearings by eliminating the current requirement to hold uncontested hearings on applications for a construction permit, an operating license, a combined construction and operating license, or a license to possess and use special nuclear material. The bill would in no way affect the right of persons whose interests are affected to request a hearing on specific matters.

H.R. 9613, the Nuclear Advisory Committee Reform Act (Rep. Harshbarger): Amends the AEA to update the role of the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards (ACRS) in providing advice to the NRC on license applications, license amendments, regulatory activities, and other matters. The legislation provides ACRS new flexibility to decline to review issues that do not merit its attention and directs the ACRS to focus on issues that are directly related to nuclear reactor facility design, are safety-significant, are noteworthy or novel, and have not been previously acted on by the Committee.

H.R. 9614, the NRC Staff Pay Alignment Act (Rep. Menendez): Amends the AEA to provide that the Chairman of the NRC may fix the compensation for career, Senior Executive Service (SES) appointees at a rate that is 10 percent higher than the maximum annual rate of basic pay for SES positions within the Commission. The legislation would help align the pay authority applicable to these career employees with workforce development and pay authority amendments made to the AEA by the ADVANCE Act. It will enable the NRC Chairman to award individuals worthy of increased compensation to help ensure high-quality management of licensing and safety oversight.

H.R. 9084, the Department of Energy Nuclear Transparency Act (Reps. Castor and Miller-Meeks): Requires DOE to announce and post information on decisions relating to the licensing and authorization of DOE nuclear facilities, as well as changes in directives and safety standards relating to such facilities, on a publicly accessible website within 24 hours of such decisions or actions. The legislation would also require the Secretary of Energy to provide an annual report to the Energy and Commerce Committee and to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee that details all such activity by DOE to authorize nuclear facilities over the previous year.

title: Statement of the Chairman and Ranking Member of the Committee on Ethics Regarding Representative Lance Gooden
text:
Pursuant to Committee Rule 7, the Chairman and Ranking Member of the Committee on Ethics (Committee) determined to release the following statement:

On June 10, 2026, the Committee received a referral from the Office of Congressional Conduct (OCC) regarding Representative Lance Gooden. Pursuant to House Rule XI, clause 3(b)(8)(A), and Committee Rules 17A(b)(1)(A) and 17A(c)(1), on July 27, 2026, the Committee extended its review of the matter. In order to gather additional information necessary to complete its review, the Committee will review the matter pursuant to Committee Rule 18(a). The Committee notes that the mere fact of conducting further review of a referral, and any mandatory disclosure of such further review, does not itself indicate that any violation has occurred, or reflect any judgment on behalf of the Committee.

In order to comply with Committee Rule 7 regarding confidentiality, out of fairness to all respondents, and to assure the integrity of its work, the Committee will refrain from making further public statements on this matter pending completion of its initial review.

title: Warren, Banks Statement on NVIDIA’s Continued Export of Advanced AI Chips Following Reports of Foreign Intelligence Operation

committee.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs

text:
Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senators Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Ranking Member of the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, and Jim Banks (R-Ind.), a Member of the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, released the following statement:

“In March, bipartisan members of Congress urged the Department of Commerce to suspend or reconsider NVIDIA’s export licenses to China and conduct a full national security review. Since then, NVIDIA has reportedly received approvals to export hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies tied to China’s military, all while attempting to influence the debate over chip controls in Washington, D.C.

“NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang’s confirmation of a relationship with a suspected spy for China’s intelligence service makes these national security concerns even more urgent and raises important questions NVIDIA must answer about the extent to which these activities were related.

“It is time for Congress to take decisive action to pass key bills like the AI Overwatch Act in the NDAA that will cut off pathways through which China accesses advanced chips. The Commerce Department should complement these efforts with immediate action to close export control loopholes and ensure that advanced AI chips are not going to China’s military.”

title: VIDEO: Heinrich and Whitehouse Urge Senate Passage of Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act

committee.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources

text:
Heinrich: “We don’t have to wait for the new Congress to start lowering costs. We can do that today. Let’s pass permitting reform.”

WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senators Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, held a press conference urging their Senate colleagues to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), bipartisan legislation to lower energy costs, hold data centers accountable for the costs they impose on American families, and create good-paying jobs.

With the Senate slated to vote on the legislation this evening, Heinrich and Whitehouse highlighted how BAAJA would help address rising electricity costs, accelerate the development of new energy infrastructure, and hold data centers accountable by forcing them to fully pay for their operational costs.

“Just one week ago Americans sent a clear message: They want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable. That’s precisely what this permitting reform bill will do,” said Heinrich. “BAAJA will save households billions of dollars in electricity costs, directly hold data centers accountable, create over 100,000 trades and manufacturing jobs, and cut emissions up to 20% from the power sector over the next decade.”

“The American people spoke loud and clear that they wanted results on affordability. BAAJA will mean billions in lower energy costs, and tens of billions of dollars more in ratepayer savings because of the provisions cracking down on data centers. And it can actually begin to happen now. People want to see Congress do big, good things. This is a big, good thing,” said Whitehouse.

Independent analyses find that BAAJA would lower Americans’ electricity bills by 3–5 percent, save families billions of dollars, nearly double the amount of solar and wind that can connect to the grid, and create up to 105,600 trades and manufacturing jobs. The legislation would also require data centers to cover the increased grid and energy costs they create, estimated at $55 billion over the next decade.

U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Ranking Member Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee Ranking Member U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) host press conference to urge Senate passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, November 9, 2026.

Watch the full video of Heinrich’s remarks here.

A transcript of Heinrich’s remarks as delivered is below:

Every once in a while, I don’t wear my Senate pin, even if it means I’m going to get stopped on the way in.

I wear this pin.

It’s my dad’s 60-year IBEW pin, and he spent those 60 years keeping people’s lights on and working to keep their electricity bills affordable.

A little over a month ago, Senator Whitehouse and myself announced, along with our Republican colleagues, our bipartisan permitting bill.

And today, just one week after Americans sent a pretty resounding message about their priorities, we are taking our first vote on that legislation.

And that message that the people sent was pretty clear: they want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable, and that’s precisely what this permitting reform bill will do.

BAAJA will save households billions of dollars in electricity costs, so that families can have money in their pockets for more than just keeping the lights on and their homes warm.

This bill directly holds data centers accountable, forcing big corporations to pay their full share instead of pushing costs on the consumers.

That one provision is worth $35 billion dollars to American households.

That’s pretty remarkable.

BAAJA will create over 100,000 trades and manufacturing jobs, good-paying jobs that workers can be certain will be around to support their families through a project’s completion.

And BAAJA will cut emissions up to 20% from the power sector over the next decade, meaning cleaner air, healthier communities, and fewer healthcare costs.

This bill’s not perfect.

We’ve never pretended it was.

It is, after all, bipartisan, and that means that neither side got everything they want.

We had to find common ground.

We had to make compromises, and we had to work through some very real disagreements.

But bipartisanship doesn’t mean we stop listening, and it doesn’t mean we stop working to make the legislation better.

I have worked hard to incorporate the feedback that we’ve heard from Tribes and New Mexicans into our Manager’s Amendment, and I want to walk you through a few of those changes because they’re pretty important.

First, on Tribal consultation, I’ve heard directly from Tribal leaders about the importance of having a meaningful voice in decisions that affect their communities and affect their ancestral lands.

We work to strengthen that dramatically in this Manager’s Amendment.

Tribes will now have an equal seat with states in transmission planning, and federal agencies will be required, and let me say that again: required “shall” consult, not “may” consult, “shall” consult early with Tribes on projects that will affect important cultural sites, including on what properties are affected, the impacts of the project, and ways to avoid, minimize, or mitigate potential harms, and basically that means that mandatory Tribal consultation is now built into every single step of the Section 106 process by law.

We’ve also extended the window for objections to agency reports.

We’ve strengthened opportunities for states to weigh in, and we’ve given states a way to ask FERC to investigate local utility projects that gouge consumers.

That, in my view, is particularly important as private equity and other outside investors seek to take a larger role in electric utilities.

States need the tools to protect their ratepayers.

Third, we’ve made sure that workers’ rights are protected.

The Manager’s Amendment preserves collective bargaining agreements for union employees of the power of bargaining administrations, so that those workers can continue to bargain collectively and stand up for workers’ rights.

And finally, we’ve added a new Department of Energy Data Center Community Assistance Program because when a community is considering whether or not to grant a permit to a major data center, it needs to understand what that project will mean for its electricity supply, costs, water resources, infrastructure, and local economy, in order for them to make a good decision.

This program will give state, local, and Tribal governments the technical assistance they need to make their own informed decisions.

These are meaningful improvements.

They reflect the feedback that we’ve heard and they make an important piece of legislation, in my view, even stronger.

And importantly, they don’t change what this bill was always about: lowering energy costs, building the infrastructure our country so desperately needs, creating good-paying jobs, protecting our communities, and making sure that data centers pay their fair share.

That’s what we set out to accomplish when we started this project, and that’s what we’re still working to deliver.

So I would urge all my colleagues: Let’s get this done.

Let’s make it possible for America to build big things in this country again.

The people sent us a very clear message on Tuesday that they expect us to lower the costs in their daily lives.

We don’t have to wait for the new Congress to start lowering costs.

We can do that today.

So let’s pass permitting reform.

title: Senate Advances Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act

committee.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works

text:
Today, U.S. Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee, spoke on the Senate floor to highlight the urgency of passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), legislation to reform our nation’s permitting and environmental review processes and make life more affordable for American families. Following Chairman Capito’s remarks, the Senate advanced BAAJA by a vote of 73-25.

Below are the floor remarks of Chairman Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) as prepared for delivery.

“Madam President, for far too long, critical investments in our nation’s infrastructure, energy production, and economy have been forced to sit on the sidelines due to endless red tape, duplicative reviews, and regulatory uncertainty.

“Businesses large and small, looking to invest meaningfully in our country, lack the certainty they need to make decisions. Communities nationwide have waited in regulatory limbo for roads, bridges, energy infrastructure, manufacturing facilities, and other investments that create jobs and strengthen local economies. All this has led to lost jobs, missed economic opportunities, and higher prices across America.

“Data from the National Association of Manufacturers shows that permitting delays are costing America’s manufacturers $12.1 billion every year, including $87 million in additional costs in West Virginia alone. According to new data from McKinsey, $1.8 trillion of investments are locked up in the federal permitting system right now, including $22.3 billion of sidelined investments in my home state of West Virginia.

“These are projects that could provide good-paying jobs, improve mobility, increase access to clean drinking water, deploy broadband in rural areas, and so much more. The environmental permitting and review processes should be tools for informed decision-making, not reasons that decisions can’t be made. This is not a sustainable way for the United States to compete with the rest of the world, and it is certainly not a sustainable way to address the energy and affordability issues we are facing today.

“It’s no secret that America’s energy demand is growing rapidly to meet the needs of a modern economy. To meet these needs, we must modernize our grid, increase our energy production, and build the infrastructure that will keep America competitive and secure for decades to come.

“It is time for Congress to act. It is, actually, well past time.

“As Chairman of the Environment and Public Works Committee, I worked with my Ranking Member, Senator Whitehouse, as well as Chairman Lee of the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and Ranking Member Heinrich, to introduce a comprehensive permitting reform solution: the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, or BAAJA. This bill will unlock economic opportunity, infrastructure development, and energy production across the United States.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act consists of two parts. The first part of the bill is in the EPW Committee’s jurisdiction, and it consists of reforms to the laws that set the framework for our environmental review and permitting processes, including the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Clean Water Act, and the Endangered Species Act. The EPW section also provides certainty that permitted projects will retain their permits if they remain in compliance with the law.

“The second part of the bill captures reforms to statutes in the ENR Committee’s jurisdiction, including the National Historic Preservation Act and the Federal Power Act. This section also includes the Ratepayer Protection Act, legislation that will make potential data centers pay their own way instead of American consumers facing increased costs through rising utility bills.

“Together, the package that our committees put together fulfills key policy priorities from members of both sides of the aisle and a diverse set of stakeholders. I believe these comprehensive permitting reforms will generate benefits for our country for years to come for three reasons.

“First, this bill is bipartisan. Senators Lee, Whitehouse, Heinrich, and I have worked together throughout this Congress to craft a solution that both Republicans and Democrats can support. That is the only way we can achieve durable and implementable reforms to our environmental review and permitting processes. There is something in this bill for everyone, because it is fair to everyone, and we owe it to the American people to come together as a body and pass this legislation in the weeks ahead.

“Second, this bill will help all types of projects. We cannot adjust the processes for some types of projects, but not others. Projects like coal mines, windmills, gas pipelines, solar farms, and steel mills will all benefit from this legislation.

“Third, the package addresses critical stages of the permitting process. This will create predictability, consistency, and finality in securing a permit. It will allow our laws to balance public health, the environment, and the needs of our economy. Finally, our legislation will prevent unnecessary delays and endless litigation that blocks growth.

“In West Virginia, investments have collapsed under the weight of legal challenges, denying potential benefits to areas that need support the most. When a project sits in the environmental review and permitting processes for years, jobs are not created, critical infrastructure is not built, energy is not brought onto the grid, and ultimately, American families and businesses face higher costs and fewer opportunities.

“The White House Council of Economic Advisers (CEA) released a report analyzing the ways that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would benefit families and businesses, and the results are clear. According to their analysis, the reforms made under BAAJA would result in $82 billion to $164 billion in additional economic output every year. Families would feel these economic benefits directly, as CEA estimates that for the average American household, real wages will increase, electricity bills will fall, and everyday expenses will be reduced. We cannot continue to let the costs of permitting delays fall onto American families.

“I am no stranger to the challenge of addressing permitting reform in Congress. Throughout my career, I have introduced multiple bills to improve this process. While Congress has passed some very limited reforms through various legislative packages, we have not passed significant reforms to NEPA in several decades.

Republicans and Democrats alike recognize the need for reforms to unlock investment to build projects that are important to our states. On both sides of the aisle, we understand that our constituents need lower costs and good jobs, communities need economic investment, businesses need certainty, and America needs to build. These are not partisan ideals. They are American principles.

“The Trump administration has also rallied behind this deal, supporting our efforts in the Senate to pass durable reforms so we can unleash our nation’s full potential. Additionally, we have made it a priority to have a robust manager’s amendment to this legislation that makes targeted changes based on feedback from our members and stakeholders to further build support.

“I am thankful for my colleagues’ efforts to strengthen BAAJA, and the contributions from members of the House of Representatives as well. This legislation reflects a vast amount of perspectives and priorities, and I’m proud of the product we are voting on today.

“We have received letters of support from over one thousand stakeholder organizations, representing a broad swath of groups across our country, including oil and gas producers and solar energy groups, labor unions, and business associations. They all recognize the urgent need for permitting reform, and the benefits that BAAJA would have on affordability, energy reliability, and economic growth across our country.

“In a statement from the American Petroleum Institute, President and CEO Mike Sommers said, ‘Washington has a generational opportunity to fundamentally transform a broken permitting system and help address the affordability challenges facing American consumers. Congress should seize this moment and finish the job.’

“In another statement from the Solar Energy Industries Association, CEO Tim Pawlenty said, ‘This is the kind of bipartisan action America needs to meet growing energy demand, put downward pressure on energy prices, and deploy more affordable, exactly reliable solar and storage for American families and businesses.’

“Xan Fishman, Executive Vice President of the Energy Program at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said, ‘[The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act] would fix our permitting processes so that we can review and build efficiently, reducing costs, improving quality of life, growing our economy, and improving economic outcomes.’

“From my home state, the Gas and Oil Association of West Virginia’s President, Rebecca McPhail, said the following, ‘GO-WV supports the [Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act]’s stated goals of modernizing federal environmental review, providing certainty for holders of federal permits and authorizations, and supporting an all-of-the-above energy strategy.’

“From the business community, Rodney Davis, Senior Vice President and Head of Government Affairs at the U.S. Chamber, said, ‘The Senate’s progress toward a comprehensive, bipartisan permitting reform deal brings us one step closer to streamlining the outdated process that is holding up critical projects of all kinds, from energy and water infrastructure to roads, broadband, and manufacturing.’

“Demonstrating the breadth of support this bill has received, the Laborers’ International Union of North America General President, Brent Booker, gave the following statement of support, “’For more than a decade LIUNA has testified before Congress, submitted comments, participated in roundtables, and endorsed numerous iterations of permitting bills… We urge lawmakers in both parties to seize this moment, pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, and finally deliver meaningful permitting reform.’

“And finally, representing a broad coalition of labor groups, in a letter from Sean McGarvey, President of North America’s Building Trades Unions, he said, ‘This legislation represents a significant step toward a more efficient permitting system that supports job creation, strengthens America’s energy and infrastructure capabilities, and helps reduce costs for working families.’

“I could not agree more. This is an unprecedented opportunity, and a legislative breakthrough we can accomplish in this unique moment. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a win for America, and we cannot let this moment pass us by.

“The reality is this: over the next several years, we will have no choice but to increase our national energy production and manufacturing capacity to meet increasing demand, and that means making sure our infrastructure projects can be built quickly, efficiently, and responsibly.

“The House has already passed several key pieces of legislation on this matter, including the SPEED Act and the PERMIT Act. Now, it’s our turn in the Senate to act on the opportunity in front of us. I encourage my colleagues to rise to the importance of this moment, and to vote in favor of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

“American growth, competitiveness, and security are at stake. With that, I yield the floor.”

title: Ernst Names Small Business of the Week, Olson Iron Works

committee.name: Senate Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship

text:
Read the release on Sen. Ernst's website HERE.

Throughout this Congress, Chair Ernst plans to recognize a small business in every one of Iowa’s 99 counties.

RED OAK, Iowa – U.S. Senator Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), Chair of the Senate Small Business Committee, today announced her Small Business of the Week, Olson Iron Works of Greene County. Throughout the 119th Congress, Chair Ernst plans to recognize a small business in each of Iowa's 99 counties.

“For the past 14 years, Olson Iron Works has forged its way to success by serving its fellow Iowans and the greater community” said Chair Ernst. “Olson Iron Works has welded such strong relationships with its customers that 80% of them are repeat buyers”

At a young age, Shane Olson discovered a love for hands-on work after learning how to weld from his father and shop teacher. He used those skills to make gifts for his family and friends. At 17, Shane enlisted in the Marine Corps, where he worked on different equipment and continued building his skills. Upon his return to Iowa, Shane joined the Iowa Air National Guard as a firefighter and further strengthened his fabrication and welding abilities. Shane’s wife, Alisa, suggested that he turn his talent and passion into a business. Shane bought and remodeled an old barn establishing Olson Iron Works as a part-time venture in 2012.

What began as a small operation has now grown into a 14,000 square foot shop and a full-time profession. Additionally, Shane remains active in the veteran community where he is a lifetime member of the American Legion and VFW. Olson Iron Works also regularly makes and donates metal flags in honor of deceased veterans and fallen first responders in the area.

Stay tuned as Chair Ernst continues to recognize outstanding Iowa small businesses with her Small Business of the Week award.

title: Trump Administration Weakens Life-Saving Silica Protections for Miners

committee.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce

text:
WASHINGTON – Ranking Member Robert C. “Bobby” Scott (VA-03), House Committee on Education and Workforce, released the following statement after the Department of Labor’s Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) published a proposed rule to change the Biden Administration’s final rule on silica dust in mines.

“Today, the Trump Administration proposed a new rule to weaken long-overdue silica dust protections, delivering a devastating blow to coal miners and their families. This proposed rule sends a clear message to coal country: profits come before people.

“For decades, we have known that silica dust is a leading cause of black lung disease, a painful and deadly illness that continues to devastate coal communities. The Biden Administration took long-overdue action to finally update MSHA’s silica dust standard, unchanged for nearly 40 years, to protect workers from the toxic exposure that has taken too many lives. Yet now, instead of defending miners’ health, the Trump Administration is rolling back protections, creating deadly loopholes and gaps that will put miners at risk of irreversible lung diseases such as severe black lung.

“This is not about regulatory red tape. It’s about whether miners can finish their careers with their lungs and health intact. This proposal only deepens this administration’s betrayal of working families in coal country.

“The Trump Administration’s actions undermine decades of progress and betray the families and communities that have sacrificed so much. Miners risk their lives every day to power this nation, and they deserve the protections and support they’ve fought for. It’s time for Congress to act and make sure miners can go to work knowing they will return home safely to their families."

Background:

The new proposal would give mine operators a get-out-of-jail-free card whenever they catch themselves exceeding the caps on silica dust. The Biden rule was clear that MSHA could bring enforcement actions whenever samples exceed the cap, whether MSHA itself conducted the sample during an inspection or the violation was revealed by the sampling that mine operators are required to perform themselves. This proposal would prohibit any enforcement unless MSHA itself takes the samples during an inspection. Keep in mind that the Trump Administration has been slashing and burning the staff and capacity of the Department of Labor, including MSHA.

The new proposal says it is keeping in place the Biden rule’s caps on dust levels, but it introduces a fudge factor that basically increases the cap. The new Trump proposal would add what it calls an “error factor” of 21 percent across the board. While the upper limit on silica dust remains officially 50 micrograms per cubic meter, this error factor effectively means that operators can effectively expose miners to close to 61 micrograms.

The new Trump proposal also gives operators a license to conduct less air sampling than before. The Biden rule had a fixed minimum schedule for air sampling, such as quarterly sampling when certain conditions are triggered. The new Trump proposal changes that to require sampling “as frequently as necessary.” MSHA argues that this could mean that operators will conduct more sampling than under a quarterly schedule, as they determine that changes in operations may generate excessive dust. However, it also puts an enormous amount of discretion in operators’ hands to determine for themselves when sampling is “necessary,” and the new proposal would eliminate a basic minimum expectation that would be clearly enforceable.

title: Huffman Puts Trump Admin, Corporate Donors on Notice to Preserve Records
text:
Ahead of the 120th Congress, Ranking Member Huffman orders 36 federal agencies and private companies to preserve every record tied to Natural Resources Democrats’ investigations of the Trump administration

Washington, D.C. – Today, House Natural Resources Committee Ranking Member Jared Huffman (D-Calif.) sent letters to 36 federal agencies and private companies ordering them to preserve documents, communications, and other records tied to the Committee’s investigations of the Trump administration.

“For two years, this administration has stonewalled us and kept the American people in the dark while Democrats have fought tirelessly to daylight and stop their corruption. Those days of obstruction are over.” said Ranking Member Huffman. “I am sending a message to President Trump and his allies: our investigations will continue full steam ahead. And to every agency official and corporate executive receiving these letters: save everything. The American people deserve to know what you did with their government and their money, and we intend to get them answers.”

The letters seek to safeguard evidence gathered or sought during the Committee’s investigations in the 119th Congress so those inquiries can continue in the new Congress. Federal agencies are directed to preserve records covered by the Federal Records Act, along with documents, communications, and other materials relevant to congressional oversight. Private companies that have been subjects of Committee inquiries also received preservation requests.

In the letters, Huffman wrote, “For the past two years, the Trump administration has repeatedly failed to provide Congress with information necessary to conduct its oversight responsibilities and obstructed numerous congressional investigations.”

The preservation letters come amid reports that the Department of the Interior and other federal agencies may already be engaging in preemptive coverups by shredding official documents and using disappearing chat messages, raising concerns that evidence could be lost before investigators can obtain it. Those reports add urgency to securing the records Congress needs to investigate allegations of corruption and misconduct.

The American people deserve to know how decisions were made, whose interests they served, and how taxpayer resources were used. These letters are an early step toward ensuring that the incoming Congress can get those answers.

Federal agency recipients included the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA), Bureau of Land Management (BLM), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), National Park Service (NPS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), U.S. Department of Commerce (DOC), U.S. Department of the Interior (DOI), U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS), and U.S. Forest Service (USFS). title: House Oversight Committee Releases Report on the Federal Government’s Mishandling of Epstein and Maxwell Criminal Investigations

committee.name: House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform

text:
WASHINGTON—The House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform today released a majority staff report titled, “A Review of the Federal Government’s Mishandling of the Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell Criminal Investigations.” The report culminates the Committee’s 15-month investigation, which included 19 transcribed interviews and depositions with key witnesses, the release of documents from the Department of Justice and the Epstein estate, and an extensive review of financial records.

The report details how Epstein and Maxwell’s network facilitated the recruitment, control, and abuse of young women. It also exposes how Epstein cultivated relationships with powerful individuals and leveraged those connections to establish financial and social legitimacy. Additionally, the report documents the federal government’s decades-long failure to hold Epstein accountable for his crimes and deliver justice for survivors.

The report offers several recommendations to deliver long-overdue justice for survivors and prevent the federal government from repeating these failures. Among its recommendations, the report calls on Congress to pass Chairman Comer’s legislation, which would ensure survivors can speak freely about sexual abuse, even if they previously signed confidentiality agreements. The report also recommends that the Department of Justice interview or re-interview key witnesses, further investigate allegations of criminal activity involving Epstein’s associates, and provide survivors with unredacted access to their records.

“The federal government has failed the survivors of Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell’s horrific crimes for decades. The House Oversight Committee conducted a review of the federal government’s mishandled investigations to bring transparency to the American people and accountability for survivors. Epstein operated with impunity, shielded and enabled by powerful connections and a justice system that repeatedly failed his victims. Governments at every level and powerful institutions must meet their legal obligations to identify these crimes, stop perpetrators, and deliver justice for survivors,” said Chairman Comer.

“The evidence we uncovered makes clear that the Department of Justice must interview or re-interview key witnesses, investigate Epstein associates accused of criminal activity, and ensure survivors have access to their records. Congress must also pass legislation protecting the ability of individuals with knowledge of sexual abuse and survivors to speak freely about these crimes, regardless of nondisclosure agreements. We cannot undo the horrific harm inflicted on these women. But we must ensure that allegations of criminal activity are thoroughly investigated, survivors are protected, and those responsible are held accountable. The failures of the past must not be repeated,” concluded Chairman Comer.

Read the report here. Key findings and recommendations include:

The federal government has failed survivors for decades.

The Committee finds that the crimes Epstein committed after 2005 could have been prevented—and justice served—if not for failures by federal investigators and prosecutors in South Florida and Washington, D.C.

Rather than pursue a federal indictment and fully investigate allegations in other states, the U.S. Attorney’s Office (USAO) for the Southern District of Florida entered into a non-prosecution agreement (NPA) with Epstein in 2007, allowing him to evade federal prosecution in exchange for pleading guilty to lesser state charges. Epstein was sentenced to 18 months in jail, received extensive work-release privileges during which he continued to abuse women, and was released early. Federal prosecutors also failed to inform survivors of the NPA, undermining their ability to pursue civil claims or publicly expose Epstein’s crimes.

While some of these failures reflected poor judgment by the USAO, others appeared to stem from Epstein’s pervasive influence and far-reaching connections, potentially including two attorneys employed by the office.

After Epstein was arrested in 2019, he died in custody at a Bureau of Prisons facility in New York. Understaffing and systemic dysfunction contributed to correctional officers on both shifts missing at least 12 rounds and three inmate counts on the night of his death. This resulted in nearly eight hours without adequate supervision of Epstein and other inmates.

Following enactment of the Epstein Files Transparency Act in 2025, the Department of Justice (DOJ) failed to adequately communicate about document releases and failed to sufficiently protect survivors. Deficient redactions exposed survivors’ sensitive personal information.

The Department of Justice must take further action to advance transparency and justice for survivors.

DOJ should ensure investigators interview or reinterview key witnesses to advance justice for survivors of Epstein’s and Maxwell’s crimes. For example, DOJ should further question and investigate Epstein’s assistant, Lesley Groff, regarding her potential knowledge of and role in facilitating Epstein’s criminal activity.

DOJ must further investigate sexual assault allegations Sarah Kellen, a longtime Epstein assistant and survivor, made against two powerful men—Philip Levine, the former Mayor of Miami Beach from 2013 to 2017, and Frédéric Fekkai, a French celebrity hairstylist—during her transcribed interview with the Committee.

DOJ should establish an appropriate process for Epstein survivors and their representatives to access their personal files and records in unredacted form.

Non-prosecution agreements must be subject to rigorous scrutiny to ensure they serve the interests of justice rather than enable and empower criminals.

DOJ and the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices must rigorously enforce policies designed to prevent conflicts of interest in federal investigations and prosecutions.

Financial institutions failed to act on clear indicators of human trafficking and immigration fraud.

U.S. and foreign government authorities failed to identify indicators of human trafficking and immigration fraud. Institutions such as American Express enabled this activity, with company agents allowing Epstein to use fraudulent decoy flights and refundable or dummy itineraries to transport foreign women across borders directly to his residences.

Financial institutions possessed substantial information about Epstein’s criminal history and repeatedly identified transactions and activities presenting heightened compliance risks. Yet they failed to adequately address those risks, in some cases reporting them years later after Epstein’s 2019 arrest, due to Epstein’s personal connections, wealth, and influence.

The U.S. Department of the Treasury and the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) should review whether financial institutions are meeting their reporting obligations designed to detect and prevent suspicious activities, including money laundering and human trafficking.

Congress must pass legislation to prevent the weaponization of nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) to silence survivors of sexual abuse.

Epstein and powerful individuals in his orbit weaponized NDAs to silence survivors and conceal criminal activity.

Congress should pass the Survivor’s Voice Protection Act (H.R. 10389), introduced by Chairman Comer, to ensure witnesses and survivors of sexual crimes are not deterred from speaking freely by nondisclosure agreements. The legislation also establishes accountability for trusted individuals by requiring them to report suspected grooming behavior to law enforcement to help protect minors. This bill would also define grooming behavior for the first time in federal law.

Democrats must put survivors—not politics—first.

During the Committee’s investigation, Committee Democrats were obsessed with trying to implicate President Trump and insinuate that he was involved in the crimes of Epstein and Maxwell. Their unfounded witch hunt continued without regard for the interests of survivors, even though the facts gathered during this investigation do not suggest President Trump is implicated in any of Epstein’s crimes.

The consensus of every witness examined before the Committee was that President Trump––to their knowledge––was not involved in any crimes committed by Epstein and Maxwell.

During the Committee’s review of documents from the Estate, U.S. Virgin Islands, JPMorgan, Deutsche Bank, and the DOJ, the Committee did not identify any documents that would implicate President Trump in any criminal activity related to Epstein and Maxwell.

title: Ranking Member Klobuchar Opening Remarks at Nomination Hearing

committee.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry

text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Senator Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, delivered the following opening statement at the Agriculture Committee nomination hearing of Gregory Ibach to be Under Secretary of Agriculture for Trade and Foreign Agricultural Affairs, and for Carl Bednarski, John Grunewald II, and James Russell Middleton to be members of the Farm Credit Administration Board.

A rough transcript of Klobuchar’s full opening statement is available below and a video can be found here.

Senator Klobuchar: Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. Thank you for those kind words.

We have a lot of work to do, as you noted, in the next few months. We are going to continue to work on this Farm Bill. It’s so important, as you noted.

I want to thank the nominees for being with us. I want to welcome you, Mr. Ibach, along with your wife, Teresa. And welcome to you, Mr. Grunewald, and your wife, Terrica. Is that right? Did I say it right? Okay, good. Also, as well as, Mr. Bednarski, thank you. A name almost as hard to say as mine. And your wife, Lisa. And finally, thank you, Mr. Middleton, for being here, and along with Renata, and your daughter Julia, and your son Jonathan.

Before we get to the subject of today's hearing, I again wanted to reiterate my support for the work on a bipartisan Farm Bill which would meet the moment to address the many challenges facing families and farms across the country, including the tariffs and the war.

Our Democratic priorities remain resolving the initial two years of the SNAP cost shifts to states. We know that with the cost of groceries and other things, that this would be a very difficult situation. And we are not going to go into the mid-level error rate states, but the way this was set up, there is a reason that we want to get it fixed. And getting to year-round E15, major priority, funding very popular voluntary conservation programs, which are important to both sides of the aisle, and I appreciate the conversations that Senator Boozman and I have been having, as well as our staff, as well as with the House Ag Committee and leadership. I hope we can find a compromise that will return the Farm Bill to a bipartisan process and bring the votes that we need to get it over the finish line.

So now to our nominees. Mr. Ibach, you have been nominated to serve as the Under Secretary for Trade and Foreign Ag Affairs, which oversees USDA’s trade policy, promotion, and food security work. As noted by the Chairman, you'd be taking over for Luke Lindberg, who recently left USDA to lead the World Food Programme. I have been supportive, as we’ve talked about, of his work.

I know you bring a wealth of experience to this role as the former Under Secretary for Marketing and Regulatory Programs, as well as a long-time state director. You are also a farmer yourself with a real understanding of the importance of trade for American agriculture.

You are coming to the role at a challenging time. I have been clear on my views on this – the administration's tariffs have been very, very bad for farmers. These tariffs have increased input costs and put markets at risk that farmers have worked for decades to expand. And the on-again, off-again, ever-changing trade policy is making longtime trading partners look elsewhere for trade deals, which is concerning not only in the short term but the long term.

The top three countries targeted with tariffs – Mexico, Canada, our neighbors in Minnesota, and China – are also our top three ag export markets and account for half of all U.S. ag exports. Think about that. This is especially important in my state – we’re the fourth largest state for ag exports, and more than one-third of our farm production is sold to customers abroad.

Our farmers have repeatedly said that they want trade – not aid. Unfortunately, we are seeing a lot of trade chaos and several rounds of ad hoc payments that are helpful – I acknowledge and I’ve said this – but they don't provide the long-term certainty, and even leave some growers out entirely.

If confirmed, Mr. Ibach, it is my hope that you will leverage your experience to try and restore some sanity and stability to our trade policy along with the Secretary of Ag.

In addition, we also have before us three nominees to serve as board members of the Farm Credit Administration. The Farm Credit System ensures that rural communities and ag producers of all types and sizes have reliable access to credit. That mission is particularly crucial today as farmers face skyrocketing costs for fuel and other inputs, coupled with global market uncertainty that has created razor-thin margins. In the face of these challenges, FCA must work to help farmers keep feeding and fueling America and to find ways to open the door for the next generation of farmers.

If confirmed to the Farm Credit Administration Board, you will be responsible for ensuring the Farm Credit System and Farmer Mac are meeting their missions.

I will also note that if you are all confirmed, it would restore the FCA board to full bipartisan capacity. Not a lot of boards can say that right now. And I hope this is the beginning of a shift back to normalcy for all independent boards and commissions across the government.

Mr. Grunewald, Mr. Bednarski, and Mr. Middleton, I appreciate the conversations I had with each of you. I believe you would each bring unique perspectives to the Board, drawing on a wealth of experience from careers in farm, the Farm Credit System, as a farmer and ag policy leader, and as a longtime civil servant who worked in Congress and at this regulator.

I look forward to hearing your testimony and today's discussion.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I yield back.

###

title: Chairman Boozman: Trade, Access to Credit Critical to American Agriculture

committee.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry

text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Chairman John Boozman (R-AR) said filling key leadership positions at the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Farm Credit Administration is critical to supporting farmers and ranchers facing economic challenges and getting a new Farm Bill across the finish line this year, as the committee considered four nominees Tuesday.

The following is Chairman Boozman’s statement as prepared for delivery:

“Good morning and welcome. It is my privilege to call this hearing to order. Today we will consider the nominations of Mr. Gregory Ibach to be Under Secretary of Agriculture for Trade and Foreign Agricultural Affairs, and Mr. Carl Bednarski, Mr. John Grunewald II, and Mr. James Russell Middleton to be members of the Farm Credit Administration Board.

“I would like to take a moment to congratulate the Ranking Member on her recent election to serve as Minnesota’s governor. I have enjoyed serving with you on this Committee, and we have accomplished some great things. Hopefully, together, we can get the Farm Bill across the finish line this year before you assume your new role. We wish you well, and you will be missed in the Senate.

“It’s important that we have the personnel in place to support farmers, ranchers and producers and that’s why considering these nominees is critical to our role.

“Starting with the Under Secretary for Trade and Foreign Agricultural Affairs. We rely on this position to lead USDA’s trade promotion programs and international food assistance work, as well as to ensure agriculture is prioritized in the administration’s broader trade discussions. I’ve always said that trade is the lifeblood of agriculture, and we know that advancing market access for U.S. agriculture is more critical now than ever.

“On October 1, the investments we made in the farm safety net last summer took effect, injecting billions of dollars in year over year support to producers who are continuing to face high input costs and low commodity prices. That includes more than doubling funding for our trade promotion programs. Congress has also come together several times over the last two years to provide emergency economic support to our farmers, as we waited for these durable changes to be felt. I spent time last month visiting with Arkansas farmers, and it’s clear that the situation in farm country remains dire.

“That is why I remain committed to working with Ranking Member Klobuchar, and our House counterparts to advance a five-year farm bill before the end of the year. I also continue to advocate for a path forward for additional emergency assistance, and I appreciate Senator Hoeven’s leadership on that as well.

“But as we look ahead, we know U.S. agriculture must build demand, both here at home and abroad. Farmers continue to look for new markets and expand access to existing markets. For one, we’re working to restore market access for our beef, in key markets like China. Additionally, several industries, such as rice, seafood, and specialty crops, are also looking for help to ensure a level playing field with imported products. The review of the USMCA agreement, which is so critical for agriculture, also remains ongoing. Mr. Ibach will play a key role in all of these efforts and more to ensure our producers have both a level playing field and long-term certainty.

“International food assistance is another tool we have to expand market access. I am pleased the farm bill that was reported out of our committee in September would permanently transfer Food for Peace to USDA. I appreciate and am proud of Luke Lindberg, who is now leading the World Food Program in Rome, for his leadership on this important program, and look forward to working with Mr. Ibach to ensure the good work of Food for Peace continues. Mr. Ibach is deeply qualified to step into this role, and I am confident he will remain a champion for U.S. agriculture on a global stage.

“Also important to American agriculture is the Farm Credit Administration. Over the past several years, our nation’s farmers and ranchers have faced significant economic headwinds, which has eroded equity, tightened credit conditions and led to more farm bankruptcies over the last year than we have seen since 2020.

“In my home state of Arkansas, farm bankruptcies are at levels not seen in a century, and we have the unfortunate distinction of leading the country in the number of bankruptcies. Many farmers have had to make the difficult decision to end farming operations that have been in their family for generations.

“According to USDA, farm sector debt is expected to increase 4.6 percent to reach $605.1 billion in 2026. Farm sector solvency is also forecast to worsen in 2026 relative to 2025, with debt forecast to grow at a faster rate than assets or equity.

“While key sector health indicators such as debt-to-asset and debt-to-equity ratios are not at levels seen during the 1980s Farm Crisis, the forecast is not encouraging.

“In order to pull out of this downturn and remain competitive in a global economy, our nation’s producers will need access to adequate levels of credit.
