title: Cantwell Leads Unanimous Senate Passage of Weather Act Reauthorization

committee.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation

text:
Weather Act would modernize weather forecasting and research

Creates an atmospheric river forecast improvement program, strengthens landslide preparedness, establishes an official Fire Weather Services Program and deploys new technology and tools to forecast droughts and heat waves that harm crops

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation, celebrated unanimous Senate passage of the bipartisan Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Reauthorization Act of 2026 (Weather Act), sending it to the House of Representatives for consideration. The Weather Act authorizes programs at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) that would strengthen weather research and forecasting to save lives and better prepare our nation against dangerous weather disasters. Led by Sen. Cantwell and Commerce Committee Chairman Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), the bill is co-sponsored by Senators Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), Brian Schatz (D-Hawai’i), Jerry Moran (R-Kan.), Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), Tim Sheehy (R-Mont.), Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), Ted Budd (R-N.C.), John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.), and John Curtis (R-Utah).

“Americans are facing increasingly dangerous and costly weather disasters, and better forecasts give communities more time to prepare and get out of harm’s way,” said Sen. Cantwell. “The Weather Act will advance next-generation weather radar, modernize lifesaving warning systems and improve forecasts for atmospheric rivers and wildfires, like the devastating fires that forced thousands to evacuate in Spokane last month. Senate passage brings us one step closer to giving forecasters, emergency managers and communities the tools they need to save lives and protect property.”

“Today, the Senate took a pivotal step toward ensuring Americans are prepared for severe weather,” said Sen. Cruz. “Texans know all too well the devastation storms can bring. The lives lost in the July 4, 2025, Texas floods are a heartbreaking reminder of what is at stake. The Weather Act brings together over a dozen bipartisan bills to modernize radar systems, deliver more accurate and timely forecasts, and improve warnings so families and first responders have more time to act, no matter where they are and no matter the time of day. These improvements will help protect property and, more importantly, save lives in Texas and across the country.”

“Delaware is the lowest-lying state in the nation. Our rapidly changing climate has changed the way we prepare for severe weather events,” said Sen. Blunt Rochester. “As severe weather damages communities more frequently, it couldn’t be more important for us to properly invest in NOAA’s weather forecasting. I’m grateful for the bipartisan coalition of colleagues on this bill. We must do everything in our power to help Delawareans, and folks across the country, prepare for whatever weather events are on the horizon. I look forward to working together to get our Weather Act passed into law.”

“We must invest in advancing and strengthening our preparedness, response, and mitigation capabilities to address natural disasters,” said Sen. Sullivan. “This is especially important for Alaska, where our vast geography, remote communities, and exposure to a wide range of hazards make accurate forecasting and timely warnings essential to protecting lives, property, and communities. The Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Reauthorization Act reinforces our existing federal programs, protects NOAA’s core weather research and forecasting framework, including authorization levels that direct adequate resources, including personnel, and bolsters NOAA’s forecasting, warning, and communication systems to be better prepared for natural disasters such as tsunamis, landslides, wildfires, and severe weather. It also incorporates bills I have introduced or cosponsored, including my Harmful Algal Bloom and Hypoxia Research and Control Amendments (HABHRCA) Act, which ensures robust prevention, identification and response to the harmful algal blooms that are increasingly found in both our coastal and inland waters, as well as several bills I have cosponsored: the NOAA Weather Radio Modernization Act; the Fire Ready Nation Act; the Accelerating Networking, Cyberinfrastructure, and Hardware for Ocean Research (ANCHOR) Act; and the Tsunami Warning, Research, and Education Reauthorization Act. I am pleased to see all these priorities for Alaska advance through this comprehensive legislation.”

“As severe weather in Hawai‘i and around the country becomes more damaging and frequent, having better forecasting can make all the difference in saving lives and livelihoods,” said Sen. Schatz. “Our bill will help improve forecasts and weather communications so that communities can better anticipate, prepare for, and respond to extreme weather.”

“Kansans, particularly farmers and ranchers, rely on access to timely and reliable weather data every day,” said Sen. Moran. “I’m pleased this bill incorporates my legislation, the FORECAST Act, to help make certain NWS offices remain staffed to provide lifesaving 24/7 weather forecasting to their communities. Passage of this legislation is an important step to improve access to timely weather data for Kansans.”

“The severity of the wildfires and extreme heat in Nevada this past summer reminded us just how important it is that we invest in the latest weather prediction technology and fund critical programs at NOAA,” said Sen. Rosen. “I’m glad that my bill, to ensure Nevada’s farmers and ranchers have access to forecasts that will improve their resilience to weather anomalies, is part of the bipartisan Weather Act that has now passed the U.S. Senate. I call on the House of Representatives to pass it soon so we can send it to the President’s desk without delay.”

“As severe weather grows more dangerous, costing us hundreds of billions of dollars in economic impact and harming thousands of Americans every year, we need to make sure communities have the tools they need to prepare and respond quickly and effectively,” said Sen. Sheehy. “Montanans know firsthand the devastation wildfires cause, and while fire season only seems to be getting worse, government response has largely stayed the same. Better forecasting helps save lives, protect homes and livelihoods, and strengthen our resilience. The Weather Act is a commonsense step toward a safer, better-prepared America, and I’m glad to see it pass the Senate.”

“This past year, communities across Minnesota faced severe weather that affected local businesses, agriculture, infrastructure, and safety. From forest fires impacting tourism on the North Shore to major crop loss from floods in Southern Minnesota, natural disasters have taken a toll on our industries,” said Sen. Klobuchar. “By investing in weather forecasting and research, the bipartisan Weather Act will help communities better prepare for severe weather. My provision to protect the Aerial Snow Survey Program was included in the bill, which is crucial for collecting data and monitoring snowpack to better predict water levels and downstream impacts for local communities.”

“North Carolina knows all too well the risks when major storms strike,” said Sen. Budd. “This bipartisan effort to reduce major gaps in our weather system will help us track future storms more effectively and efficiently, to help prevent loss of life and property. I am grateful that two bills I authored were included as provisions to the Weather Act to help enhance the accuracy of hurricane forecasts and communication, as well as modernize our radar system to get warnings out quicker.”

“Colorado and the West are facing historic drought and relentless wildfires fueled by climate change,” said Sen. Hickenlooper. “Investing in NOAA’s operations and research gives Coloradans better tools and resources to forecast extreme weather, prepare for disasters, and save lives.”

“Over the course of this year’s fire season, Utah communities have faced extreme wildfires that have led to catastrophic flooding,” said Sen. Curtis. “I’ve seen the damage these floods have caused to homes and livelihoods firsthand, and it is devastating. This bipartisan bill will help support our rural communities facing increasingly powerful fires and floods by modernizing weather communication and radio services, and I hope to see it signed into law soon.”

The Weather Act would:

Establish an atmospheric river forecast improvement program to advance accurate, effective and actionable forecasts, and warnings for atmospheric rivers.

Require NOAA to maintain and improve the system that communicates potential hazardous weather or water events to the public

Direct NOAA to upgrade outdated weather radio technology to provide reliable and continuous weather and emergency alerts.

Require the United States Geological Survey (USGS) and NOAA to incorporate risks from atmospheric rivers into landslide preparedness and response planning.

Establish an official Fire Weather Services Program within NOAA and fund the research and acquisition of new technology to improve forecasts of wildfire conditions.

Direct the National Integrated Drought Information System to advance and deploy next generation drought monitoring technologies and use observations from State or regional hydrological monitoring projects.

“Accurate weather forecasts are among the most direct ways science serves the public, and the stakes have never been higher as extreme weather grows more frequent and costly. The Weather Act Reauthorization Act would move research breakthroughs into operational forecasts faster, strengthening the nation’s ability to prepare for, respond to, and recover from severe weather. AGU applauds Congress’s bipartisan commitment to science-informed decision-making that safeguards communities across the country.” – Janice Lachance, Executive Director/CEO, American Geophysical Union

“Weather impacts everyone, every day, and the ability to provide timely, accurate weather information depends on a strong weather enterprise. The bipartisan Weather Act recognizes the importance of investing in the observations, science, technology, and forecasting capabilities that help us save lives, protect property, and support our economy. Strengthening those capabilities is an investment in the nation’s future.” – Alan Sealls, President, American Meteorological Society

“Passage of the Weather Act Reauthorization is a giant step forward for the Weather Enterprise and its delivery of forecasts that save lives, protect communities, support businesses, and bolster our national economy. This bill strengthens public-private partnerships by augmenting critical government systems with increased use of innovative commercial data, paving the way for needed advances in observations, modeling, and information delivery. The American people will benefit every day from this legislation – from improved aviation and agricultural operations to earlier warnings for extreme weather such as tornadoes and flash flooding.” – Douglas Hilderbrand, Executive Director, American Weather Enterprise Association

“Western Governors have long advocated for the improvement of forecasting abilities for weather and natural disasters, as evidenced by their efforts that led to the creation of the National Integrated Drought Information System. Western Governors are encouraged by several provisions within the Weather Act which enhance and reauthorize drought monitoring, fire weather and disaster forecasting, water quality maintenance, and soil moisture sensing. These programs are critical to enhancing the security and prosperity of the West’s communities and economies. WGA applauds the efforts of Senator Maria Cantwell and Senator Ted Cruz to advance the Weather Act through Congress and encourages the House to swiftly consider the legislation.” – Jack Waldorf, Executive Director, Western Governors’ Association

“We are tremendously appreciative of Sen. Cantwell’s continued leadership in protecting our natural resources, including our ocean. NANOOS is grateful that our policymakers understand the importance of the ocean to our weather, which is created and driven by many inter-related systems. We are excited that the Integrated Ocean Observing Systems (IOOS) network, of which NANOOS is a key component, is reauthorized as a part of the larger Weather Act reauthorization legislation. We thank the bipartisan group of Senators engaged in this effort.” – Jan Newton, Director of the Northwest Association of Networked Ocean Observing Systems (NANOOS)

“This bill has the potential to greatly improve people’s lives on an everyday basis, as it will lead to advances in many areas — from observations and modeling to warnings and decision support — to reduce loss of life and property from extreme weather. It also will accelerate innovations in uncrewed observations and artificial intelligence/machine learning-enabled forecasting by directing NOAA to coordinate across federal, academic, and private partners as well as prioritize measurable forecast improvements for high-impact hazards, including atmospheric rivers, coastal flooding and storm surge, and extreme heat.” – Shuyi Chen, Professor of Meteorology at the University of Washington

Additional Highlights of the Legislation Include:

Enhancing Federal Weather Forecasting and Innovation

Addresses NOAA’s aging radar network by directing the agency to design and deploy the next generation of weather radar technology by 2037. It also authorizes NOAA to manage existing gaps in the current radar network by supplementing weather radar coverage with data, services and technologies from third parties.

Establishes an atmospheric river forecast improvement program to develop tools and improved forecast models to address the increasingly frequent and powerful atmospheric rivers impacting the United States, especially across the West coast.

Directs the National Weather Service to include turbulence events and icing conditions in its forecasting capabilities and establishes an airborne observation program to acquire atmospheric data from commercial aircraft.

Directs NOAA to improve accuracy and timeliness of weather, water and space weather forecasts and effective dissemination of critical information using artificial intelligence.

Creates a project to improve forecasts of coastal marine fog with the goal of enhancing vessel safety and reducing the economic impact of coastal marine fog events.

Strengthening Emergency Preparedness by Improving Communication

Requires NOAA to maintain and improve how the National Weather Service (NWS) and other federal partners like the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) support emergency managers and communicate potential hazardous weather or water events to the public.

Requires upgrades to outdated weather radio technology to provide reliable and continuous weather and emergency alerts and expands radio coverage to rural areas that do not currently have access to the National Weather Radio alert system.

Modernizing Critical Research Programs

Updates the Tsunami Forecasting and Warning Program to evaluate tsunami alert levels, maintain fail-safe warning capabilities and align the analytic techniques and methodologies of the two existing tsunami warning centers in Hawaii and Alaska.

Builds on the progress of the Hurricane Forecast Improvement Project by establishing it as a long-term program that will incorporate social, behavioral, risk and communication science into modeling, forecasting and response guidance.

Expands the goals of the Tornado Warning Improvement and Extension Program to improve the effectiveness and timeliness of tornado forecasts, predictions and warnings by increasing lead times, improving forecasting and updating the system to rate the severity of tornadoes in collaboration with local communities and emergency managers.

Provides funding for weather laboratories; tornado, severe storm and next generation radar research; and transitioning the latest scientific and technological advances into operations.

Supporting Farmers and Ranchers with Better Tools for Agriculture and Water Management

Directs the National Integrated Drought Information System to advance and deploy next-generation drought monitoring technologies and transition existing drought products to probabilistic forecasts, as well as use observations from State or regional hydrological monitoring projects.

Reauthorizes the National Weather Service’s work to provide agricultural and silvicultural weather and climate information and directs NOAA to establish at least two pilot projects to support improved subseasonal to seasonal extended range precipitation forecasts for agriculture and water management.

Codifies and authorizes the National Mesonet Program, a network of automated weather stations that are used to monitor and observe weather events and microclimates. The program is directed to obtain observations to improve understanding of and forecast capabilities for atmospheric, drought, fire and water events and increase the quantity and density of environmental observations.

Expanding Commercial Data Partnerships

Increases NOAA’s access to critical forecasting data by expanding its authority to contract with the private sector to acquire commercial weather data.

Codifies the Commercial Data Program to coordinate and acquire a variety of weather and environmental data and services from the private sector for operational use.

Modifies the existing commercial data pilot program to be a testing program within the Commercial Data Program and authorizes the program to test and evaluate all sources and types of observation services, imagery, products and data from private sector entities.

Preparing for Disasters

Establishes within NOAA an interagency committee to coordinate agencies’ activities and ensure a united Federal approach to reducing health risks from heat, as well as a NOAA system to improve the delivery of data, information, forecasts, warnings, prediction and projections related to temperature and extreme heat.

Improves the monitoring, forecasting, prevention and mitigation of harmful algal blooms and hypoxia that threaten aquatic ecosystems, hurt local economies and endanger public health by reauthorizing and amending the National Harmful Algal Bloom and Hypoxia Program. Establishes a national harmful algal bloom observing network and a national incubator program and increases the avenues of assistance NOAA can provide to affected communities.

Requires the national landslide strategy to include an assessment of risks from atmospheric river flooding and extreme precipitation events and expands the National Landslide Hazards Database to cover areas needing further risk assessment due to factors such as hydrological changes and atmospheric river flooding.

Passage of the Weather Act is an important step in implementing Sen. Cantwell’s 5 Point Plan to bolster the United States’ weather readiness, which she outlined in a letter to President Donald Trump in July of last year. Sen. Cantwell continues to insist on deploying the best technology to help our weather forecasters. In June, Sen. Cantwell introduced the Hurricane Hunter Aircraft Recapitalization Act to codify NOAA’s Hurricane Hunter mission in federal law and authorize up to nine Hurricane Hunter aircraft to better prepare the nation’s first line of defense against stronger and more frequent hurricanes, atmospheric rivers and winter storms. Earlier this year, she introduced legislation to establish the Radar Next Program which will carry out deployment of the nation’s next generation weather radar system.

Last August, she introduced legislation to modernize the nation’s weather communication and radio service as the country faces increasingly powerful floods, fires and hurricanes. Both of these bills are included in the Weather Act passed today. Sen. Cantwell also called out the administration’s decision to cancel its plan to launch a large-scale test of a new advanced weather radar technology, called Phased Array Radar.

Sen. Cantwell is a long-time champion of NOAA and helped secure $3.3 billion in NOAA investments in the Inflation Reduction Act to help communities prepare for and adapt to climate change, boost science needed to understand changing weather and climate patterns and invest in advanced computer technologies that are critical for extreme weather prediction and emergency response. Her Fire Ready Nation Act, bipartisan legislation to strengthen NOAA’s ability to help forecast, prevent, and fight wildfires, passed the Senate in September of last year.

Readthe full bill text of the Weather Act HERE.

title: Senator Hickenlooper Warns of the Dangers of an FCC with Only Republican Commissioners

committee.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation

text:
[VIDEO]

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) delivered the below opening statement at today’s Commerce Committee hearing on the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs to be a Commissioner of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC). In addition to Thumann Severs, three other Trump nominees were also before the committee: Leslie Becera to be the Assistant Secretary of Governmental Affairs for the Department of Transportation (DOT); Joshua Shoemaker to be Chief Financial Officer of NASA; and Robert Steinau to be Inspector General of NASA.

Sen. Hickenlooper:

“Thank you, Mr. Chair. It’s good to be back in the familiar confines of our congressional home. Let me get this… make sure I get this right, Ms. Thumann Severs…Ms. Becera, Mr. Shoemaker, Mr. Steinau. Thank you all for being here. Thank you for being willing to take this on. Congratulations on your nominations.

“But to begin with, I want to address how the FCC, the Federal Communications Commission, brought this nomination before us. For many decades, the Senate has paired Commission nominees, a Republican and a Democrat, moving together. Congress established the FCC as an independent, bipartisan agency because having both parties at the table ensures that major policy decisions truly serve the public interest and are not restrained by a partisan agenda. A bipartisan FCC is essential to avoid things like large-scale media consolidation. I think also, more fundamentally, to protect a free and diverse press that serves everyone.

“That’s why I have deep concerns that today’s nominee is not paired with a Democrat. I strongly believe we should be considering the renomination of Commissioner Anna Gomez, the sole remaining Democrat. She is someone…I have supported, many have supported, and is serving on an expired term. Now, since the FCC requires three Commissioners for a quorum, her presence in the current two-to-one Republican majority is necessary for the FCC to conduct business.

“Thanks to the Supreme Court’s recent decision in Slaughter, if today’s nominee is confirmed, President Trump could then fire Commissioner Gomez and have an FCC with no Democratic voice at all. Unfortunately, I don’t think it’s a coincidence that today’s nomination is moving on its own, but I don’t think this strategy will age well in a new Congress or a new administration. We’re seeing the same playbook being used across other independent agencies.

“It’s also vital that any Commissioner can be trusted to exercise independent judgment in all FCC matters. Ms. Thumann Severs, your career has largely been spent serving Brendan Carr, currently as Chairman Carr’s senior counsel. Previously…legal advisor to Commissioner Carr. Your official duties include near daily meetings with Chairman Carr and working to advance his agenda [and] amplify his messaging.

“I’m particularly interested in your views related to the First Amendment and protecting the free press. In September of 2025, Chairman Carr threatened FCC regulatory action against ABC. I think the quote I have here is, ‘We can do this the easy way or the hard way,’ to take the comedian Jimmy Kimmel off the air. Unfortunately, Chairman Carr has continued to regularly threaten broadcasters over what many of us would consider First Amendment-protected speech and editorial news decisions. In fact, Chairman Carr even threatened broadcasters about airing so-called ‘fake polls’ ahead of the midterm elections, following President Trump’s attacks on low polling numbers showing or reflecting his declining popularity.

“The need for FCC oversight has never been greater. While I understand that you don’t currently work in the FCC’s Media Bureau, all media issues are going to come before you as an FCC commissioner. So I look forward to you sharing your positions on them with the committee today.

“Mr. Shoemaker, Mr. Steinau. Now, we recently celebrated the unequivocal success of the Artemis II mission and what it means for continued American leadership in space exploration. At the same time, NASA lost roughly 22 percent of its workforce in 2025, and 20 percent of its employees at the Ph.D. level. Current and former employees have raised an alarm that these losses could threaten safety and mission assurance as the agency takes on ambitious new efforts like the Moon Base. So we hope to hear how you believe NASA can reverse course and overcome these obstacles with limited personnel.

“Ms. Becera, you knew I’d get to you eventually. In September, you committed to providing information to committee staff on key priorities, and I appreciate your willingness to do so. I look forward to hearing more from you on your overall commitment to transparency and your responsiveness to Congress. So, with that, I’ll yield back to our Chair.”

###

title: What They Are Saying: Congress Must Act to Reverse Devastating Cuts to Federal Transportation Infrastructure Programs that Improve Safety, Lower Costs

committee.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation

text:
State and local stakeholders tell Congress what’s at stake

WASHINGTON, D.C. – State and local transportation officials, national road safety organizations including AAA and MADD, consumer advocates, transportation workers and other stakeholders are calling on Congress to reverse massive cuts to transportation infrastructure programs caused by failing to renew the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law’s (BIL) nearly $37 billion in advance appropriations when it expired September 30.

Last month, U.S. Senator Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation, released updated “Chopping Block” reports detailing the impact of these cuts to state and local transportation systems, roadway safety and economic development. When the law expired, states immediately lost more than 30 percent of their federal transportation funding.

“State departments of transportation depend on predictable federal investment to deliver safer, more reliable transportation systems and keep our economy moving. Continuing the Bridge Formula Program and advance appropriations transportation programs critical to individual states will help sustain progress on projects serving rural and urban communities alike. We urge Congress to work on a bipartisan basis to provide funding certainty and support states’ ability to address their transportation priorities.” – Executive Director Jim Tyman, American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials

“Four straight years of declining roadway deaths shows that sustained federal investment works. But today, states have less money to make our roads safe than they did last year because Congress didn’t extend the advance appropriations in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) when that funding expired on September 30. If we are going to continue to make progress towards eliminating fatalities on our roads, states need continued federal investment that will help them deliver programs that save lives.” – Chief Executive Officer Jonathan Adkins, Governors Highway Safety Association

“The Transportation Trades Department, AFL-CIO, continues advocating alongside dozens of other labor, industry, and government associations in urging Congress to extend IIJA advance appropriations that have been delivering tens of thousands of transportation and infrastructure projects and supporting hundreds of thousands of jobs in your districts and states and across the country. We urge the Committees to find a path forward on providing advance appropriations for modes that received such funds under IIJA, so American workers can continue to build, maintain, and operate transportation systems and infrastructure that allow our national, state, and local economies to flourish.” – President Greg Regan, Transportation Trades Department, AFL-CIO

“The investments made by the bipartisan Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) to improve roadway safety are working. After roadway fatalities surged during the COVID-19 pandemic…sustained federal investment in infrastructure safety improvements, behavioral safety programs, and data-driven enforcement has helped drive fatalities down for three consecutive years…This progress did not happen by accident. It reflects the importance of the investment Congress made in IIJA which provided a steady flow of resources to states and local communities to improve roadway safety and save lives. Reducing or delaying this funding now risks stalling or reversing that hard-won momentum.” – Letter from AAA, Advocates for Highway Safety, MADD and 18 other leading safety groups

“The IIJA demonstrated the value of providing transportation programs with a multiyear funding framework. Preserving that predictability is essential for agencies and communities making long-term decisions about infrastructure, service, and economic development. As Congress considers the next steps, the challenge is to ensure that transportation investments already underway–and the projects communities still need–are not lost to funding uncertainty. Continued federal commitment will be critical to maintaining progress toward a safer, more connected, and more reliable transportation network.” – American Public Transportation Association

“Transit and rail workers are losing work right now because of the lapse in infrastructure appropriations. Our members need certainty and strong federal investments to keep our transportation systems moving safely. Make no mistake – Congress failing to renew the advance appropriations is a job killer in every state. The TWU is calling on every member of the House and Senate to swiftly renew this funding.” – President John Samuelsen, Transport Workers Union of America (TWU) International

“Transportation funding directly impacts the safety of millions of Americans who rely on our nation’s roads every day. Communities across the United States have benefited from the historic bipartisan investments included in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act to address local challenges and deliver critical safety improvements. Extending advanced appropriations is vital to sustain the effectiveness of needed safety grants, including the Safe Streets and Roads for All grant program, which is proven to save lives.” – Chief Executive Officer Lorraine Martin, National Safety Council

“For consumers, bringing home the bacon requires a modern, reliable network of roads, rail, transit, pipelines, waterways, and airports. Building and maintaining that world-class infrastructure requires sustained investment. Just five years ago, the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law provided transformational funding to modernize America’s infrastructure, meet the needs of the 21st-century economy, and improve affordability. Today, lawmakers face a stark choice: let that progress stall or double down on the infrastructure investments needed to lower costs and strengthen American competitiveness. Senator Cantwell’s findings show that robust infrastructure investment is the right choice for American families.” – Senior Director of Consumer Protection and Product Safety Daniel Greene, National Consumers League

“Impaired driving remains one of the leading causes of fatalities and injuries on our nation’s roads, and every one of those deaths and injuries are preventable. States must be able to rely on steady funding for impaired driving prevention programs, enforcement efforts, and crash data. Advance appropriations give states that certainty. MADD urges Congress to restore this funding so critical work to save lives and prevent injuries continues.” Chief Executive Officer Stacey D. Stewart, MADD

“The Senate Commerce Committee’s ‘Chopping Block’ reports illustrate how cuts to Bipartisan Infrastructure Law funding will halt investment and innovation across the country. States are using the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) program funding to build EV charging stations, create good-paying jobs, and make driving electric more convenient. This is especially important for EV charging in rural communities, which are often overlooked by private investment. With more than 1,000 NEVI project awards already issued, Congress must ensure that states continue to make progress with the investment levels set in the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. Extending and fully funding the advance appropriations, including NEVI, is essential for completing a nationwide charging network and delivering cleaner, more affordable, and more reliable transportation for all.” – Clean Transportation for All Campaign Director Katherine Garcia, Sierra Club

“The Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance (CVSA) strongly supports continuing to fund critical state commercial motor vehicle (CMV) safety and enforcement programs at the levels established in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. The Motor Carrier Safety Assistance Program (MCSAP) received an additional $80 million per year in advanced appropriations, allowing the states to grow their CMV enforcement and safety programs, including the hiring of new inspectors, auditors and investigators. Experiencing an estimated 16% decrease in funding will result in halting that growth when programs are demonstrating positive impacts on roadway safety.” – Executive Director Collin Mooney, Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance

“Motor vehicle crashes are a leading cause of death and injury for families in every state. Kids and Car Safety is committed to reducing the unacceptable economic and emotional toll of this major public health problem by advancing safer cars, safer drivers, and safer roads. We cannot prevent crashes, deaths and injuries by withholding lifesaving technology from cars or funds for needed roadway improvements and repairs.” – Executive Director Amber Rollins, Kids and Cars Safety

“Passenger rail projects take years to plan and execute. Stable, predictable federal funding is essential to maintaining momentum, maximizing taxpayer investments, and building a stronger, more connected national passenger rail network.” – Chair Jeremy Latimer, States for Passenger Rail Coalition

“Ohio’s cities and towns have little or no useful passenger rail service today, and advance appropriations are critical in the effort to change that. Letting them lapse would cut more than $218 million from Ohio’s transportation formula funding next year alone, and federal rail funding nationwide would fall by more than 80 percent. We urge Ohio’s congressional delegation, on both sides of the aisle, to extend advance appropriations before December 11.” – Chair of the Board of Directors Mitch Radakovich, All Aboard Ohio

“The Florida Coalition of Rail Passengers urges Congress to include multiyear advance appropriations for passenger rail in the next surface transportation reauthorization. Appropriating funding for future fiscal years gives states and rail suppliers a firmer basis for commitments that extend beyond a single annual budget. Railcar production and infrastructure construction require years of planning and investment. Predictable federal funding helps manufacturers expand facilities and train workers, while enabling states to plan their own financial participation. The Railway Supply Institute identifies this funding certainty as essential to investment in American manufacturing capacity. Dependable federal support for infrastructure, equipment and service startup would strengthen Florida’s incentive to commit its own resources and pursue additional passenger trains, including expanded Amtrak service. Multiyear advance appropriations would give public agencies and private suppliers greater confidence to make the commitments these improvements require.” – President James Tilley, Florida Coalition of Rail Passengers

The Bipartisan Infrastructure Law (BIL) provided, for the first time, five years of guaranteed funding for federal transportation programs. The law spurred more than 140,000 transportation infrastructure projects across the country. The BIL expired on October 1, 2026, and without renewal, $36.8 billion in vital federal investments in freight infrastructure, mega projects, bridges, airports and seaports, passenger rail, safe streets and downtowns will be eliminated, and thousands of infrastructure projects will go unfunded. The new reports detail the impact of these cuts to formula and non-formula transportation funding programs for each state, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico.

On September 2, President Trump signed the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act (H.R. 6500) funding the government through December 11. While Congress extended surface transportation programs, it did not renew the BIL’s advance appropriations. Sen. Cantwell released her original Chopping Block reports on May 13, 2026. They looked at three key areas within our transportation ecosystem – freight, America’s main streets and rail:

American Freight Infrastructure: The United States freight transportation system moves $18.7 trillion in goods every year. It’s estimated that U.S. businesses spent $2.6 trillion last year on logistics costs.Multimodal freight investments have significant returns on investment, including improving efficiency and reducing shipping costs. Driving these transportation costs down is critical to reducing prices for American consumers and helping American businesses compete against international companies. However, if advance appropriations are not renewed, funding will decrease by 67 percent for four essential freight programs that could support hundreds of projects still in need of federal funding. U.S. Freight Infrastructure on the Chopping Block examines the benefits of the BIL’s freight investments and what is at risk for supply chains if a multiyear investment strategy is abandoned.

Local Economic Development Infrastructure: From small towns to large urban centers, the nation’s downtown districts are essential economic hubs that provide employment opportunities, access to essential services and form the building blocks of successful regional economies. The BIL provided significant support for local improvement projects through grant programs that allow local governments to apply directly for federal funds—this is critical since only 16 percent of federal highway formula funds reach local roads. If advance appropriations are not renewed, funding for three popular grant programs that support local economic development will decrease by 90 percent. American Main Streets on the Chopping Block examines what is at risk for essential business districts if a multiyear investment strategy is abandoned.

American Rail Infrastructure: Freight rail carries 29 percent of U.S. ton-miles of commodities, including shipments moved via multimodal networks. In 2025, Amtrak carried 34.5 million passengers—an all-time record. Amtrak serves 40 percent of America’s small and rural communities, and almost one in every five Amtrak riders travel to or from a station with no access to air service. The BIL provided $66 billion over five years to enhance passenger rail routes, strengthen supply chains and improve safety near the tracks. If advance appropriations are not renewed, funding for four essential rail programs will decrease 83 percent. American Rail on the Chopping Block examines the benefits of the BIL’s rail investments and what is at risk for businesses, passengers and local communities if a multiyear investment strategy is abandoned.

On May 13, 2026, Sen. Cantwell also led a letter to appropriators from all Democratic senators demonstrating the significant need for continued infrastructure investment and warning of the magnitude of harm if funding is abandoned.

The new State-by-State reports (including D.C. and Puerto Rico) are HERE.

title: Senate Unanimously Approves Bipartisan, Bicameral Comprehensive Weather Forecasting Bill

committee.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation

text:
Includes Cruz’s 2025 Hill Country Flood Weather Radio Bill

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, the U.S. Senate unanimously passed Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz’s (R-Texas) Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Reauthorization Act of 2026 (Weather Act).

Senate passage reflects a bicameral agreement on the legislation (S.3923) reauthorizing many weather forecasting and hazard communication programs at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). In light of this agreement, it is anticipated that the House of Representatives will take up and send the Weather Act to the President’s desk before the end of the 119th Congress.

Upon Senate passage, Chairman Cruz said: “Today, the Senate took a pivotal step toward ensuring Americans are prepared for severe weather. Texans know all too well the devastation storms can bring. The lives lost in the July 4, 2025, Texas floods are a heartbreaking reminder of what is at stake. The Weather Act brings together over a dozen bipartisan bills to modernize radar systems, deliver more accurate and timely forecasts, and improve warnings so families and first responders have more time to act, no matter where they are and no matter the time of day. These improvements will help protect property and, more importantly, save lives in Texas and across the country.”

Senate Commerce Committee Ranking Member Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) said: “Americans are facing increasingly dangerous and costly weather disasters, and better forecasts give communities more time to prepare and get out of harm’s way. The Weather Act will advance next-generation weather radar, modernize lifesaving warning systems, and improve forecasts for atmospheric rivers and wildfires, like the devastating fires that forced thousands to evacuate in Spokane last month. Senate passage brings us one step closer to giving forecasters, emergency managers, and communities the tools they need to save lives and protect property.”

House Science, Space, and Technology Committee Chairman Brian Babin (R-Texas-36) said: “Reliable weather forecasts and timely warnings are essential to protecting American lives and property. Last year’s devastating floods in Texas served as a tragic reminder of the need to better predict severe weather and communicate critical information to communities in harm’s way. The Weather Act Reauthorization represents an opportunity to modernize our nation’s forecasting capabilities and strengthen emergency preparedness. Building on the legislation the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee advanced last September, the Senate-passed bill reflects a bipartisan, bicameral compromise and a shared commitment to protecting American communities. I thank Chairman Cruz, Ranking Member Lofgren, Rep. Lucas, and our colleagues in both chambers for their hard work in reaching this agreement. I look forward to continuing our efforts to get this legislation across the finish line.

House Science, Space, and Technology Committee Ranking Member Zoe Lofgren (D-Calif.-18) said: “This is a long time coming. The Weather Act Reauthorization will give NOAA the support it needs to carry out its critical mission. I want to thank Chairman Babin, my former Committee partner, Mr. Lucas, and the dedicated staff on both sides of the aisle for getting this to the finish line. The World Meteorological Organization just released its State of the Climate update emphasizing that the supersized El Niño we are experiencing is expected to bring record heat, flooding, and drought conditions for the next year. Now more than ever, more observations and data are needed to bolster our nations forecasting capabilities to protect lives, property, the economy, and national security. We have to ensure that NOAA has the tools, staffing, and infrastructure to help support communities prepare for and respond to disasters. This bill will help us do that.”

More than a dozen bipartisan bills are in the Weather Act, including Chairman Cruz’s NOAA Weather Radio Modernization Act. His Radio Modernization Act upgrades weather radio equipment to make broadcasts of emergency notices during severe weather more reliable and accessible nationwide. This bill, along with numerous other underlying measures in the Weather Act came about as a response to gaps identified after the deadly July 2025 floods in Texas’ Hill Country.

In addition to Chairman Cruz and Ranking Member Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), cosponsors include Sens. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.), Jerry Moran (R-Kan.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), Tim Sheehy (R-Mont.), Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), Ted Budd (R-N.C.), Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), John Curtis (R-Utah), and John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.).

The legislation would:

Reauthorize multiple weather forecasting programs while advancing next-generation forecasting technologies and improving research-to-operations transition efforts.

Improve forecasting for flooding, hurricanes, tornadoes, droughts, landslides, wildfires, and atmospheric rivers.

Enhance public communication of weather risks — including through NOAA weather radio —to ensure warnings are clear, timely, and actionable.

Modernize NOAA’s aging radar network through planning and deployment of next-generation weather radar and targeted efforts to close radar coverage gaps, including gaps in flash-flood prone and under-observed regions such as the Texas Hill Country.

Improve coastal marine fog forecasting where dense fog can disrupt shipping and maritime commerce.

Advance long-range weather forecasting to support farmers, ranchers, and water managers by improving weather outlooks weeks to months in advance.

Sen. Sullivan said: “We must invest in advancing and strengthening our preparedness, response, and mitigation capabilities to address natural disasters. This is especially important for Alaska, where our vast geography, remote communities, and exposure to a wide range of hazards make accurate forecasting and timely warnings essential to protecting lives, property, and communities. The Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Reauthorization Act reinforces our existing federal programs, protects NOAA’s core weather research and forecasting framework, including authorization levels that direct adequate resources, including personnel, and bolsters NOAA’s forecasting, warning, and communication systems to be better prepared for natural disasters such as tsunamis, landslides, wildfires, and severe weather. It also incorporates bills I have introduced or cosponsored, including my Harmful Algal Bloom and Hypoxia Research and Control Amendments (HABHRCA) Act, which ensures robust prevention, identification and response to the harmful algal blooms that are increasingly found in both our coastal and inland waters, as well as several bills I have cosponsored: the NOAA Weather Radio Modernization Act; the Fire Ready Nation Act; the Accelerating Networking, Cyberinfrastructure, and Hardware for Ocean Research (ANCHOR) Act; and the Tsunami Warning, Research, and Education Reauthorization Act. I am pleased to see all these priorities for Alaska advance through this comprehensive legislation.”

Sen. Blunt Rochester said: “Delaware is the lowest-lying state in the nation. Our rapidly changing climate has changed the way we prepare for severe weather events. As severe weather damages communities more frequently, it couldn’t be more important for us to properly invest in NOAA’s weather forecasting. I’m grateful for the bipartisan coalition of colleagues on this bill. We must do everything in our power to help Delawareans, and folks across the country, prepare for whatever weather events are on the horizon. I look forward to working together to get our Weather Act passed into law.”

Sen. Moran said: “Kansans, particularly farmers and ranchers, rely on access to timely and reliable weather data every day. I’m pleased this bill incorporates my legislation, the FORECAST Act, to help make certain NWS offices remain staffed to provide lifesaving 24/7 weather forecasting to their communities. Passage of this legislation is an important step to improve access to timely weather data for Kansans.”

Sen. Schatz said: “As severe weather in Hawai‘i and around the country becomes more damaging and frequent, having better forecasting can make all the difference in saving lives and livelihoods. Our bill will help improve forecasts and weather communications so that communities can better anticipate, prepare for, and respond to extreme weather.”

Sen. Sheehy said: “As severe weather grows more dangerous, costing us hundreds of billions of dollars in economic impact and harming thousands of Americans every year, we need to make sure communities have the tools they need to prepare and respond quickly and effectively. Montanans know firsthand the devastation wildfires cause, and while fire season only seems to be getting worse, government response has largely stayed the same. Better forecasting helps save lives, protect homes and livelihoods, and strengthen our resilience. The Weather Act is a commonsense step toward a safer, better-prepared America, and I’m glad to see it pass the Senate.”

Sen. Rosen said: “The severity of the wildfires and extreme heat in Nevada this past summer reminded us just how important it is that we invest in the latest weather prediction technology and fund critical programs at NOAA. I’m glad that my bill, to ensure Nevada’s farmers and ranchers have access to forecasts that will improve their resilience to weather anomalies, is part of the bipartisan Weather Act that has now passed the U.S. Senate. I call on the House of Representatives to pass it soon so we can send it to the President’s desk without delay.”

Sen. Budd said: “North Carolina knows all too well the risks when major storms strike. This bipartisan effort to reduce major gaps in our weather system will help us track future storms more effectively and efficiently, to help prevent loss of life and property. I am grateful that two bills I authored were included as provisions to the Weather Act to help enhance the accuracy of hurricane forecasts and communication, as well as modernize our radar system to get warnings out quicker.”

Sen. Klobuchar said: “This past year, communities across Minnesota faced severe weather that affected local businesses, agriculture, infrastructure, and safety. From forest fires impacting tourism on the North Shore to major crop loss from floods in Southern Minnesota, natural disasters have taken a toll on our industries. By investing in weather forecasting and research, the bipartisan Weather Act will help communities better prepare for severe weather. My provision to protect the Aerial Snow Survey Program was included in the bill, which is crucial for collecting data and monitoring snowpack to better predict water levels and downstream impacts for local communities.”

Sen. Curtis said: “Over the course of this year’s fire season, Utah communities have faced extreme wildfires that have led to catastrophic flooding. I’ve seen the damage these floods have caused to homes and livelihoods firsthand, and it is devastating. This bipartisan bill will help support our rural communities facing increasingly powerful fires and floods by modernizing weather communication and radio services, and I hope to see it signed into law soon.”

Sen. Hickenlooper said: “Colorado and the West are facing historic drought and relentless wildfires fueled by climate change. Investing in NOAA’s operations and research gives Coloradans better tools and resources to forecast extreme weather, prepare for disasters, and save lives.”

Chairman Cruz, Ranking Member Cantwell and a bipartisan group of Commerce Committee members introduced the Weather Act in February 2026. The bill was unanimously advanced out of the Commerce Committee the following month.

title: Heinrich’s Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act Passes Key Senate Vote

committee.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources

text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, released the following statement after the Senate advanced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), bipartisan legislation to lower energy bills, hold data centers accountable, reduce emissions, and create good-paying jobs.

“If we have any hope of making energy cheaper and making data centers pay for their own energy costs, then we need to pass our Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act into law,” said Heinrich. “This bill delivers exactly what Americans told us they wanted on election day: Lower costs and more jobs for American workers — all while reducing our emissions and defending against the administration’s attacks on Tribal consultation.”

Heinrich continued, “Negotiating this bill hasn’t been easy and took a lot of compromise. Now, we need to roll up our sleeves, engage in the amendment process, and work across party lines to get this done. When we put working families ahead of politics, we can build a future that is affordable and put the American dream within reach.”

Independent analyses find that BAAJA will:

Require data centers to pay for increased grid and energy costs they create, estimated at $55 billion in the next 10 years;

Save $19 billion in residential electricity bills over the next 14 years;

Nearly double the amount of solar and wind that can connect to the grid;

Create up to 105,600 trades and manufacturing jobs; and

Avoid 1.5 gigatons of CO₂ emissions, the equivalent of taking 39 coal plants offline for a decade.

Earlier today, Heinrich hosted a press conference with U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, to urge their Senate colleagues to pass BAAJA and help lower electricity bills for American families. title: Chairman Capito Asks EPA Nominee About Energy Affordability, Cooperative Federalism in Nomination Hearing

committee.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee, held a hearing to consider the nomination of Justin Schwab to be Assistant Administrator for the Office of Air and Radiation (OAR) at the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). During the hearing, Chairman Capito asked Mr. Schwab how he would consider energy affordability and cooperative federalism in OAR responsibilities, and gained his commitment to work with her on Small Refinery Exemption program issues.

HIGHLIGHTS:

ENERGY RELIABILITY AND AFFORDABILITY:

Chairman Capito:

“The Biden EPA power sector strategy imposed costly requirements on coal-fired and natural gas power plants, raising serious legal questions and threatening the continued operation of reliable and affordable electricity generation units. At the same time, grid experts have warned us about the consequences of shutting down dependable power plants…and now electricity prices have increased as power supply hasn’t kept up. The Trump administration, including EPA’s Office of Air and Radiation, has taken steps to repeal these regulations in line with existing law, with the added benefit of bringing down electricity costs in the future. Mr. Schwab, how will you ensure that your office would consider electric reliability and energy affordability while carrying out the responsibilities of clean air?”

Justin Schwab, nominee to be Assistant Administrator for the Office of Air and Radiation of the Environmental Protection Agency:

“If confirmed to this position, I would ensure that energy requirements are properly taken into account. It’s important to note that multiple provisions of the Clean Air Act, including Section 111, which is the chief one under which these regulations have happened in the past, specifically requires EPA to take energy requirements into account when determining what the best system of emission reduction is, and I would pledge to take that congressional direction very seriously.”

SMALL REFINERY EXEMPTION PROGRAM:

Chairman Capito:

“Congress established small refinery exemptions, and we talked about this already, to provide relief to small refiners that experienced disproportionate economic hardships under the Renewable Fuel Standard. I’ve raised concerns about how the EPA has administered this program, including the need for timely decisions and fair consideration. Mr. Schwab, if you’re confirmed, will you commit to working with me and my staff on outstanding issues with the small refinery exemption program, to ensure that it is providing timely decisions and fair decisions for the petitioning entities?”

Justin Schwab, nominee to be Assistant Administrator for the Office of Air and Radiation of the Environmental Protection Agency:

“Yes, Senator, if confirmed to this position, I do commit to work with you and your staff, and to work inside the agency towards those ends.”

COOPERATIVE FEDERALISM:

Chairman Capito:

“This interplay between federal and state, who’s got responsibilities, are lines clearly drawn where they are, and what kind of responsibilities are better off at the state level, these are really, really important issues. I would ask you, how will you work with state environmental agencies to ensure that the OAR carries out its responsibilities consistent with cooperative federalism?”

Justin Schwab, nominee to be Assistant Administrator for the Office of Air and Radiation of the Environmental Protection Agency:

“The Clean Air Act, in its design, is a design of cooperative federalism. States, generally speaking, in the first instance, design plans to attain and maintain air quality standards. If confirmed to this position, I would work respectfully and collaboratively with the states to try to get to yes wherever legally possible and supported by evidence in the record.”

title: Crapo Statement at Hearing on Nominees for Treasury, Commerce
text:
Washington, D.C.—U.S. Senate Finance Committee Chairman Mike Crapo (R-Idaho) delivered the following remarks at a hearing to consider nominees for the U.S. Department of the Treasury and the U.S. Department of Commerce.

As prepared for delivery:

“Thank you to our nominees, Mr. Browne, Mr. Abbott and Mr. Stebbins for being here today. Congratulations on your nominations and thank you all for your willingness to serve.”

“As we approach the end of the 119th Congress, I thank my colleagues for their important work on the Committee on behalf of taxpayers over the last two years. To our departing colleagues, thank you for your service on the Committee and in Congress. To those returning to the Committee next year, I look forward to our continued bipartisan partnership.”

“I also extend my congratulations to Ranking Member Wyden as he prepares to reassume the chairmanship of the Committee in the 120th Congress. I appreciate his longstanding commitment to the Committee and our strong history of working together to advance bipartisan priorities. I look forward to building on that record of cooperation as we continue our work on behalf of the American people.”

“Today, the Finance Committee will consider three nominees who, if confirmed, will serve in important roles at the Department of the Treasury and Department of Commerce.”

“We will first hear from Francis Browne, who is nominated to serve as Under Secretary of the Treasury for Domestic Finance.”

“The Domestic Finance office develops policies and guidance for Treasury Department activities in areas involving financial institutions, federal debt finance, financial regulation and capital markets. Sensible guidance in these areas better ensures financial stability and growth, as well as the resilience of our economy.”

“Mr. Browne brings more than two decades of private sector experience in investment banking, portfolio management and financial markets to this role. His extensive background and expertise will serve him well in advancing policies that strengthen financial stability and promote economic growth.”

“Next, we will hear from Chris Abbott, who has been nominated to serve as Assistant Secretary of Enforcement and Compliance for the International Trade Administration at the Department of Commerce.”

“The Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance oversees the enforcement of U.S. trade laws—including antidumping and countervailing duty measures—to combat unfair trade practices and ensure American businesses and workers can compete on a level playing field.”

“Mr. Abbott previously served in several senior positions at the White House and most recently at the Department of Commerce. His experience overseeing trade enforcement and manufacturing policy will be critical for this important role.”

“Finally, we will hear from Bob Stebbins, who is nominated to serve as the General Counsel of the Treasury Department.”

“The General Counsel is the principal legal officer of the Treasury Department and provides important legal and policy advice to the Secretary and other senior Department officials. As the Treasury Department works to implement the Working Families Tax Cuts and other pro-growth tax policies, the General Counsel will be vital in ensuring that regulations and other guidance are developed in accordance with the law and reflect congressional intent.”

“Mr. Stebbins is undoubtedly qualified for the job, having previously served as General Counsel of the Securities and Exchange Commission and General Counsel and Acting Chief Strategic Officer of the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, in addition to his extensive private sector experience as a partner at Willkie Farr & Gallagher. His distinguished career in both the public and private sectors will be an asset as he takes on this important role at the Treasury Department.”

“I thank all the nominees for their willingness to participate in the Committee’s nominations process, meet with Committee staff prior to today’s hearing and answer their questions. I also thank you for your willingness to answer questions from Committee members during today’s hearing.”

title: Consumer Price Index Increased 0.35 Percent in October, more than Expected, Hitting 4.02 Rate for the Year
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Today, the Joint Economic Committee released its Monthly Inflation Update for October, showing that consumer prices continued to rise, and above projections.

Headline Consumer Price Index (CPI-U) increased by 0.35 percent in October and rose to 4.02 percent over the past year. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, increased 0.30 percent in October and rose to 2.81 percent over the past year. Energy price inflation increased 0.70 percent in October and was up 20.77 percent over the past year. Food price inflation rose 0.47 percent in October and was up 3.01 percent over the past year.

Inflation varied by region, with annual headline CPI inflation highest in the Northeast (4.7 percent), followed by the Midwest (4.6 percent), West (3.7 percent) and South (3.6 percent).

Note, BLS could not collect the relevant Consumer Price Index data for the October 2025 reference period due to a lapse in appropriations in late 2025. As a result, BLS did not report a year-over-year inflation figure. Instead, JEC estimated the data for October 2025 using the geometric means of September 2025 and November 2025 data. Therefore, the 4.02 percent figure is a JEC estimate calculated using an interpolated value.

In October, month over month real earnings were mostly stagnant. Real average weekly earnings for all employees increased 0.02 percent, while real average hourly earnings remained unchanged 0.00 percent.

For the full update, visit: https://www.jec.senate.gov/public/index.cfm/republicans/inflation-update

title: Durbin Calls Out Trump Judicial Nominees For Their Inexperience In The Courtroom
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, today questioned judicial nominees during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing with two panels beginning with Todd Butler, nominated to be a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. The second panel included Samuel D. Adkisson, nominated to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of Tennessee; Philip Axt, nominated to be U.S. District Judge for the District of North Dakota; Bradford Kelley, nominated to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of Louisiana; and Arthur Kleinschmidt, nominated to be Assistant Attorney General for the Office of Justice Programs.

Durbin first questioned Mr. Butler about his views on qualified immunity after Mr. Butler defended police officers for arresting a 10-year-old child in Eason v. City of Senatobia.

“You have defended a number of police officers who have been arrested for misuse of their authority. One case comes to mind. An officer arrested a 10-year-old child. You argued that the officer had probable cause that this child violated the Mississippi indecent exposure statute for urinating in public. Thankfully, the court rejected your argument because the 10-year-old cannot have the requisite state of mind to violate a statute. Would you like to comment on that defense?” Durbin asked Mr. Butler.

Mr. Butler asserted that while he has defended police officers in court, he also trains public officials and law enforcement to understand and abide by Americans’ civil rights. Notably, however, he has trained correctional institutions on how to avoid consent decrees, court-enforced legally binding performance improvement plans which are often put in place to compel such institutions to reform their correctional facilities and care of inmates.

Durbin then pressed Mr. Adkisson, Mr. Axt, and Mr. Kelley about their concerning lack of experience to serve in lifetime federal appointment.

“Mr. Adkisson, Mr. Axt, you each graduated from law school only eight years ago. You have been lawyers for less time than any judicial nominee considered by this Committee in the last 10 years. Mr. Adkisson, you have fewer than five years of litigation experience. Mr. Axt and Mr. Kelley, neither of you have ever tried a case,” Durbin said. “Most of you have little or no experience with trials.”

“How many civil juries have each of you participated in as lead or co-counsel?” Durbin asked.

Mr. Adkisson noted that he has tried only one case to judgment, a bankruptcy dispute before a judge, as a junior attorney. Neither Mr. Axt nor Mr. Kelley has participated in a civil jury trial as lead or co-counsel.

“How many criminal jury trials have each of you participated in?” Durbin followed up.

Again, Mr. Adkisson, Mr. Axt, and Mr. Kelley replied that none of them have experience with criminal jury trials as a lead or co-counsel.

“Have you ever picked a jury or conducted voir dire?” Durbin continued.

Both Mr. Adkisson and Mr. Axt confirmed that they have never conducted voir dire while Mr. Kelley could only point to the assistance he provided to the judge for whom he had clerked.

Durbin condemned the three judicial nominees’ lack of experience, saying: “To take a lifetime appointment for a federal district court, which is primarily a trial driven court, or at least preparation for trial, and not have any experience with the things I have asked you here, really raises the question of why were you on the list? Why did this Administration think you needed a lifetime appointment with so little personal experience? Fewer years of practice for two of you than any nominee in the last 10 years—10 years before this Committee…A lifetime appointment for a federal district trial judge, I just don’t see how you put it together.”

Durbin then questioned Mr. Kleinschmidt about his view on cutting federal grants aimed at improving public safety and providing services to victims. Last year, the Trump Administration terminated 373 Office of Justice Programs (OJP) grants that would have gone toward public safety funding. Mr. Kleinschmidt, despite previously advocating for more funding and accessibility for effective treatment programs, defended the Trump Administration’s cuts.

“Do you think that is key to good law enforcement, cutting back on these grants and mental health counseling?” Durbin asked Mr. Kleinschmidt.

Mr. Kleinschmidt claimed that he was not involved in any cuts to grants at the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) during his tenure there as Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary. Shortly after Mr. Kleinschmidt left SAMHSA, the Trump Administration announced that it would terminate an estimated $2 billion in grant funding from SAMHSA to treat addiction, mental health, and provide homelessness services. A day later, the Administration reversed course and reinstated those grants.

title: Durbin Slams Judiciary Committee Republicans For Violating Committee Norms To Fast-Track Judicial Nominations
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, slammed Senate Judiciary Committee Republicans for violating numerous longstanding Committee standards to fast-track unqualified MAGA extremists, all without the consent of the minority. These actions include holding nominations hearings less than two weeks apart on November 10 and 18; slating nominees for the November 18 hearing despite receiving Senate Judiciary Questionnaires (SJQ) less than 28 days in advance; slating nominees for hearings even if their FBI background investigations have not been cleared by staff in advance; and slating as many as seven nominees for a single hearing.

During his opening, Durbin criticized Republicans for fast-tracking Elliot Gaiser, reportedly nominated to be a judge on the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas, for a hearing on November 18. Mr. Gaiser is one of President Trump’s former campaign lawyers who advanced baseless legal arguments to try to overturn the 2020 election. In his current role as head of the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel, Mr. Gaiser issued an opinion claiming that the Presidential Records Act is unconstitutional and signed off on the creation of the infamous January 6 slush fund. Durbin also spoke out against a Texas Supreme Court Justice, James Sullivan, whose paperwork to be considered for a federal district judgeship was submitted to the Committee a day after he lost his re-election bid last Tuesday. Sullivan will also be slated for the November 18 hearing to be considered for a judicial vacancy in the Western District of Texas.

Durbin also criticized Republicans for continuing to withhold from Democrats committee records that Republican Senators used to question Special Counsel Jack Smith, including texts regarding Mr. Smith’s attendance at a basketball game. These records, which were used to justify unfounded accusations of perjury and personal attacks on Mr. Smith, are being withheld from the minority in violation of Senate rules and longstanding Committee practice. By departing from the Committee’s longstanding oversight and nominations practices, Republicans are setting precedents allowing future Democratic chairs to withhold committee records from Republicans and fast-track judicial nominees.

Key Quotes:

“Last week, on Election Day, the American people rejected this Administration’s corruption and cruelty overwhelmingly. President Trump responded to this stunning rebuke of his leadership by doubling down. He made baseless claims that the Democratic landslide was a result of fraud with no evidence forthcoming; he promoted Stephen Miller, the architect of the mass deportation campaign that led to the deaths of [Renée Good and Alex Pretti]. He is now chief of staff for the President of the United States. [Trump] ordered the Justice Department to criminally investigate members of Congress simply for conducting oversight hearings. Thanks to Republicans, President Trump has a loyalist as his Senate-confirmed Attorney General to carry out his [illegal] orders.”

“Unfortunately, it appears our Republican colleagues, who I thought learned a lesson from last Tuesday’s election, did not get the message… The Republican majority on this Committee continues to withhold Committee records that Republican Senators used to question Special Counsel Jack Smith. He appeared before this Committee under oath and testified. Now, the information that was used to attack him in the hearing, which we have requested and is routinely turned over, has been withheld in violation of Senate rules and longstanding Committee practice.”

“The majority is also violating numerous longstanding [Committee] standards in a desperate attempt to confirm the [un]qualified loyalists to lifetime appointments before Democrats take the majority. By departing from these practices, Republicans are further undermining the Committee’s ability [to carry out its constitutional oversight and advice and consent roles]… We cannot have one set of rules for Republicans and another for Democrats.”

“It’s not too late to change course. If [Republicans] are listening to the American people, I would suggest that you abandon these efforts [and instead] hold our regular DOJ oversight hearings; that we hold a hearing finally with Big Tech CEOs… and we need respond to Senator Curtis’s request for a bipartisan investigation of the Trump family’s famous wedding reception paid for by a Russian oligarch.”

“Mr. Chairman, there are many things we still can do… One of them is not to expedite nominees who have not been carefully vetted. I hope we don’t accept that as a standard in this Committee.”

title: Durbin Slams Senate Judiciary Republicans For Attempting To Jam Through Extreme Judicial Nominees Before Democrats Take Senate Majority
text:
WASHINGTON – During today’s Senate Judiciary Committee nominations hearing, U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, delivered an opening statement highlighting the longstanding bipartisan Committee norms that Republicans are violating to jam through the Trump Administration’s extreme and unqualified nominees during the lame-duck session. As Durbin made clear in his remarks, Committee Republicans missed multiple opportunities to slate nominees for earlier hearings, and now that Democrats are poised to lead the Senate come January, Committee Republicans are attempting to fast-track nominees.

Further, Durbin specifically called out Committee Republicans’ attempt to jam through two nominees, James Sullivan and Elliot Gaiser, for lifetime appointments to federal district courts in Texas before the new Congress in hopes of circumventing any consultation with Senator-elect James Talarico (D-TX). In a clearly premeditated move, the Department of Justice submitted Mr. Sullivan’s Senate Judiciary Questionnaire the day after he lost his election to the Texas Supreme Court. Similarly, Mr. Gaiser’s Questionnaire discloses that he was contacted by U.S. Senator Ted Cruz’s (R-TX) office about being nominated just one day after the election.

Key Quotes:

“In the waning days of this Congress, in light of the last [week’s] election, the Chairman is violating numerous longstanding Committee norms that Republicans and Democratic Chairs alike have followed for years, without consent from the minority—a key phrase when it comes to the rules of this Committee. The majority is planning to hold nominations hearings today and next week, contrary to our practice of holding nominations hearings no closer than two weeks apart. They’re slating two nominees for next week’s hearing whose Questionnaires were received 10 and 14 days before the hearing, respectively, contrary to the 28 days-[rule], which has been required by both political parties up until now. They’re calling nominees for hearings even if their FBI background investigations have not yet been cleared by staff, and they’re slating as many as seven nominees for a single hearing.”

“Why? Because the Republicans are losing the majority and they’re afraid that unqualified MAGA loyalists won’t withstand close scrutiny when Democrats are in the majority.”

“Consider two Texas nominees who are slated for next week’s hearing: James Sullivan and Elliot Gaiser. On Tuesday, November 3, James Sullivan lost his election for the Texas Supreme Court. The very next day, the Administration submitted his Senate Judiciary Questionnaire, which had obviously been prepared in advance.”

“[Gaiser’s] Questionnaire was submitted to this Committee two days ago…It says that Senator Cruz’s office contacted him the day after the election about the nomination.”

“Under the Committee’s precedents, these two nominees can’t be confirmed before the end of this Congress…So, Republicans are breaking the rules to jam through these nominees and avoid on obvious thing—on January 3, there will be a new Senator from Texas. Senator Talarico (D-TX) has the right, as all Senators do, to approve or disapprove district court nominees in a process known as the blue slip.”

“What we are seeing here is an effort to scramble quickly to resurrect defeated candidates in Texas and others to fill positions on the federal district court before Senator Talarico is sworn in on January 3. It’s pretty obvious. There’s such a scramble to do this that they are ignoring the rules of the Committee.”

“Before appointing a person to a lifetime appointment to the federal bench, shouldn’t we take a close look at their background? We have in the past, but clearly we are not any longer. I think that is a serious mistake, Mr. Chairman. When you have to live with it under a new Chairman, I’m sorry to tell you, but you asked for it.”
