title: Ranking Member Shaheen, Senator Coons Demand Elon Musk Preserve Documents Regarding Ukraine’s Access to Starlink and Starshield
text:
WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senators Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Chris Coons (D-DE) sent a letter to CEO of SpaceX, Elon Musk, demanding he and SpaceX preserve documents and communications relating to the disruption of Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starlink and Starshield satellite services. Disruptions occurred in October 2026 and again to Starshield on November 12, 2026.

In the letter, the Senators detail how the restrictions disrupted Ukraine’s critical air-defense capabilities and endangered Ukrainian civilians as well as American personnel. The Senators demand that Musk and SpaceX preserve all documents and information related to Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starlink and Starshield satellite services and provide written confirmation by November 30 that all appropriate preservation measures have been implemented.

“Between October 13 and October 24, 2026, restrictions on Starlink and Starshield disrupted communications services used by Ukrainian forces, including for interceptor drones defending civilian population centers against Russian missiles and drones. During that period, Russia launched nearly 4,000 aerial attacks against Ukraine, killing and injuring civilians. On November 12, 2026, President Zelenskyy and the Ukrainian military reported renewed disruptions to Starshield across the entire front line and Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine, hindering Ukraine’s ability to defend itself and putting civilian lives at risk,” wrote the Senators.

“The conflicting statements and reports as to who ordered and approved of these restrictions only underscore the need for a comprehensive inquiry and full accounting of the facts. For example, you asserted that limitations on Starshield were decisions made by the U.S. military and ultimately the President. Secretary Hegseth subsequently suggested that SpaceX could impose restrictions unilaterally under its terms of service, while Secretary Rubio stated that decisions regarding Starlink access likewise rested with SpaceX,” continued the Senators.

“The United States cannot permit critical national security capabilities to be subject to opaque decision-making or unilateral disruption without government authorization and accountability. As Congress evaluates the adequacy of existing contracts and the need for additional statutory safeguards, we must establish whether current arrangements provide the operational control, reliability and oversight necessary to protect American personnel and sustain Ukraine’s defense against Russian aggression,” concluded the Senators.

Full text of the letter is available HERE and provided below.

Dear Mr. Musk:

We request that you take immediate steps to preserve all documents, communications and electronically stored information of yours or of SpaceX’s relating to Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Recent restrictions on those services—which have occurred as Russia continues to carry out strikes on Ukrainian civilians—have disrupted critical air defense capabilities, endangered American personnel and raise serious questions about the control SpaceX has over critical communications capabilities essential to U.S. national security, the safety of American personnel and Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian aggression. As senior members of the Committee charged with oversight of U.S. policy towards Ukraine and the safety of U.S. diplomatic personnel abroad, the answers to these questions are critical for the Committee to ascertain whether future legislation may be warranted.

Between October 13 and October 24, 2026, restrictions on Starlink and Starshield disrupted communications services used by Ukrainian forces, including for interceptor drones defending civilian population centers against Russian missiles and drones. During that period, Russia launched nearly 4,000 aerial attacks against Ukraine, killing and injuring civilians. On November 12, 2026, President Zelenskyy and the Ukrainian military reported renewed disruptions to Starshield across the entire front line and Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine, hindering Ukraine’s ability to defend itself and putting civilian lives at risk.

These restrictions prevent Ukrainian defensive systems from maintaining connectivity at the speeds necessary to intercept certain fast-moving Russian drones, undermining Ukraine’s ability to protect its civilian population from aerial attack. As we detailed in our October 15, 2026, letter to the Department of Defense Inspector General, the October disruption also coincided with reports that American diplomatic, military and security personnel in Kyiv struggled to reach designated shelters during Russian air raids. Congressional staff in Ukraine at the time witnessed and experienced the effects of the throttling firsthand. To date, SpaceX has not provided any explanation or clarification of who authorized these restrictions, their contractual basis and the scope of SpaceX’s independent authority to impose or reverse them.

Further, the conflicting statements and reports as to who ordered and approved of these restrictions only underscore the need for a comprehensive inquiry and full accounting of the facts. For example, you asserted that limitations on Starshield were decisions made by the U.S. military and ultimately the President. Secretary Hegseth subsequently suggested that SpaceX could impose restrictions unilaterally under its terms of service, while Secretary Rubio stated that decisions regarding Starlink access likewise rested with SpaceX.

This is not the first time SpaceX’s control over satellite communications has raised national security concerns. Previous restrictions affecting operations near Crimea demonstrated the risks of relying on commercial infrastructure whose availability could be determined by a single corporate executive. The development and procurement of Starshield were intended, in part, to address the military’s need for more reliable and government-controlled communications. The October and November restrictions now raise the disturbing possibility that these vulnerabilities persist even within systems on which the U.S. government relies.

There remain critical unanswered questions about SpaceX’s contract terms, its compliance with that contract and who is ultimately responsible for directing and approving restrictions on these communications services. Given the importance of SpaceX’s systems to U.S. national security as well as the defense of a vital partner, it is imperative that Congress have a complete and accurate picture of what led to these restrictions and how they can be prevented in the future.

To better inform the Committee as it evaluates potential legislation addressing these topics, we request that SpaceX immediately preserve all documents, communications and electronically stored information relating to Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. This preservation demand includes, but is not limited to:

All contracts, task orders, amendments, statements of work and technical specifications governing Starlink and Starshield services in Ukraine, including materials addressing availability, speed restrictions, allowable uses, geofencing, suspension, termination, modification authority and notice requirements.

All technical records, network logs, configuration changes, software instructions, operational directives and records identifying when restrictions were proposed, activated, modified, removed or reinstated, including the identities of individuals who authorized or implemented those changes.

All communications related to Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine, including authorized use thereof, speed restrictions or changes in access or speed, compliance with contractual terms, and including communications involving you, SpaceX executives and employees, President Trump, White House officials or employees and Department of Defense employees or contractors.

All internal communications, legal analyses, risk assessments and decision memoranda addressing the rationale for the restrictions, their contractual or legal basis and their anticipated or actual effects on Ukrainian air defenses, unmanned systems, civilian protection or American personnel.

All records concerning reports of failed Ukrainian interception missions, degraded defensive capabilities, civilian casualties or risks to U.S. diplomatic, military or security personnel, including any warnings received before or during the restrictions.

All records concerning representations made to the U.S. government, Congress, investors or the public regarding who controlled Starlink and Starshield, who ordered the restrictions, whether services were degraded and the circumstances under which normal operations were restored.

All documents related to required public disclosures, contract disputes and compliance or noncompliance with any federal contract, congressional request or investigation.

This demand applies to records in the possession, custody or control of SpaceX, its officers, employees, agents and contractors, including communications conducted through personal devices, encrypted messaging applications or other noncorporate channels used for company business. It encompasses records created from September 1, 2026, to the present, as well as subsequently created records relating to these events. For purposes of this request, “preserve” includes taking reasonable steps to prevent the partial or full destruction, alteration, testing, deletion, shredding, incineration, wiping, relocation, migration, theft, mutation or negligent or reckless handling that could render the information incomplete or inaccessible.

We request that you provide written confirmation no later than November 30, 2026, that the preservation measures described above have been implemented. We further request answers to the following questions no later than November 30, 2026:

How were any restrictions on Starlink or Starshield services affecting Ukraine since October 1, 2026, communicated, approved and/or directed? Identify the specific restrictions, the dates they took effect, the authority under which they were carried out and whether anyone outside of SpaceX authorized or directed those actions. If applicable, identify the individual or entity responsible for each decision, including any relevant U.S. government officials, and explain the extent of your knowledge of those decisions.

Did SpaceX conduct any assessment of the potential consequences of restrictions on Starlink or Starshield for Ukrainian air defenses, civilian lives or American personnel? If so, provide a copy of those findings and identify who conducted those assessments and who received those findings. Provide a complete chronology of all restrictions, restorations and subsequent modifications, including the technical parameters and geographic scope of each change.

Which restrictions since October 1, 2026, remain in effect, and which have been reinstated? Identify who authorized each change and explain the renewed restrictions reported on November 12, 2026.

The United States cannot permit critical national security capabilities to be subject to opaque decision-making or unilateral disruption without government authorization and accountability. As Congress evaluates the adequacy of existing contracts and the need for additional statutory safeguards, we must establish whether current arrangements provide the operational control, reliability and oversight necessary to protect American personnel and sustain Ukraine’s defense against Russian aggression. We expect your full cooperation with this congressional oversight request and written confirmation by November 30, 2026, that all appropriate preservation measures have been implemented.

###

title: October Ends with $404 billion Deficit, 42.10 Percent Above Same Period in FY2026
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Today, the Joint Economic Committee released its Monthly Fiscal Update. In October, the federal government ran a deficit of $404.064 billion. From the beginning of the fiscal year to October, deficits were $404.064, meaning 52.27 percent of outlays in FY2027 were not paid for by revenues, and for every dollar the federal government received in revenue, it spent $2.10.

In the comparable fiscal year to date in FY2026, total federal deficits were $284.350 billion, which means the total deficit in the current fiscal year to date period is 42.10 percent higher than in the same period last fiscal year.

In FY2026, deficits were $1.992 trillion. The most recent 10-year budget projection from the CBO projected a total deficit of $1.887 trillion in FY2027, $2.080 trillion in FY2028, and $2.020 trillion in FY2029.

In October, total federal net outlays were $773.004 billion. From the beginning of the fiscal year to October, net outlays were $773.004 billion. In the comparable fiscal year to date in FY2026, total federal net outlays were $688.721 billion, which means the net outlays total in the current fiscal year to date period is 12.24 percent higher than in the same period last fiscal year.

In FY2026, net outlays were $7.396 trillion. The most recent 10-year budget projection from the CBO forecasts outlays of $7.772 trillion in FY2027, $8.151 trillion in FY2028, and $8.340 trillion in FY2029.

In October, total federal net receipts were $368.940 billion. From the beginning of the fiscal year to October, net receipts were $368.940 billion. In the comparable fiscal year to date in FY2026, total federal net receipts were $404.371 billion, which means the net receipts total in the current fiscal year to date period is 8.76 percent lower than in the same period last fiscal year.

In FY2026, net receipts were $5.403 trillion. The most recent 10-year budget projection from the CBO forecasts that total receipts will be $5.885 trillion in FY2027, $6.071 trillion in FY2028, and $6.320 trillion in FY2029.

Please see the full Monthly Fiscal Update for greater detail of the nation's receipts, outlays and deficit.

title: ICYMI: “Grassley Targeted the Kratom Killing our Kids”
text:
Grassley targeted the kratom killing our kids

By Wendy Chamberlain

November 9, 2026

The Cedar Rapids Gazette

‘Kratom is killing our kids."

Sen. Chuck Grassley posted those words in October, and then did something about it. He led a letter, joined by Sens. Mike Lee and Susan Collins, urging the DEA and FDA to finish the emergency scheduling of a kratom compound called 7-OH and to begin permanently scheduling the whole kratom plant. He gave the agencies a deadline to answer in writing.

Those are the words every parent who has buried a child to kratom has been hoping to hear from Washington.

My son Joe was 38 when he sat down in his recliner to watch TV, drifted off to sleep and never woke up. He was my only child and a father to three boys. His toxicology report listed one cause of death: mitragynine toxicity. Mitragynine is the main drug in kratom. It was the only substance in his body.

Joe started taking kratom because he was told it was a natural, healthy pick-me-up. It hooked him the way opioids hook people. Kratom works on the same receptors in the brain as heroin and morphine. People who try to quit go through withdrawal. Some never wake up.

Grassley's letter says what families like mine have been saying at city halls and statehouses for years. He and his colleagues wrote they "worry the availability of these products is providing consumers with a false sense of security because they are readily available and marketed as 'natural.'"

The senators put numbers on the record. Poison control centers received 3,434 kratom exposure reports in 2025, roughly 1,200 percent more than a decade ago. Emergency crews logged 3,672 suspected nonfatal kratom overdoses across 38 states in just over three years. The FDA has told consumers not to use kratom at all. And the DEA has found that some semi-synthetic compounds sold in kratom-labeled products are more potent than morphine.

Iowa has confirmed 45 kratom-associated deaths since 2024, across 23 counties, with 16 of them in the first seven months of this year. Iowa Poison Control calls about kratom are up 467 percent in two years. A ban passed the Iowa House.

The industry behind kratom runs a powerful lobbying operation that fights hard against anyone who opposes it. Grassley has spent his career taking on people who thought they were too big to be questioned on behalf of families who have no lobbyist at all.

For a mother who lost her only child to a product sold next to the gum, that means more than I can say. When the chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee puts his name on a letter like this, every grieving parent in the country knows we are not making this up, and every agency knows someone with real authority is watching.

Iowans should keep an eye on what the DEA and FDA do next. The agencies still have to act.

I can't bring Joe back. His boys are growing up without him. But for the first time in a long time, someone in Washington said out loud what killed my son. Thank you, Sen. Grassley.

Wendy Chamberlain is the founder of Kratom Danger Awareness. Her son, Joe, died of mitragynine toxicity in 2020.

title: Ranking Members Larsen, Carson Statement on Last Night’s Nationwide Ground Stop

committee.name: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure

text:
Washington, D.C.—Today, Ranking Member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure Rick Larsen (D-WA) and Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Aviation André Carson (D-IN) released the follow statement regarding last night’s nationwide ground stop and this morning’s press conference with U.S. Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford.

“Thank you to our air traffic controllers, safety technicians and all transportation workers who sprang into action to protect travelers during yesterday’s nationwide ground stop,” Ranking Members Larsen and Carson said. “This ground stop left the flying public and aviation workforce in disarray and seeking answers that the Trump administration waited hours to share. The safe travel of the flying public must always be our top priority. Our committee, on behalf of the flying public, will hold the administration accountable for what happened to make sure this chaos does not happen again.

“Let’s look at the facts. Congress approved $12.5 billion for the Department of Transportation to make necessary safety upgrades to our air traffic control system. Fifteen months later, the administration’s obligated $4.3 billion but only spent $1 billion, leaving $8 billion unobligated and $11 billion unspent. Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money?

“FAA and DOT staff will brief our staff on Monday about the additional $30 billion originally requested by the administration. We also expect to receive clear answers from FAA Administrator Bedford at our early December hearing—unless that can happen sooner.

"Heading into the next Congress, T&I Democrats are reconstituting the Oversight and Investigations staff of the Committee, and the rollout of ‘BNATCS’ will be a top priority of this new team. With holiday travel around the corner, we must avoid chaos that leads to mass, unexpected travel delays.”

title: MEDIA ADVISORY: Chairman Garbarino Announces Annual Worldwide Threats Hearing
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. –– Today, House Committee on Homeland Security Chairman Andrew R. Garbarino (R-NY) announced the date for the Committee’s annual Worldwide Threats hearing:

“Today we face a far broader and more complex threat landscape than 25 years ago, but our shared mission remains the same as it was in the aftermath of 9/11: to protect the American people. From the emergence of AI-enabled cyberattacks and adversaries such as Iran targeting U.S. critical infrastructure to terrorist organizations utilizing new tools to recruit and inspire across the globe, next week’s hearing comes at a pivotal moment. The Committee has consistently held this annual hearing for over a decade, and it remains an important touchpoint between lawmakers and the executive branch to help ensure our federal partners have the necessary coordination, resources, authorities, and personnel to fulfill their no-fail missions today and prepare for the threats of tomorrow.”

When: Wednesday, November 18, 2026, at 10:00 AM ET

Where: 310 Cannon House Office Building

WITNESSES:

The Honorable Markwayne Mullin

Secretary, Department of Homeland Security (DHS)

The Honorable Jay Clayton

Director of National Intelligence, Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI)

Christopher Raia

Deputy Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)

title: MEDIA ADVISORY: Subcommittee Chairman Strong Announces Hearing with FEMA Administrator Hamilton
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. –– Today, Subcommittee on Emergency Management and Technology Chairman Dale Strong (R-AL) announced a hearing for Thursday, November 19, to review the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (FEMA) capabilities and readiness:

“Having served as a first responder for over four decades, I have seen firsthand the critical role FEMA plays in disaster preparedness, response, and recovery, and I remain committed to the success of its mission. However, continued Congressional oversight is essential to ensuring the agency operates effectively and efficiently and that states and local communities have the resources they need before, during, and after disaster strikes. The Committee looks forward to hearing from Administrator Hamilton on how we can strengthen our nation’s emergency management capabilities and better support state, local, tribal, and territorial governments in protecting lives and property from devastating disasters.”

DETAILS:

What: A Subcommittee on Emergency Management and Technology hearing entitled, “Beyond the Storm: Assessing FEMA’s Mission Readiness.”

When: Thursday, November 19, 2026, at 10:00 AM ET

Where: 310 Cannon House Office Building

WITNESS:

The Honorable Cameron Hamilton

Administrator, Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA)

Witness testimony will be added here. The hearing will be livestreamed on YouTube and will be open to the public and press. Press must be congressionally credentialed and should RSVP in advance.

BACKGROUND:

Next week’s hearing will include assessments of recent developments regarding FEMA’s structure and governance, including the addition of the delivery of federal disaster assistance to the Government Accountability Office’s (GAO) High-Risk List, FEMA’s administration of preparedness grants, and FEMA’s absorption of certain functions of the now-dissolved U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction Office (CWMD).

In March 2025, the subcommittee also held a hearing entitled, “Future of FEMA: Perspectives from the Emergency Management Community.”

title: Moolenaar: Accountability Does Not End With Resignation. ﻿NVIDIA Must Have Thorough, Independent Investigation

committee.name: House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party

text:
Earlier this week, Chairman John Moolenaar of the Select Committee on Chinasent a letter to Stephen Neal, the lead independent director of the NVIDIA Board of Directors. The letter addresses former CEO Jensen Huang's failure to uphold his fiduciary responsibilities to the company and his violations of the NVIDIA Code of Conduct. Hours after the letter was sent, Huang tendered his resignation. However, serious questions remain as to whether Huang violated his duties and U.S. national security interests during his tenure. Nvidia’s future is critical to America’s technological leadership and winning the high-stakes AI race against China. The board must complete a thorough investigation as the first step towards rebuilding trust with investors, Washington, and the American public.

In the letter, Moolenaar writes:

"I write to you with grave concerns about the investigation NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has announced following the revelation that NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang carried out an improper relationship with alleged People’s Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset Alice Huang, while NVIDIA conducted billions of dollars of business with her company, which itself is reportedly involved in subverting U.S. national security laws. While I commend the board for opening an independent investigation into the matter I am troubled that the board’s announcement appears to pre-conclude the investigation’s outcome. The Board asserts that it “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” before any investigation has begun.

I fully support NVIDIA’s critical role in the American AI industry, and hope to see it thrive. But to restore shareholder and public trust, the company must conduct a truly open-minded, thorough investigation. The November 10th shareholder lawsuit against your company for allegedly misleading investors about Mr. Huang’s relationship with Ms. Huang is a powerful sign that the incident raises numerous questions concerning Mr. Huang’s commitment to his fiduciary duties as NVIDIA’s chief executive.

A thorough investigation is absolutely essential because, if media reports are correct, Mr. Huang may have violated multiple compliance requirements, including NVIDIA’s own Code of Conduct (Code)."

title: Cabinet Heads Must Take Responsibility for Their Own Mismanagement of Funds
text:
***NEW RESOURCE*** The Ground Stop: A Crisis of Mismanagement

Cash Grab, the Trump Administration Only Has Itself to Blame as $9 Billion Remains Unspent

WASHINGTON – House Appropriations Committee Ranking Member Rosa DeLauro (D-CT-03) and Transportation, Housing and Urban Development Subcommittee Ranking Member James E. Clyburn (D-SC-06) released funding facts questioning the mismanagement of resources at the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) under Secretary Duffy’s tenure.

“First and foremost, I am proud of the dedication and professionalism of our nation’s air traffic controllers and every worker involved in keeping the country’s airspace and travelers safe. They have been failed by the Secretary of Transportation,” DeLauro said. “Americans and their families across the entire country watched with confusion, frustration, and fear on Friday as the Trump administration halted thousands of flights carrying passengers, critical medication and supplies, and our nation’s goods. The cause of this nationwide crisis remains largely unexplained after the performance we witnessed from Secretary Duffy and Secretary Mullin. Instead of laying out the facts, Secretary Duffy commanded the public’s attention to demand a $50 billion ransom without a real plan to deliver. Secretary Duffy and the Federal Aviation Administration have received historical and monumental investments over the last two years, over $12.5 billion of which was provided without meaningful guardrails or accountability requirements and largely remains unspent. No federal leader should be free to do their work without Congressional oversight. Congress has shown its willingness to modernize the FAA’s systems and support its workforce as part of annual bipartisan legislation, but we need a competent partner at the Department of Transportation to carry this out in a sustainable, transparent manner. Right now, it is clear that we lack such a partner.”

“Modernizing the FAA’s air traffic system is critical, that is not debatable. However, this Administration seems to be forging ahead with broad deployments, without the confidence of Congress, the FAA workforce, or the flying public,” Clyburn said. “Congress, and this Committee, have demonstrated their willingness to be bipartisan partners to provide the resources the FAA needs to maintain and advance aviation safety. As the lead Democrat on the Transportation and Housing Subcommittee, I support adequate investments in technologies and systems that increase safety and efficiency in the National Airspace System, but it cannot and must not be at the expense of public transparency and accountability. Recent events are not the result of a lack of funding or support from this Congress. They result from leadership decisions that continue to put politics and private interests above the public's interests.If more taxpayer dollars are desired, the Secretary must submit his justifications to this Committee and the nation's taxpayers.”

The timeline shows the monumental financial resources that Congress has provided to support the FAA over the last two years and contrasts those Congressional investments with the questionable, unclear progress Secretary Duffy has made in using those funds, $9.1 billion of which remains unspent.

In addition to low reimbursement rates, the Members highlight that SNAP eligibility, as well as certain other programs, allows low-income students to be certified for free and/or reduced-price school meals without their families needing to complete burdensome school meal applications. However, because of Republicans’ ‘Big, Ugly Bill,’ millions of eligible families have been kicked off SNAP, and their children have lost access to free school meals.

title: Higgins Announces Hearing on the ATF’s Out-of-Business Records Retention Practices

committee.name: House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform

text:
WASHINGTON—Subcommittee on Federal Law Enforcement Chairman Clay Higgins (R-La.) today announced a hearing titled “Oversight of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives’ Out-of-Business Records Retention Practices.” During the hearing, members will examine the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives’ (ATF) out-of-business records system and assess whether this system operates as a de-facto national firearms registry. Members will also weigh the value of gun tracing against the right guaranteed by the Second Amendment and the implications of retaining out-of-business records in light of recent ATF rulemaking.

“Federal law requires licensed federal firearms dealers to turn over their sales records to the ATF when they go out of business. While federal law prohibits the ATF from abusing these records to create a national firearms registry, the agency’s historical actions raise serious questions about whether that prohibition is being respected. The Subcommittee is concerned that the ATF’s recent proposed rulemaking of retaining out-of-business records for multiple decades too closely resembles a lifetime gun registry, potentially creating conflict with the Second Amendment. The federal government has no business maintaining a backdoor registry of law-abiding American citizen gun owners. I look forward to hearing from witnesses on where the line can be drawn between respecting the rights of firearms owners and ensuring the ATF can effectively do its job,” said Subcommittee Chairman Higgins.

title: Moolenaar Speaks at Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation on the Upcoming APEC Meeting, Manufacturing, and the Future of the Select Committee

text:
Chairman John Moolenaar of the Select Committee on China participated in a fireside chat with Dr. Adrian Zenz at the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation in Washington, D.C. on November 10. Moolenaar discussed the future of the Select Committee, President Donald Trump's upcoming trip to APEC, Chinese espionage, securing critical minerals supply chains to break China's chokehold on the global industry, and more.

On the future of the Select Committee:

"It truly is an honor to chair the Select Committee. A select committee has to be reauthorized each Congress, and ultimately the leadership of the majority party makes the decision on what's going to be in the rules package to be voted on.

"I feel very fortunate that when I first started on the committee, Kevin McCarthy was the Speaker and Hakeem Jeffries was the Minority Leader, and both had strong support. That has continued under Speaker Johnson and Leader Jeffries.

"... The issues are not going away. In fact, just this last week's events with NVIDIA and some of the other stories around that illustrate the significance of this competition and how high the stakes are.

"...My belief is that the committee's success has been primarily because it's bipartisan, and we want to continue that, because, as you know, there's not a lot in Washington, D.C., right now that's bipartisan. Starting in January, you're going to see a lot of investigations, you're going to see a lot of attacks. And boy, we've got to keep our eye on the ball. This relationship with China, to me, is foundational for the future of our country."

On advice he would give President Trump leading up to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting next week in Shenzhen:

"I would advise him that he doesn't need a "deal" -- I think it's good that he is fostering a relationship, and I would say there are real limits to ... dialogue - the CCP would just love dialogue dialogue dialogue and just keep doing their thing. I would encourage him to keep building relationships with likeminded allies and partners."

On economic entanglements and China's attack on U.S. manufacturing:

“But whereas China would focus on that solely, the iceberg under the surface is that they are desperately trying to advance their military capabilities and commercial [capabilities]. They're trying to drive manufacturing businesses in the United States out of business, and they have a very different view of human dignity, and communism simply brings that about.”

On protecting U.S. supply chains:

"China had a very serious, deliberate approach that said, let's dominate mining, processing, and refining, and they figured out ways to develop their capacities in other countries through the Belt and Road. And we saw how they were willing to leverage that when we stepped outside of what they thought was good policy. Suddenly they were threatening and leveraging things that we rely on commercially as well as militarily.”

title: Murray, Shaheen, Baldwin Call for Inspector General Investigation into How Trump and RFK Jr. Worsened the Cyclospora Outbreak
text:
Murray, Shaheen, Baldwin Call for Inspector General Investigation into How Trump and RFK Jr. Worsened the Cyclospora Outbreak

Washington, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senators Patty Murray (D-WA), Vice Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee; Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Ranking Member of the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies; and Tammy Baldwin (D-WI), Ranking Member of the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education, sent a letter to Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Inspector General Thomas March Bell, asking him to open an investigation into how the Trump administration’s personnel and policy changes at the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) contributed to this summer’s extensive Cyclosporiasis (Cyclospora) outbreak.

“We write to request that you open an investigation into how personnel and policy changes at the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) contributed to this summer’s Cyclosporiasis (Cyclospora) outbreak, which was an unusually large, multistate outbreak that resulted in more than twelve thousand confirmed cases and two deaths,” the lawmakers wrote. “It is clear that the FDA and CDC failed to adequately prevent and respond to this outbreak, and we believe that is, in no small part, due to this Administration’s illegal staffing cuts over the last 18 months. Additionally, we are concerned that political interference resulted in delayed recalls and inspections of facilities linked to this outbreak.”

Noting that the Trump administration pushed out over 4,600 FDA staff since taking over, the lawmakers state that: “The FDA failed to quickly inspect the suspected source of the outbreak. It took the FDA over a month to access the Taylor Farms facility and farms that have now been linked to this Cyclospora outbreak. It is also important to note that the facility’s most recent inspection took place in 2019, meaning that the FDA has not had eyes on the conditions of this facility for at least seven years.”

The lawmakers also addressed the failure to respond to the outbreak from the CDC: “It is clear it was not just the FDA that failed to quickly and effectively respond under this administration. Similar personnel, funding, and policy decisions at CDC call into question how the agency responded to this outbreak—and its ability to effectively address others. The Trump administration has pushed out approximately 3,000 CDC staff members since January 2025, greatly diminishing the agency’s ability to respond to public health emergencies. Due to attrition and probationary staff firings, the CDC lab that responds to outbreaks of cyclospora was downsized from eleven people to just three last year.”

They also write that the Trump administration’s decision to remove mandatory reporting of cyclospora by the Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network (FoodNet) and its failure to fully staff and operate the White House Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response (OPPR) have contributed to the administration’s failure to respond to the outbreak.

The full letter is available HERE and below:

Dear Inspector General Bell,

We write to request that you open an investigation into how personnel and policy changes at the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) contributed to this summer’s Cyclosporiasis (Cyclospora) outbreak, which was an unusually large, multistate outbreak that resulted in more than twelve thousand confirmed cases and two deaths. It is clear that the FDA and CDC failed to adequately prevent and respond to this outbreak, and we believe that is, in no small part, due to this Administration’s illegal staffing cuts over the last 18 months. Additionally, we are concerned that political interference resulted in delayed recalls and inspections of facilities linked to this outbreak.

According to data from the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), the Trump administration has pushed out over 4,600 FDA staff since January 2025. Through a series of mass reductions in force (RIFs), the Trump administration has fired key staff working in policy, human resources, IT, procurement, and communications, as well as staff who worked to write guidance documents, regulations, and issue press releases about the FDA’s activities such as recalls. These policy and communications staff are not dispensable; they play a key role in ensuring the American people have information about disease outbreaks that could jeopardize their health. Having staff working to disseminate this information is especially important during recalls, like during the cyclospora outbreak, in order to quickly share information to keep people safe. The absence of clear, consistent communication from the FDA was evident during this outbreak, led to unnecessary confusion, delayed responses, and likely led to more people getting sick. Furthermore, Secretary Kennedy’s comments that the cyclospora outbreak was “under control” only led to more confusion for the public as the FDA continued to expand the outbreak to more and more states.

Last year, the Trump administration pushed out support staff who worked directly with inspectors to ensure they can seamlessly visit FDA-regulated facilities. This has left inspectors responsible for coordinating their own travel, scheduling their inspections, communicating with FDA-regulated facilities, and filling out paperwork for which they used to have additional support—all of which simply meant that they were able to conduct fewer inspections and keep our food supply safe. The FDA reports that outside of the years of COVID-19, 2025’s inspection count was the lowest since 2011, and based on available data, inspections for 2026 will be at a similarly low rate. The FDA has struggled to retain inspectors for many years, and instead of working to hire and retain more and ensure they have the support they need to effectively do their jobs, the Trump administration destroyed their support base. The U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) made three recommendations about ways to improve retention of inspectors to better protect the U.S. food supply in January of 2025, and as of June 2026, the FDA had concurred with the recommendations but has failed to respond to several of the key recommendations, including defining the appropriate size and workload for its foreign investigators to meet the FDA's foreign inspection needs to protect the American food supply and developing performance management processes to improve inspection goals.

The FDA failed to quickly inspect the suspected source of the outbreak. It took the FDA over a month to access the Taylor Farms facility and farms that have now been linked to this Cyclospora outbreak. It is also important to note that the facility’s most recent inspection took place in 2019, meaning that the FDA has not had eyes on the conditions of this facility for at least seven years. It is also troubling that Taylor Farms appears to have interfered in the FDA and CDC’s ongoing investigation of this cyclospora outbreak, including by potentially delaying access to their facility directly linked to this outbreak in Mexico. Of similar concern is the fact that Taylor Farms reportedly met with the White House and made contributions to Republican Political Action Committees in order to change the course of the investigation. We request an investigation into whether political interference from Taylor Farms put the American people at further risk by delaying the time it took to remove their products from the market, thus increasing the number of cyclospora cases this summer.

It is clear it was not just the FDA that failed to quickly and effectively respond under this administration. Similar personnel, funding, and policy decisions at CDC call into question how the agency responded to this outbreak—and its ability to effectively address others. The Trump administration has pushed out approximately 3,000 CDC staff members since January 2025, greatly diminishing the agency’s ability to respond to public health emergencies. Due to attrition and probationary staff firings, the CDC lab that responds to outbreaks of cyclospora was downsized from eleven people to just three last year. CDC staff are already stretched thin responding to other outbreaks, including a rapidly worsening Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Further impacting CDC’s ability to respond to the cyclospora outbreak is the loss of $40 million in funding from the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) after the Trump administration illegally dismantled it in 2025. While CDC hopes to recover some of that funding, it will only be a fraction of what it used to receive from USAID. The reduction in funding has resulted in the loss of staff who would often be called upon to assist in an emergency response situation. Fewer staff and experts make it impossible to respond quickly to an outbreak, where timely response is vital.

The Trump administration’s decision to remove mandatory reporting of cyclospora by the Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network, (FoodNet) is also confounding—and has put our food supply at risk. While FoodNet is not used to track outbreaks in real time, the removal of cyclospora mandatory reporting risks negatively affected the ability for the program to understand this outbreak and provide an analysis on trends of cyclospora outbreaks over time, which in turn could help reduce the risk of future wide-spread outbreaks.

Lastly, the Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response (OPPR) was created by Congress to coordinate the federal government’s response to public health crises like this outbreak. This administration has utterly failed to ensure it is fully staffed and operational to protect Americans from disease outbreaks and ensure coordination across government. For over a year, OPPR did not so much as have a director or even any staff. It has been widely reported that the administration appointed Dr. Sara Brenner, a former FDA official, to lead OPPR in July of this year. But it’s not clear how long she will remain in the position, or if a single additional person is serving on staff.

For all these reasons, we request that you open an investigation that evaluates the following questions:

Have RIFs of support staff for inspectors affected inspectors' ability to meet demand for inspections?

Has the loss of support staff taken inspectors away from the critical parts of their jobs?

Will the FDA meet inspection targets for the Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA) in 2026 and if not, what is needed to meet those targets in future years?

Why hasn't the FDA implemented all of the GAO's recommendations for retaining inspectors?

Are there additional challenges that are affecting the inspectorate at the FDA that are not outlined in the GAO report?

Does HHS OIG have additional recommendations to improve recruitment and retention for inspectors?

How will the July 2028 implementation of the FDA’s Food Traceability Rule impact any corrective actions that should be taken in the wake of future foodborne illness outbreaks?

Should the FDA implement inspection targets for international food facilities like those of domestic facilities to have better oversight of all the food entering the U.S. market?

Why did it take over a month for the FDA to access the Taylor Farms facility in Mexico that has now been linked to this outbreak?

In areas where the U.S. government may have security concerns internationally, what contingencies has the FDA put into place to ensure that the FDA’s inspectors are able to access facilities to ensure the safety of the FDA-regulated products?

If there are not contingencies in place, should the U.S. government consider preventing imports from areas with international security concerns to protect the FDA’s inspectors and the American public until contingencies are created?

Prior to accessing the Taylor Farms facility in Mexico in July, why hadn’t the facility been inspection since 2019?

Did meetings or communications with the White House or donations to Trump-associated Political Action Committees delay the FDA's response to this outbreak and identifying Taylor Farms as the culprit?

We appreciate your work on this important inquiry.

###

title: Murray, Warren, Larsen, to FTA and OMB: Again, Stop Holding Infrastructure Dollars Hostage
text:
Murray, Warren, Larsen, to FTA and OMB: Again, Stop Holding Infrastructure Dollars Hostage

Washington, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator Patty Murray (D-WA), Vice Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-WA), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs, and Representative Rick Larsen (D-WA), Ranking Member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, wrote to Federal Transit Administration (FTA) Acting Deputy Administrator Matthew Cahill and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Administrator Russell Vought following up with their concerns that the Trump administration continues to delay the advancement of public transportation projects funded by the Capital Investment Grants (CIG) program, as they continue to hold up significant projects instead of spending its infrastructure dollars. The members also submitted comments opposing FTA’s proposal that will kick projects out of the CIG pipeline and withhold funding from worthy projects.

“You have failed to respond to an initial letter on August 11th concerning the growing backlog of projects currently in the CIG pipeline that are in limbo due to FTA and OMB inaction,” the members wrote. “Your failure to respond to earlier correspondence and offer explanation for the irresponsible delays could signal that FTA and OMB are intentionally delaying approvals for the advancement of targeted CIG projects.”

“We remain very frustrated by reports that OMB is partially responsible for these avoidable and costly delays. At present, there has been only one CIG grant agreement signed since this Administration took office…” the members continued.

“These delays are inexcusable. As noted in our prior correspondence, project sponsors and taxpayers will end up footing the bill for delay-induced cost increases,” the members continued. “The construction workforce and the broader transportation supply chain are left waiting for critical job-creating investments.”

“…[W]e believe that if FTA’s proposed guidance were implemented, more than half of the projects currently in the CIG project pipeline could either become ineligible and be kicked out of the program or could face termination because of reduced FTA funding,” the members wrote about the proposed new guidance.

The members concluded by demanding FTA stop stonewalling the qualified CIG projects and drop their proposed rewrite of the CIG rules.

Full text of the letter is available HERE and below.

Dear Director Vought and Acting Deputy Administrator Cahill,

We write again to express deep concern that the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) are continuing to delay the advancement of public transportation projects within the Capital Investment Grants (CIG) pipeline, and your agencies are now failing to sign grant agreements for finalized projects. We also write to express equally deep concerns that FTA’s proposed changes to the CIG Policy Guidance (DOT docket number FTA-2026-0331), if adopted, will result in many projects currently in the CIG program becoming ineligible for FTA assistance and could disincentivize or stop future projects from ever applying to enter the CIG program. These unacceptable delays and the threat to projects from FTA’s policy proposal could waste the state and local taxpayer funds that have already been spent to develop and design transit projects and deny communities better transportation options.

Further Project Delays in the CIG Program and Reduced CIG Funding

You have failed to respond to an initial letter on August 11th concerning the growing backlog of projects currently in the CIG pipeline that are in limbo due to FTA and OMB inaction. As Ranking Members of the Senate Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs, House Transportation and Infrastructure, and Senate Appropriations Committees, we have an obligation to ensure that the CIG program is carried out in accordance with statutory requirements. Your failure to respond to earlier correspondence and offer explanation for the irresponsible delays could signal that FTA and OMB are intentionally delaying approvals for the advancement of targeted CIG projects. As noted previously, we have watched for months as FTA and OMB have stonewalled the progress of worthy transit projects. Your agencies have neglected for a year to advance the Boston Green Line Transformation project and the Los Angeles Southeast Gateway Line to the CIG Engineering phase under current program rules that were adopted in November of 2025—without any justification or explanation for the delay.

In August, the Salt Lake City region’s Frontrunner 2X project was moved into the Engineering phase, and last month the Broward Commuter Rail South project in Florida was advanced to Engineering too. The Florida project and the projects in Massachusetts and California have each received a cumulative rating of “Medium-High,” and the Utah project received a qualifying lower rating of “Medium”— all sufficient ratings to move forward.

The projects in Massachusetts, California, Utah, and Florida requested to enter the Engineering phase in 2025 under current program rules, but FTA did not determine the Florida project submitted complete information for the request until late March of this year. FTA and OMB have left two well-rated projects in limbo but inexplicably moved two other projects forward.

FTA and OMB should advance all projects that meet statutory criteria, and your agencies should not impose any further delays. Under the most recently enacted appropriations law and prior appropriations laws since fiscal year 2020, FTA, OMB and the Administration are prohibited from using any federal funds to “impede or hinder project advancement or approval for any project seeking a Federal contribution from the capital investment grants program of greater than 40 percent of project costs,” which includes the delayed projects.

In addition, while the projects in Florida and Utah have been allowed to move forward in the pipeline, we are very concerned that FTA has significantly reduced the amount of CIG funding that FTA pledges to contribute to these projects to levels far below the amounts requested by the project sponsors. While the Utah project was reduced to a 40 percent CIG share, which would comply with current law, FTA reduced the Broward Commuter Rail South project CIG funding to a 23 percent CIG share, cutting nearly $188 million from the sponsor’s request, creating an additional obstacle to initiating construction, and flouting Congressional intent by approving a CIG share lower than 40 percent.

FTA and OMB Failure to Execute Grant Agreements

We remain very frustrated by reports that OMB is partially responsible for these avoidable and costly delays. At present, there has been only one CIG grant agreement signed since this Administration took office, and FTA and OMB are failing to execute grant agreements for at least two projects that have been fully funded by Congress and have met all FTA requirements to receive their CIG grant. Both the Veirs Mill Road Flash Bus Rapid Transit Project in Montgomery County, Maryland and the NorthSouth Bus Rapid Transit Project in Chapel Hill, North Carolina are ready to receive their grant agreements, but FTA and OMB have failed to act.

These delays are inexcusable. As noted in our prior correspondence, project sponsors and taxpayers will end up footing the bill for delay-induced cost increases. The construction workforce and the broader transportation supply chain are left waiting for critical job-creating investments.

A total of 30 CIG projects across the nation hope to receive grant agreements in late 2026 or in 2027, and FTA and OMB’s failure to advance projects and execute grant agreements in a timely manner threatens each of these projects. FTA has executed just one $149.9 million grant agreement under the Trump Administration. However, there are ample funds available to advance these projects.

Congress has appropriated funds to FTA to execute CIG grant agreements, not OMB, but OMB has inappropriately restricted the availability of CIG funds. As highlighted in reporting on project delays under the Trump Administration, OMB has “designated more than $5.2 billion for next fiscal year— effectively putting it out of reach should the F.T.A. want to use it to sign a grant today.”

Specifically, in fiscal years 2025, 2026, and 2027, OMB apportioned CIG funding in Category B (to Lines 6011 through 6110, available for obligation in the current fiscal year) and took an unusual step to apportion the vast majority of funds in Category C (to Lines 6170 through 6173, available for obligation in future fiscal years),thereby locking up and pushing CIG funding availability into future fiscal years. Category C was not used in this same manner by OMB for CIG in fiscal years 2022, 2023, and 2024, when all CIG funding was apportioned by OMB for use by FTA in the current fiscal year.

OMB should immediately make funds available for FTA to sign grants agreements for all projects that are ready.

FTA’s Proposal to Make CIG Projects Ineligible and Improperly Limit Funding Assistance

FTA published proposed Policy Guidance for the CIG program on October 1 and requested public comment on the proposal, as required prior to the agency implementing new guidance. For the reasons detailed in the attached appendix, we believe that if FTA’s proposed guidance were implemented, more than half of the projects currently in the CIG project pipeline could either become ineligible and be kicked out of the program or could face termination because of reduced FTA funding. Looking to the future, FTA’s proposed changes to project evaluation and new limits on CIG funding would likely bar many communities from ever applying to the CIG program.

We believe the proposed Policy Guidance is so deeply flawed and fundamentally unsound that FTA should withdraw its proposal and continue to utilize the program’s current guidance. This letter and the appendix is being submitted to DOT docket number FTA-2026-0331 to detail the most concerning flaws in FTA’s proposed guidance. If FTA does not withdraw its proposal, the agency should address each of the concerns below and address additional concerns that stakeholders identify in their comments to the docket.

Staff for the Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs, House Transportation and Infrastructure, and Senate Appropriations Committees have spoken to the sponsors of more than half of the 47 projects currently in the CIG pipeline, and each of those sponsors expressed significant concerns with FTA’s proposed guidance. The project sponsors raised concerns that their projects’ cumulative rating could be reduced to below a “Medium” under the proposed guidance, resulting in their projects becoming ineligible for CIG funding, or stated concerns that FTA’s proposed reductions in CIG funding share threaten their ability to move to construction, possibly resulting in project termination. FTA is changing program rules after sponsors have spent considerable amounts of state and local taxpayer funds to design projects and prepare federal applications. FTA’s proposal would offer no relief to projects that have followed all current rules.

We also note that FTA has refused to provide Congress with the agency’s analysis of the effect of the proposed Policy Guidance on projects currently in the CIG pipeline. We are concerned that FTA is refusing to provide the analysis because that document would further confirm the harm that would result to project sponsors if the proposed Policy Guidance were to go into effect.

Because of the large number of disruptive and unsound elements of the proposed Policy Guidance, we must consider if FTA’s intent is to undermine the CIG program and discourage future applicants. Should FTA move forward to implement any of the proposals we identify below, we will use all legislative and oversight tools to undo damage to the CIG program and preserve efforts to develop and construct long-overdue public transportation projects.

Conclusion and Requests to FTA and OMB

Transportation policy is historically bipartisan, and we remain proud of this reputation. We have hoped that President Trump’s Administration would work in good faith to help build long-overdue infrastructure projects. However, FTA and OMB’s continued mismanagement of the CIG project pipeline and the disruptive and reckless policies proposed by FTA for the CIG Policy Guidance threaten to do serious harm to the bipartisan coalition that supports federal infrastructure investment.

We request that you immediately advance the two stalled projects in California and Massachusetts into Engineering and sign CIG grant agreements for all projects that are ready, including the projects in North Carolina and Maryland. Further, we ask that FTA withdraw the proposed CIG Policy Guidance and ensure that any final CIG guidance remedy the concerns raised in this letter. In addition, we ask that you immediately provide the Committees with FTA’s analysis of the effects of the proposed Policy Guidance on projects currently in the CIG pipeline and preserve all documents and records related to this request. Please respond in writing to this correspondence not later than December 1, 2026.

Sincerely,

###

title: Cantwell Tells Lutnick: You Failed to Protect National Security & America’s Tech Edge

committee.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation

text:
“America cannot maintain its leadership in AI if the agency responsible for protecting that advantage fails to enforce its own controls.”

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation, sent a letter to Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick demanding that he use the Department’s authority to protect U.S. national security and American technological leadership by stopping the flow of advanced AI chips to companies with ties to the People’s Republic of China (PRC). The letter comes as Secretary Lutnick prepares to travel to the PRC with the President later this week for the APEC summit.

“The Department of Commerce is charged with export controls to protect America’s technological edge and to keep sensitive technology out of the hands of our adversaries,” wrote Sen. Cantwell. “Despite clear authority from Congress, the Department of Commerce has allowed advanced AI chips to flow through companies with ties to the People’s Republic of China (PRC).”

“The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology,” continued Sen. Cantwell. “These failures to carry out the law help give away America’s technology advantage in AI.”

Under the Export Control Reform Act of 2018, the Commerce Department clearly has the authority and the responsibility to protect sensitive American technology and to defend the nation’s national security by restricting access to such technology. Sen. Cantwell explains how since Secretary Lutnick has been at the helm, the Department has failed to enforce these authorities and protect U.S. national security.

Specifically, the Department of Commerce:

Gave the PRC access to America’s most advanced AI computing power, undermining our technological edge. Chinese companies are using overseas companies to train advanced AI models using advanced American chips. The Department of Commerce has refused to close a well-known loophole in the U.S. export controls that China has exploited

Resisted efforts by the Departments of Treasury, State and Defense to keep sensitive American technology away from high-risk PRC-linked companies. Despite multiple warnings over many months from these agencies to restrict Megaspeed, the Department failed to act, putting America’s lead in AI at risk.

Suspended an investigation into the suspected diversion of America’s most advanced AI chips to the PRC, risking further transfers of sensitive technology. Reports indicate that, after outreach by Nvidia’s general counsel, the Department suspended its investigation of Megaspeed, enabling Megaspeed to continue to acquire advanced AI chips.

Promulgated a loophole that weakened previous standards designed to keep America’s most sensitive technology out of the hands of blacklisted PRC companies. The Department has twice suspended a Bureau of Industry and Security rule that extended export restrictions to subsidiaries majority-owned by restricted companies. As a result of this suspension, Commerce reopened a loophole that allows restricted companies to seek sensitive American technology through these subsidiaries.

In addition, financial conflicts raise serious questions about whether the Department of Commerce is putting business interests ahead of national security. Reports indicate thatCantor Fitzgerald, controlled by Secretary Lutnick’s sons, held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. The Administration has also imposed an unprecedented 25 percent fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to the PRC, creating a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology.

“America cannot maintain its leadership in AI if the agency responsible for protecting that advantage fails to enforce its own controls,” concluded Sen. Cantwell. “The Administration must account for its failure to enforce these protections and take immediate action to prevent America’s most sensitive technology from strengthening our adversaries.”

The text of the letter to Secretary Lutnick can be found below and HERE.

November 15, 2026

Dear Secretary Lutnick:

The Department of Commerce is charged with export controls to protect America’s technological edge and to keep sensitive technology out of the hands of our adversaries. Despite clear authority from Congress, the Department of Commerce has allowed advanced AI chips to flow through companies with ties to the People’s Republic of China (PRC). The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology. These failures to carry out the law help give away America’s technology advantage in AI.

The Export Control Reform Act of 2018 empowers the Department of Commerce with broad authority and responsibility to protect sensitive American technology, investigate violations, and restrict companies that threaten national security. Your failure to use these authorities has undermined America’s national security.

First, the Department of Commerce is giving the PRC access to America’s most advanced AI computing power, undermining our technological edge. The Financial Times reported that Alibaba and ByteDance used overseas data centers equipped with advanced Nvidia chips to train advanced AI models. These companies are exploiting a loophole in U.S. export controls by using advanced American chips in foreign data centers even when those chips are restricted from the PRC. Despite warnings from the Bureau of Industry and Security that certain arrangements may violate existing restrictions, the Department of Commerce failed to close this loophole, allowing PRC companies to advance their AI capabilities using sensitive American technology.

Second, the Department of Commerce has resisted efforts by the Departments of Treasury, State, and Defense to keep sensitive American technology away from high-risk companies. White House and intelligence officials reportedly urged the Department of Commerce to restrict Megaspeed beginning in fall 2025. You received a classified warning in May 2026, yet the Department of Commerce did not act. Treasury Secretary Bessent has now publicly confirmed that the Departments of Treasury, Defense, State, and the U.S. Trade Representative supported restricting Megaspeed for months. Despite these warnings, the Department of Commerce delayed action on repeated national security warnings, putting America’s technological advantage in AI at risk.

Third, the Department of Commerce suspended an investigation into the suspected diversion of America’s most advanced AI chips to the PRC, risking further transfers of sensitive technology. Department of Commerce investigators were examining Megaspeed when Nvidia’s general counsel reportedly contacted them in August 2025, apparently with permission from Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler. The Department of Commerce subsequently suspended its administrative investigation when the Department of Justice requested that the matter be transferred for criminal investigation. By suspending its investigation without restricting Megaspeed, the Department of Commerce left the company free to continue obtaining advanced American AI chips despite serious national security concerns.

Fourth, the Department of Commerce promulgated a loophole that weakened previous standards designed to keep America’s most sensitive technology out of the hands of blacklisted PRC companies. In September 2025, the Bureau of Industry and Security established a rule extending certain export restrictions to subsidiaries majority-owned by restricted companies. The Department of Commerce suspended the rule in November 2025 and extended that suspension through January 10, 2027. The result is a continuing loophole that allows restricted companies to seek American technology through subsidiaries.

Finally, financial conflicts raise serious questions about whether the Department of Commerce is putting business interests ahead of national security. Cantor Fitzgerald, now controlled by your sons, reportedly held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of your nomination. The Administration has also imposed an unprecedented 25 percent fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to the PRC, creating a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology. America’s national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge.

America cannot maintain its leadership in AI if the agency responsible for protecting that advantage fails to enforce its own controls. The Administration must account for its failure to enforce these protectionsand take immediate action to prevent America’s most sensitive technology from strengthening our adversaries.

Sincerely,
