title: Heinrich Op-Ed: A Plan to End America’s Most Expensive Bottleneck

committee.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources

text:
WASHINGTON – In an op-ed published by The Economist, U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, highlighted the need for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), explaining how the legislation will speed up the federal approval process for energy projects to get more power onto the grid, lowering electricity bills for Americans and creating more jobs – while codifying into law Tribal consultation, maintaining key environmental protections, and holding data centers accountable for their costs.

“In June, the largest clean-energy-infrastructure project in the western hemisphere came online in New Mexico. “The[SunZia] project took 17 years to permit and build—and SunZia isn’t alone. Across America, energy-infrastructure projects take far too long to permit… Indeed, permitting might be the economy’s most expensive bottleneck,” began Heinrich.

“America’s ability to meet the energy demands of the 21st century depends on its ability to build a modern, clean energy economy… That process is now standing in the way of getting new clean energy online and unlocking important economic investment,” continued Heinrich. “The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act—which the Senate voted to advance on November 9th and which I co-sponsor with another Democrat and two Republicans—does not remove environmental considerations, the ability to litigate projects or the ability for local communities to comment… But it does make these reviews a standardized part of a predictable process.”

“Modelling by Resources For the Future suggests that BAAJA could cause a decline in cumulative CO2 of about 1.8 gigatons—more than if the entire light-duty vehicle fleet was taken off America’s roads for a year—between now and 2041. Similarly, the Solar Energy Industries Association, a trade body, estimates that BAAJA’s adoption would mean solar and wind would provide 37.4% of America’s electricity generation in 2035, against 19.6% if the current permitting regime remains in place. These forecasts starkly illustrate the heavy drag America’s permitting regime places on the economy. For the nation’s future prosperity and security, it must be reformed,” concluded Heinrich.

Heinrich’s full op-ed is here and below:

A plan to end America’s most expensive bottleneck

By: U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee

In June, the largest clean-energy-infrastructure project in the western hemisphere came online in New Mexico. TheSunZia Wind and Transmission Project’s 916 wind turbines now power over 1m homes. It’s a momentous accomplishment I was proud to help deliver, but it’s one that should have come a dozen years sooner. The project took 17 years to permit and build—and SunZia isn’t alone. Across America, energy-infrastructure projects take far too long to permit. The approval process can stretch on a decade or more, before a single digger has moved in. Indeed, permitting might be the economy’s most expensive bottleneck.

America’s ability to meet the energy demands of the 21st century depends on its ability to build a modern, clean energy economy. Its permitting regime tells companies what they can build and how: projects like transmission lines, pipelines, energy-generation facilities, manufacturing plants and transport infrastructure require multiple approvals from multiple federal agencies across several environmental and permitting statutes. That process is now standing in theway of getting new clean energy online and unlocking important economic investment. McKinsey estimates that more than $3trn in American economic activity is tied to infrastructure projects awaiting federal permits.

At the same time, America’s electricity needs are expected to grow dramatically over the next decade, threatening grid reliability, energy affordability and economic competitiveness. I see the effects of this growing strain on my constituents every day.

Fortunately, there is a plan for tackling these problems head-on, and it goes by the acronym BAAJA. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act—which the Senate voted to advance on November 9th and which I co-sponsor with another Democrat and two Republicans—does not remove environmental considerations, the ability to litigate projects or the ability for local communities to comment. Those are necessary. But it does make these reviews a standardized part of a predictable process.

First, BAAJA creates standardized timelines for these processes, from authorization decisions to public comment periods to litigation windows. BAAJA takes reviews that drag on and on—because there is no legally mandated timeline—and creates a predictable workflow. Legitimate environmental considerations, legal challenges and community input are protected, but those processes would be efficient. For both project developers and consumers, this means getting electrons on the grid faster, more cheaply and more predictably. A study by Columbia University estimates that BAAJA would save eight years for transmission projects, three years for solar projects, two and a half years for geothermal projects and about two years for offshore and onshore wind projects.

BAAJA also creates new policies that would benefit energy production. It codifies federal transmission planning so that different regions all plan together instead of separately. It bans right-of-refusal rules, which currently give incumbent utilities the first chance to build new regional lines—creating a more competitive marketplace. It opens wholesale markets and requires grid operators to allow aggregators to energize the grid, which would allow small-scale power sources like solar panels to connect to the grid in times of high usage. And BAAJA would make it financially costly and virtually impossible for an administration to block or undo permits on a whim, so worthwhile renewables projects couldn’t be shut down by a president overnight simply because he is skeptical of clean energy.

BAAJA is also the first federal legislation to meaningfully hold data centers accountable for their costs. The bill requires them to pay the costs of connecting to the grid, a burden American citizens are currently shouldering. By requiring electric utilities to charge data centers for transmission services, we can drive down transmission charges to other customers. Grid Strategies, an energy consultancy, estimates that $55bn in transmission costs could be collected from data centers over ten years under BAAJA.

Now, this is a bipartisan bill that demanded compromise. While there are strict timelines under BAAJA, deadlines should not be mistaken for lack of review. The requirement that infrastructure projects consider the environments and communities they affect remains. Environmental Impact Statements—detailed documents on a project’s potential environmental consequences— are given two years with BAAJA, still substantial time for consideration. The bill mandates consultation with Native American tribes and other communities that may worry about the impact of cutting “red tape” for a clean-energy transition; the current administration, by contrast, has threatened to eliminate those requirements.

And although it is true that BAAJA will make it easier to permit any kind of project, clean or not, the reality is that a huge share of the energy waiting to connect to the grid is renewable energy and storage. Modelling by Resources For theFuture suggests that BAAJA could cause a decline in cumulative CO2 of about 1.8 gigatons—more than if the entire light-duty vehicle fleet was taken off America’s roads for a year—between now and 2041. Similarly, the Solar Energy Industries Association, a trade body, estimates that BAAJA’s adoption would mean solar and wind would provide 37.4% of America’s electricity generation in 2035, against 19.6% if the current permitting regime remains in place.

These forecasts starkly illustrate the heavy drag America’s permitting regime places on the economy. For the nation’s future prosperity and security, it must be reformed.

title: Heinrich Statement on Interior’s Plans to Sell Public Lands

committee.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources

text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, released the following statement in response to the Department of the Interior’s (DOI) new plan to sell off public lands:

“The Interior Department says it’s going to sell off lands that aren’t of ‘national interest.’ But anyone who lives in the West knows that some of our most beloved public lands don’t meet that definition. They’re the places where our kids have their favorite picnic spot, where we go fishing on the weekends, or where we hike with our dogs.

“There is nothing in our public lands laws that says a place needs to be of ‘national interest’ to remain in public hands. These lands belong to the American people — not private interests or corporations looking to cash in.

“I’ve fought before to stop efforts to sell off millions of acres of public lands, and I’ll do it again. I will keep fighting to protect all of our public lands — from Yosemite to the Organ Mountains to all the places with no line around them on a map that mean so much to the communities who know and love them.”

Background:

The Federal Land Policy and Management Act (FLPMA) authorizes the sale of BLM-managed public land only if the land is difficult or uneconomic to manage as public land and can’t be used be another Federal agency; if the land was acquired for a specific purpose and is no longer needed for that or any other Federal purpose; or if the sale will serve important public objectives that can’t be achieved “prudently or feasibly” on other land, and which outweigh other public objectives like recreation or scenic values. There is no authority to sell land based on whether they are “nationally significant.”

In addition, the proceeds from the sale of BLM land cannot be transferred back to the purchasing entities, as proposed in DOI’s strategic plan. The Federal Land Transaction Facilitation Act requires proceeds from BLM land sales to be used to acquire new public land for conservation and recreation.

The Department of the Interior does not have the authority to sell land managed by agencies other than the Bureau of Land Management without explicit Congressional direction.

As Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Heinrich is leading the fight in Congress to protect our public lands, expand access to national parks, and hold the Trump administration accountable for its attacks on our treasured places — from efforts to erase history in our national parks to diverting funding to Trump’s vanity projects.

This month, Heinrich demanded answers from Bureau of Land Management Director Steve Pearce about the Trump administration’s push to develop AI data centers on public lands. Heinrich raised concerns about the administration’s consideration of at least 15 proposals spanning more than 17,000 acres across six Western states, emphasizing that public lands must be managed in the best interests of the American people and the communities directly impacted by development. Heinrich called on BLM to provide transparency about the authorities it is using to approve data center development, the projects under consideration, and the public lands identified as eligible for development.

In October, Heinrich successfully pressured Major League Baseball to abandon its proposal to host a professional baseball game in Grand Teton National Park. After Heinrich sent a letter to MLB Commissioner Robert Manfred urging the league to withdraw its proposal, MLB confirmed it would no longer consider Grand Teton as a potential site. Heinrich emphasized that national parks are no place for commercial sporting events and warned that allowing such development would set a dangerous precedent for future uses of public lands.

In September, Heinrich joined a bipartisan group of 153 lawmakers in urging the DOI to abandon a proposed transfer of federally managed public land within Yosemite National Park that would facilitate private access to and development of an 83-acre parcel adjacent to the park known as Hazel Green Ranch. During a U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee hearing, Heinrich criticized the Trump administration for its plan to exchange public land in Yosemite National Park for private development.

In September, Heinrich led his Senate colleagues in sending a letter to DOI Secretary Doug Burgum demanding that the Trump administration stop work on President Trump’s commemorative arch on federal property, which federal officials have admitted will harm historic sites on public lands, including Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial.

In September, Heinrich spoke in support of the Roadless Rule at a New Mexico Wild community event, encouraging New Mexicans to submit public comment in support of preserving the Roadless Rule. The public had until October 6, 2026 to submit comments on the Trump administration’s repeal of the Roadless Rule. You can read more about Heinrich’s actions to protect the Roadless Rule here.

In August, Heinrich led his colleagues in opposing the Bureau of Land Management’s (BLM) proposal to overturn the 2024 Waste Prevention, Production Subject to Royalties, and Resource Conservation rule (the 2024 Waste Prevention Rule). The move will increase pollution on public lands, reduce domestic energy supply, expose nearby communities to avoidable health risks, and waste publicly owned natural gas, costing Americans tens of millions in foregone revenue.

In August, Heinrich joined top Senate Democrats in sending a letter to the Government Accountability Office (GAO) Acting Comptroller General Orice Williams Brown to audit and assess the full scope and cost of the White House ballroom project.

In August, Heinrich sent a letter requesting that the DOI Deputy Inspector General Caryl Brzymialkiewicz investigate what Department officials knew – and when they knew it – about engineering failures at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and whether Department employees withheld evidence from federal prosecutors.

In July, Heinrich criticized legislation that removes protections for public lands, emphasizing the need for bipartisan collaboration within the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee. Heinrich additionally fact-checked Trump administration actions that undo protections for the Chaco Canyon Cultural Protection Zone. You can read about Heinrich’s actions to protect Chaco Canyon here and here.

In July, Heinrich sent a letter to DOI Secretary Doug Burgum and U.S Park Chief of Police Scott Brecht demanding answers and transparency about the U.S. Park Police’s new vehicle pursuit policy following news reports that an innocent bystander, Nolberto Armando Sanabria Meza, a 46-year-old food delivery driver, was hit and tragically killed in D.C. by a driver being chased by U.S. Park Police.

In June, Heinrich helped advance the America the Beautiful Act, bipartisan legislation introduced by U.S. Senators Steve Daines (R-Mont.) and Angus King (I-Maine) to reauthorize the National Parks and Public Land Legacy Restoration Fund, out of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

In June, Heinrich sent a letter demanding answers from DOI Secretary Doug Burgum about the Trump administration redirecting tens of millions of dollars from fees paid to the NPS to fund President Trump’s vanity projects in Washington, D.C. – including redirecting funds collected at New Mexico sites such as Carlsbad Caverns National Park and Bandelier National Monument.

In April, during a U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee hearing to examine the Trump administration’s Budget Request for the DOI Fiscal Year 2027 (FY27), Heinrich grilled DOI Secretary Doug Burgum about the Department’s draconian staff cuts at the NPS.

In March, Heinrich joined lawmakers in filing an amicus brief that would put a stop to President Trump’s plan to construct a commemorative arch on federal property. The amicus brief argues that the President’s plan is illegal unless Congress authorizes it.

In March, Heinrich led his colleagues in delivering remarks on the Senate floor in condemning and drawing attention to the Trump administration’s efforts to erase American history from public lands.

In March, Heinrich sent a letter to DOI demanding answers from the NPS following reports that NPS staff across the country are removing signage from national parks about slavery, Tribal history, and climate change.

In February, Heinrich led his colleagues in calling on DOI Secretary Doug Burgum to halt efforts to create the Department’s new U.S. Wildland Fire Service (USWFS), citing potential life-or-death consequences that could come as a result of decoupling wildfire management from land management agencies, and emphasizing concerns related to recent reductions in staffing, combined with improperly severing wildfire management from land stewardship.

Last December, during a U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Subcommittee on National Parks hearing to consider 26 pending bills, Heinrich criticized the Trump administration for removing fee-free admission on Juneteenth and Martin Luther King, Jr. Day.

Last October, Heinrich delivered remarks on the Senate floor, criticizing Republicans for pushing forward Congressional Review Act (CRA) resolutions of disapproval targeting BLM Resource Management Plans (RMPs) that would undo protections for national parks, including the Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve.

Last October, during the government shutdown, Heinrich urged the DOI Secretary Doug Burgum to classify the Department’s staff as essential during the Republican government shutdown to maintain the health and safety of Americans who visit public lands, wildlife refuges, and national park sites.

In June of 2025, Heinrich successfully fought Senate Republican provisions to sell off public lands in the Big Bad Bill, lead an amendment to prevent the privatization of our public lands, hosted a roundtable and sounded the alarm about New Mexico public lands that were at risk of being sold off by Republicans, continuously uplifted New Mexicans’ voices who called his office to raise their concern with Republicans’ plan to sell off these lands, and released a statement immediately criticizing Senate Republicans’ plan to sell off public lands following the release of the reconciliation text.

In June 2025, Heinrich blasted the Trump administration for its plans to transfer national park units to state control, criticizing the administration for “cutting off our access to public lands and devastating state economies in the process, overwhelming state budgets and dismantling the systems that keep public lands running.”

In June 2025, Heinrich grilled the DOI Secretary Doug Burgum over the Trump administration’s Fiscal Year 2026 (FY26) budget request for the Department, which slashes funding for national parks and guts staffing for the agency.

In May of 2025, Heinrich sent a letter to DOI Secretary Doug Burgum, demanding answers from the Trump administration regarding its plans to transfer National Park System units from federal management. The letter followed Heinrich’s questioning of Secretary Burgum during a Senate Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies Appropriations Subcommittee hearing, where Burgum failed to provide sufficient answers on the Trump administration’s plan to transfer hundreds of sites managed by the NPS to the states.

In January 2025, Heinrich’s Simplifying Outdoor Access for Recreation (SOAR) Act and Every Kid Outdoors Extension Act, which extends free access to national parks and other public lands to all American fourth grade students and their families through 2031, were signed into law as part of the Expanding Public Lands Outdoor Recreation Experiences (EXPLORE) Act. The broader bipartisan package bolsters outdoor recreation and promotes public lands in New Mexico and across the United States.

title: Grassley Leads Colleagues in Seeking Explanation, Urging Reconsideration of Changes to Kratom-Derived Scheduling
text:
WASHINGTON – Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and seven of his Republican colleagues are urging the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to explain and reconsider changes to the emergency scheduling order for semi-synthetic, kratom-derived substances, including deadly 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MP).

Following a revised recommendation from FDA, the DEA in October issued an updated proposal that doubled the threshold originally established for 7-OH and removed MP from Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act. DEA’s October decision would allow both chemicals to be present in over-the-counter kratom products at levels higher than those found naturally in the kratom plant. Prior to DEA’s updated proposal, Grassley, along with Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Mike Lee (R-Utah), had urged DEA and FDA to implement the agencies’ original scheduling order and permanently place all harmful kratom-derived substances into Schedule I.

“Kratom is a drug in any form with addictive properties, and we believe this combined threshold level for 7-OH and MP set by DEA is inappropriately high and unsound… If the administration’s goal is to remove all unsafe products from the shelves, particularly synthetic or enhanced kratom products, this order misses the mark,” the senators wrote.

“The psychoactive alkaloids of the kratom plant are potentially dangerous substances that should be treated with caution, particularly given the lack of adequate regulation on its products… The American people deserve peace of mind about what is sold on marketplace shelves and a public health system that makes sound regulatory decisions,” the senators continued.

Specifically, the senators are requesting DEA and FDA:

Provide Congress the scientific and medical evaluations the agencies relied on to set a higher threshold limit for 7-OH.

Explain how a higher threshold for 7-OH better protects American families than the original, lower threshold.

Reconsider the updated threshold level for 7-OH and place kratom substances containing any amount of MP in Schedule I.

Grassley is joined by Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine), Rick Scott (R-Fla.), Mike Crapo (R-Idaho), Bill Cassidy (R-La.), Jerry Moran (R-Kan.), Shelley Capito (R-W.Va.) and Jim Risch (R-Idaho).

Read the full letter HERE. A fact sheet on kratom and the timeline for DEA’s proposed scheduling order is available HERE.

Background:

Kratom leaves contain two major psychoactive ingredients: mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH). These substances can be concentrated and chemically modified to produce extremely potent, semi-synthetic compounds – MP, MGM-15 and MGM-16. Kratom and kratom-derived substances are sold over the counter across the country, available to all age groups as “natural” energy boosters, mood lifters and pain relievers.

According to the FDA, known side effects of kratom include liver toxicity, seizures, substance use disorder and, in rare cases, death. According to the DEA, state health authorities have linked the use of 7-OH products and concentrated extracts to dependence, addiction, acute psychosis, slowed breathing, cardiac arrest and death.

Kratom-derived 7-OH has been identified as having a similar abuse potential to heroin or fentanyl and is known to be 13-times more potent than morphine. Other kratom-derived compounds, like MP, are known to be 20-times more potent than morphine.

title: ICYMI: “Public Safety is a Rare Bipartisan Win Congress Shouldn’t Let Slip Away”
text:
Public safety is a rare bipartisan win Congress shouldn’t let slip away

By Rachel Wright, National Policy Director for Right on Crime

November 13, 2026

The Hill

...It isn’t a new feeling, but [partisan tension] is increasingly a roadblock to good policy that improves Americans’ lives. However, Congress now has a real opportunity to set that tension aside and deliver meaningful public safety solutions through a package of bipartisan bills.

Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Ranking Member Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) have offered a set of public safety bills as amendments to the National Defense Authorization Act. Together, they show what a thoughtful, targeted approach to crime looks like, tackling online child sexual exploitation, organized retail crime and contraband in federal prisons.

Their approach? Address each problem narrowly and specifically, so the policy actually moves the needle on community safety. Rather than piling on punishment for its own sake, the bills aim for consequences that fit the threat and are serious enough to hold offenders accountable for reprehensible conduct.

Government’s first duty is to protect the most vulnerable among us, especially children. That responsibility does not disappear when crime moves online. Sextortion, which means coercing someone into sending sexually explicit images, often by threatening to expose them, can reach any child with an internet connection. In 2024 alone, the FBI received nearly 55,000 sextortion complaints, a 59 percent jump from the year before.

Federal law has not kept pace. The proposed James T. Woods Act, named for a victim of online sextortion, would update federal sentencing laws for child sexual abuse material. It would also create two new crimes targeting sextortion and violent online networks like 764, which coerce children into harming themselves or others. The goal is simple — hold predators accountable and ensure fewer children become victims.

Additionally, law-abiding citizens and businesses also should not bear the cost of organized crime. Organized retail theft is not petty shoplifting. It is driven by sophisticated networks that operate across state lines, raising prices and putting workers at risk. Because these schemes cross jurisdictions, the federal government has a role to play. The Combating Organized Retail Crime Act would strengthen the federal response by creating a multi-agency task force, improving coordination between retailers and law enforcement, and giving authorities new tools to recover stolen goods.

Public safety also extends behind prison walls. Incarceration should protect the public and prevent further crime, not give offenders a way to keep operating from their cells. Contraband cell phones let inmates continue directing criminal activity on the outside. The Lieutenant Osvaldo Albarati Stopping Prison Contraband Act would make possessing a contraband phone in federal prison a felony rather than a misdemeanor. What happens inside prisons can feel out of sight, out of mind. But safe, secure prisons are essential to public safety, officer safety, and the integrity of the justice system...

Online exploitation, interstate theft rings, and federal prisons are inherently federal challenges. And the National Defense Authorization Act, which has passed every year for more than six decades, is one of the few reliable vehicles in what feels like a gridlocked Congress.

The real question is not whether a policy sounds tough, but whether it offers a targeted, effective response to serious criminal conduct. Today, sizable gaps in federal law leave children exposed, let criminal networks profit, and allow offenders to keep operating behind bars. These bills close those gaps.

In a climate in which distrust of the political process seems to be at an all-time high, lawmakers should seize every chance to show that protecting the public is a shared priority. This is one of those chances. Congress should keep this package in the final National Defense Authorization Act and not let the moment slip away.

title: Blumenthal Applauds Sweeping House Passage of the Major Richard Star Act, Calls for Immediate Senate Vote
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), incoming Chairman of the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee, today called for immediate passage of the Major Richard Star Act—bipartisan legislation to deliver nearly 59,000 combat-injured veterans their full military benefits. This legislation passed in the House last week by a vote of 392-18 and does not include a funding offset proposed by Republican leadership to cut veterans’ disability benefits.

“Combat-injured veterans deserve justice— long overdue—ending the disgraceful Wounded Veteran Tax. Last week’s sweeping bipartisan passage of the Richard Star Act in the House of Representatives shows this legislation has the votes to pass without cutting benefits to other deserving disabled veterans. The Senate must act immediately and decisively. I am eager to lead this fight.”

The Major Richard Star Act is bipartisan legislation to fix an injustice preventing combat-injured veterans from receiving their full military benefits. Currently, only veterans with disability ratings above 50 percent and more than 20 years of service are eligible to receive the full amount of their Department of Defense retirement and Department of Veterans Affairs disability payments—leaving behind nearly 59,000 combat-injured military retirees.

Blumenthal has led the effort on the Senate side to pass the Major Richard Star Act and oppose attempts to fund the legislation by cutting nearly $57 billion in veterans’ benefits for veterans with sleep apnea and tinnitus. Senate Republican leadership has blocked eight attempts from Blumenthal, including in October, March, May, and June, to advance or vote on the bill.

This legislation has overwhelming support from the majority of both chambers of Congress, with 80 bipartisan cosponsors in the Senate and 342 bipartisan cosponsors in the House.

title: PASSED: Sens. Moran, Blumenthal Bipartisan Legislation to Deliver Cost-of-Living Increase for Veterans
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) – chairman of the Senate Committee on Veterans’ Affairs – on Veterans Day requested unanimous consent on the Senate floor to pass legislation he introduced with Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) – ranking member of the Senate Committee on Veterans’ Affairs – to make certain the rate of disability compensation and other financial benefits for veterans, their families and military survivors keeps pace with the rate of inflation. The legislation passed unanimously and now heads to the President’s desk to be signed into law.

The Veterans’ Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2026 (COLA) will increase certain VA benefits by 3.6% to reflect changes in the everyday cost of living and align with annual benefit increases by the Social Security Administration. The increased COLA rate goes into effect December 1, 2026.

“Veterans and their families deserve peace of mind knowing their VA benefits will keep pace with changes in our economy,” said Sen. Moran. “On Veterans Day and every day, we have a commitment to support those who have sacrificed for our nation’s freedoms. The annual cost-of-living adjustment makes certain that VA can continue delivering support to those who have served, while alleviating the stresses of financial uncertainty due to circumstances that are out of their control.”

“The nation’s affordability crisis hits veterans hard—in fact, harder than others—and they urgently deserve relief,” said Sen. Blumenthal. “As the cost of housing, food, and fuel continues to skyrocket, our bipartisan legislation will ensure veterans’ benefits keep pace. I urge the President to sign it into law without delay to help veterans during this crushing cost of living crisis.”

title: Trump Administration Carries out $9 Billion Violation of Appropriations Clause of the Constitution
text:
Government Accountability Office (GAO) Identifies Over $9 billion

in Unappropriated Funds Drawn from the Treasury

WASHINGTON –Today, the non-partisan Government Accountability Office (GAO) issued a legal decision affirming that the Executive Branch unlawfully drew over $9 billion in taxpayer dollars from the United States Treasury.

House Appropriations Committee Ranking Member Rosa DeLauro (D-CT-03) issued the following statement on the decision:

“In 2025, the House of Representatives originated appropriations legislation – passed by the Senate and signed into law by the President – providing that $12.5 billion in the Treasury would become available to the Executive Branch for housing support, foreign assistance, domestic law enforcement, and scientific research if, and only if, the President designated that the full $12.5 billion was for emergency requirements. Because the President did not designate the full $12.5 billion, the law made none of the funds available. Nevertheless, the Executive Branch drew and spent billions in taxpayer dollars from the Treasury in violation of the appropriations legislation, the Antideficiency Act, and the Appropriations Clause of the United States Constitution.

“Today’s decision emphasizes that it is Congress that holds the power of the purse, not the President, and not Executive Branch agencies. Indeed, the nonpartisan GAO has found and notified the Executive Branch that these obligations and expenditures violate the Antideficiency Act, which carries criminal penalties for knowing and willful violations. These unlawful actions must be immediately halted, and the Executive Branch must report all relevant facts and a statement of actions taken to the Committee, as required by the Antideficiency Act, to further inform next steps.”

Ranking Member DeLauro previously identified the Office of Management and Budget’s central role in the unlawful spending in her March 2025 letter to Director Vought.

For more details on the circumstances surrounding today’s decision, see the joint request for a legal decision from the Comptroller General, sent by Ranking Member DeLauro and Vice Chair Murray in December 2025.

title: Scott Introduces New Bill to Restore the Office for Civil Rights

committee.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce

text:
WASHINGTON— Today, Ranking Member Robert C. “Bobby” Scott (VA-03), House Committee on Education and Workforce, will introduce the Defend Students’ Civil Rights Act of 2026. The bill would prohibit the Secretary of Education from transferring the functions of the Department of Education (ED) Office for Civil Rights (OCR) to other federal agencies through interagency agreements or any other means and require ED to provide Congress with detailed cost analyses of the interagency agreements it has already entered into.

OCR enforces federal civil rights laws that protect students from discrimination based on race, color, national origin, sex, disability, and age in schools and colleges that receive federal funds. In June 2026, ED announced an interagency agreement to move OCR’s core investigation and enforcement work to the Department of Justice (DOJ), leaving students and families with fewer places to turn when their rights are violated.

"The Department of Education (ED)’s most important function is to protect and defend students’ civil rights and ensure every student can access a high-quality public education. In a move that is contrary to congressional intent, ED announced plans in June to move the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) to the Department of Justice (DOJ). Most civil rights complaints at ED are resolved through administrative enforcement, with a focus on students, and institutions are provided an opportunity to cure the harm they caused, not a lawsuit,” said Ranking Member Scott. “By contrast, DOJ is ill-equipped to implement education policy. Moving these offices reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of students’ and families’ needs. I will not stand by while this Administration continues to dismantle ED brick by brick. This legislation will ensure OCR stays at ED and that students’ civil rights are protected by the experts Congress intended.”

The legislation:

Prohibits the Secretary of Education from transferring OCR’s functions, programs, or authorities to any other federal agency through interagency agreements or other means

Requires the Secretary of Education to provide detailed cost analysis data on all of the interagency agreements ED has undertaken since January 2025.

Background:

In March 2025, the Administration laid offroughly half of OCR’s staff and closed seven of its twelve regional offices.

In February 2026, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) reported that ED paid OCR investigators up to $38 million not to work.

In April 2026, the Senate HELP Committee released a report that in 2025, OCR reached zero resolution agreements involving sexual harassment, sexual violence, seclusion or restraint, racial harassment, or discriminatory school discipline — despite more than 2,700 pending cases.

title: E&C Democrats Expand Measles Investigation After “Woefully Inadequate” Briefing from CDC Director Schwartz

committee.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce

text:
Washington, D.C. – Energy and Commerce Committee Democratic leaders today blasted Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Director Erica Schwartz for her failure to meaningfully answer questions raised in a briefing last month with Committee staff on CDC’s suppression of the total number of national measles-related deaths on its public dashboard.

The Committee briefing was scheduled in response to a September letter from Full Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone, Jr. (D-NJ), Health Subcommittee Ranking Member Diana DeGette (D-CO), and Oversight and Investigations Subcommittee Ranking Member Yvette D. Clarke (D-NY). The Committee leaders described the briefing from Schwartz as unresponsive and, at times, misleading.

“While we appreciate that you took time to personally lead the briefing, it was woefully inadequate,” the three Ranking Members wrote in their follow-up letter Director Schwartz. “As the crisis worsens, we are concerned that you continue to direct an effort at CDC to downplay the outbreak and artificially reduce the number of measles deaths that CDC reports to the public, concealing the fact that ten people have died of measles-related deaths this year alone.”

“Instead of providing information and support to the many communities across the nation that are facing measles outbreaks, CDC is seemingly focused on manipulating data, delaying diagnostic development, and obstructing medical updates to doctors,” Pallone, DeGette, and Clarke continued in their letter.

As measles cases and deaths continue to rise, leading to the United States losing its measles elimination status, Schwartz has worked to artificially deflate the total number of deaths on the agency’s dashboard. Under her leadership, CDC changed its method of reporting measles deaths from trusted real-time reporting by state public health departments to death certificate data, which could take upwards of three to 12 months between death and reporting.

The Democratic Committee leaders voiced concern that this was an intentional choice made to keep the public in the dark on how diseases are affecting their communities and downplay the way Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s ideological campaign has contributed to the spread of infectious diseases nationally.

“Since your briefing did not provide meaningful answers regarding critical decisions you are making to lead CDC’s reporting and response to the largest measles outbreak in three decades, we are expanding our investigation to examine the threat your actions pose to Americans’ health and whether changes to your statutory authority are required,” the Committee leaders continued.

“You can expect many more requests from Democratic Committee staff, and we expect your briefings to be substantive and complete,” Pallone, DeGette, and Clarke warned. “As the 120th Congress begins in January, you can expect that any information not provided voluntarily will be compelled using all the tools that will be at our disposal in the majority.”

The Committee leaders also asked for confirmation that CDC officials and staff have been notified of the requirement to preserve records outlined in the September letter, and noted the Committee would be following up with specific document requests.

title: Neal & Pallone Demand Answers from Trump Administration on Actions to Disenroll Americans from Their Health Care Coverage

committee.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce

text:
Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E. Neal (D-MA) and Energy and Commerce Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone, Jr. (D-NJ) sent a letter demanding answers from Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Administrator Mehmet Oz on the Trump Administration’s decision to arbitrarily terminate health care coverage for more than 750,000 Americans enrolled through the Affordable Care Act (ACA), with over 400,000 additional people at risk of losing coverage.

The Democratic leaders raised concerns about the Administration's willful lack of transparency and accountability, the alleged use of AI to wrongfully disenroll Americans, and reports of CMS re-enrolling people who should not have had their coverage terminated.

“The Trump Administration is rushing to purge Americans from their ACA plans reportedly with the help of AI, and forcing consumers that were wrongly terminated to navigate burdensome requirements and red tape to re-enroll in coverage,” wrote Neal and Pallone. “This haphazard approach—cutting first and asking questions later—leaves families and children to bear the brunt of the collateral damage. All the while, Trump continues pardoning health care fraudsters while Administration officials engage in rampant corruption.”

title: Select Committee Launches Bipartisan Investigation into Mercedes-Benz’s Ties to Chinese Communist Party-Linked Entities

committee.name: House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party

text:
WASHINGTON – Today, Ranking Member Ro Khanna (D-CA) and Chairman John Moolenaar (R-MI) of the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party launched a bipartisan investigation into Mercedes-Benz’s ownership ties, technology partnerships, and business relationships with entities in the People’s Republic of China (PRC), citing national security and supply chain concerns raised by the company’s deepening integration with China’s automotive industry.

In a letter to Mercedes-Benz senior executives Jason Hoff and Ola Källenius, the Committee seeks records and information, including copies of all relevant agreements, regarding the company’s relationships with Beijing Automotive Group (BAIC), Geely founder Li Shufu, and other PRC-based companies. BAIC and Li-affiliated companies reportedly each hold nearly 10 percent stakes in Mercedes-Benz, collectively accounting for approximately 20 percent of the company’s ownership and likely an even greater share of votes at shareholder meetings.

“These records and responses will not only assist with the Select Committee’s oversight of national security and supply chain risks in the automotive sector, but also inform Congress’s consideration of legislation to mitigate the profound threat presented by PRC cars in the U.S. market,” the lawmakers write in the letter.

Furthermore, the Committee raises concerns about the potential influence and information access of these PRC entities, particularly given BAIC’s status as a Chinese state-owned enterprise and Geely’s leading role in the PRC’s strategy to dominate global automotive markets. The investigation will also examine Mercedes-Benz’s expanding technology partnerships with Chinese companies, including Hesai, Tencent, Momenta, and other PRC-based technology and automotive firms.

Among other issues, the Committee is seeking information about Beijing’s influence over Mercedes-Benz’s strategic decisions, technology sharing, access to proprietary Mercedes research and development by PRC entities, Chinese components used in vehicles manufactured or sold in the United States, and the company’s engagement with PRC government officials.

Given bipartisan legislative concerns that PRC dominance of the global automotive sector would pose profound data security risks, undermine our national security, and erode the industrial base of the U.S. and our allies, the Committee also aims to understand how Chinese investment in Western automakers may seek to circumvent existing and potentially forthcoming restrictions.

The Committee requests that Mercedes-Benz produce the records and information by December 1, 2026, and preserve all documents and electronic communications relevant to the investigation.

The Committee further requests an in-person oversight meeting with company leadership.

title: Key House and Senate Committee Leaders Agree on Aviation Safety Legislation Framework

committee.name: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure

text:
Washington, DC – Key transportation committee leaders in the House and Senate today announced they have reached a bipartisan, bicameral agreement in principle on the civil aviation provisions of aviation safety legislation that addresses the National Transportation Safety Board’s (NTSB’s) recommendations following its investigation of the tragic 2025 midair collision between American Airlines Flight 5342 and a UH-60 Army Black Hawk helicopter near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA).

Statements from House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Chairman Sam Graves (R-MO); House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Ranking Member Rick Larsen (D-WA); Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee Chairman Ted Cruz (R-TX); and Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee Ranking Member Maria Cantwell (D-WA):

Chairman Graves: "The January 2025 midair collision in Washington, DC was a terrible tragedy, and Congress owes it to the victims and their families to get this safety legislation right. That’s been our goal, and working with House and Senate leaders, the NTSB and FAA, and safety stakeholders, including the victims’ families, I’m happy that we’ve reached an agreement in principle for the civil aviation components of the legislation, and that we are very close to a final agreement on the entire bill. We will continue working to see a final House-Senate bill signed into law before the end of this Congress that addresses the NTSB’s safety recommendations, honors the victims of this tragedy, and helps ensure this kind of disaster never happens again.”

Ranking Member Larsen: “The DCA midair collision was a stark reminder that we must remain vigilant in our pursuit of aviation safety – more can always be done to make air travel safer. We owe it to the victims, their families and friends, and the flying public to leave no stone unturned and to learn every lesson we can. I want to thank the friends and families of the victims; their presence keeps their loved ones’ memories alive, and their advocacy reminds us to always stay focused on improving aviation safety. Due in no small part to their efforts, today we have announced an agreement in principle with the Senate on a requirement for ADS-B In and other needed reforms for our civil aviation system. I am confident that we will soon reach a final agreement on the entire comprehensive bill and pass it into law. Safety is always my highest priority – let’s get this bill done.”

Chairman Cruz: “I made a promise to the Families of Flight 5342 that Congress would pass comprehensive safety legislation. Today, the Senate and the House have reached an agreement in principle to mandate ADS-B In. Under this agreement, all aircraft required to broadcast their location via ADS-B Out will now be mandated to receive those same signals through ADS-B In. Although a few details are still being worked out with the House and Senate Armed Services Committees, it is critical that Congress pass comprehensive safety legislation by the end of the 119th Congress, and I am confident we will. I want to thank the families for their persistence in ensuring that the legacy of the 67 lives lost will be a change in the law to protect millions upon millions flying in our country’s airspace.”

Ranking Member Cantwell: “We reached an agreement with the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, in principle, on the civil aviation provisions of this legislation. But our work is not done. We need a comprehensive bill that holds everybody to the same standards. We need the flying public to know their safety comes first – always first – and we need the standards that meet that. I look forward to working with my Armed Services Committee members, military partners, and the FAA to make sure this gets done. To the families, we know how long you’ve waited. It’s long enough. Let’s get this bill signed into law.”

The lawmakers have been working to resolve differences between H.R. 7613, the Airspace Location and Enhanced Risk Transparency (ALERT) Act of 2026, which was previously passed by the House, and S. 2503, the Rotorcraft Operations Transparency and Oversight Reform (ROTOR) Act, which previously advanced through the Senate.

title: Statement of the Committee on Ethics
text:
The Committee on Ethics (Committee) has scheduled a public meeting to be held in 1015 Longworth House Office Building on November 19, 2026 at 2:30 p.m., to consider adopting changes to the Rules of the Committee pursuant to House Rule XI, clause 2(a)(1)(A).

The Committee has undertaken a review of the rules with the goal of improving the speed of investigations and increasing transparency, particularly with respect to allegations of sexual misconduct. While the Committee has identified areas for improvement, the Committee also seeks to preserve the procedures that ensure fairness, due process, and bipartisanship in all investigations. At its next meeting, the Committee will consider adopting changes to its existing rules, to include the following:

Codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct in violations of clauses 9 or 18 of the Code of Official Conduct, while explicitly prohibiting publication of the identify of any victim of such conduct.

Delegating subpoena authority to the Committee’s Chairman and Ranking Member, acting jointly, rather than requiring a vote of the full Committee.

Adjusting the role of an investigative subcommittee to conclude following the adoption of findings, so that the full Committee and/or an adjudicatory subcommittee can more quickly begin consideration of a matter’s resolution.

Consolidating deadlines for a Respondent to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings, preserving Respondents’ ability to address concerns within a reasonable period of time while minimizing the potential for dilatory motions practice.

Clarifying the potential for the Committee or a Respondent to seek to adjudicate a matter based on the available record in lieu of a burdensome hearing.

Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.

As required by the Rules of the House, the Committee will meet in open session to vote on whether to adopt these reforms.

title: House Advances Legislation to Conserve Resources and Species, Support Tribes
text:
Today, the U.S. House of Representatives advanced legislation to support experimental forestry research, bolster tribal communities, responsibly manage cormorant populations and develop water infrastructure. Chairman Bruce Westerman (R-Ark.) issued the following statement in response:

"Today, House Committee on Natural Resources Republicans passed legislation aimed at conserving our natural resources and supporting tribes. Throughout the 119th Congress, Committee members have delivered real results to communities across the country to improve lives, create jobs and responsibly manage our natural resources. The legislation passed today continues this important work."

Background

H.R. 2400, the Pit River Land Transfer Act of 2025, as amended, introduced by U.S. Rep. Doug LaMalfa (R-Calif.), would place approximately 557 acres of U.S. Forest Service land, commonly referred to as the “Four Corners,” into trust for the Pit River Tribe.

H.R. 7954, the Don Young Doug LaMalfa Indian Buffalo Management Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd (R-Colo.), directs the Secretary of the Interior to work alongside tribes and tribal organizations to support the restoration, management and conservation of buffalo and buffalo habitat on tribal lands. The legislation also authorizes the Secretary to enter into agreements to transfer surplus buffalo from federal lands to Indian lands in support of tribal-led conservation efforts.

H.R. 8195, the Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act of 2026, introduced by U.S. Rep. Tim Walberg (R-Mich.), supports local fisheries and economies by establishing regional management frameworks for overseeing the responsible taking of double-crested cormorants. These measures are intended to ensure effective, science-based management of the species.

H.R. 8483, the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians Land Transfer Act of 2025, introduced by U.S. Rep. Darrell Issa (R-Calif.), places approximately 1,847 acres of culturally significant land into trust for the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians while maintaining existing rights-of-way, permits and water rights.

H.R. 9785, the South Dakota Water Feasibility Studies Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson (R-S.D.), directs the Secretary of the Interior to conduct studies to determine the feasibility of constructing projects to supply municipal, rural and industrial water in South Dakota and surrounding regions.

H.R. 10136, the Crossett Experimental Forest Act of 2026, introduced by Chairman Bruce Westerman (R-Ark.), directs the transfer of the Crossett Experimental Forest to the State of Arkansas to continue its nearly century-long legacy of forestry research, education and demonstration in coordination with the University of Arkansas at Monticello and the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture.

H.R. 9269, the Renewing the African American Civil Rights Network Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. James Clyburn (D-S.C.), reauthorizes the African American Civil Rights Network for an additional 7 years.

H.R. 9600, the Common Sense 250 Act of 2026, introduced by U.S. Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), authorizes the Thomas Paine Memorial to be located within Area I on the National Mall in Washington, D.C.

title: Chairmen Babin, McCormick Seek Answers from NIST on Manufacturing Extension Partnership Oversight

committee.name: House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology

text:
(Washington, D.C.) – Today, House Science, Space, and Technology Committee Chairman Brian Babin and Investigations and Oversight Subcommittee Chairman Rich McCormick sent a letter to National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Director and Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology Dr. Arvind Raman, requesting a briefing on NIST's oversight of the Hollings Manufacturing Extension Partnership (MEP) following four Department of Commerce Office of Inspector General (OIG) reports identifying unreliable performance data, financial noncompliance, and inadequate oversight.

In the letter, the Chairmen raise concerns about NIST's use of unreliable economic-impact data to report MEP's performance to Congress and the public. A September 2024 OIG report found that nearly half of the reviewed fiscal year 2022 reported sales impacts and a quarter of reported available jobs were unreliable. The OIG further found that NIST relied on inaccurate data to overstate MEP's economic impact in reports to Congress and the American public over several years.

The Chairmen also cite additional OIG findings involving unallowable costs, unreported program income, and conflicts of interest at MEP Centers. Most recently, an August 2026 OIG audit of Ohio's MEP awards questioned more than $20 million in costs and identified additional unreported program income.

The letter further notes that although NIST agreed to implement corrective actions in response to OIG recommendations, 22 of 23 recommendations remain open. The Chairmen are seeking a detailed accounting of NIST's corrective actions, amounts demanded and recovered from MEP Centers, additional enforcement actions, and procedures for ensuring MEP performance data are accurate and reliable, as well as safeguards addressing potential conflicts of interest.

The Committee requested that NIST provide a briefing by December 11, 2026.

title: Ranking Member Klobuchar Opening Remarks at Nomination Hearing

committee.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry

text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Senator Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, delivered the following opening statement at the Agriculture Committee nomination hearing of Nathan Anonick and Matthew Rowland to be Commissioners of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

A rough transcript of Klobuchar’s full opening statement is available below and a video can be found here.

Senator Klobuchar: Well, thank you so much, Chairman Boozman, and I'm delighted to welcome our two nominees, Mr. Anonick and Mr. Rowland, and congratulate them both on their nominations. Both have worked closely with Members of this Committee, and we know firsthand their knowledge of the markets and the responsibilities of the CFTC.

I'd like to also welcome their guests today. Welcome to Mr. Anonick's wife, Nichole, and his daughter, Charlotte. Charlotte seems immersed in a book in the back on the workings of the CFTC, I'm sure. I just wanted to acknowledge she was a little bit of a moment here, and now she is like all studying up to assist you and pass you notes if you need it. Also, your parents, Patrick and Robin. Welcome also to Mr. Rowland's wife, Emily, and his children, who I just got to meet, Ryan and Tali, his parents Patrick and Cecilia, and his in-laws Linda and Elliot Goldberg. Always good to have the support of your in-laws.

The CFTC is an important regulator that has a fundamental responsibility to ensure that farmers, ranchers, and businesses can rely on fair, transparent, and well-functioning derivatives markets to manage risk. That responsibility is especially critical as producers confront rising input costs and market headwinds due to tariffs, the war, and continuing uncertainty in global markets.

But these markets are always changing, and the CFTC we are discussing today already faces challenges that have evolved substantially since Chairman Selig's nomination hearing a year ago. Prediction markets have expanded dramatically. The CFTC has asserted broad federal authority over a wide range of event contracts, even as federal courts have reached differing conclusions about whether these products fall within the Commodity Exchange Act. At the same time, novel products, including perpetual derivatives and contracts tied to individual stocks, are raising new questions about consumer protection.

I support innovation. But the CFTC's core mission – managing risk for farmers and ranchers – should always be at the center of its work. And the Commission must protect consumers by maintaining strong market safeguards, respecting state and tribal authority, and ensuring financial products under its authority are held to the protections that Congress established.

These are not abstract concerns. Farmers, businesses, and American consumers depend on markets where the rules are enforced fairly and no participant has an improper advantage. Which brings us to today's hearing.

For nearly a year, Chair Selig has been the Commission's sole member. Congress designed the CFTC to be a five-member, bipartisan, independent commission, not an agency governed by one individual.

The CFTC has challenging, important issues to tackle and it requires capable, experienced Commissioners from both sides of the aisle ready to work constructively from day one.

That's why we are glad that you have been both nominated together. Mr. Anonick and Mr. Rowland, you each bring valuable experience to this nomination. Mr. Anonick, your work for Chairman Boozman on CFTC and derivatives policy has given you a solid background for the role you take on if confirmed. And Mr. Rowland, your experience at the CFTC as a litigator in the enforcement division and a senior attorney in the General Counsel's office, as well as a detailee to this Committee and to me, provides a strong foundation for the work of a Commissioner. If you are both confirmed, it would not result in a complete five-member Commission, but adding both of your voices would provide different thought as intended by Congress in creating bipartisan, independent agencies like the CFTC.

I look forward to hearing how you would restore confidence in the Commission, strengthen its core oversight and enforcement mission, and ensure that American markets remain fair, competitive, and resilient.

Thank you again to both of you for being here and for your willingness to continue serving the American public in this new role. And I look forward to the discussion.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

###

title: Chairman Boozman Opening Statement in Hearing to Consider CFTC Nominees

committee.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry

text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Chairman John Boozman (R-AR) emphasized the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s (CFTC) role in protecting consumers in emerging financial markets and ensuring farmers and ranchers have access to tools to manage risk during a hearing to consider the nominations of Nathan Anonick and Matthew Rowland to serve as CFTC commissioners.

The following is Chairman Boozman’s opening statement as prepared for delivery:

“Good afternoon and welcome. It is my privilege to call this hearing to order to consider the nominations of Nathan Anonick and Matthew Rowland to be Commissioners of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

“We welcome both of you to the committee and congratulate you on your nominations. Thank you for your willingness to serve.

“The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has played a critical role in our agricultural economy for decades, but over time, the responsibilities of the agency have evolved far beyond its foundational mission of regulating grain futures. In addition to its agricultural roots, the commission now oversees not only platforms facilitating trading of corn and energy futures but is also tasked with regulating more modern financial tools like interest rate swaps and digital asset futures.

“While these markets have evolved and expanded, the principles-based structure this commission was founded on has proven to be reliable and effective across commodities and products.

“This is by design. The commission regulates the deepest, most liquid markets in the world, and is equipped with the flexibility needed to ensure these markets continue to operate effectively.

“In recent years, financial products have become more retail facing, and as technology advances, we have seen increased participation in event contracts and in the digital asset space. Gone are the days of our derivatives markets only being utilized by sophisticated players.

“As both of you know very well from your time working on this committee, Congress recently contemplated a proposal for regulating the digital asset spot market. While the CLARITY Act did not pass the full Senate, the need for certainty in those markets remains significant. We are seeing an increasing number of Americans participating in digital asset markets, and without a comprehensive regulatory scheme, bad actors continue to go unchecked.

“It is my hope that the commission continues to use its existing authority to help protect American consumers. I believe that the CFTC is the right regulator to oversee the digital asset spot market. The commission has the experience regulating commodities and commodity-based contracts and has the right regulatory approach to navigate emerging technologies.

“My final note is this, should you be confirmed, you will be overseeing the markets that our farmers and ranchers use every day. Farm country is in crisis, and producers are being squeezed in every direction. They need every tool in their toolbox to manage their risk, including our futures markets.

“I look forward to hearing from both of our nominees on their vision for the commission. I have said this before, the CFTC, like any agency, works best when there is a full slate of commissioners. Today is a step in that direction, and I look forward advancing these nominations in the near future.”

title: Watchdog Concludes Trump & Vought Broke Law When Cherry Picking What Emergency Funds to Spend
text:
Watchdog Concludes Trump & Vought Broke Law When Cherry Picking What Emergency Funds to Spend

Washington, D.C. – Today, Senator Patty Murray (D-WA), Vice Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, issued the following statement responding to the Government Accountability Office’s (GAO) determination that the Trump administration broke the law when refusing to spend some, but not all, of the emergency funding provided in the fiscal year 2025 continuing resolution.

“Once again, GAO has made clear what’s been obvious from the start: Russ Vought brazenly broke the law when refusing to spend billions of dollars in emergency funding Congress provided on a bipartisan basis. The law does not allow the White House to cherry pick what emergency funds to spend. Congress, not Russ Vought and not Donald Trump, controls the power of the purse, and Democrats are going to ensure this tactic is never on the table for this administration again.”

In March 2025, at Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Russ Vought’s recommendation, President Trump refused to spend some emergency funding provided by Congress, while spending other funds—expressly violating the text of the law, which made clear all or none of the funds must be designated by the president as emergency funds and made available to spend. Vice Chair Murray immediately called out the illegal maneuver and sent a bipartisan letter to Director Vought calling on him to reverse it.

###

title: Cantwell, Baldwin Call on Chair Cassidy to Hold Hearing for NSF Director Nominee BEFORE Voting on His Nomination

committee.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation

text:
“The Committee and the public should hear directly from Mr. O’Neill about how he would lead NSF…and ensure that the United States remains the global leader in science and technology.”

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senators Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation, and Tammy Baldwin (D-Wisc.), Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Science, Manufacturing and Competitiveness, sent a letter to Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) Chairman Bill Cassidy (R-La.) calling on him to hold a nomination hearing before moving forward with the nomination of James O’Neill to be Director of the National Science Foundation (NSF). The HELP Committee has scheduled a markup for November 18th to vote on Mr. O’Neill’s nomination, despite not having held a hearing on his nomination.

“Given the scale of recent changes at NSF and the importance of the agency to American competitiveness, national security, and the scientific workforce, the Senate should have an opportunity to hear directly from the nominee about how he would lead NSF,” wrote the Senators. “The Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee has jurisdiction over authorizations for the NSF and a strong vested interest in its next leader.”

For more than 70 years, NSF has worked to promote the progress of science, advance the nation’s health, prosperity and welfare, and secure the national defense. The Trump Administration has severely undercut the agency’s ability to fulfill its mission. It has cut staffing by 30 percent, frozen and terminated research grants and removed the entire membership of the National Science Board. In addition, the Trump Administration has sought to abandon merit-based grantmaking and instead put senior political appointees as the final arbiters of whether a grant can move forward.

“The Committee and the public should hear directly from Mr. O’Neill about how he would lead NSF, restore confidence in the agency, rebuild the NSF workforce, and ensure that the United States remains the global leader in science and technology,” their letter continued.

“With the future of American research, science, and innovation at stake, the Senate should fully perform its constitutional role of advice and consent by hearing directly from Mr. O’Neill before acting on his nomination,” concluded the Senators. “Therefore, we respectfully ask that you notice a public hearing and bring Mr. O’Neill before the Committee before any vote on his nomination.”

The text of the letter can be found below and HERE.

November 16, 2026

Dear Chairman Cassidy,

We write to urge you to hold a full Committee public hearing on the nomination of James O’Neill to be Director of the National Science Foundation (NSF) before moving his nomination forward. Given the scale of recent changes at NSF and the importance of the agency to American competitiveness, national security, and the scientific workforce, the Senate should have an opportunity to hear directly from the nominee about how he would lead NSF. The Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee has jurisdiction over authorizations for the NSF and a strong vested interest in its next leader.

NSF was created in 1950, in the aftermath of World War II, to promote the progress of science, advance the nation’s health, prosperity, and welfare, and secure the national defense. For more than seven decades, NSF has supported the discovery science that leads to new industries, medical advances, critical technologies, and a stronger national defense. At this moment, the question before the Senate is not only who will manage NSF, but who can be trusted to restore and strengthen it.

Since January 2025, the Trump Administration has repeatedly frozen and terminated research grants, reduced the NSF workforce by more than 30 percent, and removed every member of the National Science Board. The Administration has also proposed budget cuts, including a $4 billion cut for FY 2027 that would represent a 55% reduction from the prior year and would further weaken the agency. Although Congress rejected these cuts in FY 2026 by appropriating more than $8.75 billion for NSF, the Administration has withheld an unprecedented $1.4 billion. Finally, on April 24, 2026, the Administration removed every member of the National Science Board without explanation. With the Board vacant, the Director will be without the independent scientific expertise, continuity, and oversight Congress intended the Board to provide. Together, these actions have created uncertainty across the research community and raised serious questions about the future of the agency responsible for supporting the basic research that underpins American innovation, economic competitiveness, public health, and national security.

Furthermore, the Office of Management and Budget’s (OMB) May 29, 2026 proposed government-wide grant rule would threaten NSF’s merit-review system. The proposed rule would require senior appointees to review discretionary awards before they are issued and would expand agencies’ authority to terminate any active awards. If finalized, the rule would move NSF funding decisions away from the independent peer-review process that has guided the agency for decades and toward greater control by political leadership. While we oppose OMB’s change to the rule, it makes it even more essential for the Senate to hear how Mr. O’Neill would protect scientific merit and NSF’s core mission.

At this moment, NSF needs credible, trusted, and capable leadership. A nominee preparing to lead this agency should explain how he intends to implement the important authorities Congress has vested in the NSF before the Senate votes, not after. The Committee and the public should hear directly from Mr. O’Neill about how he would lead NSF, restore confidence in the agency, rebuild the NSF workforce, and ensure that the United States remains the global leader in science and technology.

With the future of American research, science, and innovation at stake, the Senate should fully perform its constitutional role of advice and consent by hearing directly from Mr. O’Neill before acting on his nomination. Therefore, we respectfully ask that you notice a public hearing and bring Mr. O’Neill before the Committee before any vote on his nomination.

Thank you for your consideration.

###

title: Cantwell Remarks at Families of Flight 5342 “Safer Skies for All Memorial”

committee.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation

text:
“Our work is not done. We need a comprehensive bill that holds everybody to the same standards.”

[VIDEO]

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation, delivered the following remarks at the Families of Flight 5342 “Safer Skies for All Memorial.” The Families call on Congress to pass comprehensive aviation safety legislation following the tragic January 29, 2025 midair collision near DCA that took the lives of 67 people. A full transcript of her remarks is below:

“Thank you to the families of Flight 5342, not just this event, but everything you have done to this point to bring awareness and certainty to the fact that we need to pass new legislation. I want to thank you for your willingness to turn tragedy and grief into action.

“The dedication today [in honor] of those 67 souls who were lost on January 29, 2025, is a reminder that safety is a 365-day-a-year job, and we need to stay on it until the tasks are accomplished. Today, I’m glad to be joined by so many people who also want us to be successful: the Secretary of Transportation, the Administrator, pilots […]. Also, the NTSB chair, as Chairman Cruz said, has played a critical role over a long period of time, advocating for these changes.

“As was mentioned last Thursday, we reached an agreement with the House Transportation Infrastructure Committee, in principle, on the civil aviation provisions of this legislation. Speaking with Chairman Graves, we were able to reach a deal on ADS-B In, helicopter route operations, ADS-B Out, and fees. And we need to get this agreement over the goal line. I know that Chairman Cruz and I, and Chairman Graves and Ranking Member Larson, who have all been working on this all summer long, are excited for this breakthrough in having these provisions settled among the four of us. Most importantly, I want to thank the families of the victims, whose advocacy has kept this effort focused on preventing another tragedy.

“But let me be clear about where we are right now. While we have a deal in principle on the civil provisions, we do not have an agreement on the military provisions. We must have strong military accountability in the national airspace. The military must be a willing partner with the Department of Transportation and the FAA to make sure that what happened last January never, ever happens again.

“When military aircraft operate in the same airspace, they must meet the same safety standards that protect everyone. Allowing a military loophole for routine or training operations in that immediate area undermines the very safety provisions we have agreed upon with Chairman Graves, Ranking Member Larson, Senator Cruz, and myself.

“It is the FAA’s job to ensure that everyone in the flying airspace is safe. That responsibility requires effective oversight, [and] full cooperation, [from] everyone flying in our skies.

“Our agreement on the civil provisions is important progress, but our work is not done. We need a comprehensive bill that holds everybody to the same standards. We need the flying public to know their safety comes first — always first — and we need the standards that meet that. So I look forward to working with my Armed Service Committee members, military partners, and the FAA to make sure this gets done. To the families, we know how long you’ve waited. It’s long enough. Let’s get this bill signed into law.”
