title: Commerce Committee Democrats Demand Clear & Fact-Based Answers From DOT, FAA on Root Cause of Nov. 13th Nationwide Ground Stop

committee.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation

text:
“Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety.”

WASHINGTON, D.C. – All Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation, led by Ranking Member Senator Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), sent a letter to Department of Transportation (DOT) Secretary Sean Duffy and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Administrator Brian Bedford demanding clear, fact-based answers about the root cause of last Friday’s nationwide ground stop. The DOT and FAA leaders have blamed a router malfunction in Arkansas and FAA contractor L3 Harris’ work converting the FAA’s communications network from copper to fiber for the disruption.

“The Department of Transportation (DOT) and FAA must explain how this failure occurred and identify the corrective actions and oversight needed to prevent a recurrence,” the Senators wrote. “Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed. FAA must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues.”

According to information provided by L3 Harris, the Senators learned that the copper-to-fiber transition involves converting more than 3,600 routers to Juniper devices. To date, according to the contractor, 400 devices have been installed and 69 are operational. While a small sample of the Juniper routers were tested before installation, the Senators expressed concerns about continued deployment of the new routers until the root cause of the failure has been identified.

“We request an immediate pause on the deployment of additional Juniper devices,” the Senators continued. “Deployment should resume after the FAA demonstrates the devices’ readiness for safe deployment through improved operational testing, independent validation, verified failover capability, and rollback procedures. Congress expects a briefing on these improvements before the FAA resumes deployment of the routers.”

The letter comes as Duffy and Beford are demanding $50 billion in funding for air traffic control modernization, up from a request for $30 billion just last week and after prior outages earlier this year in Philadelphia Terminal Radar Approach Control and Minneapolis Air Route Traffic Control Center.

“DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13,” the Senators wrote. “Congress deserves clear answers on how the FAA is ensuring the safety of the aviation system for the traveling public while these new systems are being deployed.”

“Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety,” they concluded.

Along with Sen. Cantwell, the letter was signed by Sens. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawai’i), Ed Markey (D-Mass.), Gary Peters (D-Mich.), Tammy Baldwin (D-Wisc.), Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.), John Fetterman (D-Pa.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.) and Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.).

The text of the letter can be found below and HERE.

November 16, 2026

Dear Secretary Duffy and Administrator Bedford,

The November 13 nationwide ground stop disrupted air travel across the country, eroded public trust in our aviation system, and raised serious questions about the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) ability to ensure reliable and resilient operations. Congress expects clear, fact-based answers about the root cause of this disruption and why existing safeguards failed to prevent it. The Department of Transportation (DOT) and FAA must explain how this failure occurred and identify the corrective actions and oversight needed to prevent a recurrence.

Based on information provided to our offices from L3 Harris, the copper-to-fiber transition involves converting 3,648 routers to Juniper devices. To date, it is our understanding that 400 devices have been installed, and 69 are operational. With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation.

Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed. FAA must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues.

We understand the FAA Technical Center tested a sample of Juniper devices before installation. The devices passed pre-deployment testing. The November 13 failure raises serious questions about whether that testing adequately reflected operating conditions or evaluated all potential failure modes or outcomes.

We request an immediate pause on the deployment of additional Juniper devices. Deployment should resume after the FAA demonstrates the devices’ readiness for safe deployment through improved operational testing, independent validation, verified failover capability, and rollback procedures. Congress expects a briefing on these improvements before the FAA resumes deployment of the routers.

The ground stop demonstrated a breakdown in a system Americans rely on, and Congress was left to piece together critical facts. We expect accurate information as soon as it is available. Concerningly, the DOT attributed the November 13 network disruption to “old switches [and] old routers,” when in fact the deployment of the new Juniper routers seem to be the problem. This discrepancy between the FAA’s contractor and the DOT further fuels our concern that the root cause of the disruption has not yet been identified, leaving the potential for another failure.

The DOT and FAA have assigned blame to L3 Harris and used this moment to call for $50 billion in funding for Brand New Air Traffic Control System (BNATCS). This is notably $20 billion more than the request from DOT and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) that was sent on Thursday, November 12. DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13. DOT and FAA must also take full responsibility for managing contractors working to modernize the NAS.

Congress deserves clear answers on how the FAA is ensuring the safety of the aviation system for the traveling public while these new systems are being deployed.

Further, we request a joint technical briefing with FAA, L3Harris, and Juniper, and the following information no later than November 23, 2026:

An initial safety assessment of operational Juniper devices in the NAS, identifying shared infrastructure dependencies and common points of failures, vulnerabilities in primary and backup telecommunications paths, and the adequacy of failover, rollback, and recovery procedures.

An explanation of why the FAA’s operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy to recover immediately from the November 13 outage

An explanation of how a cut fiber-optic line or other localized telecommunications failure could result in widespread operational disruption, including actions taken to reinforce network redundancy following the Philadelphia Terminal Radar Approach Control and Minneapolis Air Route Traffic Control Center outages.

Given recent events, Congress is concerned about the FAA’s oversight of the BNATCS program. Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety. We expect a prompt response and look forward to working with the FAA to ensure the safety, reliability, and resilience of the NAS.

We are grateful for the air traffic controllers, pilots, flight attendants, and all aviation workers who continue to be impacted by Friday’s events.

Sincerely,

###

title: Committee Democrats Call on Chair to Pull Controversial FCC Nominee from Wednesday Markup

committee.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation

text:
“As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree.”

WASHINGTON, D.C. – All Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation, led by Ranking Member Senator Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), wrote to Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) calling on him to remove Danielle Thumann Severs from the markup scheduled for November 18, 2026. Ms. Thumann Severs is a Republican nominated to serve as a Commissioner on the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), and Democrats are united that Ms. Thumann Severs should only advance if joined by the renomination of current Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez and the nomination of another Democrat.

“There is no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks,” wrote the Senators. “As such, we request the removal of Ms. Thumann Severs’ nomination from the Executive Session agenda scheduled for November 18, 2026. Ms. Thumann Severs’ nomination should be postponed until the next Congress and paired with Commissioner Gomez’s renomination and the nomination of an additional Democratic commissioner.”

Along with Sen. Cantwell, the letter was signed by Democratic Sens. Ben Ray Luján (N.M.), Amy Klobuchar (Minn.), Brian Schatz (Hawai’i), Edward J. Markey (Mass.), Gary Peters (Mich.), Tammy Baldwin (Wis.), Tammy Duckworth (Ill.), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Ben Ray Luján (N.M.), John Hickenlooper (Colo.), John Fetterman (Pa.), Andy Kim (N.J.) and Lisa Blunt Rochester (Del.).

The text of the letter to Chairman Cruz can be found below and HERE.

November 16, 2026

Dear Chairman Cruz:

Following the recent elections, which returned control of both chambers of Congress to the Democrats, we strongly oppose the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a Republican, to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), without the renomination of current Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez and the nomination of another Democrat. There is no mandate for the outgoing majority to rush through a partisan FCC nomination in its final weeks. As such, we request the removal of Ms. Thumann Severs’ nomination from the Executive Session agenda scheduled for November 18, 2026. Ms. Thumann Severs’ nomination should be postponed until the next Congress and paired with Commissioner Gomez’s renomination and the nomination of an additional Democratic commissioner.

In January, Democrats will hold the Senate majority and will set the Commerce Committee’s agenda, including the pace at which nominations move. The Administration will have additional nominees for agencies and departments within the Committee’s jurisdiction over the next two years, and confirming them will require the cooperation of the incoming majority. Pairing this nomination with Commissioner Gomez’s renomination and a nominee for the seat vacated by former Commissioner Geoffrey Starks would allow the Committee to begin the new Congress with the bipartisan approach to nominations that has served both parties. In fact, the President has recognized the benefits of bipartisan nominations to other agencies within the jurisdiction of this Committee, renominating Democrats to seats on the National Transportation Safety Board and the Surface Transportation Board earlier this year. And last week, the President nominated Democrats to open seats on the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

At last week’s Committee hearing, Senate Democrats voiced concerns about Ms. Thumann Severs’s close relationship with FCC Chairman Carr and how that would impact her support for Chairman Carr’s controversial policies, some of which you have opposed as well.

As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees “should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.” We agree.

We therefore request that you remove the nomination of Ms. Thumann Severs from the Executive Session agenda scheduled for November 18, 2026. We believe her nomination, or any Republican nominee to the FCC, should be paired with the renomination of Commissioner Anna Gomez, and the nomination of another Democrat to the open seat of former Commissioner Starks.

Thank you for your consideration of this pressing matter.

Sincerely,

###

title: Key Senate and House Leaders Agree on ADS-B Safety Legislation Framework

committee.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation

text:
WASHINGTON, DC – At today’s press conference honoring the victims of the tragic January 2025 midair collision between American Airlines Flight 5342 and a UH-60 Army Black Hawk helicopter at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA) and calling for action, Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) announced an agreement in principle on a bipartisan, bicameral framework for aviation safety legislation. This includes an ADS-B In requirement first proposed in Chairman Cruz and Commerce Committee Ranking Member Maria Cantwell’s (D-Wash.) Rotorcraft Operations Transparency and Oversight Reform (ROTOR) Act.

Key transportation committee leaders on the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee and the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee touted the agreement in principle, but noted lawmakers on the House and Senate Armed Services Committees have yet to sign on to reforms for military aircraft operating in civilian skies.

Upon announcing the agreement, Chairman Cruz said: “I made a promise to the families of flight 5342 that Congress would pass comprehensive safety legislation. Today, the Senate and the House have reached an agreement in principle to mandate ADS-B In. Under this agreement, all aircraft required to broadcast their location via ADS-B Out will now be mandated to receive those same signals through ADS-B In. Although a few details are still being worked out with the House and Senate Armed Services Committees, it is critical that Congress pass comprehensive safety legislation by the end of the 119th Congress, and I am confident we will. I want to thank the families for their persistence in ensuring that the legacy of the 67 lives lost will be a change in the law to protect millions upon millions flying in our country’s airspace.”

Ranking Member Maria Cantwell said: “We reached an agreement with the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, in principle, on the civil aviation provisions of this legislation. But our work is not done. We need a comprehensive bill that holds everybody to the same standards. We need the flying public to know their safety comes first — always first — and we need the standards that meet that. I look forward to working with my Armed Service Committee members, military partners, and the FAA to make sure this gets done. To the families, we know how long you’ve waited. It’s long enough. Let’s get this bill signed into law.”

House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Chairman Sam Graves (R-Mo.-06) said: “The January 2025 midair collision in Washington, DC was a terrible tragedy, and Congress owes it to the victims and their families to get this safety legislation right. That’s been our goal, and working with House and Senate leaders, the NTSB and FAA, and safety stakeholders, including the victims’ families, I’m happy that we’ve reached an agreement in principle for the civil aviation components of the legislation, and that we are very close to a final agreement on the entire bill. We will continue working to see a final House-Senate bill signed into law before the end of this Congress that addresses the NTSB’s safety recommendations, honors the victims of this tragedy, and helps ensure this kind of disaster never happens again.”

House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Ranking Member Rick Larsen (D-Wash.-02) said: “The DCA midair collision was a stark reminder that we must remain vigilant in our pursuit of aviation safety – more can always be done to make air travel safer. We owe it to the victims, their families and friends, and the flying public to leave no stone unturned and to learn every lesson we can. I want to thank the friends and families of the victims; their presence keeps their loved ones’ memories alive, and their advocacy reminds us to always stay focused on improving aviation safety. Due in no small part to their efforts, today we have announced an agreement in principle with the Senate on a requirement for ADS-B In and other needed reforms for our civil aviation system. I am confident that we will soon reach a final agreement on the entire comprehensive bill and pass it into law. Safety is always my highest priority – let’s get this bill done.”

The lawmakers are wrapping up a final deal on the full text for a bill that resolves differences between S. 2503, the ROTOR Act, which unanimously advanced through the Senate and fell one vote short of House passage, and H.R. 7613, the Airspace Location and Enhanced Risk Transparency (ALERT) Act of 2026, which previously passed the House.

title: Durbin Calls For Passage Of Stop CSAM Act & Better Protections For Kids Online During Opening Statement At Senate Judiciary Subcommittee Hearing On Dangers Of Roblox
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, delivered an opening statement during today’s Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism hearing entitled “Roblox and Online Gaming: Digital Playgrounds Endangering America’s Children.” Today’s hearing explored the dangers posed to children on Roblox and the gaming platform’s efforts to prevent victims of online grooming or abuse while on the site from receiving justice.

Following their joint investigation into Roblox earlier this year, Durbin and U.S. Senator Josh Hawley (R-MO) this week introduced new bipartisan legislation to empower families of children harmed by tech products and by child sexual exploitation online. The No Forced Arbitration for Child Sexual Exploitation and Cyber Injuries Act would allow the families of minor children who are harmed to take their claims to court, even if a company’s terms of service require private arbitration. Notably, Roblox requires users to give up their constitutional right to a trial when creating a user account on their platform.

In his opening remarks, Durbin commended the bipartisan work done by the Senate Judiciary Committee to protect children online, and he called for final passage of his bipartisan STOP CSAM Act to hold Big Tech accountable for abuses occurring on their platforms.

Key Quotes:

“Two years ago, I was Chair of this Committee, honored to be, and we started working on legislation to protect children. We found out very quickly it was a bipartisan cause. I remember the day that I was going to bring my STOP CSAM bill to the floor and I didn’t have a Republican sponsor. Then there was a tap on my shoulder, and the Senator from Missouri was standing there and said, ‘I’d like to cosponsor the bill.’ It was Senator Hawley.”

“This has been a bipartisan effort from the start, and it should be. It has nothing to do with whether the families are Democrat, Republican, [or] independent. It’s about their kids, innocent kids who are being lured into this terrible situation.”

“What is the STOP CSAM Act? It’s pretty basic. Before I came to Congress, I was a trial lawyer. Want to get someone’s attention? Serve them with a complaint. Let them know they’re going to have to answer in court, under oath, as to what they’ve done… That’s what we’re facing here.”

“We will examine today at this hearing how predators have used the online gaming platform Roblox to exploit kids; how Roblox has responded to these tragedies; and what more needs to be done.”

“Roblox is a massively popular online gaming platform with 138 million daily active users. By its own estimates, 75 percent of kids ages 9 to 12 play Roblox games regularly, and the company markets itself to kids as young as five years old. Not surprisingly, child predators have recognized Roblox as a good hunting ground.”

“Roblox has long been aware of platform features—like its virtual Robux currency—that have been used by predators to facilitate sexual exploitation. There have been too many stories of predators using Roblox to trade child sexual abuse material, participate with kids in sexually explicit and violent games, bribe and extort kids, and connect with kids they later lured into in-person meetings.”

“Let me tell you a tragic story about a nine-year-old boy in Cook County, Illinois. He was groomed by an adult male predator posing as a child on the platform. The adult cultivated the child’s trust and then manipulated him into sharing explicit photographs.”

“In 2025, Roblox submitted 65,381 reports of suspected child exploitation to NCMEC, the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. Each of these reports represents an individual, a family, forever impacted by this experience.”

“And when lawsuits have been filed against the company, the response has been to attempt to silence victims by arguing that these minor users agreed to arbitrate all disputes. A five-year-old making a legal agreement? Get real.”

“Let me put that differently. According to Roblox’s arguments, a kid as young as five could agree to give up their constitutional rights to a trial simply by going to Roblox, creating a username, and entering a birth date. That’s it. That’s wrong.”

“While Roblox recently has taken steps [to address the risks on their platform], they haven’t done enough. The fact that they aren’t here today says that they’re ashamed of what they’re doing, but they’re still raking in the money.”

“This Committee has a long history of working on a bipartisan basis. We want this to be bipartisan.”

“We have pending legislation [the STOP CSAM Act] in the National Defense Authorization Act, which is pending on the floor, which we can pass in the closing days before the end of December. Protecting children is an important part of it. Let’s make it real. Let’s make it the law of the land. Let’s tell parents across the country that we got the message, and we did something on a bipartisan basis.”

title: Durbin Continues To Call Out Judiciary Committee Republicans For Violating Committee Norms To Fast-Track Judicial Nominations
text:
WASHINGTON – During his opening statement at today’s Senate Judiciary Committee executive business meeting, U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, slammed Committee Republicans for continuing to violate numerous longstanding Committee norms to fast-track unqualified MAGA nominees, all without the consent of the minority. These actions include holding nominations hearings less than two weeks apart on November 10 and 18; slating nominees for the November 18 hearing despite receiving Senate Judiciary Questionnaires (SJQ) less than 28 days in advance; slating nominees for hearings even if their FBI background investigations have not been cleared by staff in advance; and slating as many as eight nominees for a single hearing.

Key Quotes:

“Observers of the Senate Judiciary Committee know we typically meet on Thursday mornings at 10:00 a.m., as specified in our rules. Yet here we are, second week in a row, meeting on Tuesday at 9:00 a.m., prior to a previously-scheduled hearing on a different topic. What’s going on? Republicans are in a mad scramble to confirm as many judicial nominees as possible before the Democrats take majority control of the Senate in January.”

“My Republican colleagues argue this is business as usual. In fact, the majority is violating longstanding bipartisan Committee norms to jam through nominees in the Senate in this lame-duck session.”

“Republicans claim they aren’t acting any differently than Democrats did when we were in the majority. That simply is not true. The reality is these practices have been followed for years by Republicans and Democrats to ensure both sides have adequate time to review prospective lifetime nominees to the federal bench and to fulfill our advice and consent responsibility under the Constitution.”

“On the rare occasions that we’ve deviated from these rules it has only been with the consent of the minority. There is no consent with what we are doing now.”

“The Chairman is within his rights to schedule any nominee he would like for a hearing. But I want to warn my Republican colleagues: you will regret changing the 28-day rule to the 7-day rule… Remember this day when a future Democratic Chair moves judicial nominees through the Committee with one week for you to review their background and qualifications for a lifetime appointment.”

“Why are [Republicans] doing this? Simple: under the 28-day rule, nominees put forward after the election can’t be confirmed before the end of the Congress. So, Republicans decided change the rule, in fact break the rule, and the hell with the minority’s consent.”

“Senate Republicans turned obstruction of judicial nominees into an art form under President Obama. So, forgive me if I shed no tears when Republicans complain about Democrats refusing to rubberstamp unqualified MAGA nominees once we take the majority in January.”

At one point he wrote, ‘We need more diversity in these institutions.’ But while working for the Trump Justice Department, he got religion. He has frequently attacked diversity initiatives and stated, ‘DEI will either die on its own or we will kill it.’”

“Considering his record, I have my doubts as to whether Mr. Osete is able to be a neutral arbiter on the federal court. He’s going to have a lifetime to prove me wrong [with] this Republican majority.”

title: Durbin Pushes For Medicare To Have More Authority To Negotiate Prescription Drug Costs During Senate Judiciary Committee Hearing
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, today questioned witnesses during the Senate Judiciary Committee hearing entitled “Prescribing Sunshine: How Competition & Transparency Lowers Prescription Drug Costs.” During the hearing, Durbin spoke about the benefits of providing the federal government with more authority to negotiate the cost of prescription drug prices as the provisions in the Inflation Reduction Act have allowed Medicare to negotiate directly with Big Pharma, yielding enormous savings for taxpayers while allowing Americans to receive their medications at a lower cost.

Durbin began his questioning by emphasizing that research done at the National Institutes of Health (NIH), a taxpayer-funded medical research center, lays the foundation for nearly all new prescription drugs that enter the market.

“Is it true or not true that 95 percent of the new drugs that are available in America started with federal research at the National Institutes of Health?” Durbin asked, to which the witnesses agreed. “The starting point is: the American people are already paying for the basic research that leads to the drugs which they need to stay healthy, true?”

The witnesses affirmed Durbin’s analysis.

Durbin then spoke in favor of the Inflation Reduction Act’s provision that allowed Medicare to negotiate the price of 10 of the most commonly used prescription drugs.

“Let’s talk about the call that many politicians are making for Medicare for All. Let’s take a look at Eliquis under Medicare… Eliquis fell into these Part D drugs, the 10 that were reduced in cost through Medicare [under the authority granted by the Inflation Reduction Act]. Eliquis was originally $521 for a 30-day supply. It’s now $231 for a 30-day supply. A pretty dramatic [decrease in] cost because the government said to the maker of Eliquis, ‘You’re entitled to a profit, but you’re charging too much. We won’t pay it under Medicare,’” Durbin said.

“Out of the 70 million people who are under Medicare, which some politicians brand as socialism, four million take Eliquis. What has happened to the cost to the federal government of this Part D mandate by the government to reduce the 30-day cost of Eliquis from $521 to $231? The federal taxpayers have saved $10 billion for this blood thinner. That’s pretty amazing,” Durbin continued.

“So the question in my mind is, why don’t we just go ahead and go all the way? Why don’t we put everyone under Medicare?” Durbin said.

Durbin posed a question to Mr. Alex Oshmyansky, CEO and co-founder of Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company, about how his company is able to pay less for prescription drugs than the federal government.

“Mr. Oshmyansky, I listened to you explain how Mr. Cuban has been able to give people discounts on drugs just by paying what the drug companies are charging, but the federal government is paying more. Why?” Durbin asked.

Mr. Oshmyansky replied that intermediaries mark up the cost of these medications. He explained that cutting out the middleman and allowing the federal government to negotiate directly with pharmaceutical companies will reduce the cost of these medications.

Durbin then asked the witnesses about their stance on Medicare for All.

“Anybody here opposed to Medicare for All?” Durbin asked the panel at large.

While Professor Neeraj Sood of the USC Schaeffer Institute for Public Policy and Government Service expressed some hesitation, Ms. Merith Basey, CEO of Patients for Affordable Drugs Now, spoke about the necessity of tackling the list price of prescription drugs to achieve Medicare for All.

Durbin then spoke out against pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), which have grown into powerful intermediaries that have contributed to the rise of prescription drug costs by steering patients toward their affiliated pharmacies and marking up the costs.

“If you read a PBM defense what they’re doing, it sounds perfectly reasonable. [They say,] ‘We’re bringing competition and rebates and cuts and discounts,’ and yet, when it’s all over, Americans pay four times as much as other people around the world for the same [brand-name] drugs. So the system with PBMs is hardly working to the benefit of the consumers,” Durbin said.

Turning to Dr. Karriem Watson, CEO of UI Health Mile Square Health Center in Chicago, Durbin asked about the anticipated impact of congressional Republicans’ so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cuts nearly $1 trillion to Medicaid and threatens the ability for hospitals to provide care to uninsured patients.

“Dr. Watson, I’ve been to Mile Square [Health Center]. The people who come in there, some of them are covered by Medicaid, and now there’s talk about taking $1 trillion out of Medicaid. What is that going to do?” Durbin asked.

Mr. Watson explained that he anticipates a drastic impact on his patient population. According to Mr. Watsom, more than 60 percent of their adult patients are covered by Medicaid, and if those patients become uninsured under the Republicans’ Medicaid cuts, the cost of health care would go up as these uninsured patients would be more likely to seek treatment in emergency rooms only after their medical condition has worsened.

Durbin concluded by underscoring that eliminating health care coverage for millions of Americans leads to a sicker population and severe harms to hospitals’ ability to provide care to patients. Durbin invoked his personal experience as an uninsured father desperate to find treatment for his newborn daughter with a serious heart condition.

“How could this be good for the country, for more and more people to be uninsured? Have you ever been uninsured with a sick baby? Yes [Durbin raises his own hand]. You will never forget it as long as you live. And we’re going to do this to millions of people now?” Durbin concluded his questioning.

title: Durbin Raises Alarm About Abuses Occurring On Roblox, Discord During Senate Judiciary Subcommittee Hearing
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, today questioned witnesses during the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism hearing entitled “Roblox and Online Gaming: Digital Playgrounds Endangering America’s Children.” During his questioning, Durbin underscored that social media and gaming platforms, including Roblox, must take accountability for the abuse they have allowed to occur on their platform and do more protect their users.

Durbin began by asking Myriam Gilles, Professor of Law at Northwestern Pritzker School of Law, about how Roblox approaches legal disputes brought against them by families of children abused on the platform.

“Is it my understanding that they’re arguing that the user, the child in this case, can consent to forced arbitration?” Durbin asked Professor Gilles.

Professor Gilles confirmed that Roblox does ask all users, regardless of age, to consent to forced arbitration.

“I’m trying to remember that contracts course I took a long time ago. If I do remember it properly, if a child showed up at an auto dealership and signed up to buy a car for $25,000, that would be a voidable contract, wouldn’t it? Why?” Durbin asked.

Professor Gilles explained that, under common law, children cannot consent to those types of purchases.

“Why is this an exception? That a child can consent under Roblox[’s terms of use] to activity which is potentially so dangerous?” Durbin followed up. “This is hard to imagine that any court, any judge, can see a nine- or ten-year-old and say they have the capacity to consent to conduct and activity that is potentially so dangerous.”

Professor Gilles explained that both Roblox and the platform Discord claim that under their user agreements, only an arbitrator can decide whether a child validly “opt-ed out” of a mandatory arbitration provision. In other words, a child’s family would have to go to arbitration and ask an arbitrator to decide whether they have a right to go to court in a process kept secret from the public. Professor Gilles pointed out that in two recent cases, courts have upheld the argument that young children have the ability and did consent to arbitration. She went on to note that the Supreme Court’s interpretation of the Federal Arbitration Act has resulted in arbitration provisions being treated differently than other contracts.

“They’re basically setting up a scenario where they always win it. As long as they can keep it secret, you don’t know what’s happening. As long as the courts give a nod of approval, this will continue,” Durbin said.

Durbin then asked Michael Schlep and Woody Doe, both online safety advocates and survivors of abuse themselves, about what dangers exist on Discord.

Mr. Schlep spoke about the cases of child exploitation on Discord, noting that there have been accounts flagged for child safety violations, yet those accounts are allowed to remain active on the platform.

“Mr. Doe, your story is nothing short of amazing,” Durbin said of Mr. Doe’s background as a Marine Corps veteran and an engineer. As a child, Mr. Doe experienced sexual abuse on Roblox, and his abuser later lured him to his home to continue the abuse. In 2025, Mr. Doe sued Roblox, alleging design defect, negligence, and misrepresentation claims, and he continues to speak out against predators who use Robux—the currency on Roblox—to manipulate children.

“What you’ve been through, your life’s journey with the Marine Corp and your own family, you had courage to come here today,” Durbin told Mr. Doe. “You really are saving lives by this testimony. I believe that some people watching this are going to change their attitude towards this dangerous situation.”

Durbin then asked Khari James, Senior Legal Counsel at the National Center on Sexual Exploitation (NCOSE), about the volume of complaints filed at the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC).

“Ms. James, you must see this in the organization you work for coming at you on a regular basis, thousands of complaints…What are we talking about in terms of volume of victims across the United States?” Durbin asked.

Ms. James noted that NCMEC received more than 65,000 reports related to Roblox in 2025, more than double the reports received from Roblox in 2024.

Durbin concluded his questioning by reflecting on the harms done to children on these platforms, and he called on his colleagues to hold Big Tech accountable by passing the STOP CSAM Act.

“First, this isn’t just a child signing a contract for a car. It’s signing a contract for a car with no brakes. That to me, ought to be taken into consideration as well when you consider the danger,” Durbin said.

“The second thing I observed is—what in the hell are we thinking as a nation? We let our kids and grandkids be lured into this kind of a horrible situation and dream up legal theories to justify it. What is wrong with us? The answer is nothing is wrong with us, and the richest people in the world who are exploiting these kids need to be held accountable. It’s up to us, put the party aside, to do the right thing for the people and families of this country,” Durbin said.

“Senator Hawley, he and I are as different as night and day on some issues, we really see this the same way. I hope we can get something done before the end of the year. There is no excuse for why another child is exploited while we twiddle our thumbs and think of some reason why we can’t get around to it. We have a bill before us on the floor, the STOP CSAM Act. It’s in the defense authorization bill, and it’s time to pass it,” Durbin concluded his remarks.

Video of Durbin’s questions in Committee is available here.

Audio of Durbin’s questions in Committee is available here.

Footage of Durbin’s questions in Committee is available here for TV Stations.

Durbin has used his role on the Senate Judiciary Committee to prioritize child safety online through hearings, legislation, and oversight efforts. Today, Durbin and Hawley introduced new legislation, the No Forced Arbitration for Child Sexual Exploitation and Cyber Injuries Act, to allow families of minor children who are harmed online to take their claims to court, even if a company’s terms of service require private arbitration. Their bipartisan bill introduction comes after the two Senators launched an investigation into Roblox last year.

On January 31, 2024, while Durbin was serving as Chair, the Committee held a hearing featuring testimony from the CEOs of social media companies Discord, Meta, Snap, TikTok, and X (formerly known as Twitter). This hearing highlighted the ongoing risk to children and the immediate need for Congress to act on the bipartisan bills reported by the Committee.

Last year, Durbin and Hawley joined forces to reintroduce the bipartisan STOP CSAM Act, which would combat online child sexual abuse material. The bill passed the Judiciary Committee unanimously and awaits action on the Senate floor.

In addition, Durbin’s bipartisan Disrupt Explicit Forged Images and Non-Consensual Edits Act of 2024 (DEFIANCE Act) passed the Senate unanimously in July 2024 and again in January 2026. The legislation would hold accountable those responsible for the proliferation of nonconsensual, sexually-explicit “deepfake” images and videos. The bill awaits consideration by the House.

Durbin also introduced the Sunset Section 230 Act with the late U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham (R-SC), which would repeal Section 230 two years after the date of enactment so that those harmed online can bring legal action against the companies that caused the harm. The bill awaits consideration by the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.

title: Durbin Shares 154th Dreamer Story on the Senate Floor
text:
WASHINGTON – In a speech on the Senate floor, U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, shared his 154th Dreamer story. During his time in Congress, Durbin has continuously shared stories of Dreamers—young people who have lived in America since they were children, built their lives here, and are American in every way except for their immigration status. Under current law, there is no pathway to citizenship for Dreamers. Eighty-one percent of Americans support citizenship for Dreamers, including 56 percent of Republicans.

“It has been 25 years since I first came to the Senate Floor with a simple request—for Congress to protect the Dreamers. Dreamers are immigrants who were brought to the United States as children. They grew up pledging allegiance to the same flag that we do. But because of a decision on immigration that they had no control over, they are forced to live their lives in fear of deportation,” Durbin said. “I joined forces with Republican Senator Orrin Hatch of Utah, and together, we introduced the Dream Act.”

Durbin has introduced the Dream Act every Congress since 2001. The Dream Act is bipartisan legislation that would allow noncitizens without lawful status who were brought to the United States as children and meet certain education, military service, or work requirements to earn lawful permanent residence. This Congress, Durbin introduced the bill with U.S. Senator Lisa Murkowski (R-AK).

“Since then, I have come to the floor of the Senate over 150 times to share the stories of Dreamers who are doctors, nurses, business owners, educators, parents, and members of our military,” Durbin said. “I have pushed for this legislation to be included in bipartisan measures like the 2013 ‘Gang of Eight’ immigration bill, which passed the Senate with 68 votes… Over the years, the Senate has passed the Dream Act… and the House of Representatives has passed it too, but never at the same time, so that we could send the legislation to the President’s desk to be signed into law.”

In 2010, Durbin sent a letter, joined by the late U.S. Senator Richard Lugar (R-IN), asking then-President Obama to stop the deportation of Dreamers. Fourteen years ago, President Obama responded by announcing the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program. More than 830,000 Dreamers have since come forward and received DACA, which has allowed them to contribute more fully to their country as teachers, nurses, doctors, engineers, and small business owners.

Durbin continued, “I am not going to give up on the Dreamers. Just last week, President Trump said that he was willing to work with Democrats on a bipartisan immigration deal… I ask the President of the United States now to keep his word. Work with us to pass the Dream Act, and do it now. We have enough time left to get it done this year. As I near the end of my Senate career, I ask my colleagues to support these young people who are American in every way, except for their immigration status.”

Durbin then shared the story of Brenda Bedolla, the 154th story of a Dreamer he has shared on the Senate floor. Brenda arrived in Little Village, a lively neighborhood in Chicago, from Mexico when she was just two years old. From a young age, her parents instilled in her a deep desire to learn and to use her education as a means to become something greater.

As she began to apply to college, Brenda realized that she was ineligible for financial aid due to her immigration status. But Brenda refused to let that stop her, and she earned a full-ride scholarship to Morton College. At Morton, Brenda ran on the school’s cross-country team, reported for the college newspaper, served as student body vice president, and received the Lincoln Academy of Illinois Student Laureate for outstanding achievement.

Brenda then transferred to Northeastern Illinois University, where she served as student body president and worked in an on-campus job, as well as at a restaurant on nights and weekends to support her education and her family. These experiences exposed Brenda to what it meant to advocate, organize, and represent others. They led her on the path to becoming an organizer for the Service Employees International Union, or SEIU, representing Illinois and Indiana.

Since 2019, Brenda has served as the representative of more than 90,000 care workers in essential jobs in home care, child care, nursing homes, and hospitals. She has helped hospital workers organize and supported members who have workplace grievances. Brenda also serves as a board member of the Morton College Foundation to fundraise for scholarships for students at her alma mater, as well as Arise Chicago, a faith-based worker center educating and organizing low-wage workers about fighting injustice. Brenda says her family’s own experiences with exploitative working conditions are what led her to this rewarding job.

“Brenda is exactly the type of person we need in America. This is whom we might lose if we fail to pass the Dream Act. To my Republican colleagues, I ask you, is this a person you want to remove from the United States? An advocate for health care workers who care for the elderly, our children, and our grandchildren, and our sick? Does Brenda sound like ‘the worst of the worst’? No. She is one of the hundreds of thousands of Dreamers who serve our country every day, even as they worry about being forced to leave this nation,” Durbin said.

Durbin concluded, “We owe it to these talented young people to help. And there is still time in the final weeks of the 119th Congress to get it done. To all of my Republican colleagues, please join me and Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska in standing up for these people who epitomize the American Dream. We have an opportunity to finally give Dreamers the justice they deserve. We can do it. We have the time to do it. Let’s get to work.”

title: In Opening Statement During Senate Judiciary Committee Hearing, Durbin Calls For Bipartisan Action To Lower Cost Of Prescription Drugs
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, delivered an opening statement during today’s Senate Judiciary Committee hearing entitled “Prescribing Sunshine: How Competition and Transparency Lowers Prescription Drug Costs.” Today’s hearing examined competition and transparency in the prescription drug supply chain, specifically consumers’ lack of access to pharmacy services; how brand name drug companies’ patent practices can inhibit competition from generics; and the role played by pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) in drug pricing and access.

In his remarks, Durbin emphasized that Americans are paying the highest prescription drug prices in the world—on average four times more than people in similar countries for brand-name drugs. To address these sky-high prices and crack down on Big Pharma, Durbin advocated for the passage of his legislation with U.S. Senator Chuck Grassley (R-IA), the Drug-price Transparency for Consumers (DTC) Act, which would require price disclosures on advertisements for prescription drugs in order to empower patients and reduce Americans’ colossal spending on medications.

Key Quotes:

“It is no secret: People in the United States pay the highest prescription drug prices in the world—on average, four times more than people in similar countries pay for brand-name drugs. Patients are forced to choose between [prescription] drugs and food.”

“Compounding this challenge is the lack of access to brick-and-mortar pharmacies. In the last 15 years, more than 800 community pharmacies in my state of Illinois have been forced to close their doors because of increased drug costs and declining reimbursement rates.”

“Congress took a first step forward to address the high cost of [prescription] drugs by passing the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022. This law capped the price of insulin at $35 per month. It set an annual out-of-pocket expense limit for seniors—$2,100 in 2026. It also let the executive branch negotiate with Big Pharma to lower prices under Medicare—something President Biden used to reduce drug prices by up to 79 percent.”

“There’s more work to do. Where should we start? Let me suggest, direct-to-consumer drug ads. There are only two countries in the world that allow consumer television ads for drugs… Big Pharma spends billions of dollars to flood the airwaves with advertisements. Why? To get American viewers to get to the point where they can not only pronounce Xarelto but spell it.”

“In July, a citizen petition was filed with the FDA asking to ban these ads… If we cannot get rid of them, we should at least require Big Pharma to let people know how much these drugs cost. Is that an outrageous idea?”

“Chairman Grassley and I have a simple bill that we put together that would require direct-to-consumer ads to disclose the price charged by the drug company. It’s a basic transparency issue to inform patients, and it’s been supported by President Trump in the past. I hope we pass it before the end of the year.”

“We must also address Big Pharma’s anti-competitive schemes to maintain monopolies. The Senate Judiciary Committee has taken a leading role in stopping these abuses. In April 2025, this Committee unanimously reported six bipartisan bills to address this issue. This includes my bill with Republican Senator Tillis to improve information sharing between the FDA and Patent Office. Congress must pass these bills sooner rather than later.”

“This hearing is going to make clear that our work to address the high cost of prescription drugs is far from over. Let’s work together, on a bipartisan basis, to do something to help families afford their prescription drugs.”

title: Grassley Opens Judiciary Committee Executive Business Meeting on District Judges and Executive Nominees
text:
Prepared Opening Statement by Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa

Chairman, Senate Judiciary Committee

Executive Business Meeting

Tuesday, November 17, 2026

On today’s agenda, we have 14 nominations and one bill.

We’ll vote on three district court nominees: Robert Long, Peter Mansfield and Jesus Osete.

We’ll also vote on several other nominees: Stephen Husk, for the U.S. Parole Commission; three U.S. attorney nominees: Samuel Lee, Gretchen Shappert and Robert Troester; and four U.S. marshal nominees: Reid Creswell, James Edge, Christopher Inabinett and James Jackson.

The remaining nominations and the bill will be held over for future consideration.

We have a lot to get through on today’s agenda, and we have a hearing right after this, so I’ll be brief.

I understand that there’s disagreement about the scope of protections that’d been afforded in the Right to Worship bill. It’s being held over so that Ranking Member Durbin and Senator Cruz’s offices can continue to work through those differences, but I’m hopeful we can vote on it at an upcoming markup.

As for today’s votes, I’d note that the committee remains steadfast in its commitment to serve the American people.

As chairman, I’ve worked diligently to ensure that high-caliber nominees get processed and advanced efficiently, and I thank my colleagues for helping me to do so.

Federal judges, U.S. attorneys and U.S. marshals are among the most important nominations that this committee reviews. They’re the backbone of our justice system, and the American people need good folks in these roles to keep the wheels of justice moving.

Today’s judicial nominees are highly qualified.

Their track records demonstrate a commitment to the Constitution and the rule of law. I’m confident that they will preside over cases without fear or favor.

I’m also pleased to have so many U.S. attorney and U.S. marshal nominees on the agenda.

These men and women have the experience and qualifications to lead federal law enforcement in their respective jurisdictions, and I’m confident that they’ll work hard to keep Americans safe.

title: Grassley Opens Judiciary Hearing Examining Avenues to Make Prescription Drugs More Affordable
text:
Prepared Opening Statement by Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa

Chairman, Senate Judiciary Committee

“Prescribing Sunshine: How Competition & Transparency Lowers Prescription Drug Costs”

Tuesday, November 17, 2026

I’d like to welcome everyone to this hearing examining how competition and transparency can lower prescription drug costs.

Today, we’re examining questions that matter to every family. Why do prescription drugs cost so much? How do we make them affordable?

Needless to say, the prescription drug supply chain is complicated.

Manufacturers set list prices. Wholesalers and distributors move products. Pharmacy benefit managers set prices, build formularies, process claims and create pharmacy networks.

Insurers and employers design benefits. Pharmacies fill the prescriptions. Each one of these participants affects the final cost.

However, when the transactions are hidden behind confidential contracts, rebates, fees and payments to affiliated companies, patients and consumers have a hard time following the money.

When companies are allowed to engage in anticompetitive and abusive tactics, drug prices remain high for patients.

Last year, the Senate Judiciary Committee advanced six bipartisan bills that address the high cost of prescription drugs and the abusive practices that keep prices too high for too many American families.

They’ll help make medications more affordable for the patient.

These bills address anticompetitive tactics in the pharmaceutical supply chain, including opaque pharmacy benefit managers’ (PBMs) practices, product hopping, patent games, sham citizen petitions, pay-for-delay deals and the need to strengthen collaboration in the drug patent process between the FDA and Patent Office.

I’m glad the Senate unanimously passed the Affordable Prescriptions for Patients Act in July.

It’s time for the Senate to pass the five other bills.

Last year, the Senate Judiciary Committee held a hearing focused specifically on PBMs. We learned that these entities originally existed to process pharmacy claims. Then, they began negotiating prices and managing drug benefits.

In recent years, PBMs’ role has continued to evolve. They now exercise significant power over what medications patients can access, how much the patient will pay, how the pharmacy gets paid and much more.

My two-year bipartisan investigation into insulin price gouging, cited by the FTC, found that PBMs encourage drug makers to spike a drug’s list price in order to offer a greater rebate. This, in turn, allows manufacturers to secure priority placement on covered meds – all at the expense of patients.

For years, I’ve pressed the FTC to study PBMs, and their impact on competition and drug costs.

I’m glad that the FTC listened to me and began their study into PBMs in 2022.

While the FTC’s two interim staff reports are helpful, I’m eager to get their full report with legislative recommendations. Last month, I asked the FTC for an update on when Congress will see the report.

I also appreciate that the FTC has issued two proposed consent orders with major PBMs. The enforcement of those settlements will need to be monitored to ensure they benefit patients.

While a report on PBMs is crucial, we can address some anti-competitive behavior today. In February, Congress took some action on PBM reform in Medicare Part D and the private insurance market.

I’m glad the Department of Labor implemented its regulation last month. I look forward to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services completing its regulatory work next year. I’m watching both regulations closely to ensure they help patients and lower drug costs.

These are good first steps, but more PBM reform is needed. I’m on the record calling for more transparency and accountability of PBMs.

The PBM industry may try to argue that they’ve changed their ways and they’re more accountable, but I disagree.

PBMs are still too opaque and powerful, while patients, pharmacies and taxpayers are being hurt by these powerful drug middlemen.

The efforts to lower prescription drug costs are bipartisan.

The Senate should also consider the Drug-price Transparency for Consumers Act. This bill is a priority of Senator Durbin and mine. If a drug company can advertise a prescription drug directly to the public, it should disclose the product’s price to the public too.

Sunlight gives patients information to ask better questions about price and lower-cost alternatives before they purchase at the pharmacy counter.

I appreciate President Trump’s commitment to lowering drug costs, holding foreign countries accountable for benefiting from American medical innovation and protecting rural health care through price transparency and the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Fund.

The Trump administration’s work to root out fraud, waste and abuse in health care programs is also ensuring resources are going to those who most need them while protecting taxpayers.

Today’s hearing is about the prescription drug supply chain as a whole. The entire prescription drug supply chain needs to be put under a magnifying glass.

Accountability must follow the decision maker.

No participant can hide behind the complexity of the system or conveniently shift responsibility.

I appreciate Senator Durbin’s partnership in holding this hearing.

Today, we’ll hear testimony from a patient advocacy organization, the co-founder of a transparent cost-plus pharmacy, the Iowa Pharmacy Association, a health economist and a CEO of Illinois health clinics.

They bring different perspectives. I thank each of the witnesses for being here, and I look forward to the discussion.

title: Judiciary Committee Witnesses Urge Congress to Pass Grassley-Backed Bills to Lower Prescription Drug Costs, Echo Grassley’s Calls for PBM Transparency & Accountability
text:
WASHINGTON – Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) today chaired a hearing to examine the high cost of prescription drugs and proposed legislative solutions. Last year, the Judiciary Committee advanced six Grassley-backed, bipartisan bills to lower prescription drug prices through competition transparency and to address anticompetitive tactics in the pharmaceutical supply chain. One of those bills, the Affordable Prescriptions for Patients Act, passed the Senate unanimously in July. The remaining bills have not received a vote on the Senate floor.

Today’s witnesses urged Congress to pass bipartisan legislation and echoed Grassley’s calls for the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to complete its 6(b) study of pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs). The witnesses also detailed how PBMs increase the cost of prescription drugs and outlined mechanisms to hold PBMs accountable.

Grassley questioned the following witnesses:

Matthew Pitlick, PharmD, chief executive officer of the Iowa Pharmacy Association

Merith Basey, chief executive officer of Patients For Affordable Drugs Now

Alex Oshmyansky, MD, PhD, cofounder and chief executive officer of the Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company

Neeraj Sood, PhD, senior scholar and professor at the University of Southern California Shaeffer Institute for Public Policy & Government Service

Video and excerpts of Grassley’s questions follow. Read Grassley’s opening statement HERE.

VIDEO

On the FTC’s Final PBM Report:

GRASSLEY: “It’s been four years since the FTC began their study of PBMs. Patients, rural pharmacies and Congress are still waiting for the study and its recommendations. Dr. Pitlick, how is the delay of the FTC’s final report on PBMs impacting patients and rural pharmacies? Why is getting this report so important?”

PITLICK: “The interim reports are non-binding, but they gave great information and great insight. Like you said in your opening statement, we are waiting for the full report with legislative action that Congress can take. I think that Congress is deserving of that, the public is deserving of that, and taxpayers deserve it as well.”

On the impact of Grassley-backed, bipartisan drug pricing bills:

GRASSLEY: “Ms. Basey, last year, this committee took a comprehensive [approach] to reducing drug costs… These bills will bring cheaper treatment faster to the market and hold drug companies and PBMs accountable. The Senate has now passed just one of these six competition bills. So, for you, what impact would these remaining five bills have on patients, and why should the Senate act now?”

BASEY: “Lower cost competition is essential for the one in three Americans who are struggling to afford their prescription drug prices. These bills, if passed together, would help close some of the loopholes in the patent and regulatory systems that the pharmaceutical industry uses to abuse the system and keep prices high at the expense of American patients…

“We need lower cost drugs sooner, so that patients can benefit and so that taxpayers can benefit too. These bills would all save money, and they would make a difference for millions of patients around the country.”

On PBMs driving up the prices of prescription drugs:

GRASSLEY: “Dr. Oshmyansky, according to a recent study, Part D Medicare could save as much as $8.6 billion dollars annually if it were using the same pricing for certain generic drugs as the Cost Plus Drug Company uses. In other words, you're getting a better deal for patients, while under the Part D program, PBMs drive up the cost for seniors and taxpayers.

“So, how does the Cost Plus Drug Company achieve these lower prices, and what barriers does a company face when entering or expanding in the prescription drug market?”

OSHMYANSKY: “We try to go back to the 1850s in terms of our pricing model. You can go to our website, and you can see what it is exactly we pay for the drugs… we add a 15% margin as our markup, a $5 fee to pay our pharmacist, a $5 shipping and handling [fee], and that's the total cost of the medication. Everything else – that entire $8.6 billion difference – that's just intermediaries in the supply chain, adding their markup...

“You might get asked to pay a $3,000 copayment for Imatinib for Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia. From us, [the] exact same drug [from the] exact same drug company [would be] about $30... The one thing we cannot do at the moment is get access to the branded, patented and specialty drug products. If we could break through that, I think we could drive down drug costs for the country much further.”

On the positive impact of establishing fiduciary responsibilities on PBMs:

GRASSLEY: “I'm glad the Department of Labor recently implemented PBM reform for some employer-sponsored health plans. Under federal rules for employer-sponsored health plans, there's a question as to whether PBMs have a fiduciary responsibility to health plan sponsors. PBMs would argue that they're getting the best deal for their clients. PBMs' opaqueness and tactics made me question that position. I'm all in for regulating PBMs, but we ultimately need a comprehensive mechanism to hold these PBMs accountable. Otherwise, we're playing whack-a-mole with PBM behavior.

“You talked about this in your 2025 testimony before this committee. So, why would establishing an explicit fiduciary duty standard, given the recent Department of Labor recommendation, help ensure PBMs have a duty to work for the benefit of the consumer?

SOOD: “What the new laws do, the Department of Labor regulations and the [Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2026], is they ask PBMs to disclose to employers how they are making money and their contracts with pharmacies. But disclosure is not enough to change their practices. As Dr. Alex said, there's only three PBMs, and if every PBM is doing the same games, switching PBMs is not going to help.

“What you need is accountability ultimately to plan members. As the [PBM] FAIR Act does, it gives fiduciary responsibility to PBMs. That fiduciary responsibility is owed to employees and plan members. So, even if employers don't act under [the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA)], the Department of Labor or employees could act and hold PBMs accountable. If PBMs say they’re doing a great job for our patients, be [held] accountable for it – that's what fiduciary responsibility does.”

title: Ernst Names Small Business of the Week, American State Bank

committee.name: Senate Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship

text:
Read the release on Sen. Ernst’s website HERE.

Throughout this Congress, Chair Ernst plans to recognize a small business in every one of Iowa’s 99 counties.

RED OAK, Iowa – U.S. Senator Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), Chair of the Senate Small Business Committee, today announced American State Bank of Clarke County as her Small Business of the Week. Throughout the 119th Congress, Chair Ernst plans to recognize a small business in each of Iowa's 99 counties.

“For nearly 40 years, American State Bank has made it their mission to deposit joy throughout Iowa communities” said Chair Ernst. “From financial services to investing in the local community, American State Bank continues to make customers its highest priority and interest.”

In the spring of 1987, the town of Osceola, Iowa, lost its primary banking institution due to economic conditions in the Midwest. This left $8.6 million in assets and $7.7 million in deposits available for acquisition. To address this situation, a group of five families came together to acquire the bank, ensuring that locals would continue to have a choice in where to do their banking. On April 24, 1987, the American State Bank was officially established in Osceola.

Since then, the bank has expanded its presence by establishing a central office in downtown Osceola and additional locations in Winterset and Lamoni. Today, the bank focuses primarily on agricultural lending while providing a wide range of services including personal and business banking, investments, insurance, and financial education. Beyond its banking services, American State Bank supports the communities it serves through donations to local agriculture, education, and community initiatives.

Stay tuned as Chair Ernst continues to recognize outstanding Iowa small businesses with her Small Business of the Week award.

###

title: Cole Statement on End-of-the-Year Appropriations Work
text:
Washington, D.C. – House Appropriations Committee Chairman Tom Cole (R-OK) issued the following statement on the release of all twelve Senate FY27 appropriations bills and the push to enact full-year funding before year’s end:

“Funding the federal government is a constitutional obligation. It’s a duty that belongs to Congress as a whole – not one political party or legislative chamber. As Chairman, I’m used to long odds and tight timelines. Neither has ever deterred me from doing the work.

“A lame duck doesn’t have to leave full-year bills dead in the water. I’ve been actively working with my counterparts to advance negotiations, avoid an unnecessary shutdown, and get full-year FY27 legislation signed into law. With all twelve Senate bills now public and the House measures long on the table, we have what we need to negotiate in earnest.

“The biggest disservice to the American people would be not to try. I refuse to let any opportunity available pass us by simply because some are already looking at the next Congress while this one still has votes to take. No appropriator charged with upholding Article I should be more willing to put off these measures than to negotiate small packages right now.

“I’m ready and determined to move as many full-year FY27 bills as possible before the end of the year.”

###

title: Chairman Arrington Urges Colleagues to Pass the Preventive Health Savings Act
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – House Budget Committee Chairman Jodey Arrington (R-Texas) delivered the following remarks on the House floor urging the passage of H.R. 4464, The Preventive Health Savings Act, which ensures Congress fully captures the long-term savings potential of preventive health care measures over a 30-year window:

Watch here

Remarks as Delivered:

Mr. Speaker, first, let me congratulate my colleague and friend Brendan Boyle from the Keystone State. We've been working together, side by side, in partnership to address some of the biggest problems facing our country that are fiscal in nature.

We know that the current trajectory, I believe, has come about as a result of both parties' neglect or lack of political courage to address it in a more meaningful way. We are on a terribly unsustainable course, and I just want to say publicly and for the record that he's just been a great partner.

We have different views on issues pertaining to budget and across the board, but he has helped me set the kind of tone in the committee that could provide the context for real debate, not performative stuff that too many people watch on cable news and social media that gets us nowhere, but meaningful discussion about the issues that we must confront.

And many of these, and the largest ones, I think, will only be addressed when we work together.

So, congratulations to my friend, who will go from Ranking Member to Chairman. And while I grieve that on some level, and profoundly so, in our personal friendship, and because I know the kind of person you are and the caliber of person, I'm happy for you and for your family, and I'm looking for big things from you, and especially continuing the culture that I think we created together that has served our country well.

Now, this is one example. The ranking member and I have worked with our colleagues in a bipartisan way to pass 14, I believe, bipartisan bills, the most in the 50-year history of the House Budget Committee. Two have become law of the land, and we have one here today that was initiated by a former Member and dear friend from Texas, Dr. Michael Burgess, who used to say, ‘An ounce of prevention is better than a pound of cure.’

That's true for people who need life-saving therapeutics, vaccines, or who need better prevention on the front end. But it's also true of our budget, the federal budget, where we can save, especially in a category of spending—I'm talking about health care, Mr. Speaker—which is $5.3 trillion in its total expense, private sector and public sector. It's a third of the federal budget.

So, when we can bend that curve, save money, make for more efficacious drugs to treat our fellow Americans, it's a win-win. It's a double, triple bottom line, and that's what this Preventive Health Savings Act does.

Let me make it real simple. In this business, and with the oversight of the Budget Committee, the Congressional Budget Office scores health-related legislation, and that score is over a time horizon of 10 years.

But some of the most innovative, life-changing, or, in some cases, life-saving drugs, vaccines, et cetera, they have tremendous cost on the front end, but over time, they may break even on the latter side of that 10-year window and return savings beyond the 10-year window.

And so, having an arbitrary 10-year window to judge whether or not the ROI is good for the American people, good for our health care system, especially in the space of health care innovation, just doesn't make sense.

We're not blowing up the 10-year window. We're just saying, in some cases, we need to look at 15 years out, 20 years out, and even 30 years out to see what benefits are accruing to the American people and to the balance sheet of the United States of America.

And I think we're long overdue to innovate ourselves as a Budget Committee and to not get stuck on arbitrary.

###

title: Ranking Members Meeks, Raskin, and Kamlager-Dove Probe Whether Lutnick’s Family Finances Shaped His Response to the NVIDIA Spy Scandal
text:
Lutnick Family Firm’s Massive Holdings in NVIDIA Stock and Other Foreign Data Center Investments Boosted by Secretary Lutnick’s Refusal to Enforce Export Controls and Stop Diversion of Highly Sensitive Chips to China

Washington, DC — Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, Ranking Member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee; Rep. Jamie Raskin, Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee; and Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove, Ranking Member of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia with jurisdiction over export controls, sent a letter to Cantor Fitzgerald Chairman Brandon Lutnick demanding records to determine whether his father, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, blocked efforts to stop the suspected smuggling of advanced NVIDIA chips to China while his family’s firm held hundreds of millions of dollars in NVIDIA stock. The letter comes days after NVIDIA announced that its CEO, Jensen Huang, had resigned amid revelations of an alleged Chinese intelligence operation tied to the suspected smuggling of billions of dollars in restricted chips.

“[T]he American people deserve to know: Did the Secretary of Commerce seriously and perhaps irreversibly compromise U.S. national security interests to make money for his adult children and Cantor Fitzgerald?” wrote the lawmakers.

From September 2025 to March 2026, White House and U.S. intelligence officials examined whether a Chinese intelligence operation had targeted NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang to help smuggle restricted AI chips to China. China’s Ministry of State Security reportedly recruited Alice Huang, the former chief executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based NVIDIA customer, to compromise him. Jensen Huang resigned after admitting that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with the alleged Chinese asset.

As U.S. officials pressed to cut off Megaspeed’s access to advanced NVIDIA chips, Secretary Lutnick reportedly resisted. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said four federal agencies had backed blacklisting Megaspeed for months while Lutnick’s Commerce Department, which controls the blacklist, held out.

Before Lutnick became Commerce Secretary, Cantor Fitzgerald had disclosed holding more than 3.5 million NVIDIA shares. After his confirmation, Lutnick agreed to transfer ownership of the firm to trusts benefiting his adult children. While U.S. officials were scrutinizing Megaspeed, Cantor Fitzgerald cut its reported NVIDIA shareholdings by nearly half. The firm still held roughly $310 million in NVIDIA shares at the end of March 2026.

Secretary Lutnick’s push to weaken proposed chip export restrictions raises another question about whether Cantor Fitzgerald’s business interests influenced his decisions. The New York Times reported that Secretary Lutnick pushed to narrow proposed restrictions on overseas data centers that use advanced NVIDIA chips to serve Chinese customers. One project that could be affected is a Malaysian data center run by a Cantor Fitzgerald client.

The lawmakers are demanding records identifying every NVIDIA trade Cantor Fitzgerald has made since January 2024, along with an accounting of the firm’s business dealings in China and Southeast Asia. They are also seeking internal and client communications about U.S. export controls and suspected chip smuggling, communications with the Commerce Department about NVIDIA, Megaspeed, and Asian data center projects, and records concerning President Trump’s reported NVIDIA investments.

title: Himes Statement on Recent Computer Network Outages

committee.name: House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence

text:
Washington, DC -- U.S. Representative Jim Himes (D-CT), Ranking Member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, today released the following statement:

“Over the past week, I have heard from many concerned Americans about the series of high profile and disruptive computer network outages, including Microsoft Outlook, an Air Traffic Control system, JP Morgan Chase, and an internal National Security Agency system. I want to be clear that as Ranking Member of the House Intelligence Committee, I have seen no evidence to suggest any of these outages were the result of a malicious actor. To the contrary, the owners of these systems have acknowledged publicly that the outages were caused by internal actions, not by an outside attacker.

“Stepping back, the risk of disruptive or even damaging cyberattacks is very real, and we need to do more to harden our critical infrastructure against attack. The rapid advent of highly cyber capable AI models, including open-weight models, has accelerated the ability of both attackers and defenders to discover vulnerabilities and create exploits, necessitating even greater urgency to patch systems regularly. It is possible that the increased pace of vulnerability discovery and patching could cause more frequent outages, but the breakneck pace of patching we have seen in recent months is vital to shore up the security of all IT infrastructure. Disruptions in networks, whether through internal errors or outside attack, are a fact of life, but we can do much more to be prepared and resilient.”
