title: Select Committee Democrats Call on Trump to Uphold U.S. Interests and Values in Meeting with Xi and Putin

committee.name: House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party

text:
WWASHINGTON – Today, Ranking Member Ro Khanna (CA-17) of the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), alongside Committee Democratic Members Representatives Raja Krishnamoorthi (IL-08), Jill Tokuda (HI-02), Shontel Brown (OH-11), André Carson (IN-07), Kathy Castor (FL-14), Seth Moulton (MA-06), Greg Stanton (AZ-04), Tom Suozzi (NY-03), and Ritchie Torres (NY-15) issued the following statement ahead of President Trump’s Thursday meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China:

“As Members of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, we strongly urge President Trump to stand up for American interests and democratic values in Thursday’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

President Trump must make clear that American workers, manufacturers, and security will not be sacrificed to advance the interests of Beijing or Moscow. Concerning AI, it is vitally important that the U.S. leads the conversation on an AI treaty that establishes clear guardrails to reduce the risk of conflict, prevent the misuse of advanced AI systems, and promote transparency while preserving American technological leadership.

President Trump should use this opportunity to directly address China’s enabling of Russia’s illegal war in Ukraine and demand the two leaders cease their military, economic, and gray-zone coercion of U.S. allies and partners in the Indo-Pacific and Europe. The security of Taiwan’s people must under no circumstance be a bargaining chip. Similarly, the future of Ukraine must not be discussed without Ukrainians at the table.

Meanwhile, we urge President Trump to call for the release of Americans unjustly imprisoned in both countries and for the humane treatment of political prisoners. Xi must immediately end the CCP’s ongoing genocide against the Uyghur people and reverse its inhumane policies.”

title: Chairman Walberg: Taxpayer Dollars Should Support Team USA, Not the Competition

committee.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce

text:
Today, Education and Workforce Committee Chairman Tim Walberg (R-MI) joined former U.S. Davis Cup captain Patrick McEnroe at a press conference on H.R. 10351, TEAM USA Act, legislation aimed at protecting college athletic opportunities for American students.

Excerpts from Chairman Walberg’s remarks:

“…In some college sports, international athletes now make up more than half the roster. At Alabama State the tennis team is made up 100 percent with international athletes. Too often, those spots are going to older international athletes, instead of American high school graduates.

“That means fewer spots are available for American students who have worked their entire lives for the chance to compete.

“American colleges and universities should be opening doors for American students, not making it harder for them to pursue their dreams. And that’s why I introduced the TEAM USA Act alongside Senator Jon Husted…

“American taxpayers invest billions of dollars in higher education every year. It's reasonable to expect our colleges and universities to prioritize opportunities for American students…

“College athletics is also one of the most important training grounds for America's future Olympians.

“At the 2024 Olympics, catch these numbers, 65 percent of Team USA had ties to NCAA athletics. That’s a good thing. Yet of those 1,036 NCAA Olympians in Paris, only 385 competed for Team USA—the other 63 percent competed for foreign nations. Let that sink in.

“The U.S. is subsidizing rival nations through our taxpayer-funded pipeline. And why wouldn’t they want that pipeline. We are the best.

“When we limit opportunities for American students to compete at the college level, we also risk weakening the pipeline that helps produce our next generation of Olympic champions…

“The TEAM USA Act is about making sure the next generation of American athletes gets a fair shot…”

title: Chairman Guthrie Requests Briefings from Nvidia and Department of Commerce Over Megaspeed and National Security Concerns

committee.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congressman Brett Guthrie (KY-02), Chairman of the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, sent letters to Nvidia Interim CEO Colette Kress and U.S. Department of Commerce Secretary Lutnick and Under Secretary Kessler requesting briefings following recent reporting on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with alleged Chinese intelligence asset and Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.

Key Excerpt from the Letter to Nvidia:

“These reported events raise questions about the company’s compliance with existing federal law regarding the export of advanced technologies, as well as the robustness and efficacy of the company’s security controls. Understanding what happened, how it happened, and how to move forward are critical to mitigating the impacts of this ongoing situation, ensure national and economic security, and ensure that the U.S. continues to be a global leader in the AI stack.”

Key Excerpt from the Letter to Secretary Lutnick:

“The Committee seeks further information from the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) regarding the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”

BACKGROUND:

The Committee on Energy and Commerce holds broad jurisdiction over interstate commerce, including domestic manufacturing, supply chains, and most of the U.S. AI stack.

As part of the Committee’s oversight mandate, Chairman Guthrie is formally requesting briefings from both Nvidia and the Department of Commerce on the allegations in these reports and the threats to economic and national security posed as a result.

The Chairman’s letters request briefings with both Nvidia and the Department of Commerce no later than December 2, 2026.

title: Homeland Republicans Lead Legislation to Strengthen, Modernize DHS’s Cybersecurity Mission as AI Reshapes the Threat Landscape
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. –– As artificial intelligence (AI) transforms the cybersecurity landscape and reshapes the resilience of America’s critical infrastructure, House Committee on Homeland Security Republicans introduced four bills this week to ensure the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) have the frameworks, expertise, personnel, and coordination structures needed to accomplish their core cybersecurity mission amid technological advancements. These bills would help secure AI agents operating on federal networks, enhance CISA’s AI workforce, and prepare for future AI-enabled cyber threats by learning from past intrusions. Read more in NextGov.

Upon their introduction, Committee Chairman Andrew R. Garbarino (R-NY) said:

“In the past year, the Homeland Security Committee has engaged directly with AI developers, critical infrastructure operators, security researchers, and government officials to better understand rapid advancements in AI and the associated security risks. Today’s technological and cyber threats demand informed Congressional action and stronger partnerships between industry and all levels of government, with DHS and CISA leading efforts to promote the secure adoption of AI, understand how adversaries use it, and protect the critical infrastructure Americans rely on.

“With China nipping at our heels, now is the time to ensure America leads in AI and is prepared for the security challenges this technology brings. The bills introduced by Committee members this week complement the Administration’s work to secure advanced AI and take valuable steps forward in helping DHS lead a whole-of-society cybersecurity mission. I look forward to working with colleagues on both sides of the aisle to see these priorities through.”

Rep. Matt Van Epps (R-TN) introduced the “Improving Nonhuman-Agent Security, Identification, Governance, Handling, and Traceability Act,” or AI INSIGHT Act, which would establish a framework for securing AI agents operating on federal civilian information systems, with CISA providing operational support, guidance, and technical assistance.

“We need commonsense AI safeguards. Agentic AI can help streamline workflows and automate cybersecurity tasks in both the public and private sectors. However, oversight and transparency measures are essential to ensure agents are properly managed and secured as they interact with systems and data. Every agent with access to a federal network presents a new opportunity to harness efficiencies, but also a new potential target for adversaries,” Rep. Van Epps said. “The AI INSIGHT Act would build on existing cybersecurity programs and controls to help agencies identify which agents are operating on their networks, limit their access to what their tasks require, monitor their activity, and suspend or revoke access when necessary. This legislation is an important step to ensure federal agencies can take advantage of this cutting-edge technology to deliver services to the American people without opening new doors for adversaries.”

Rep. Vince Fong (R-CA) introduced the “Bridging Resources for Innovative Defense and Government Expertise in Artificial Intelligence Act” or BRIDGE AI Act, which would establish a pilot program within CISA to help recruit AI and emerging technology experts from the private sector, academia, federally funded research and development centers, National Labs, and other technical talent pipelines.

“Communities and critical industries across the country are trying to keep up with the surge in AI-driven cyberattacks that steal sensitive data and disrupt operations,”Rep. Fong said. “In the Central Valley, cyberattacks have increasingly targeted schools, hospitals, and water systems, threatening the critical services our communities depend on. These attacks are becoming more frequent and sophisticated. These threats are real, and they aren’t waiting for the government to catch up. By bringing in AI and emerging technology specialists from the private sector, the BRIDGE AI Act ensures our nation’s cybersecurity experts receive the additional tools and expertise needed to modernize our systems, address vulnerabilities, and protect the essential services Americans rely on.”

Rep. Morgan Luttrell (R-TX) introduced the “Reviewing Origins, Outcomes, and Threats from Cyber and Artificial Intelligence to Understand Security Events Act,” or ROOT CAUSE Act, which would establish a National Cyber and AI Investigations Board (NCAI Board) within CISA to examine significant cyber incidents, including those involving AI or cyber terrorism, identify root causes, and recommend measures to prevent similar incidents from happening in the future. The NCAI Board would have no regulatory or enforcement authority, and its reviews would not assign civil or criminal liability. The bill also includes provisions governing board membership, conflicts of interest, access to information, and protection of sensitive material, along with published incident selection criteria, a majority vote to open an investigation, and regular congressional oversight. Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY) is an original cosponsor.

“When it comes to warfare, cyber is the next phase of evolution. We are living in a world where no individual, business, or industry is protected from cyberattacks,” Rep. Luttrell said. “As our adversaries become increasingly sophisticated in this space, it is more critical than ever that we take action. I am grateful for Rep. Torres’ efforts on this bill, and urge its passage through Congress.”

Subcommittee on Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Protection Chairman Andy Ogles (R-TN) introduced the “Sector Engagement for Cybersecurity through Unified Responsibility and Expertise in Information Technology Act,” or SECURE IT Act, which would codify DHS’s existing responsibility as the Sector Risk Management Agency (SRMA) for the Information Technology Sector, with DHS, through CISA, serving as the designated SRMA. Chairman Garbarino is an original cosponsor.

“Last week’s global Outlook outage and recent cyberattacks have exposed America’s dependence on shared IT infrastructure. As cyber threats grow, we need stronger coordination between government and industry,” Subcommittee Chairman Ogles said.“My SECURE IT Act would establish DHS, through CISA, as the federal partner responsible for protecting the critical technology infrastructure Americans rely on.”

BACKGROUND:

The House Committee on Homeland Security continues to engage with the private sector on AI through roundtables, briefings, and hearings on the future of cybersecurity and best practices for developing secure AI technology. In May, Anthropic provided Committee Members with one of the first live demonstrations of Mythos given to Congress, allowing Members to see firsthand how advanced AI can find software vulnerabilities. The demonstration reinforced the urgency of ensuring that federal agencies, including our civilian cyber defenders, can responsibly use advanced U.S. models to find and patch vulnerabilities.

In June, the Subcommittee on Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Protection convened a hearing on AI and policy solutions to secure our networks, strengthen America’s domestic technology base, and ensure the United States maintains its leadership in AI. Testimony was provided by representatives from Google Threat Intelligence, the Frontier Model Forum, Corridor Security Inc., and the Electronic Frontier Foundation.

In April, Chairman Garbarino and Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar (R-MI) launched a joint investigation into the growing adoption of artificial intelligence models developed by the People’s Republic of China (PRC). The investigation is examining the potential cybersecurity, data security, and critical infrastructure risks associated with the deployment of PRC-developed AI systems in American products and services.

That month, the Subcommittee on Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Protection held a hearing to examine whether DHS has the authorities, resources, and sector risk management structure necessary to defend the interconnected communications and information technology IT systems, assets, and underlying infrastructure that support American economic and national security.

In December 2025, the Subcommittee also convened a joint hearing to examine threats stemming from the use of emerging technologies like AI, quantum computing, and hyper-scale cloud infrastructure, as well as how to use this technology to defend our networks from malicious actors.

title: House Advances Legislation to Map America’s Vast Natural Resources
text:
Today, the U.S. House of Representatives passed H.R. 9640, the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI) Reauthorization Act of 2026, led by House Committee on Natural Resources Vice Chairman Rob Wittman (R-Va.). Chairman Bruce Westerman (R-Ark.) issued the following statement in response:

“America cannot secure its mineral future without knowing what resources lie beneath our feet. H.R. 9640 reauthorizes the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative through 2031 and incorporates modern sensing technologies to improve our understanding of our nation’s mineral wealth. I commend Vice Chairman Wittman for being a champion of this program that strengthens the data available to support domestic resource development and build more secure American mineral supply chains.”

Background

H.R. 9640 reauthorizes the U.S. Geological Survey's Earth MRI through 2031. The bill expands the program's scope to incorporate modern sensing technologies and to support the identification of critical mineral resources and other geologic data.

title: Committee Delivers Legislation to Conserve America’s Lands and Resources
text:
Today, the House Committee on Natural Resources favorably reported 23 pieces of legislation. Chairman Bruce Westerman (R-Ark.) issued the following statement in response:

“The House Committee on Natural Resources is the hardest-working and most productive committee in the 119th Congress. Today, we passed 23 bills by unanimous consent to recognize America’s historic sites, improve visitor experiences to our public lands, support tribal communities and conserve species habitat. I look forward to moving these bills through regular order to deliver real results for the American people.”

Background

H.R. 1031, the Fort Ontario Holocaust Refugee Shelter National Historical Park Establishment Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. Claudia Tenney (R-N.Y.), creates the Fort Ontario National Monument in N.Y., where 982 World War II refugees were housed from August of 1944 until February of 1946.

H.R. 2323, the Big Bend National Park Boundary Adjustment Act, championed by U.S. Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas), authorizes the acquisition of approximately 6,100 acres of land to be added to Big Bend National Park.

H.R. 3286, the Mammoth Cave National Boundary Adjustment Act of 2025, introduced by U.S. Rep. Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.), expands Mammoth Cave National Park by 551 acres to include two new cave systems.

H.R. 5470, the Route 66 National Historic Trail Designation Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. Darin LaHood (R-Ill.), designates the 2,400-mile Route 66 corridor as a National Historic Trail ahead of its 100th anniversary.

H.R. 7031, the Making National Parks Safer Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher (R-Idaho), improves public safety by assisting with the transition to Next Generation 9-1-1 systems in America’s national parks, facilitating improved emergency response efforts and interoperability across the National Park System.

H.R. 7466, the Safeguarding America’s Food Economy and Controlling Agricultural Threats to Livestock and Enterprises (SAFE CATTLE) Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. Ronny Jackson (R-Texas), strengthens the federal response to New World Screwworm by requiring coordinated surveillance, prevention and eradication efforts between the Departments of Agriculture and the Interior to safeguard wildlife, livestock and the U.S. food supply.

H.R. 7495, introduced by U.S. Rep. Scott Fitzgerald (R-Wis.), authorizes the establishment of memorials to the Wisconsin infantry officers and enlisted men who fought in the Battle of Antietam and the Second Battle of Bull Run in the U.S. Civil War.

H.R. 8276, the Quindaro Townsite National Historic Landmark Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt (R-Kan.), designates the Quindaro Townsite in Kansas City, Kan., as a National Historic Landmark.

H.R. 8473, the Veterinary Services to Improve Public Health in Rural Communities Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. Nick Begich (R-Alaska), authorizes veterinary public health services for Indian tribes and tribal organizations to address zoonotic diseases and other public health initiatives in Indian Country.

H.R. 8546, the Pechanga Band of Indians Water Rights Settlement Technical Amendments Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. Darrell Issa (R-Calif.), makes technical corrections to the Pechanga Band of Luiseño Mission Indians Water Rights Settlement Act.

H.R. 8674, the Geese House Site Conveyance Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. Nick Begich (R-Alaska), transfers ownership of the Geese House Site from the National Park Service to Doyon, Limited, to ensure the culturally significant site is managed by the Alaska Native Athabascan people.

H.R. 8954, the Tribal Regulatory Reform Implementation Act of 2026, introduced by U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd (R-Colo.), updates the Indian Tribal Regulatory Reform and Business Development Act of 2000 by transferring certain administrative responsibilities for implementing the law to the Secretary of the Interior, to improve efficiency and program delivery.

H.R. 9148, the Scipio Jones House Assessment Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. French Hill (R-Ark.), directs the Secretary of the Interior to conduct a special resource study of the Scipio A. Jones House in Little Rock, Ark.

H.R. 9416, the Ocmulgee Mounds National Park Redesignation Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. Austin Scott (R-Ga.), redesignates the Ocmulgee Mounds National Historical Park as Georgia’s first national park.

H.R. 9590, the Study and Assessment of Future Ecosystems (SAFE) for Manatees Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. Daniel Webster (R-Fla.), directs the Secretary of the Interior to conduct a study on alternative habitat for certain manatees.

H.R. 2785, the New Mexico Land Grant-Mercedes Historical or Traditional Use Cooperation and Coordination Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez (D-N.M.), establishes a formal framework through a memorandum of understanding to improve coordination, permitting clarity and communication between federal land agencies and New Mexico land grant-merced communities.

H.R. 6869, introduced by U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez (D-Calif.), amends the Aamodt Litigation Settlement Act to modify a provision relating to the extension of certain dates for the completion of the Regional Water System.

H.R. 7269, the Helping Our People Act of 2026, introduced by U.S. Rep. Emily Randall (D-Wash.), amends the Puyallup Tribe of Indians Settlement Act of 1989 to clarify that amounts in the Puyallup Tribe of Indians Settlement Trust Fund may be withdrawn by the Puyallup Tribe of Indians.

H.R. 8735, the American Sovereignty and Monterey Historic Military Site Study Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. Jimmy Panetta (D-Calif.), directs the Secretary of the Interior to conduct a special resource study to assess whether the Lower Presidio Historic Park in Monterey, Calif., meets the criteria for designation as a unit of the National Park System.

H.R. 9779, the Hands Off Our Boca Chica Beach Act of 2026, introduced by U.S. Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D-Texas), formally names “Boca Chica Beach” in Texas and requires federal references to use that name.

S. 282, the Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument Access Act, introduced by Sen. Angus King (I-Maine), improves road access to the Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument in Maine.

S.1051, the Historic Greenwood District—Black Wall Street National Monument Establishment Act, introduced by U.S. Sen. James Lankford (R-Okla.), establishes the Historic Greenwood District—Black Wall Street National Monument in Tulsa, Okla.

S. 1377, the Theodore Roosevelt National Park Wild Horses Protection Act, introduced by U.S. Sen. John Hoeven (R-N.D.), directs the Department of the Interior to maintain a genetically diverse herd of feral horses, with a population of no fewer than 150 horses, in the South Unit of Theodore Roosevelt National Park in N.D.

title: Higgins Opens Hearing on the ATF’s Out-of-Business Records Retention Practices

committee.name: House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform

text:
WASHINGTON—Subcommittee on Federal Law Enforcement Chairman Clay Higgins (R-La.) delivered opening remarks at today’s hearing on “Oversight of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives’ Out-of-Business Records Retention Practices.” In his statement, Subcommittee Chairman Higgins raised concerns that the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives’ (ATF) record retention process could eventually become a national firearms registry, threatening lawful firearm owners’ Second Amendment rights. He also highlighted how ATF’s new proposed rule that would limit firearm dealers’ sales records retention requirements to 20 or 30 years could create loopholes for establishing a lifetime national firearms registry.

Below are Subcommittee Chairman Higgins’s opening remarks as delivered:

Welcome to today’s hearing of the Subcommittee on Federal Law Enforcement.

Today, we are examining a collection of records most Americans have never heard of: more than 1.4 billion firearm sales records held by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.

When someone buys a gun from a licensed dealer, they fill out a federal form with their name, address, and date of birth, along with the gun’s make, model, and serial number.

When a dealer closes without a successor, federal law requires that those records go to ATF.

And ATF keeps them indefinitely.

In Fiscal Year 2025, ATF took in roughly 6.8 million new records per month.

Federal law forbids the creation of a national gun registry.

This is to protect the Second Amendment rights of all Americans from being infringed by any future tyrannical government engaged in firearm confiscation.

Federal law thus bars ATF from creating any system to register firearms, gun owners, or gun sales.

It bars ATF from consolidating dealers’ records.

And it bars ATF from electronically searching out-of-business records by name or any other personal identifier.

ATF says it follows those rules. It says the records are pulled only to trace guns recovered by police as a result of a crime.

And the Government Accountability Office has found that the system does not currently cross the line into a registry. That’s the opinion of GAO.

So ATF’s Out of Business Records Imaging System, or OBRIS, is an existent digital record, a massive digital record. When out-of-business records are scanned, a buyer’s name can be captured as searchable data.

Searching by name is a function that ATF has simply “turned off” to remain compliant with federal law. It could just as easily be turned on.

Think about that. The difference between this database and an illegal national gun registry may come down to a software setting that ATF itself controls.

These records do have some law enforcement value, of course. I’m well aware. Tracing a gun used in a crime to its first retail buyer might give investigators a lead, and out-of-business records were used in nearly half of the crime gun traces ATF handled in 2022 and 2023.

2023. I can say from personal experience and observation that the impact on local and state law enforcement, crime investigation is almost nonexistent in these records, but nonetheless, a lead in a criminal investigation is not a conviction and a prosecution.

And ATF cannot say whether any given trace led to a successful prosecution. It doesn’t track that.

And the older a gun is, the more likely it has changed hands. That’s generally always the case. By the time a gun is recovered on a crime scene, the odds that that gun still belongs to its original owner is very slim. Perhaps it’s changed hands multiple times on the secondary market where no records are kept.

That brings us to ATF’s recent proposed rulemaking on records retention. There has never before been a cap on how long ATF is allowed to retain out-of-business dealer records. The rule for dealers has swung back and forth.

Prior to 1985, dealers were required to retain their sales records indefinitely. After 1985, a new ATF rule limited the requirement to 20 years. That 20-year mark generally settled in as acceptable across the board for a dealer to maintain records. This rule was again changed in 2022 under the Biden Administration, which again required indefinite retention.

This year, ATF proposed a new rule which would limit to either 20 or 30 years the sale records retention requirement for dealers and, for the first time, cap at either 20 or 30 years­–how long ATF itself is allowed to keep those records.

Some see that as a step in the right direction. I’m not necessarily one of those people. But those two clocks, those two 30-year clocks can stack. A record could sit with a dealer for 30 years, and then if that dealer goes out of business without a successor, [could] sit with ATF for another 30 years. That is 60 years on file for a law-abiding American’s name, address, and gun purchase data.

And what [is] more significant, perhaps–that’s 30 Congresses. And we see what can happen with the way the pendulum swings in America from one Congress to the next, the variance of laws. And what we seek today in today’s hearing is just [to] objectively put the truth on the table for the American people to consider. We have Second Amendment rights to protect, and we have an obligation to do so.

So, the question before us is not whether law enforcement should have the lawful tools it needs to solve gun crimes, of course. We support that.

But our observation, based upon accurate historical data for a long time, is that this this record retention is precariously close to an illegal federal registry. And with one push of a button, [it] could become quite a tool of oppression against American people, whereas the benefit for law enforcement is almost nonexistent.

The question before us is whether a collection this large, reaching back this far–60 years–is worth the risk to law-abiding Americans’ privacy and the risk that a gun registry would erode the Second Amendment’s guarantee that the right to keep and bear arms shall not be infringed.

With today’s hearing, we hope to weigh the principled Second Amendment concerns around ATF’s records retention practices against federal law enforcement’s interest in holding those records for some period of time.

We are honored to have expert witnesses with us today to help examine this important issue.

title: House Passes Select Committee-Supported Legislation Cracking Down on China-Linked Scam Centers

committee.name: House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party

text:
Today, the House passed Select Committee on China-supported legislation cracking down on China-linked scam centers. H.R.5490 – the Dismantle Foreign Scam Syndicates Act led by Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar (R-MI) and Congressman Jefferson Shreve (R-IN) establishes a federal task force to shut down the China-linked criminal syndicates ripping off Americans and stealing their life savings.

"Thank you to my colleagues for their strong bipartisan support of this Select Committee-supported bill. Working with Congressman Shreve and our Democratic colleagues we have passed important legislation that will go after the ruthless China-linked scam centers ripping off Americans. My committee led a bipartisan investigation into these scam centers and exposed how they are stealing more than $10 billion a year from American families. The Senate should quickly advance this legislation and put it on President Trump’s desk for him to sign into law,” said Moolenaar.

In May, Moolenaar and Select Committee Ranking Member Ro Khanna (D-CA) released a bipartisan investigation into China-linked scam centers. Crime, Corruption, and Power: CCP-Linked Transnational Crime and the Rise of a Distributed Threat to U.S. National Security, exposing a China-linked scam center network that has defrauded Americans of at least $10 billion annually while fueling human trafficking, cybercrime, and illicit finance.

“These scam centers with deep links to China are a broad network of fraud, human trafficking, cybercrime, and illicit finance that are ripping off Americans and threatening our national security,” warned Moolenaar at the time. “If the Chinese government wanted to act against these criminals, it could, but it chooses not to.”

“This investigation is about standing up for the millions of Americans who have lost billions of dollars to these scams, as well as the human trafficking victims who have been lured into scam compounds by China-linked crime syndicates. Verifiable bilateral cooperation with Beijing, alongside engagement with and funding for civil society groups, is essential to getting justice and compensation for victims of CCP-linked transnational fraud and holding these scammers accountable,” said Khanna when the report was released.

The Select Committee found that the scam centers concentrated in southeast Asia, particularly in Cambodia and Burma, are part of a distributed criminal ecosystem linking cyber fraud, human trafficking, and money laundering.

Rather than direct state control or any state-backed conspiracy, the report concludes that Chinese governance and enforcement patterns have enabled the growth of these criminal networks. Their operations rely heavily on Chinese underground banking networks, cryptocurrency brokers, and shell companies to move and launder funds across borders. The report highlights the widespread use of trafficked labor, with thousands of individuals coerced into conducting scams under threat of violence inside fortified compounds.

title: ICYMI: Moolenaar Joined Face the Nation to Discuss Nvidia and Jensen Huang

committee.name: House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party

text:
Chairman John Moolenaar of the Select Committee on China recently joined Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan to discuss Nvidia, President Donald Trump's trip to Asia, and the urgent need for Congress to pass bipartisan export control legislation.

On Trump’s Trip to Asia

“…I think it's important that the president meet with these leaders. Obviously, it's in everyone's interest to decrease the risk involving nuclear weapons, and to have those conversations is important. I don't believe any agreements are going to be made, but certainly China has resisted being part of any agreements, and if there's a way to provide more security for the American people through those kinds of discussions, I think it's important to have it.”

On Jensen Huang and Nvidia

“They said they will be forthcoming and work with the committee. Actually, three committees: Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and our China Select Committee. And we think that's going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, also to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia's philosophy, and that may have had an influence on some of our policies with respect to AI and- and export controls…

…there is an ongoing investigation into Alice Huang, but what we do know is this, she's a Chinese national, set up a company that has been able to access over $12 billion of high-end chips, and- and there's an investigation as to whether those chips were illegally smuggled into China. And for Jensen Huang to be in a relationship like that, knowing that every Chinese national can be pressured by the Chinese Communist Party to comply whatever directives they have from the intelligence, that was simply irresponsible and a direct threat to our national security. These are vital technologies that our military depend upon, our commercial entities depend upon, and for Nvidia and for Jensen Huang, not to view that as a national security risk is outrageous.”

On the Commerce Department

“I think ... we need to examine why the Commerce Department did not update their entity list for the past year. Why did Megaspeed- why was it not thoroughly investigated? We know that Singapore wanted to investigate. And now it appears that there may be a criminal investigation, or some kind of Justice Department investigation. So, why is it that export controls were so adamantly opposed by Commerce? And to what degree did Jensen Huang influence that? And to what degree was he influenced by a Chinese national?”

On AI Chip Export Controls

“Well, I think the key question is what type of chips? You know, you have the Advanced, the Blackwells, the Rubins, which the Trump administration has prohibited sales of those...we have to safeguard these crown jewels. We have to make sure that we aren't helping China's military-industrial complex, and that's why it's so important that Megaspeed should have been on the entity list because they were partnering with Alibaba, which is a designated, by Department of War, as a Chinese military company. So we have to differentiate between types of chips. We need to know where those chips are going. We need to make sure American companies have first access. We need to make sure there's not remote access or smuggling. And so all of these require- and we need to build upon some of the safeguards the Trump administration has put in place and prosecutions they have done, but also have this codified in Congress, and that's why it's going to be so important in the next few weeks that we don't let up on the gas pedal on this.”

On Why Export Controls Need to Be Law

“I think Congress has an important oversight role, but for certainty for the private sector and for continuity between administrations, you actually need acts of Congress to put that in place. And we've been working very hard to codify Trump administration policies, whether it's outbound investment or biosecurity, all of these, which are positive initiatives by the Trump administration, need to be followed up and codified in law.”

title: Moolenaar, Aderholt, Smith Lead Members in Urging Trump to Raise Political Prisoners with Xi in Shenzhen

committee.name: House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party

text:
Chairman John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China (R-MI), Values Action Team Chairman Robert B. Aderholt (R-AL), and Co-Chairman Chris Smith of the Congressional-Executive Commission on China (R-NJ), today called on President Trump to raise the issues of wrongfully detained Americans and other political prisoners with Chinese leader Xi Jinping when the two leaders meet Thursday in Shenzhen.

The lawmakers pointed to the release of Pastor Ezra Jin in July as an example of productive diplomatic engagement from the Trump administration, while encouraging recognition that other prisoners remain.

The lawmakers released the following statement:

“The fundamental freedoms of religion, of speech and of free association are endowed by our Creator on every human being, but the CCP continues to strip them from innocent people. Pastor Ezra Jin spent nearly nine months in prison for leading a church. He is free today, but there are still pastors, believers and journalists sitting in Chinese cells because of political persecution. Their welfare and freedom are a top priority.

Jimmy Lai is 78 years old and was handed a 20-year sentence for running a newspaper. A sentence that long for a man his age is a death sentence. The American people have not forgotten him and Joshua Wong, who turned 30 in jail and was recently sentenced to an additional 10 years in prison. We will continue speaking their names and advocating for their cause until they are free.

It is unconscionable that two Americans, Dr. Youlin Chen and Min Zin, and other prisoners of conscience like Dr. Gulshan Abbas; Pastor Gao Quanfu and his wife Pang Yu; members of Pastor Jin’s Beijing Zion Church; and Ilham Tohti still suffer in CCP prisons. They should all be released immediately.”

The House and Senate have already passed resolutions calling for the release of wrongfully detained Americans and prisoners of conscience. These and others include the following:

Dr. Youlin Chen and Min Zin, wrongfully detained American scholars engaging in academic research held by China on baseless suspicions of endangering national security.

Jimmy Lai, founder of Hong Kong's pro-democracy Apple Daily. He has been jailed since December 2020 and was sentenced on February 9, 2026, to 20 years.

Joshua Wong, pro-democracy student leader and activist. He has been jailed since November 2020 and was recently sentenced to 10 additional years in prison.

Dr. Gulshan Abbas, a retired Uyghur physician. She disappeared in September 2018, days after her sister Rushan Abbas spoke publicly about the persecution of Uyghurs.

Pastor Gao Quanfu and his wife, Pang Yu, Christians imprisoned for their faith.

Members of Beijing Zion Church who are still detained after the October 2025 crackdown in which Pastor Ezra Jin was arrested.

And Ilham Tohti, who was awarded the Sakharov Prize in absentia in 2019, has been unjustly imprisoned since his arrest and life sentence in 2014.

Members co-signing the statement include: Rep. Josh Brecheen (R-OK), Rep. Mary Miller (R-IL); Rep. Riley Moore (R-WV); Rep. Gary Palmer (R-AL), Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-IN); Rep. Sheri Biggs (R-SC)); Rep. Vince Fong (R-CA); Rep. Russ Fulcher (R-ID); Rep. Glenn Grothman (R-WI); Rep. Andy Harris (R-MD); Rep. Mark Harris (R-NC); Rep. Mark Messmer (R-IN); Rep. Barry Moore (R-AL) Rep. John Rutherford (R-FL); Rep. Glenn “GT” Thompson (R-PA); Rep. Randy Weber (R-TX); and Rep. Joe Wilson (R-SC).

title: Subcommittee on Contracting and Infrastructure Holds Hearing on Cybersecurity Challenges for Small Business Contractors
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congressman Tony Wied (R-WI), Chairman of the Small Business Subcommittee on Contracting and Infrastructure, held a hearing titled “Protecting Main Street, Securing America: Examining Cybersecurity Challenges for Small Business Contractors” to examine how Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) compliance requirements are affecting the small businesses that make up the backbone of America’s defense industrial base.

“At a time when cybersecurity concerns are at the forefront, it is critical for small businesses to maintain the highest-quality and most up-to-date cybersecurity infrastructure, especially when they are contracting with the federal government,” said Chairman Wied. “However, small businesses shouldn't be forced to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars to obtain a level of cybersecurity they don’t need simply because Washington has failed to provide clear rules. Today’s hearing was focused on providing that clarity and ensuring small businesses have access to the resources they need to protect their businesses, employees, and our national security."

---

Watch the full hearing here.

Below are some key excerpts from today’s hearing:

Chairman Wied:“So last week we touched on the bill, my bill H.R. 10238, which is the Cybersecurity for Small Businesses Act, passed the House. Among other things, this bill requires the Small Business Administration to coordinate with the Department of War when providing information to these small businesses about CMMC compliance. How should the Department of War use the Phase II pause to make CMMC practical for small businesses, of course, without weakening the protections?”Mr. Lattie: “Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The best way was echoed here multiple times. It’s to make sure you mark CUI correctly. That comes not only from the Department of War but also to the primes and to the tier ones. They tend to pass this along, and by the time it gets to a machine shop like Ms. Giddens, it has already been deemed CUI, when it probably shouldn’t have been. So, very clear, disciplined instructions for labeling CUI are the best first step we can take. Coordinating that for smaller businesses means that, as you pass that down to them, you give them a clear path. Show them how to do it, give them a portal, give them things that are easy to use to maintain the security.”

Chairman Williams: “Your company holds several ISO certifications, including standards that overlap significantly with CMMC’s security requirements, yet CMMC gives no formal credit for them. So, my question is: would recognizing existing certifications like these reduce the burden on small businesses without weakening security? Would that help?”Mr. Dimlich:“Absolutely. I think most of the defense industrial base got independent third-party certifications before CMMC was created. ISO 27001:2022 is actually the newest standard of NIST 800-171. It would be amazing if there were reciprocity. It would really help us.”

title: Health Subcommittee Chairwoman Dr. Miller-Meeks Leads Oversight Hearing to Examine Future of Psychedelic-Assisted Treatments for Veterans
text:
Today, Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-Iowa), the Chairwoman of the House Committee on Veterans’ Affairs Subcommittee on Health delivered the following opening remarks, as prepared, at the start the subcommittee’s oversight hearing to look into the Department of Veterans Affairs’ (VA) research into psychedelic-assisted therapies and the role they could play in addressing PTSD, depression, substance abuse disorders, and other health conditions facing veterans.

Good afternoon.

This oversight hearing of the Subcommittee on Health will now come to order.

Without objection, the Chair may declare a recess at any time.

I would like to welcome our Members and witnesses to today's hearing on psychedelic-assisted therapies for veterans.

Before we discuss the promise of these emerging therapies, I think it is important to recognize the challenges we are trying to address.

According to VA's latest National Veteran Suicide Prevention Annual Report, an average of 17 veterans died by suicide every single day in 2024.

That is more than 6,400 veterans in a single year.

And despite years of congressional attention, significant federal investments, and countless suicide prevention initiatives, those numbers have remained somewhat stagnant.

That should trouble every Member of this Committee.

As a physician and a 24-year Army veteran, I know that the wounds of military service are not always visible.

For many veterans, the effects of post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, and substance use disorders persist long after their military service has ended.

While there have been numerous advancements in research and mental healthcare, far too many veterans continue to struggle to find treatments that work for them.

We cannot accept these outcomes as inevitable.

Something needs to change.

We must continue supporting the treatments and programs that work, while recognizing that conventional approaches do not always provide relief for every veteran.

And if there are emerging therapies that could improve veterans' mental health, reduce suffering, and potentially save lives, then we have a responsibility to at least explore them at the federal level.

That is why I am proud to be leading today's hearing on psychedelic-assisted therapies for veterans.

As a physician, I understand the importance of ensuring that new treatments are supported by credible scientific evidence and appropriate safeguards.

But medical innovation also requires a willingness to explore new approaches to care.

Emerging research into substances such as MDMA and psilocybin has shown promise for treating PTSD, treatment-resistant depression, and other serious mental health conditions.

And while more research is needed, these developments should give us all a reason to be optimistic.

Fortunately, VA is uniquely positioned to help lead this effort.

With one of the largest integrated healthcare systems in the country, a robust research enterprise, and decades of experience treating veterans with complex mental health conditions, VA has the capabilities to help move these therapies from research toward clinical practice.

I am encouraged by the progress we have already seen.

In 2024, VA announced funding for its first clinical trial examining MDMA-assisted therapy for veterans suffering from PTSD and alcohol use disorder.

Earlier this year, that research moved forward with a randomized clinical trial at VA facilities in Rhode Island and Connecticut.

VA has also launched the PIVOT trial, examining the safety and effectiveness of psilocybin for veterans suffering from treatment-resistant depression.

I also want to recognize Secretary Collins and the Trump administration for the steps taken to further advance this forward-thinking research.

In April of this year, the Trump administration issued an Executive Order directing greater federal coordination to accelerate the development of treatments for serious mental illness.

Following that Executive Order, VA entered into agreements with the Department of Health and Human Services and the Food and Drug Administration to strengthen research collaboration, improve information sharing, support workforce training, and prepare for the potential clinical deployment of these therapies.

The Trump administration has also taken steps to accelerate the regulatory review of promising treatments through FDA's existing expedited development and review pathways.

These are meaningful developments, and I appreciate Secretary Collins' commitment to advancing innovative, evidence-based treatments for veterans.

But today's hearing is also about what comes next.

Because some of these emerging therapies are already in advanced stages of clinical development, and there is a real possibility that certain treatments could receive FDA approval within the next year.

That raises an important question.

Will VA be ready?

Will VA have the trained clinicians, appropriate facilities, and clinical protocols necessary to safely administer these treatments?

How quickly could approved therapies become available to eligible veterans?

And how will VA ensure that access to these treatments is not determined by where a veteran happens to live?

These are questions we should be answering now.

Preparing for the next generation of mental health care cannot begin the day a treatment receives FDA approval.

And while FDA approval is a critical milestone, it is only one part of the process.

Many of these substances remain subject to strict federal controlled-substance requirements.

Additional coordination with the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Department of Justice may be necessary to address scheduling, registration, handling, and distribution requirements.

VA, HHS, FDA, DEA, and DOJ must work together to ensure that each agency understands its responsibilities and that unnecessary regulatory delays do not prevent veterans from accessing safe and effective treatments.

We must also consider how these therapies would fit into VA's broader healthcare delivery system.

VA may not have the specialized workforce or facilities to provide these treatments at every medical center.

That is why we should examine the potential role of qualified community providers in expanding access while maintaining appropriate clinical oversight.

Congress also has an important role to play.

We need to understand whether VA has the authorities, resources, and flexibility necessary to prepare for these emerging treatments.

And we need to identify whether additional congressional action may be needed to support research, workforce development, and eventual implementation.

Today, I look forward to hearing from our witnesses about the current state of psychedelic-assisted therapies, what we have learned from the research conducted so far, and what challenges remain.

I hope to better understand what the future of these treatments could look like within VA, how prepared the federal government is for their potential approval, and how Congress can meaningfully support these efforts.

If these emerging therapies can help improve outcomes, restore hope, and save lives, then we owe it to our veterans to responsibly pursue that opportunity.

They have earned nothing less.

title: Chairman Rick Scott Holds Hearing on Reforming Programs to Reward Work

title: Chairman Johnson Releases Hearing Memo: “Social Security: The Reality… a Legal Ponzi Scheme”
text:
WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), chairman of the Committee on the Budget, released a Chairman’s Hearing Memo titled “Social Security: The Reality… a Legal Ponzi Scheme.”

Excerpts from Chairman Johnson’s Memo:

“The history and name of the program are important because they specifically describe what the original program was designed for, and by default, what it was not designed to do. It was insurance. It was not a fully funded investment and retirement plan. It provided insurance in the event a worker outlived his or her life expectancy of 62 by three years and attained the age of retirement of 65. Only then did it pay an Old-Age benefit. Disability insurance was added in 1957.

“For most of its existence, the program collected more in FICA tax revenue than it paid in benefits. That surplus was never invested in an asset that had value outside the federal government. Instead, the surplus was spent along with other tax revenue coming into the general fund, and special issue Treasury Bonds were placed in a four-drawer file in Parkersburg, West Virginia — the Social Security Trust Fund.”

…

“Unfortunately, politicians from both parties — either from their own ignorance or willful deception — have misled the American public for decades by promoting the fiction that their entire payroll deduction for Social Security was being invested in a real asset (often using the term ‘lockbox’) to earn compound interest yielding an adequate amount for retirement. Nothing could be further from the truth.”

…

“Once a Ponzi scheme begins to collapse, it can’t be fixed. It can only be liquidated, with late investors often receiving only pennies on the dollar for their end-of-scheme investments. Their only hope is that an underlying financial entity can provide a backstop to limit their losses.”

…

“A better solution would be to repeal that portion of the law that reduces Social Security benefits and quit scaring seniors. We should then roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem — our massive debt and deficits.”

Text of the memo is available HERE.

title: Cantwell, Rounds Warn AI Cyber Threats Are Outpacing U.S. Defenses; Call for Urgent White House Action to Protect Critical Infrastructure

committee.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation

text:
Citing new AI-threats to banks, websites and critical systems, Senators call for coordinated national effort to deploy AI-powered defenses and establish security standards

WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senators Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation, and Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), Chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee Subcommittee on Cybersecurity today warned that rapidly escalating AI-enabled cyber threats are outpacing the nation’s defenses and urged the White House to take immediate action to protect critical infrastructure, financial institutions and widely used software.

“AI is rapidly increasing the ability to discover and exploit weaknesses in software, and our defenses are not keeping pace,” the Senators wrote in a letter to Jay Clayton, Chair of the White House Super Intelligence Task Force. “We cannot meet these threats with yesterday’s cybersecurity infrastructure or rely on individual companies to solve a problem that spans the entire digital economy.”

The Senators cited four recent developments exposing new cybersecurity risks and called for a coordinated national effort to deploy AI-powered defenses and establish security standards for autonomous AI agents:

AI exposes global website vulnerabilities. “AI uncovered decades-old serious vulnerabilities in PHP, software used by millions of websites, leading to governments and companies shutting down their websites to patch the flaws,” they wrote. CNN reported that this vulnerability could affect up to 70% of websites globally.

Unauthorized AI agents access bank accounts. Major U.S. banks reported that unauthorized AI agents have accessed customer accounts, with banks unable to distinguish, in some cases, between authorized AI agents and rogue actors.

Cyberattacks hit Japan companies and financial institutions. A recent wave of attacks against Japanese business and financial institutions have led to large-scale data breaches and leaks, illustrating the growing threats to our digital infrastructure from AI-enabled cyberattacks.

Foreign-developed AI models raise security concerns. Researchers at Cohere reported that a Chinese-developed Qwen model attempted an unauthorized connection to a server in China during testing, highlighting the risk that AI models could access or compromise sensitive systems without users’ knowledge.

In their letter, the Senators called on the White House to move urgently on two defensive actions, bringing together leading AI developers including open-source developers, cybersecurity companies, critical infrastructure operators, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), other appropriate federal agencies, and the National Laboratories.

Speed development and deployment of defensive AI-powered tools. Deploy AI-powered tools that continuously identify vulnerabilities, develop and test fixes and block attacks before they spread. Direct NIST to develop standards for defensive AI tools and CISA to help accelerate adoption across critical infrastructure like banks, hospitals, utilities, small businesses, and government agencies.

Establish strong security standards for autonomous AI agents. Direct NIST to develop security standards for defensive AI agents to prevent them from introducing vulnerabilities, exceeding access and permission limits. These standards should strive to make AI agent behavior explainable, independently verifiable through testing, and subject to audits that assess whether organizations maintain effective security controls.

“The United States has the technological expertise to lead this effort,” the Senators concluded. “What is missing is a coordinated national strategy to bring these capabilities together, establish common security standards, and put effective defenses into widespread use.”

Today’s letter follows a letter the Senators sent to Clayton on October 13 which urged the Administration to develop a comprehensive national AI safety and cyber defense strategy.

Last month, Sen. Cantwell released her comprehensive AI governance framework to address catastrophic risks and other harms from frontier AI models.

The text of the letter can be found below and HERE.

Dear Director Clayton:

We write to urge the Super Intelligence Task Force to launch a national effort to confront a new generation of AI-enabled cyber threats. AI is rapidly increasing the ability to discover and exploit weaknesses in software, and our defenses are not keeping pace.

Four recent developments underscore the urgency:

First, last month, AI uncovered decades-old serious vulnerabilities in PHP, software used by millions of websites, leading to governments and companies shutting down their websites to patch the flaws. CNN reported that this vulnerability could affect up to 70% of websites globally.

Second, major U.S. banks have reported they are confronting unauthorized AI agents that have accessed customer accounts. In some instances, banks cannot tell whether the AI agent has been deployed on behalf of the customer or is a rogue actor. Banks are concerned that agents could access sensitive financial information or initiate transactions without proper authorization, and are strengthening security protocols to identify and control such activity.

Third, in Japan, a recent spate of cyberattacks against companies and financial institutions led to large-scale data breaches and leaks, which the Japanese government is now seeking to contain. These developments illustrate the growing exposure of our digital infrastructure to sophisticated cybersecurity threats bolstered by the power of AI.

A fourth concern is emerging with foreign-developed AI models. In a recent security test, researchers at Cohere reported that a Chinese-developed Qwen model attempted an unauthorized connection to a server in China. Although the finding does not establish deliberate malicious behavior, it underscores the risk that AI models could introduce vulnerabilities, make unauthorized connections, or compromise sensitive systems without users’ knowledge.

The fundamental problem is that AI can discover software weaknesses and help attackers exploit them faster than many organizations can respond. Even when fixes are available, testing and installing patches across interconnected systems can take weeks or months, potentially disrupting essential services. At the same time, autonomous AI agents capable of writing code, accessing sensitive systems, and taking actions independently are introducing new security risks. We cannot meet these threats with yesterday’s cybersecurity infrastructure or rely on individual companies to solve a problem that spans the entire digital economy.

We therefore urge the Super Intelligence Task Force to convene leading AI developers including open-source developers, cybersecurity companies, critical infrastructure operators, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), other appropriate federal agencies, and the National Laboratories around two urgent defensive priorities:

Use the full suite of cyber tools to secure our existing digital infrastructure. This includes using defensive AI-powered tools that continuously identify vulnerabilities, develop and test fixes, and detect and block attacks before they spread. But finding vulnerabilities is not enough. Organizations also need ways to protect exposed systems immediately, including patching to block attacks and installing permanent fixes. NIST, working with relevant federal agencies, industry, academic researchers, and independent security experts, should develop risk-based guidance, evaluation methods, and standards for defensive AI tools.

CISA should help accelerate their adoption across critical infrastructure. To protect our U.S. economy and the public, these capabilities must reach banks, hospitals, utilities, small businesses, and government agencies—not just the largest technology companies. Priority should also be given to securing federal websites, widely used software that underpins the internet, and the supply chains supporting national security, including defense contractors. This effort should build on existing open cybersecurity standards and industry initiatives, including the Linux Foundation’s Open Secure AI Alliance.

Secure the AI agents we use to discover vulnerabilities in systems. The same agents that can discover vulnerabilities and repair software can also introduce dangerous code, exceed their instructions, or gain unauthorized access to sensitive systems. These risks include agents that introduce vulnerabilities into software, conceal unauthorized activity, or make connections to external systems without authorization. NIST should lead the development of security standards for defensive AI agents and the environments in which they operate, including standards for secure testing environments, limits on system access and permissions, and continuous monitoring. These standards should also address the security of the models and software supply chains on which agents depend, including risks associated with foreign-developed models. These standards should strive to make AI agent behavior explainable, independently verifiable through testing, and subject to audits that assess whether organizations maintain effective security controls.

These two priorities must advance together. More powerful defensive AI will accomplish little if organizations cannot use it quickly and safely. And expanding autonomous AI without effective security controls risks creating new vulnerabilities even as we close existing ones.

To translate these priorities into action, we urge the Task Force to launch a national cyber defense grand challenge. Building on proposals such as the Institute for Progress’s Operation Patchlight, the initiative should mobilize government, industry, National Laboratories, and researchers to use AI to find and fix vulnerabilities in widely used software and critical parts of the web. The challenge should demonstrate, across participating federal systems, critical infrastructure, and defense supply chains, that AI-enabled defenses can cut the time from discovery of a critical vulnerability to effective protection. NIST should establish independent methods to measure performance and security, including the speed and reliability of fixes and relevant agencies should coordinate practical deployment and help scale successful approaches nationally.

The United States has the technological expertise to lead this effort. What is missing is a coordinated national strategy to bring these capabilities together, establish common security standards, and put effective defenses into widespread use.

We urge the Super Intelligence Task Force to make these priorities central to its mission and develop a concrete plan for federal agencies and industry to act. That plan should identify a national grand challenge, assign agency responsibilities, establish measurable milestones, and specify the resources and authorities needed to carry it out. AI is changing cybersecurity at unprecedented speed. Our national response must match that urgency.

Sincerely,

###

title: Statement from Commerce Committee Democrats

title: Commerce Republicans Advance Slate of Bipartisan Bills and Nominations

committee.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee advanced four of President Trump’s nominations, twelve bills, and multiple Coast Guard promotions. For the second time in the 119th Congress, Committee Democrats boycotted the committee markup, which advanced bipartisan legislation and followed the typical nomination process.

The following actions were taken during today’s Executive Session:

Nominations advanced by roll call vote:

Nomination of Ms. Leslie Becera, of Virginia, to be an Assistant Secretary of Transportation

15 Yeas

Nomination of Ms. Danielle Thumann Severs, of North Carolina, to be a Member of the Federal Communications Commission

15 Yeas

Nomination of Mr. Joshua Shoemaker, of Virginia, to be Chief Financial Officer of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration

15 Yeas

Nomination of Mr. Robert Steinau, of Maryland, to be Inspector General of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration

15 Yeas

Legislation advanced by voice vote:

S. 69, COLLUDE Act, as amended by the Schmitt substitute and Cantwell 5

S. 2586, MARA Act of 2025, as amended by the Wicker substitute, as modified, and Sullivan 1

S. 2883, Quantifying Uncertainty and Action to Help Optimize Growth of Shellfish Act of 2025, as amended by the Blunt Rochester substitute

S. 3301, Chip EQUIP Act, as amended by the Blackburn substitute

S. 3741, Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026, as amended by the Klobuchar substitute, as modified

S. 3954, No Lifeline for Dead People Act, as amended by the Cruz substitute, as modified, Markey 1, as modified, and Markey 5

S. 4256, Airmen Certificate Accessibility Act, as amended by the Sheehy-Kim substitute

S. 5251, ACPAC Modernization Act

S. 5332, Cooperative Institute Act of 2026, as amended by the Cantwell substitute, as modified

S. 5508, Telecommunications Cybersecurity and Resilience Act, as amended by the Cruz substitute, as modified

S. 5663, PROOF Act, as amended by the Lummis substitute, as modified

S. 5718, Trucker Bathroom Access Act, as amended by the Blunt Rochester substitute, as modified

Nominations advanced by voice vote:

Coast Guard Promotions (PN 1355, PN 1356, PN 1357, PN 1438, PN 1470, PN 1471)

Chairman Cruz’s remarks as delivered:

“Yesterday, I received a letter from members of the minority urging me to postpone a vote on Danielle Thumann, who’s been nominated to the Federal Communications Commission. The opening sentence of the letter explained that ‘The recent elections returned control of both chambers of Congress to the Democrats.’ Apparently, that means the Democrats don’t need to show up for work anymore.

“Look, Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January, but today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent for our full terms. As Senator Cantwell put it a few years ago, ‘Advice and consent isn’t an option. It’s an obligation.’ So we’re going to be doing our job today, even if the Democrats refuse to show up to do theirs.

“It’s a shame, really, because this is now the second time that the Democrats have boycotted a markup this Congress. We never saw that at this committee last Congress when the Democrats had the majority, when Senator Cantwell was chairman. Not once did Republicans do what Democrats have done twice now, which is boycott the meeting and throw a temper tantrum because they did not like the choice of the American voters at the previous election. And candidly, it’s a terrible harbinger heading into next year. What it should tell all of us is the Democrats have zero intention of processing any of the president’s nominees. We are heading into two years of total obstruction, total war. Partisan warfare is what the Democrats are promising us. By the way, on the campaign trail, they talked about affordability. Affordability is now gone. This is just open Democrat war.

“Ms. Thumann’s nomination followed a typical process. President Trump nominated her way back in August. She was scheduled to testify before this committee in September, but she went into labor just before the hearing, leading us to have to postpone it to last week. So the Democrats who love to boast about their support of working mothers are now punishing a woman for having a baby and taking a few days of maternity leave. We’ve had plenty of time to vet Ms. Thumann, and all throughout that time, my colleagues never suggested that moving this nomination was a red line. We didn’t learn about this boycott until last night, after staff on both sides had spent countless hours preparing for the markup.

“So what’s the issue? Some Democrats oppose Ms. Thumann because President Trump did not pair her with a Democrat FCC nominee, but there’s no evidence that Democrats actually worked with the Trump administration to have a Democrat nominated to the FCC.

“The administration has shown it’s willing to move Democrats this week. Senate committees are voting on bipartisan pairs for the CFTC and the SEC. Of course, there’s nothing that requires the president to nominate in pairs, and this committee has moved FCC nominees separately in the past. The law merely says that no more than three of the commissioners may be from the same party. If confirmed, Ms. Thumann would be the third Republican FCC commissioner, consistent with that requirement.

“I’ll also note that while the Supreme Court decided in Trump v. Slaughter that President Trump has the authority to dismiss commissioners of independent regulatory agencies, he has not fired any FCC commissioners. Commissioners Nathan Simington and Geoffrey Starks voluntarily resigned in June of 2025. Ms. Thumann is nominated to fill the vacancy left by former commissioner Simington, a Republican. This is an ordinary nomination to fill a vacancy previously held by someone of the same party.

“There’s ample precedent for advancing nominations during a lame duck session. In fact, in December 2024, I want us to remember back to what we did in December 2024. This committee under Democratic leadership and despite the Democrats getting trounced in an election the month earlier, November of 2024, this committee advanced eight of President Biden’s nominees before the new Congress was sworn in.

“Republicans didn’t boycott that markup. We could have. I even praised the committee chair for her leadership at the time. I made the motion to advance the nominees. So let’s evaluate our nominees on their own records. Let’s actually do our jobs. Ms. Thumann, for her part, has substantial experience at the FCC and in communications law. This committee on the merits should advance her nomination today.

“By the end of this markup, the committee will have advanced more than 120 pieces of legislation in the last two years. It’s a record we should all be proud of Republicans and Democrats alike. I’d intended to commend both the Republicans and Democrats on this committee for a remarkable record of success. Unfortunately, half the members of this committee decided not to be here. Although I can’t tell her in person this morning, I look forward to working hand in hand with Ranking Member Cantwell when she takes over the gavel in January. And this committee will continue to be productive, but having half the committee refuse to show up for work is not helpful to getting our work done.”

title: ICYMI: Schools Urge House to Vote Now on Protect College Sports Act

committee.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Student athletes, coaches, professors, and presidents from universities and colleges across the country continue to rally behind the bipartisan Protect College Sports Act and urge the House of Representatives to quickly vote on the bill. Authored by Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas), Ranking Member Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), and Senators Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) and Chris Coons (D-Del.), the Protect College Sports Act passed the Senate with a broad bipartisan vote of 77-22.

Nick Saban, legendary college football coach, and Gordon Gee, university president for over four decades, stated in their op-ed: “The Senate seized the opportunity. The House should do the same and send the Protect College Sports Act to President Trump’s desk without delay when it returns to session. Not for universities, and not for coaches, but for young people whose futures will be shaped by college sports.”

Colleges, universities, and stakeholders across the country are urging the House of Representatives to take up and pass the Protect College Sports Act before the end of the 119th Congress, including:

Colleges and Universities in California, Connecticut, New York, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, and Washington

Members of the President’s Roundtable on Fixing College Sports

United States Olympic and Paralympic Committee

Individuals and organizations representing colleges and universities, conferences, and student-athletes, fans, and alumni

AJ Larkin, a student at the University of Maryland, wrote in his op-ed: “This bill does exactly that. We are running out of time to get meaningful legislation passed. There is a reason why so many coaches, universities, athletic directors, student-athletes, major sports leagues and law professionals across the country support this bill. The House should do the right thing for student-athletes and pass this bill without delay.”

TJ Johnson, a student at the Virginia Military Institute, wrote in his op-ed: “The Protect College Sports Act would provide that stability while also preserving many of the opportunities that today’s student athletes have fought to earn. It would protect our ability to benefit from our name, image and likeness, establish clearer transfer and eligibility standards, strengthen protections for scholarships and medical expenses, and give student-athletes a greater voice in decisions that directly affect us. Just as importantly, it would provide structure to a system that has changed at a pace few athletes, coaches or fans have been able to keep up with.”

The Connecticut Legal Roundtable stated: “Some may think our national legislators ought to have better things to do with their time than try to protect college sports. But if Congress can get this right, maybe the many people deeply invested in college athletics will recognize that Congress, like a championship coach, can have a real and positive impact on our lives.”

Op-eds supporting the Protect College Sports Act:

Kadence Berry, student athlete, cross-country and track athlete, Lindenwood University

Ruben Rojas Betanzos, student athlete, cross country, Syracuse University

Lumpy (Liam) Deweese, student athlete, football, University of West Florida

Sophia Stylianos, student athlete, rowing, University of Michigan

Temple Landry, student athlete, gymnastics, Stanford University

Henry Gibbs, student athlete, swimming and diving, Georgia Tech

Ella Brooks, student athlete, track and field, Clemson University

John Davis, Vice President and Director of Athletics, Florida A&M University

Matthew Mittin, Professor of law and senior advisor at Marquette University Law School’s National Sports Law Institute

Chicago Tribune Editorial Board

Jerry Brewer, senior sports columnist, The Athletic

Jay Hartzell, President, Southern Methodist University

Dwayne Yancey, founding editor, Cardinal News

Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas)

Senate Commerce Committee Ranking Member Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.)

The Protect College Sports Act additionally has the support of 32 collegiate athletic conferences and more than 380 colleges and universities across all 50 states and Washington, D.C., including Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs). Additional endorsements for the bill include: the National Football League (NFL), Major League Baseball (MLB), the National Hockey League (NHL), the National Basketball Association (NBA), the players associations for the NFL and the NBA, the American Football Coaches Association (AFCA), and the National Association of Basketball Coaches (NABC), FBS Athletics Directors Association. To emphasize this support, Chairman Cruz hosted a press conference in September with coaches and student athletes.
