title: EPW Committee Advances Schwab Nomination, Approves Resolutions at Business Meeting

committee.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee, led a business meeting where the EPW Committee advanced the nomination of Justin Schwab to be Assistant Administrator for the Office of Air and Radiation (OAR) at the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and voted in favor of eight resolutions to approve prospectuses from the General Services Administration.

Below is the opening statement of Chairman Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) as delivered.

“Today, we will consider the nomination of Justin Schwab, we had him before the committee last week, to be Assistant Administrator for the Office of Air and Radiation at the Environmental Protection Agency. Mr. Schwab is well-qualified and equipped to serve in the role to which he has been nominated.

“He previously served as General Counsel at CEQ, as well as Deputy General Counsel at the EPA during the first Trump Administration. In between the first and second Trump Administration, Mr. Schwab founded a law practice in Washington D.C., where he represented regulated entities and provided legal counsel on Clean Air Act and other environmental matters.

“Last week, we heard from Mr. Schwab on how he plans to use his wealth of experience in environmental law to ensure that the EPA continues to carry out its role in protecting public health and environment, consistent with the statutory authority that Congress has provided to the Agency. His testimony and answers demonstrated his deep understanding of the Clean Air Act and related programs administered by OAR.

“Mr. Schwab highlighted the importance of cooperative federalism and recognized the significance of durable and legally defensible regulations. I have confidence that Mr. Schwab will help the Agency to fulfill its core mission and reject pushing unlawful regulations that threaten energy affordability and the reliability of our electric grid.

“I look forward to working with him to strengthen communities across the country. I urge my colleagues to support Mr. Schwab’s nomination.

“We will also have a roll call vote on a prospectus to authorize the relocation of the Department of Energy’s headquarters. This will allow for the long-anticipated disposal of the James V. Forrestal Building.

“Finally, we will consider seven prospectuses en bloc from the General Services Administration that concern leases for various Veterans Administration facilities and federal buildings throughout the country. I urge my colleagues to vote to approve these prospectuses.”

title: Crapo Statement at Executive Session to Consider Treasury and Commerce Nominations
text:
Washington, D.C.—U.S. Senate Finance Committee Chairman Mike Crapo (R-Idaho) delivered the following remarks at an executive session to consider the nominations of Francis Browne to be an Under Secretary of the Treasury, Christopher Abbott to be an Assistant Secretary of Commerce and Robert Stebbins to be General Counsel for the Treasury.

As prepared for delivery:

“We meet today, in executive session, to consider favorably reporting the nominations of the following individuals: Francis Browne to be Under Secretary of the Treasury for Domestic Finance; Christopher “Chris” Abbott to be Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance at the Department of Commerce; and Robert “Bob” Stebbins to be General Counsel of the Department of Treasury.

“As is our usual process, members will have an opportunity this morning to offer their remarks on the nominees.

“Members will be notified of the time and location off the Senate floor to conduct the vote later today on the nominees.

“During last week’s hearing, Mr. Browne emphasized the importance of maintaining strong and stable financial markets, including preserving the strength of the Treasury market, promoting appropriately tailored financial regulation and supporting innovation in the financial sector.

“I appreciated his commitment to ensuring our financial system continues to support economic growth, expand opportunities for American families and businesses and maintain our nation’s leadership in global finance.

“Mr. Abbott discussed the important responsibility of the Department of Commerce’s Office of Enforcement and Compliance to administer our nation’s trade remedy laws and ensure American workers and businesses can compete on a level playing field.

“I was encouraged by his commitment to enforcing our trade laws fairly and effectively, including by addressing unfair foreign subsidies and pricing practices, while ensuring decisions are transparent, well-reasoned and grounded in the law.

“Mr. Stebbins highlighted his past experiences as the General Counsel of the Securities and Exchange Commission and the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation.

“He also emphasized the important role the Treasury Legal Division plays in providing sound legal counsel on matters critical to our nation’s financial and economic interests. I welcomed his commitment to issuing timely guidance and maintaining a productive working relationship with Congress.

“I am voting in favor of each nominee and encourage my colleagues to do the same.”

title: Finance Committee Advances Treasury and Commerce Nominations
text:
Washington, D.C.—The U.S. Senate Finance Committee advanced the nominations of Francis Browne to be an Under Secretary of the Treasury by a vote of 14-13, Christopher Abbott to be an Assistant Secretary of Commerce by a vote of 14-13 and Robert Stebbins to be General Counsel for the Treasury by a vote of 14-13.

Following the vote, Chairman Mike Crapo (R-Idaho) issued the statement below:

“I commend the Committee’s action and congratulate each nominee.

“Mr. Browne understands the importance of maintaining strong and stable financial markets and supporting innovation in the financial sector. His commitment to these priorities will be valuable in maintaining our nation’s leadership in global finance.

“Mr. Abbott recognizes the critical role the Department of Commerce’s Office of Enforcement and Compliance plays in enforcing our trade laws fairly and effectively. His commitment to addressing unfair foreign trade practices will help to ensure American workers and businesses can compete abroad on a level playing field.

“Mr. Stebbins has extensive legal and regulatory experience from his service as the General Counsel of the Securities and Exchange Commission and the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation. His background will serve him well in providing sound legal counsel on matters critical to our nation’s financial and economic interests.

“I am confident in each nominee’s qualifications and look forward to their confirmation by the full Senate.”

title: Wyden Statement at Finance Committee Markup on Treasury Nominees
text:
The Finance Committee met with these nominees last week, just a few days after voters across the country made clear that they don’t like the direction the Trump administration is taking on just about anything.

Members on this side of the dais were hoping these nominees would demonstrate at least a bit of independence. Would they show us they’re prepared to approach these important jobs in an evenhanded way, or would they continue to be Trump loyalists? From where I sit, I didn’t come away reassured.

These are serious jobs they’re nominated to fill. The general counsel of the Treasury Department needs to be prepared to stand up to the secretary and the White House when people want to break the law. The Undersecretary of Domestic Finance at the Treasury has their hands on some of the most sensitive and highly protected data in our government. Assistant Commerce Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance is a role with big influence over tariffs and trade policy.

So what’s at stake here is lawlessness at the Treasury Department, the abuse of Americans’ personal data, and failed tariff policies that are driving up costs for families nationwide. On these issues, the American people need a change of direction. I don’t expect they’ll get it from these nominees.

Here’s my bottom line on Trump nominations. From the top on down, the Trump administration is a corruption machine that occasionally dabbles in federal policymaking. It doesn’t make sense to me why anybody wants to sign up to be a part of it. Working for this president will be a black mark people ought to carry around forever.

The Trump administration is a trainwreck. The Congress cannot allow it to be staffed with a bunch of loyalists and yes-men. I will not support these nominees.

###

title: Ranking Member Shaheen, Senate Foreign Relations Democrats Statement Ahead of President Trump's Meetings with Xi and Putin
text:
WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senators Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Chris Coons (D-DE), Tim Kaine (D-VA), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Brian Schatz (D-HI), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) and Jacky Rosen (D-NV) released the following statement ahead of President Trump's meetings with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit:

“President Trump must use this summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin to defend American interests and values and confront the growing threats posed by Beijing and Moscow—not simply look out for his own bottom line.

“This meeting must not be yet another convergence of would-be-strongmen, carving up the world into spheres of influence, but an American president fighting for American values, including the rule of law. He must stand up to President Xi and make clear that the United States will strictly enforce export controls to prevent Beijing from exploiting American technology to erode our economic and national security advantages. He must confront China’s military intimidation of Taiwan and reaffirm our commitments under the Taiwan Relations Act and the Six Assurances by following the law and sending $14 billion in previously approved arms sales to Taiwan. He must also demand the release of Jimmy Lai, Min Zin and all other Americans wrongfully detained in China.

“China and Russia are cooperating in unprecedented and dangerous ways to undermine American security and prosperity. Xi and Putin cannot be allowed to use this meeting as a forum to advance their interests at the expense of the United States. The President should not let China’s indispensable support for Russia’s brutal war against Ukraine continue; he must crack down on Chinese suppliers and financial institutions facilitating Putin’s war machine that murders Ukrainian civilians with every passing day. This can only be achieved by standing up to Xi and Putin, rather than accommodating their imperial impulses. President Trump must be prepared to tell Putin unequivocally that European security is non-negotiable and that there will be no talks about Ukraine without Ukraine.

“American security cannot be traded away for photo opportunities or personal aggrandizement. President Trump must demonstrate that he is prepared to impose real costs on Putin for his aggression, rather than reward him with concessions that undermine Ukraine, our NATO Allies and U.S. national security. It is clear that the American people want lower prices, not more pageantry. We urge President Trump to use this summit to make Americans safer, strengthen our alliances and counter the destructive actions of our adversaries.”

title: Chairman Cassidy Delivers Remarks Before Advancing Labor, Education Nominations

committee.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions

text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Bill Cassidy, M.D. (R-LA), Chairman of the U.S. Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) Committee, delivered remarks before today’s vote on nominations for the U.S. Department of Education, Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission, and Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC). Mark Priebe, Michael Doyle, and Catherine Eschbach were all advanced by a 12-10 vote. All nominations will now move to the Senate floor for a final vote at a later date.

The approved nominations include:

Mark Priebe, of Virginia, to be Inspector General, Department of Education.

Michael Doyle, of Pennsylvania, to be a Member of the Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission.

Catherine Eschbach, of Texas, to be General Counsel of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

Click here to watch the full executive session.

Cassidy’s opening remarks as prepared for delivery can be found below:

The Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee will please come to order.

Last night, the White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton, saying she did not have the votes to pass. Which is odd because I was having productive conversations with members. I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate. My conversations with her convinced me she would follow the science and push back against decisions that put Americans’ health at risk. The other issue was that pro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding their commitment to life issues. Rather than making such commitments, the Administration withdrew Dr. Overton, Unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats.

We will also not consider the nomination of Jim O’Neill. As Acting CDC Director, Mr. O’Neill did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements from Secretary Kennedy. His role in the firing of Dr. Susan Monarez raises further concerns about the independent judgment he would bring to NSF. Several members of the committee had concerns regarding this. I like Jim personally, but this time requires leadership and fortitude in standing up for what is right.

As for the other nominees.

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission needs a General Counsel who will enforce federal civil rights laws in an even-handed manner and give all workers the legal representation they deserve. Catherine Eschbach is that person. Her legal experience in private practice, judicial clerkships and significant pro bono work on behalf of domestic abuse victims will serve her well in the role for which she is nominated. As Acting General Counsel and Principal Deputy General Counsel of the EEOC, Ms. Eschbach has the experience needed to be successful.

Michael Doyle is another qualified nominee. As a member of the Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission, Mr. Doyle will be tasked with reducing the backlog of cases and improving the timeliness of decisions, while serving as a fair and neutral arbiter of disputes between OSHA and employers. Mr. Doyle will bring with him a valuable 20 plus years of legal experience at the Department of Labor.

I also look forward to supporting Mark Priebe’s nomination to be Inspector General of the Department of Education. He has already proven himself capable, as he has been successful as Acting Inspector General for almost a year and brings more than 22 years of experience in auditing, financial management, and government oversight with him. I have full confidence in his ability to combat federal student aid fraud, reform grant oversight and make the Office of Inspector General more efficient. We held a bipartisan meeting to review concerns raised about Mr. Priebe individuals at OIG. I am satisfied with his answers and am comfortable moving forward with his nomination.

With that, I recognize Senator Sanders.

title: As Republicans Shirk Committee Norms, Durbin Grills Judicial Nominees About Their Lack Of Judicial Temperament, Involvement In Baseless Prosecution Of James Comey
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, today questioned judicial nominees during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing with two panels beginning with Justice James Cody Hiland, nominated to be a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit. During the second panel, Durbin pressed Philip Lawrence Aubart, nominated to the Middle District of North Carolina; Judge Brian Meyers, nominated to the Eastern District of North Carolina; and Justice James Sullivan, nominated to the Western District of Texas.

Before questioning Justice Hiland about his temperament, Durbin raised the alarm about Republicans abandoning the longstanding 28-day-rule, which requires that the Committee receive a nominee’s Senate Judiciary Questionnaire at least 28 days before their hearing. Justice Hiland’s Questionnaire was transmitted just seven days ago.

“You’re asking to be given that opportunity for life, for the rest of your natural life, to serve in that capacity. To say that we take this seriously is exactly what we’re supposed to do up here,” Durbin said to Justice Hiland. “We’re asked to ask serious questions so we can understand whether you are right for that job. It is also quite possible that we are troubled by the fact that we’ve had the response to your extensive questionnaires about your background, we’ve had access to that for seven days. That’s it. You would be the shortest period of time of any nominee that we received a questionnaire in the 28 years I’ve served on this Committee. To think we’re asking tough questions, that’s the reason. We have limited opportunity to review your background, and you are seeking the second highest court in the land for a lifetime appointment.”

Durbin then pressed Justice Hiland about his lack of judicial temperament when White House staff offered him a nomination to a district court in August 2026 rather than a nomination to the Eighth Circuit, which he was expecting. Months after he rejected the nomination to the district court vacancy, Justice Hiland was nominated to the Eighth Circuit after the Trump Administration withdrew Judge Lee Rudofsky’s nomination to the seat. Durbin questioned Justice Hiland on whether he has the temperament to serve in this lifetime appointment.

“In August, you spoke to a group of law students about the selection process to the federal bench. You told them that you had expected to receive a call from President Trump informing you of his intent to nominate you to this Eighth Circuit. Instead, you received a call from staff at the White House asking if you would be interested in filling a district court vacancy. Calling yourself ‘belligerent,’ you declined the offer. When asked by White House staff if they should ‘go back into the Oval Office and tell the President of the United States that you’re rejecting an opportunity to be appointed to the federal bench?’ You responded, ‘Yes, that’s exactly what I want you to tell the President of the United States,’” Durbin said.

“Do you still consider yourself ‘belligerent?’” Durbin asked Justice Hiland. “Can you control your emotions if you’re given this opportunity?” Durbin asked.

Justice Hiland claimed that his career as a prosecuting attorney and Arkansas Supreme Court justice has shown that he is capable of separating his emotions from the facts.

Durbin then asked Justice Hiland about a recent scandal at the Office of Professional Programs, which is overseen by the Arkansas Supreme Court, where he has served since 2023. In 2026, Nancie Givens, the former executive director of the Arkansas Office of Professional Programs, was arrested and charged with 65 felony counts of tampering with a public record. Investigators allege that, between July 2020 and July 2025, Givens had been deliberately altering bar exam scores. According to a press release signed by six of the seven justices on the Arkansas Supreme Court, including Justice Hiland, the court was informed about the irregularities in test scores and recordkeeping as early as February 2026; however, the criminal investigation was not initiated until April 2026. Further, a seal order has been put in place, eliminating any transparency about where the case stands.

“Earlier this month, the former executive director of the Arkansas Supreme Court’s Office of Professional Programs was arrested and charged with 65 felony counts for allegedly tampering with bar exam scores in the state of Arkansas, including adding points to scores that allowed them to pass rather than fail. The alleged misconduct took place between 2020 and 2025. You have sat on the Supreme Court since 2023… When were you first made aware of these irregularities with the bar exams?” Durbin asked Justice Hiland.

Justice Hiland claimed he was made aware in May of this year, though months earlier he had signed the press release issued by the Arkansas Supreme Court noting that it was aware of the test score irregularities.

“When were the individuals who should have failed the bar exam but are now practicing notified of the discrepancies in their scoring?” Durbin asked.

Justice Hiland replied that because this is an ongoing criminal investigation, there has been no communication with those who were incorrectly informed that they had passed the bar exam.

“For clarity, I would like to have you state for the record, under oath, whether you played any role… in the wrongdoing that’s been alleged,” Durbin said.

Justice Hiland said he was not involved in any wrongdoing.

Video of Durbin’s questions in Committee for Panel I is available here.

Audio of Durbin’s questions in Committee for Panel I is available here.

Footage of Durbin’s questions in Committee for Panel I is available here for TV Stations.

During the second panel, Durbin grilled Justice Sullivan about his nomination to the Western District of Texas, which the Committee was notified of just one day after he lost his election to the Texas Supreme Court and only two weeks before his scheduled hearing.

“What an amazing story. I have been a candidate in a lot of elections, but I’ve never had a consolation prize like this. So here you are running for the Texas Supreme Court, and you don’t know you have lost until the night before, but yet you have a Questionnaire filled out to file the next day for this federal court position. What am I missing here?” Durbin asked Justice Sullivan.

Justice Sullivan said that he first expressed interest in federal judicial service in March 2025.

“You certainly have friends in high places if you can lose an election one night and file a Questionnaire the next morning for a different judgeship. That’s quite a rebound,” Durbin replied.

Durbin then turned to Mr. Aubart and Judge Meyers, asking them about their involvement in the Trump Administration’s efforts to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey. Durbin first asked Mr. Aubart about his time serving as the First Assistant U.S. Attorney in the Eastern District of North Carolina.

“At President Trump’s urging, the Justice Department is implausibly claiming that former FBI Director Mr. Comey threatened to kill the President because he posted a picture of seashells in the formation of ‘86 47’ on social media….You [have] served as First Assistant U.S. Attorney in the Eastern District of North Carolina since 2025…[The First Assistant] typically oversees the office’s operations and supervises a large staff of prosecutors and professional staff…yet you have taken an unusually hands-on approach to the Comey prosecution,” Durbin said.

“In April 2026, you and a case agent directed the FBI to conduct keyword searches of trial transcripts from U.S. vs. Gambino, a case Comey prosecuted more than 30 years ago. What were you looking for?” Durbin asked Mr. Aubart.

Mr. Aubart said he was searching for any reference to “86” during the Gambino trial.

“Did you find it?” Durbin followed up.

Mr. Aubart said he found no reference to “86.”

“You traveled around the country to interview multiple witnesses, including to Phoenix. What did you do in Phoenix?” Durbin continued.

“Sammy the Bull was interviewed in Phoenix,” Mr. Aubart replied, referring to Salvator Gravano, who was a witness in the Gambino trial.

“What did he have to do with seashells?” Durbin pressed.

Mr. Aubart said he spoke with Mr. Gravano about his knowledge of the term “86,” but Mr. Aubart declined to provide additional details about their conversation.

“Did this case ever come up in your interviews with the Justice Department or the White House Counsel Office for this judgeship?” Durbin asked Mr. Aubart.

Mr. Aubart said he raised it as a potential topic of questioning during his nomination hearing.

Two months after signing the search warrants, Judge Meyers was contacted by U.S. Senator Ted Budd (R-NC) about his interest in serving as a district judge.

“Did this case ever come up in your interviews with the Justice Department or the White House Counsel?” Durbin asked Judge Meyers.

Judge Meyers replied that it did not.

title: Durbin Criticizes Senate Republicans For Violating Committee Norms To Jam Through Extreme, Unqualified Judicial Nominees Before Democrats Take Senate Majority
text:
WASHINGTON – During today’s Senate Judiciary Committee nominations hearing, U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, delivered an opening statement again calling out Senate Republicans for violating longstanding bipartisan Committee norms to jam through the Trump Administration’s extreme and unqualified nominees during the lame-duck session. In addition to calling out Committee Republicans for missing multiple opportunities to slate nominees for earlier hearings and bypassing standards that allowed Committee staff to review each nominee’s FBI background check, Durbin criticized the Trump Administration for nominating extreme and unqualified individuals to lifetime appointments.

Nominees considered during today’s hearing include James Cody Hiland, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Eighth Circuit; Philip Lawrence Aubart, to be U.S. District Judge for the Middle District of North Carolina; Brian S. Meyers, to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of North Carolina; Eric James Hamilton, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Nebraska; William Grayson Lambert, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of South Carolina; Joseph Patrick Falvey, to be U.S. District Judge for the Northern District of Indiana; and James P. Sullivan, to be U.S. District Judge for the Western District of Texas.

Key Quotes:

“Just eight days after the Committee’s last nominations hearing, we’re back again because Senate Republicans are determined to confirm as many nominees as possible before control of the Senate shifts in six weeks. We’re here because the Trump White House has been slow to send nominations to the Senate.”

“Now the majority has resorted to breaking, if not changing, longstanding bipartisan Committee norms that Committee Chairs of both parties followed for decades to ensure that every member had adequate time to evaluate the nominees before us.”

“A longstanding rule, going back to at least the George W. Bush Administration, is that the Committee does not hold a hearing on a nomination until at least 28 days after the nominee’s Senate Judiciary Questionnaire is submitted. Today, we have nominees before us whose Questionnaires were received 14 days ago, and in one case, 7 days ago. This is for a lifetime appointment. It’s understandable that we’d ask for a little time to review a person’s background before the decision is made.”

“As I said yesterday, the Chairman and majority are within their rights to slate any nominee they’d like for a hearing. But it bears repeating: my Republican colleagues will regret changing our 28-day-rule to a 7-day rule.”

“We received Justice Cody Hiland’s Questionnaire one week ago. This came after Justice Hiland publicly complained about the White House passing him over for another nominee, Judge Lee Rudofsky. The nomination of Judge Rudofsky, who already had a hearing before this Committee, was withdrawn, and Justice Hiland received the nomination he publicly asked for.”

“I have deep concerns with Justice Hiland’s record. His partisan roles as Chairman of the Arkansas Republican Party and a Senior Advisor on Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders’s campaign led to a seat on the state’s Supreme Court. On the bench, he has made it harder for Arkansans to vote and upended 75 years of precedent to weaken voter initiatives.”

“We have another state Supreme Court Justice before us today, James Sullivan, nominated to the Western District of Texas. This is an amazing political story. Two weeks ago, Justice Sullivan lost his bid to be reelected to the Texas Supreme Court. The very next day, the Administration submitted his Questionnaire, which had obviously been prepared in advance. It appears that a federal district court appointment for life is the consolation prize if you lose an election for the Texas Supreme Court.”

“Republicans are violating Committee norms to rush through this nominee because they want to deny the incoming Senator any voice in the process.”

“Also on today’s slate is Eric Hamilton, nominated to the District of Nebraska. He is currently a senior DOJ official, defending the Trump Administration’s blatantly unconstitutional actions in court…A federal judge said, ‘the Court is left with little confidence that [he] can be trusted to tell the truth about anything.’”

“Finally, the two North Carolina nominees before us today have played leading roles in the prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey for the alleged crime of posting a picture of seashells—one of President Trump’s efforts to seek revenge against his political enemies.”

“Here’s what one Republican member of this Committee said about this prosecution, quote: ‘Some bonehead in North Carolina thinks that’s a crime…Well, they better damn sure have information to back it up, because if all it is, is a picture, that person should lose their job.’ But instead of losing their jobs, they’re getting lifetime appointments.”

title: In Speech On The Senate Floor, Durbin Calls For Guantánamo Bay Detention Facility To Finally Be Closed
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, called on the next generation of leaders to continue to fight for the ideals that make this nation great and finally close the Guantánamo Bay detention facility. Durbin has been a vocal advocate for shuttering the detention center at Guantánamo Bay. After holding the Senate’s first hearing on the need to close Guantánamo in 2013, Durbin held another hearing in 2021 where he reiterated his frequent calls to close the detention facility. Durbin emphasized that keeping the detention center open undermines America’s moral standing and credibility around the world and wastes taxpayer dollars.

“What makes America great is our aspiration to uphold the inherent dignity, equality, and inalienable rights of all of our people. All too often though, when we are faced with threats, there are those who would cast these foundational ideals aside. Unfortunately, after the terrorist attacks on September 11th, that view prevailed, promoted by those in power who believed that the risk of another attack justified compromising our basic values,” Durbin said. “This January marks the 25th anniversary of the opening of detention camps for suspected terrorists at Guantánamo Bay.”

Durbin continued, “The express purpose of sending captured suspects to Guantánamo was to detain them in a legal black hole. Our nation’s leaders wanted a place where detainees could be held and interrogated beyond the reach of our laws, our courts, our Constitution, and our ideals of justice and dignity. Detainees were tortured and subjected to unspeakable abuse at Guantánamo, as well as at secret CIA black sites around the world. Most were held in indefinite detention without charges or trial. The few who were charged were in makeshift military commissions.”

Durbin continued, “This betrayal of our values weakened America. Rather than making us safer, we fueled terrorist recruitment, surrendered the moral high ground in the argument, wasted the good will of our allies, and damaged our standing in the world. This astronomically expensive offshore prison also cost American taxpayers—and continues to—billions of dollars more than if we had used our time-tested federal court system. Meanwhile, thousands of 9/11 families continue to suffer from the emotional and financial loss of their loved ones, loss compounded by the failure of our government to give them a modicum of justice. Twenty-five years after the attacks, the 9/11 trial still has not begun, and key confessions have been ruled too tainted by torture to be admissible in a court or hearing.”

Durbin has also spoken out against the Trump Administration’s unlawful transfer of immigrants to Guantánamo Bay, and he has led other Senators in demanding answers for the legal justification for using the base as an immigration detention center.

In October, Durbin’s office released insights from an oversight visit of immigration detention at Guantánamo Bay. The staff noted that the Trump Administration staffs the facilities whether any immigrants are being detained at Guantánamo Bay or not, including during extended periods of time when there are none present. Detaining immigrant detainees at Guantánamo Bay comes at an exorbitant cost to taxpayers, with a total of approximately 852 immigrants being held at the facility since January 2025 at the cost of more than $100 million.

“We should have learned by now that we are strongest as a nation and as a people when we uphold human dignity and the rule of law. Instead, we left the Guantánamo playbook open and available for President Trump and Stephen Miller. Trump vowed during his presidential campaign in 2016 that he would not only keep Guantánamo open, but he would also ‘load it up with some bad dudes.’ And now, in his second term, the President is making good on his threat—by sending immigrants to this grotesque facility,” Durbin said. “Most migrants come to America seeking safety from persecution and torture or simply a better life. But Trump and Miller are seeking to avoid our laws and our courts by shipping these immigrants off to legal black holes around the world faster than the courts can stop them.”

Durbin then shared the story of Victor Omar Bonilla Alvarez. Victor escaped years of torture and abuse at the hands of MS-13 and law enforcement in El Salvador. He has no criminal record. An immigration judge granted him withholding of removal to El Salvador based on his credible fear of torture if he were sent back. After months of confinement in the United States, our government sent him to Guantánamo. Then, after months of confinement there, the government transferred him to Arizona and then swiftly removed him to Mexico. They did this all without informing his counsel and without any assurances from Mexico that he would not be sent to El Salvador.

“This Administration has sent an estimated 25,000 people to third countries, denying them due process and their legal protections against persecution or torture,” Durbin said. “Many, like Victor, risk being returned to torture. Others are being indefinitely detained, in abysmal conditions, and with little to no access to the rule of law or any hope for the future.”

Durbin concluded, “Violating the law to send people away to be persecuted or tortured? Is this who we are? Is this American? Is this who we aspire to be? With a new year and a new Congress on the horizon, I hope our next generation of leaders will continue to fight for the ideals that make this nation great and finally close the Guantánamo detention facility.”

title: Sens. Moran, Murray Introduce Legislation to Improve Support & VA Response Times for Veterans in Crisis
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senators Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) and Patty Murray (D-Wash.) – chairman and member of the Senate Committee on Veterans’ Affairs – introduced legislation to improve the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Veteran Crisis Line (VCL). This legislation was released in response to committee oversight and reports published by the VA Office of Inspector General and the Government Accountability Office (GAO) that showed several areas of needed improvement.

The Veterans Crisis Line Improvement Act would decrease VA’s emergency response time when veterans present an imminent risk of harm to themselves or others, require VA’s local suicide prevention coordinators to connect with veterans the same day they contact the VCL when appropriate, track the scheduling and provision of follow-up care, close after-hours safety gaps and increase transparency and oversight through evaluations of outreach methods.

“Veterans who are contacting the VCL for support deserve the best available tools and resources as quickly as possible,” said Sen. Moran. “This legislation would help close the gaps that are delaying care to veterans when they are reaching out for help and make certain they receive the care they need when they need it. I appreciate GAO’s investigation and will work to see this legislation pass in the Senate.”

“When I chaired the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee, thousands of servicemembers were coming home from Iraq and Afghanistan, and I saw firsthand the toll their service took on their mental health,” said Sen. Murray. “For a veteran struggling with PTSD or their mental health, picking up the phone to ask for help can be the hardest step there is. When they finally call the Veterans Crisis Line, we owe them more than a voice on the other end. We owe our veterans real follow-through and a direct path to care. Our legislation strengthens the Crisis Line so that every veteran who reaches out gets the support they need, not only during the call, but also long after it ends. We made a promise to take care of our servicemembers when they come home, and I will always fight to keep it.”

In February 2025, Sen. Moran requested GAO examine VCL’s post-contact interactions with veterans after an earlier GAO investigation, that Sen. Moran also initiated, found a lack of oversight and significant risks with complex callers, chat and text operations as well as critical-incident disclosures at the VCL. The second GAO report found that the VCL received over a million interactions via phone call and text in FY25. Throughout those interactions, VCL employees requested emergency dispatches 60,261 times but local authorities did not dispatch responders in 2,494 cases. The report also found that, while VA closed more than 98% of their over 195,000 referrals to suicide prevention coordinators within three days, VA did not track whether those veterans were contacted or received care after their initial contact with the crisis line.

The full text of the legislation can be found here and a one-page summary of the legislation can be found here.

“For warriors experiencing a mental health crisis, reaching out for help is a critical first step,” said Jose Ramos, Senior Vice President of Government & Community Relations at Wounded Warrior Project. “Wounded Warrior Project supports the Veterans Crisis Line Improvement Act because it would help strengthen efforts to connect veterans in crisis with the care and support they need. Ensuring veterans who seek help are effectively connected to services is an important part of broader efforts to prevent suicide and save lives, and we thank Chairman Jerry Moran and Senator Patty Murray for their bipartisan leadership on this important issue.”

This legislation is also supported by The American Legion.

title: Chairman Arrington, Reps. Obernolte and DeGette, Applaud Passage of Legislation to Reform How Congress Estimates the Cost of Preventive Health Care
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – House Budget Chairman Jodey Arrington (R-Texas), joined by sponsors Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Diana DeGette (D-Colo.), released the following statements applauding House passage of the Preventive Health Savings Act, H.R. 4464, by a vote of 401-0:

Chairman Arrington lauded the historic passage of the legislation:

“A former Member of Congress and dear friend from Texas, Doctor Michael Burgess, used to say, ‘an ounce of prevention is better than a pound of cure.’

That's true for people who need life-saving therapeutics, preventive health care treatments on the front end, but it’s also true of the federal budget. Health care is a $5.3 trillion industry that spans across public and private sectors, and health care spending accounts for one-third of the federal budget.

When we can save money, make for more efficacious drugs to treat our fellow Americans, it's a win-win. And that's what this Preventive Health Savings Act does. It allows us to take a step back and see the full cost-saving potential of preventive health care policies.

Life-saving drugs, vaccines and other preventive measures may have a high price tag on the front end, but it’s misleading to judge their cost or cost-savings potential against a ten-year window, as we currently do. By opening up the window to 30 years, we are better able to see what the benefits of these treatments are to both the American people and the balance sheet of the nation.

I want to extend my sincere thanks to Ranking Member Brendan Boyle as well as my colleagues Representatives Jay Obernolte and Diana DeGette for helping us change the dynamic in a way that will be better for all Americans.”

Representative Jay Obernolte’s (R-Calif.) Statement:

“Preventive health care has the potential to improve patient outcomes while reducing long-term health care costs, and our budget process should reflect those impacts. The Preventive Health Savings Act will help Congress make more informed decisions by accounting for potential savings that extend beyond the traditional budget window. I'm pleased to see this bipartisan legislation pass the House and move us one step closer to a more accurate and responsible approach to evaluating federal health care investments.”

Representative Diana DeGette’s (D-Colo.) Statement:

“I am proud to have worked on The Preventive Health Savings Act for over a decade. This bill will revolutionize and modernize how Congress assesses health initiatives by accurately gauging the long-term savings from preventive health programs. Passage of this bill is a huge win for our country's fiscal health and a big step towards a healthier, more affordable future for all Americans. Now, the Senate must act quickly to pass this bill so that it can be signed into law.”

title: House Democrats Oppose USDA Effort to Take Food Assistance Away from Millions of Americans
text:
House Agriculture Committee Ranking Member Angie Craig (MN-02) led 213 members of the House Democratic Caucus in a letter to U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins opposing a new proposed rule that would kick an estimated 6.3 million Americans – primarily older or disabled recipeints and families with children – off the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). Experts have argued that the rule is illegal and that only Congress has the authority to change broad-based categorical eligiblity (BBCE).

The proposed rule would undercut BBCE, an optional mechanism used by U.S. states and territories to improve efficiency and reduce administrative burdens by granting SNAP eligibility to Americans in need if they already qualify for similar means-tested programs.

“BBCE has been used by red and blue states alike for nearly 30 years to reduce administrative red tape, ease SNAP’s benefit cliff, and allow families to save for their future,” write the lawmakers.

They continue, “According to the Department’s own regulatory impact analysis of the proposed rule, 6.3 million individuals in 3.2 million households will lose their SNAP benefits entirely.”

“This proposed rule comes a little over a year after the largest cut to SNAP in history, with 5.5 million people having lost food assistance due to the changes advocated for by this administration,” the letter writers note.

The Democratic lawmakers conclude, “This rule will increase hunger, cost states more, exacerbate the affordability crisis for millions and make passing a farm bill more complicated.”

Read the letter here.

title: Ranking Member Angie Craig Opening Statement at Rural Development Hearing
text:
Today, House Agriculture Committee Ranking Member Angie Craig (MN-02) delivered the following opening statement at a Subcommittee on Commodity Markets, Digital Assets, and Rural Development hearing entitled "Strengthening Rural America Through USDA Rural Development Programs and Partnerships." Watch the hearing here.

[As prepared for delivery.]

Thank you, Chairman Johnson and Ranking Member Davis, for holding today’s hearing, and a thank you to our witnesses for being here today to discuss the power and promise of USDA Rural Development. I am especially excited to see Ms. Lori Blair here from my home state of Minnesota.

The United States Department of Agriculture touches every family in America. Whether you’re a farmer growing food or a working parent trying to put dinner on the table – USDA programs and policies stretch from the farmgate to the grocery store shelf.

President Lincoln called it the “People’s Department.” Today, it is living up to that nickname. Anchored in its network of local offices, USDA has one of the most widespread footprints of any federal department.

USDA field offices and staff are present – and have roots – in almost every county, no matter how rural, no matter how geographically remote, no matter the population size.

USDA staff don’t just work in rural America; they live there. They know their neighbors; they know the pressures and concerns of their local communities.

That makes USDA uniquely situated not only to understand and connect with, but also to help rural communities, whether it’s providing technical assistance for farmers or helping someone afford their first home.

That is why I, and many of my colleagues, have forcefully opposed this Administration’s reorganization efforts, which courts have at least for now stayed on legal grounds. Whether it’s relocating offices, closing offices or downsizing staff, this reorganization hurts rural America.

For the same reason, taking Rural Development away from USDA and placing it elsewhere, like the Small Business Administration, will undermine its mission and make it harder for farmers, rural business owners, working people and municipalities to access Rural Development programs.

We say that in rural America, “neighbors help neighbors.” And yet, there are some in this country who would like to see our neighbors fired, our neighborhood offices closed and the experts that know the neighborhood issues outsourced to strangers hundreds of miles away.

The work USDA Rural Development does matters because the communities it serves matter. The people who live there are important. Abandoning them by downsizing vital staff and relocating USDA Rural Development programs sends the wrong message.

I look forward to hearing your testimony and to learning more about the amazing things you are doing in partnership with USDA RD.

Thank you again for being here today, and I yield back.

title: Trump Administration Cancels Raises for Head Start Teachers
text:
WASHINGTON – House Appropriations Committee Ranking Member Rosa DeLauro (D-CT-03) issued the following statement after the Trump administration announced it was repealing a federal rule that would increase Head Start teacher compensation to bring it in line with local public preschool teachers.

“More than 700,000 of the nation’s poorest children are taught by Head Start teachers. These selfless educators forgo higher salaries in other schools to help children and families who are struggling to stay afloat. Now, as the Trump administration continues to dismantle the Department of Education, they are canceling a planned pay-raise for Head Start teachers. It is unconscionable.

“The Trump administration will move Heaven and Earth to find money for foreign wars, tax cuts for billionaires, and White House renovations, but when it comes to paying preschool teachers they somehow cannot do it. This is not a matter of resources; it is a matter of priorities.

“As the Ranking Member of the House Appropriations Committee, and the Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Labor, HHS, and Education, I have long fought this administration to increase funding for education. The Trump administration should reverse course, acknowledge the crucial service these hard-working teachers provide, and require that they receive the pay they deserve. If they will not lead, Congress will. I will fight to secure the resources necessary to support strong cost of living wage increases for Head Start teachers - and strengthen American education—not continue dismantling it.”

title: Ranking Member Maxine Waters Blasts HUD’s Cruel Attack on Mixed-Status Families
text:
Today, Congresswoman Maxine Waters (D-CA), the top Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, released the following statement condemning the recently published U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) final rule, “Housing and Community Development Act of 1980: Verification of Eligible Status.” This rule ends long-standing prorated housing assistance for families with mixed immigration status, while creating cumbersome new citizenship verification requirements for all assisted households.

“HUD has finalized an inhumane rule that will force families to make an unthinkable choice: lose your housing or be torn apart. As a result, nearly 80,000 people in mixed status households could face eviction or homelessness this winter, including 37,000 children, the vast majority of whom are citizens and eligible for assistance. And this rule goes even further, imposing new burdensome citizenship requirements on all assisted households through an outdated, unreliable system that will strain public housing authorities. In fact, this latest action also doubles down on Trump’s efforts to block formerly incarcerated people from housing assistance, which also disproportionately impacts Black and Brown communities.

“I commend my constituents and the national organizations who are taking Secretary Turner to court this week to challenge this reckless rule.

“And that’s not all. HUD is also cutting homelessness assistance, rescinding resources for critical housing counseling, rolling back LGBTQ+ and fair housing protections, and manufacturing fake coalitions to pressure housing providers to bend to their political will and circumvent Congress. This Administration is out of control and making the affordable housing crisis worse. They must stop.

“Secretary Turner must reverse this rule immediately. Americans need housing relief, not more political cruelty. I will use every tool at my disposal to hold this Administration accountable.”

title: After One Law Firm Reveals Being Coerced into Providing $11.8 Million in Free Legal Work to Trump Administration, Ranking Members Raskin and Blumenthal and Sen. Schiff Slam Nine Other Law Firms For Stonewalling Congressional Inquiry
text:
Washington, D.C. (November 19, 2026)—Rep. Jamie Raskin, Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee, Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations Ranking Member Richard Blumenthal, and Sen. Adam Schiff demanded records from nine law firms after their investigation uncovered that the law firm Kirkland & Ellis LLP (Kirkland) provided at least $11.8 million in free legal services to federal agencies and federal entities after being threatened with an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission investigation and retributive Executive Orders that the Trump Administration had leveled against other firms. The probe also uncovered that Kirkland balked at helping the Trump Administration rename the Kennedy Center and build the President’s triumphal arch, raising questions about whether other firms that struck deals with the Administration took on those projects.

The lawmakers sent follow-up letters to Latham & Watkins LLP (Latham); Simpson Thacher & Bartlett LLP (Simpson Thacher); Willkie Farr & Gallagher LLP (Willkie); Sullivan & Cromwell LLP (S&C); Hogan Lovells Cadwalader LLP (Cadwalader); Allen Overy Shearman Sterling US LLP (A&O Shearman); Milbank LLP (Milbank); Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison LLP (Paul, Weiss); and Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom LLP (Skadden Arps).

“We have recently received substantial and profoundly troubling information that this corrupt bargain went much further than originally understood. Kirkland & Ellis LLP provided at least $11.8 million in free legal services to numerous federal agencies and entities engaged in questionable activities, including approximately $4 million to the U.S. Department of Commerce, $2.2 million to the U.S. Department of Defense, $1.6 million to the U.S. Postal Service, $2 million to the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, and $1.8 million to represent an investment entity negotiated between the Trump Administration and Japan to create a $550 billion slush fund. The Trump Administration also unsuccessfully tried to involve Kirkland & Ellis in work supporting the President’s political vanity projects, such as the renaming of the Kennedy Center or supporting the illegal construction of his triumphal arch in Washington, D.C.—raising serious questions of whether other firms acceded to these demands,” the lawmakers wrote.

The lawmakers received this information from Kirkland just two days after the November midterm elections. Since April 2025, the lawmakers have repeatedly demanded answers about the ten firms’ dubious multimillion-dollar deals with President Trump. However, to date, the vast majority of the firms still have yet to provide any substantive answers or turn over a single responsive document.

The lawmakers renewed their demands for all outstanding records about the Executive Order and directed the firms to prioritize records of requests for free or discounted legal services from the White House, any executive branch agency, or any public or private associate of the President. They are seeking the nature of each request, who made it, what services each firm agreed to provide, and the hours and billable value of any work performed.

Today’s letters are the latest salvo in an investigation Ranking Members Raskin and Blumenthal launched in April 2025 into Trump’s unprecedented official coercion of major law firms and the deals firms struck to avoid retaliation. Joined by Sen. Schiff, they subsequently scrutinized firms’ free legal work for the Commerce Department, sought records of Epshteyn’s role in Kirkland’s deal and pressed Skadden over potential conflicts involving its work for Intel and the Commerce Department. In October, the lawmakers rejected Kirkland’s claims of privilege and renewed their demands for records on its $125 million deal after the firm failed to produce a single responsive document and refused to meet with congressional staff.

The lawmakers warned that they will use every tool at their disposal to pursue the investigation in this Congress and the next. As the initial phases of this investigation make clear, the President of the United States abused the power of the federal government to extract nearly $1 billion in free legal services from some of the nation's largest law firms. Worse, the agreements announced on Truth Social effectively made the President the sole judge of whether those firms were complying with their obligations—putting these firms at the political mercy of the Administration and the personal mercy of the President, driving major firms away from both existing and potential clients and causes that could put them at odds with the mercurial shakedown artist in the White House. For people and communities who rely on pro bono lawyers to defend their rights, that could mean facing the full power and intensifying fury of the federal government alone.

title: Ranking Member Takano After Oracle Hearing: No Answers on $17.5 Billion, and Ellison is Next
text:
WASHINGTON – House Veterans’ Affairs Committee Ranking Member Mark Takano (CA-39) released the following statement after today’s full committee hearing with Oracle CEO Mike Sicilia and Oracle Health Executive Vice President Seema Verma. Sicilia appeared under subpoena after refusing to appear at the Committee’s September 2 hearing.

“After yet another hearing on VA’s electronic health record, I am no more confident in this program, and I did not hear a justification for the $17.5 billion increase in its cost,” said Ranking Member Takano. “In September, VA blamed Oracle. Today, Oracle pointed the finger back at VA. Nobody wants to take responsibility, but both want a blank check from taxpayers while veterans are being harmed.”

On Oracle’s contract: Asked by Rep. Maggie Goodlander (NH-02)whether Oracle kept its 2022 promise to this Committee to bear cost overruns, Sicilia said, “I don’t believe the promise was broken.” Asked by Rep. Julia Brownley (CA-26) roughly how much Oracle has absorbed, however, neither Sicilia nor Verma could give a figure. Verma said, “I don’t have a rough estimate in front of me.” The contract ceiling has gone from about $10 billion to about $27 billion, and the system is live at 19 of 170 sites, or 11 percent. This led Rep. Herb Conaway (NJ-03), an internal medicine specialist, to ask,“Why is Oracle charging the VA so much more for the same work that Cerner did before you bought it?”

On patient safety: Asked by Rep. Kelly Morrison (MN-03), an obstetrician-gynecologist, why taxpayers should accept the increase while patient safety concerns remain unresolved, Sicilia said he is “not aware of any direct patient safety concerns that are yet unresolved.” VA’s own data, cited at the hearing by Rep. Goodlander, show 4,601 cases of harm involving the system, 10 of them classified as catastrophic. “There are five other deaths directly accountable to the EHR system that you are deploying,” said Rep. Maxine Dexter (OR-03), a pulmonologist. "The fact that we are only in 19 of 170 facilities, and we are continuing to fund this, knowing people are dying, is absolutely on our heads and we need to do something about it.”

On veterans’ data: Rep. Nikki Budzinski (IL-13), ranking member of the Technology Modernization Subcommittee, told Sicilia and Verma it was her understanding that Oracle’s sales team has been pursuing the inclusion of its commercial terms and conditions on data privacy, “which would virtually allow you to own this data.” “Do you believe Oracle should be able to stand above statutory protections for veterans’ data so you can improve your bottom line?” Rep. Budzinski asked. Verma answered, “We have zero access to the data of the veterans… We do not use that data for any purpose.” RM Takano then told them VA staff described a “long, feisty discussion” with Oracle on exactly that.

On Larry Ellison. Sicilia acknowledged he never asked Larry Ellison directly whether Ellison had spoken with the President or White House officials about Oracle’s VA contract. “I did not ask him directly,” he said.

“Without that information, I am still unconvinced that Larry Ellison’s relationship with the president has not tipped the scales in Oracle’s favor,” RM Takano said. “I do expect to see Larry Ellison on December 10, as required by Dr. Dexter’s unanimous subpoena. Continued pressure from Oracle’s lobbyists will not result in us looking the other way.”

On Oracle meeting the contract terms. After being asked directly by RM Takano, Sicilia committed to Oracle owning the health record business through 2031, then added, “I can’t imagine there’d be a lot of buyers that signed up to take on this program right now.”

“If I read a headline that Oracle is selling off this business, it’s going to look like you fooled us twice,” RM Takano told him.

Takano entered into the hearing record Oracle’s responses to the Committee’s pre-hearing requests and email communications between Oracle’s sales team and the contracting team at VA’s Technology Acquisition Center, which handled the $17.5 billion contract augmentation.

“Oracle has not delivered what it promised for veterans,” RM Takano said. “Taxpayers should not be asked to keep sending good money to a failed program until Mr. Sicilia’s and Mr. Ellison’s promises are fulfilled.”

RM Takano and Democratic Members of the Committee have asked Oracle to produce all documents and communications with White House and VA officials about its work at VA. The Committee will hear from Oracle Chairman Larry Ellison next month.

title: A Win for Worker Freedom

committee.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce

text:
Today, Education and Workforce Committee Chairman Tim Walberg (R-MI) issued the following statement on the Department of Labor’s final rule protecting the freedom of Americans to work as independent contractors:

“Workers should have the freedom to choose how they earn a living. For many Americans, independent contracting means setting their own hours, being their own boss, and having more control over their careers. This final rule protects that freedom and makes it easier for workers to pursue opportunities that best fit their lives and their families.”

title: Chairman Brian Mast Exercises Legislative Authority to Publicly Release AI Chip License Information for China
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. - This afternoon, Chairman Brian Mast exercised his authorities under the Export Control Reform Act to publicly reveal export control license application information regarding NVIDIA and AMD's AI chip licenses for the People's Republic of China.

The findings include requested sales of 3.4 million AI chips to China, and the approval of more than 879,000 by BIS-including approvals for AI chip exports to Department of War-designated Chinese Military Companies like Alibaba and Tencent. It also includes requests by NVIDIA to depend on possible chip-smuggling fronts to facilitate their sales of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies. This is the most detailed public disclosure in the history of the Export Control Reform Act.

title: Chairman Mast Applauds President Trump Signing H.R. 1744
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast released the following statement after President Trump signed H.R. 1744, the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom Reauthorization Act of 2026, into law:

“Thank you to President Trump for signing this important bill into law, protecting America’s ‘first freedom’, the free exercise of religion, abroad,” said Chairman Brian Mast. "Americans have always stood firmly with all those jailed, tortured, or killed for their faith around the world, and oppose the rampant religious persecution taking place in China, Nicaragua, Nigeria, Pakistan, the Middle East, and so many other places.

"I want to thank Rep. Chris Smith for leading this bipartisan effort, and the Senate for taking up this time-sensitive bill and sending it to the President’s desk. This Committee will continue to work with USCIRF, including the newly appointed Commissioners, to ensure our foreign policy distinguishes between nations that protect internationally recognized human rights and those that trample on them.”

The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom, or USCIRF, was established by Congress in 1998 to provide recommendations to Congress and the Executive Branch on promoting religious freedom abroad. During the 119th Congress, the House Foreign Affairs Committee held numerous roundtables with USCIRF to exercise its oversight duty and ensure USCIRF maintains strict fidelity to its statutory mandate. H.R. 1744 extends the Commission until the end of 2028.

title: Strengthening Tribal Sovereignty and Expanding Access to Tribal Healthcare
text:
Today, the Subcommittee on Indian and Insular Affairs held a legislative hearing on proposals to strengthen tribal sovereignty, maintain access to traditional subsistence activities and improve healthcare access in tribal communities. Subcommittee Chairman Jeff Hurd (R-Colo.) issued the following statement in response:

“Tribal sovereignty means ensuring that tribes have the authority and resources to make decisions that best serve their communities. The legislation before our Subcommittee today addresses practical challenges facing tribal communities, from preserving access to traditional subsistence activities and strengthening tribal control over ancestral lands to expanding healthcare access and addressing workforce shortages. I’m pleased to chair this hearing and work with my colleagues on both sides of the aisle to advance commonsense, bipartisan solutions that respect tribal sovereignty, strengthen self-determination and improve the quality of life in Native communities.”

Background

H.R. 10307, the Anaktuvuk Pass Food Security Access Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. Nick Begich (R-Alaska), amends the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act to ensure residents of Anaktuvuk Pass can use motorized transportation within Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve for subsistence purposes.

H.R. 10751, the Tribal Oral Health Sovereignty Act, introduced by U.S. Rep. Jack Bergman (R-Mich.), amends the Indian Health Care Improvement Act to remove the dental therapist caveat from the Indian Health Service's Community Health Aide Program, allowing tribal health programs to employ more dental therapists to serve native populations.

H.R. 10956, the IHS Workforce Parity Act of 2026, introduced by U.S. Rep. Mike Kennedy (R-Utah), amends the Indian Health Care Improvement Act to allow Indian Health Service scholarship and loan repayment recipients more flexibility to fulfill their service obligations through half-time clinical practice rather than requiring full-time service.

H.R. 10458, the Grand Ronde Land Transfer Act of 2026, introduced by U.S. Rep. Andrea Salinas (D-Ore.), transfers approximately 18,628 acres of federal land into trust for the Confederated Tribes of the Grand Ronde Community of Oregon.

For more information on the hearing, click here.

title: Hearing Wrap Up: ATF Must Ensure Record Retention Policies Do Not Violate Americans’ Second Amendment Rights

committee.name: House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform

text:
WASHINGTON—Yesterday, the Subcommittee on Federal Law Enforcement held a hearing titled “Oversight of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives’ Out-of-Business Records Retention Practices.” During the hearing, members examined the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives’ (ATF) out-of-business records system to assess whether this system operates as a backdoor national firearms registry. Members also weighed the value of gun tracing against the right guaranteed by the Second Amendment and the implications of retaining out-of-business records in light of recent ATF rulemaking.

Key Takeaways:

ATF is amassing an enormous collection of firearm purchase records, raising Second Amendment and privacy concerns.

Aidan Johnston, Director of Federal Affairs at Gun Owners of America, testified that “The ATF holds more than 1.4 billion records that identify which Americans own which guns. Those records are searchable, and they can be weaponized against law abiding gun owners for mass gun confiscation. Gun Owners of America spent years exposing ATF’s registry because it is a direct threat to the right of the people to keep and bear arms. Here’s how ATF’s registry works: After a firearm is serialized, the manufacturer records which dealer received it. The dealer then records which individual bought it using the information collected on the Background Check Form 4473 the buyer gives his or her full name, address, date of birth, height, weight and race. The dealer then records the make, model and serial number of the gun. What many gun owners do not realize is that when the dealer closes, every single firearm transaction record is sent to ATF. ATF then digitizes these transaction records into a centralized database.”

ATF claims its proposed records retention rule helps law enforcement, but it could have significant implications for Americans’ privacy and Second Amendment rights.

ATF’s proposed rule would cap out-of-business records retention at 20 or 30 years. However, the two retention periods effectively stack: a record could sit with a dealer for 30 years, then with ATF for another 30, meaning the personal information and firearm purchase history of a law-abiding American could remain in government hands for up to 60 years.

Wally Nelson, retired ATF Deputy Assistant Director, testified that “The purpose of ATF record keeping and the [National Tracing Center] out of business records process is to provide information and support of federal, state and local agencies, law enforcement agencies and their fight against crime and violence. In support of that effort, the NTC traces firearms 24 hours a day, seven days a week. The ATF has proposed to change the record retention requirement for dealers from the current permanent regulation to 20 or 30 years. ATF had a 20-year requirement from 1985 to 2022. In 2022, the regulations were changed to make them permanent. ATF’s own data that they wrote up in the [Notice of Proposed Rulemaking] for this proposed change indicated that the number of traces coming on records that are over 20 years old has been reduced quite a bit in the last 15 years.”

Christopher Chiafullo, Founder and National Coordinating Counsel at FFLGuard, testified that “The proposed rule would replace indefinite record retention with defined limits, limits that were already addressed 40 years ago, and that this industry already successfully navigated from 1985 to 2022, using a 20-year records retention window. Most importantly, the proposed records retention rule would set corresponding limits on how long ATF can retain those records at the NTC, the National Tracing Center, before their destroyed.”

The Subcommittee on Federal Law Enforcement is examining how to balance legitimate law enforcement needs with the constitutional rights and privacy interests of law-abiding Americans.

Policymakers must determine whether retaining a collection this large, reaching back decades, is worth the potential risks to law-abiding Americans’ privacy and the right guaranteed by the Second Amendment.

Member Highlights:

Subcommittee Chairman Clay Higgins (R-La.) exposed how current ATF record retention practices creates a database that is searchable by name.

Subcommittee Chairman Higgins: “So these records are continuously coming into ATF. It’s a hell of a lot of manpower and energy being invested to add to the already existing 1.4 billion digital records that we have on file. And is it true, Mr. Nelson? Mr. Johnston? Mr. Chiafullo… is it true that with very easy IT adjustment, this record compilation will be searchable by name. Is that true, Mr. Johnston?”

Mr. Johnston: “Yes. This this weekend I wrote a program using­––“

Subcommittee Chairman Higgins: “Is that true, Mr. Nelson?”

Mr. Nelson: “It could be, I don’t know. I’m not a computer expert.”

Mr. Chiafullo: “ChatGPT gave me directions on how to get here today, Mr. Chairman. So I think anything’s possible.”

Rep. Andy Biggs (R-Ariz.) asked whether searching firearm owners by address turns the ATF’s firearm owner database into a registry.

Rep. Biggs: “Our founders understood that an armed citizenry is essential to preserving a free nation. That’s why they enshrined the Second Amendment in the Constitution, protecting the right to keep and bear arms as a safeguard against foreign threats, government tyranny, and the erosion of liberty…I’ll just remind you that the reason that FISA, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, is so dangerous is because it is a database that is searchable and abused. And so we on this Committee have been fighting to restrain that government surveillance ever since I came to Congress and have been unsuccessful. But there’s been loads of abuses there. So let’s find out here. Do we actually have a registry? I mean, Mr. Johnston, you talked about this database as a database; they’re accumulating information putting into database, right?”

Mr. Johnston: “That’s correct.”

Rep. Biggs: “And they’re putting it in, and the very purpose of that database is to make it searchable. Is that not true?”

Mr. Johnston: “It’s to know who owns the gun so it can be traced.”

Rep. Biggs: “Right. So that doesn’t work if it’s not searchable, right?”

Mr. Johnston: “Correct.”

Rep. Biggs: “And everyone who has testified here today has said this database is searchable. What makes it a registry? Is it a registry? If it’s if it’s searchable by address only, is it a registry? If you if it’s searchable by make model and serial number, and all four of those things are where it’s currently searchable. Is that not true, Mr. Nelson.?”

Mr. Johnston: “That’s correct. And that’s all you need to say, ‘confiscate AR-15s.”

Rep. Biggs: “Mr. Nelson?”

Mr. Nelson: “I don’t know that that’s true. My understanding is that they have––it’s a flat tiff file, and it goes into a file of all the images of the records for that FFL. And when they get a trace, they have to go through them one at a time to find the file.”

Rep. Biggs: “So you’re saying it’s not searchable?”

Mr. Nelson: “I don’t believe so, sir.”

Rep. Biggs: “You just described a way to search it.”

Mr. Nelson: “Shuffling through, going through the reels of the record, the individual photos or optical scans to find the firearm they’re looking for.”

Rep. Biggs: “Right, so what they’re doing, they’re looking––another word for that would be searching––to find the information they want. That makes it a searchable database.”

Rep. Michael Cloud (R-Texas) asked about the ways ATF could digitize records to create a searchable database and national gun registry.

Rep, Cloud: “[The number of gun records has] grown to about 1.4 billion. One of the ways we got there was in between this period, and that was the Biden Administration, which took the 20-year limit and extended it forever, then placed a zero-tolerance policy on FFLs and began to intimidate them to force them out of business so that they could collect the gun records, it would seem, to grow the database. And then we’re told that this is not a searchable database, it’s not a registry. It’s definitely a searchable database. And they’ll say, ‘oh, well, we’re not scanning the name.’ I’ve gone and I’ve actually watched them scan the documents in. They scan the names and it’s a patch that they basically place in the software to keep the name from kind of being withheld, but that seems like it could very easily be solved. Mr. Johnston, can you speak to how easily this would be to change that paradigm?”

Mr. Johnston: “So it would be very easy to change this into a digital––into a completely searchable database by name, by address. It’s been said already. These are kept in like TIFF files, a type of image with no data, and it’s accompanied by metadata, and all ATF would have to do is rescan the images using optical character recognition in order to get all of the data that’s written on each page.”

Rep. Cloud: “Well, now in the world of AI––“

Mr. Johnston: “I wrote a little software, the ATF could convert them all in about an afternoon using federal government technology.”

Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga.) noted that the Biden Administration violated the Firearm Owners Protection Act, which prohibits the creation of a national firearms registry

Rep. Clyde: “[C]ongress has already spoken out on this matter through the Firearm Owners Protection Act, which bars and I quote, ‘any system of registration of firearm, firearm owners or firearm transactions or dispositions.’ It also prohibits the recording of out of business records…So it prohibits two things. It prohibits: one, the recording of the records, and, number two, the creation of a system of registration of firearms. That is the Firearm Owners Protection Act. That is the law. That’s today’s law. So question for each of you. Or, Mr. Johnston, for you first. Am I reading this wrong? [Does] that not seem like there’s a prohibition on recording of records?”

Mr. Johnston: “There is a prohibition and President Biden directly violated with a new rule.”

Mr. Chiafullo: “It would definitely seem that way, yeah. Absolutely.”

Mr. Clyde: “All right. Thank you. Furthermore, a permanent appropriations rider, and I’m an appropriator, prohibits the ATF from spending money on, quote, ‘consolidating or centralizing dealers records within the Department of Justice.’ Read together, these two provisions explicitly block the ATF from digitizing records at all, no matter how long the agency keeps them…yet the ATF’s proposal on the length of records kept does not address either law.”
