title: Investigation Details How Western Government Policy Enabled China's Rise in the Skies

committee.name: House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party

text:
November 19, 2026

Today, Chairman John Moolenaar of the Select Committee on China released a new report on the threats posed to American national security by U.S. and allied aerospace companies collaborating with the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and Chinese companies. The investigation details how American and European aerospace contractors inadvertently participated in the CCP's national strategy of military-civil fusion to develop lethal and advanced technology for the Chinese military.

"American and European companies transferred technology to China that could be used against our brave men and women in uniform. With the CCP’s military-civil fusion there are no private companies in China. The PLA will exploit civilian technology and use it to advance its military ambitions and that is what happened here,” said Moolenaar. "The U.S. and its allies should strengthen export controls and tighten investment restrictions on the aerospace sector to stop the transfer of vital technology that will empower our foremost adversary.”

Investigation Findings

Western aerospace companies entered lawful commercial arrangements that transferred advanced technology, technical know-how, and Western expertise to Chinese aerospace firms.

Honeywell, GE Aerospace, and Collins repeatedly sought and obtained licenses for controlled technology transfers involving PRC military end users and other military-linked entities as part of Chinese commercial aerospace platforms.

Export controls relied on company due diligence even where commercial incentives favored continuity and past enforcement actions revealed compliance weaknesses.

PRC-based joint ventures created a structural gap in U.S. national security review by allowing sensitive capabilities to move offshore outside the principal Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) framework.

Unilateral U.S. restrictions would disadvantage American aerospace companies without denying China access to many Western technologies when allied firms backfill the resulting business.

Policy Recommendations

The United States should not allocate taxpayer dollars to companies that build adversary military capabilities that can be turned against the United States and its allies.

The Treasury Department should restrict outbound investment into China’s aerospace sector under its Outbound Investment Security Program, and Congress should codify this prohibition by amending it into the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act of 2025 (COINS Act).

The Federal Aviation Administration should not certify aircraft manufactured in China.

Congress should pass H.R. 11047 Aerospace Transparency Act, requiring aerospace contractors doing business with DOW to disclose their relationships with U.S.-designated Chinese military companies, giving the Department the visibility it needs to assess and act on these entanglements.

The State and Commerce Departments should fundamentally reapproach how licensing for aerospace technologies is handled, reducing exports to adversaries generally, requiring full beneficial ownership transparency for all interested parties, denying dual-use exports or exports accessible by Chinese military companies, and enforcing violations with genuinely deterrent penalties.

Congress should pass H.R. 11048 Geospatial Intelligence Transparency and Security Act, directing the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency to assess the full landscape of commercial geospatial AI capabilities, identify those presenting the greatest national security concern, and transmit the findings to the Departments of Commerce and State to inform export control rulemaking and international negotiations.

Subject acquisition of American aerospace companies by French companies to heightened scrutiny and a presumption of denial until they unwind ties to China’s civil-military ecosystem.

Read the reporthere.

title: Chairman Bost Gavels in Subsequent Oversight Hearing on VA’s Electronic Health Record Modernization for Veterans and Servicemembers
text:
Today, House Committee on Veterans’ Affairs Chairman Mike Bost (R-Ill.), delivered the following opening remarks, as prepared, at the start of the Full Committee’s oversight hearing to further examine the Department of Veterans Affairs’ (VA) federal electronic health record modernization effort and the federal contract cost following 2026 deployments and going into 2027 to ensure veterans – current and future – can get their health records through one, modern, efficient system to access the high-quality healthcare they have earned. Today’s hearing with Oracle CEO Mike Sicilia comes as the Committee previously heard from VA officials on the status update, project cost, and plan for 2027 deployments in September.

The Committee will come to order.

Without objection, the Chair may declare a recess at any time.

Good morning.

Thank you to our witnesses, for being here today.

In September, this Committee held a status check on V.A.’s EHRM program.

At the end of that hearing, members on both sides of the aisle voted unanimously to hear directly from Oracle.

That is why we are here today.

As of today, V.A. has completed its new system deployments for 2026.

Cleveland and Anchorage went live last month, bringing this year’s total to 13 medical centers.

More than 780,000 veterans are now being served by the new system.

That is real progress.

I want to recognize the V.A. and Oracle teams, and the frontline V.A. staff, who made it happen.

It is well known that I have been skeptical of this program from the very beginning.

I still have questions. But I also believe in giving credit where it is due.

This year’s deployments have gone far more smoothly than those that came before.

Now we need to make sure that progress lasts without driving up the contract price tag.

In August, V.A. raised the ceiling on its contract with Oracle from about 10 billion dollars to about 27 billion dollars.

That is a big number, and veterans and taxpayers deserve to understand why the price tag keeps changing.

Congress deserves a clear accounting of what has changed since 2018.

We need answers to why the price tag has grown out of control.

We need to know who is responsible for keeping costs under control.

Congress needs to know how much of the higher price tag reflects the cost of delays.

In 2022, Oracle told Congress it was prepared to bear the cost of overruns within the scope of the contract.

Mr. Sicilia, today is your opportunity to explain to this Committee what costs Oracle has absorbed.

We need you to explain whether that commitment still stands.

We also want to hear about what comes next.

V.A. plans to deploy the new health record system at 26 more V.A. medical centers in 2027, starting in January.

That pace will test everyone: V.A., Oracle, and the clinicians and schedulers who use this system every day.

Congress needs transparency.

Veterans deserve accountability.

As I have always said, at the end of the day, this is still about the veteran sitting in an exam room.

This is also about making sure the contract with Oracle Health delivers for veterans, not shareholders.

Our focus must remain on providing veterans with the best healthcare in the world.

With that, I again welcome our witness and look forward to his testimony.

title: Ahead of Committee Vote, Warren Releases Concerning Responses from Trump’s Treasury, HUD, EXIM Nominees

committee.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs

text:
Text of Wiggins Response (PDF) | Text of Jones Response (PDF) | Text of Slade Response (PDF) | Text of Rigas Response (PDF)

Washington, D.C. – Ahead of the committee vote, U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Ranking Member of the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, released the troubling responses from President Donald Trump’s nominees to the Questions for the Record (QFRs) she submitted following their respective confirmation hearings on October 1, 2026.

Treasury Assistant Secretary for International Trade and Development Nominee Jeremy Wiggins

Ranking Member Warren’s questions pressed Wiggins on President Trump’s chaotic tariff policies and failed economic agenda, as well as on his view of international financial institutions like the World Bank and IMF. In his response, Wiggins failed to acknowledge the impact of Trump’s tariffs and war in Iran on American families, declining even to confirm that grocery and gas prices have increased and that diesel prices have reached record highs. He also refused to answer a straightforward question about who won the 2020 presidential election, saying only that “Congress certified Joseph R. Biden President on January 7, 2021.”

See Wiggins’s responses HERE.

HUD Assistant Secretary and FHA Commissioner Nominee Matthew Jones

Ranking Member Warren’s questions pressed Jones on America’s housing crisis and the Administration’s plans to lower costs and enforce our fair housing laws. In his response, Jones failed to directly answer whether the Fair Housing Act and other laws prohibit housing discrimination on the basis of race, national origin, sexual orientation, and other specific characteristics. He also refused to explain what more he would do to help Americans avoid foreclosure or justify cuts to programs meant to help homebuyers make informed purchase decisions. He also refused to answer a straightforward question about who won the 2020 presidential election, saying “(t)he FHA Commissioner and Assistant Secretary for Housing has no oversight over the federal election process and/or results.”

See Jones’s responses HERE.

EXIM First Vice President and Vice Chairman Nominee David Slade

Ranking Member Warren’s questions pressed Slade on two publicly disclosed complaints against him based on his past conduct at EXIM, as well as on reports that the bank was considering a loan to a Kazakhstani mining operation tied to the Trump family. At the nomination hearing and in his QFR responses, Slade refused to commit to establishing ethics safeguards on Trump family corruption. He also refused to answer a straightforward question about who won the 2020 presidential election, saying that “Congress certifies the electoral votes cast pursuant to the Constitution and applicable law” and that “(t)he candidate who receives the required electoral votes, or who is selected through the applicable constitutional contingent-election process, wins the presidential election.”

See Slade’s responses HERE.

EXIM Board of Directors Nominee Michael Rigas

Ranking Member Warren’s questions also pressed Rigas on reports that EXIM was considering a loan to a Kazakhstani mining operation tied to the Trump family, as well as on EXIM’s role in providing a $10 billion loan for the Project Vault initiative. At the nomination hearing and in his QFR responses, Rigas refused to commit to establishing ethics safeguards on Trump family corruption. He also refused to answer a straightforward question about who won the 2020 presidential election, saying that “Congress certifies the electoral votes cast pursuant to the Constitution and applicable law” and that “(t)he candidate who receives the required electoral votes, or who is selected through the applicable constitutional contingent-election process, wins the presidential election.”

title: Ahead of Markup, Warren Calls on White House to Pause EXIM First Vice President, Vice Chairman Nomination Given Pending Investigation by the Office of Special Counsel

committee.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs

text:
“I urge the Administration to pause Mr. Slade's nomination until his pending complaint is fully investigated and resolved.”

Text of Letter (PDF)

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, wrote to White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, expressing concerns regarding David Slade’s nomination to be First Vice President and Vice Chairman of the Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM). The letter follows Mr. Slade’s public disclosure, during his confirmation process, of complaints about his conduct while at EXIM, including one that has yet to be resolved.

“As part of the confirmation process, Mr. Slade publicly disclosed two specific complaints that were filed against him,” wrote Ranking Member Warren. “First, he indicated that the Office of Special Counsel (OSC) is actively investigating an allegation that he improperly removed a probationary employee while serving on the Beachhead team at EXIM for the current Trump Administration.” Mr. Slade explained that he had consulted with EXIM’s Office of Human Capital and concluded that “the employee’s performance did not meet the requirements of the position,” but he acknowledged that the OSC investigation is ongoing.

Mr. Slade was also the subject of a personnel-related complaint during the first Trump Administration, when he served as EXIM General Counsel. In response to questions for the record, Mr. Slade explained that the matter was ultimately “resolved through a settlement agreement rather than further litigation.”

“I support a strong EXIM that strengthens critical supply chains and helps small businesses in the United States grow and compete. That requires Congress to closely examine the character and qualifications of the people nominated to lead EXIM,” Ranking Member Warren concluded. “The White House should therefore hold Mr. Slade’s nomination until the Committee can be briefed on the results of the ongoing OSC investigation into his conduct.”

title: At Nominations Markup, Ranking Member Warren Calls Out Nominees for Turning a Blind Eye to Corruption, Enabling Trump’s Failed Economic Agenda

committee.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs

text:
“In November's elections, the American people sent a very clear message: they are worried about corruption in the Trump Administration, and they are sick and tired of rising prices. And they are appalled at the connection between the two.”

Watch Remarks Here (YouTube)

Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, delivered opening remarks ahead of a Committee markup to vote on the nominations of Jeremy Wiggins to be Assistant Secretary of the Department of the Treasury, Matthew Jones to be Assistant Secretary of the Department of Housing and Urban Development, David Slade to be Vice Chairman and First Vice President of the Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM), and Michael Rigas to be a Member of the Board of Directors at EXIM.

In her remarks, the Ranking Member highlighted the nominees’ unwillingness to commit to addressing corruption in the Trump administration, as well as their support for President Trump’s disastrous economic agenda. Sen. Warren also discussed the Office of Special Counsel’s ongoing investigation into Mr. Slade, urging a pause in his nomination process. She encouraged her colleagues to vote no on all four nominees.

A transcript of Ranking Member Warren’s opening statement is below:

Mr. Chairman, in November’s elections, the American people sent a very clear message: they are worried about corruption in the Trump Administration, and they are sick and tired of rising prices. And they are appalled at the connection between the two.

But after that cry for help from American voters, this markup is a cold, hard, slap in the face.

We are marking up four nominees today. And each either has a blind eye to corruption, or has championed Trump policies that increase costs.

Mr. Jones, is the nominee to be Assistant Secretary for Housing and FHA Commissioner at HUD. But his office has cut resources for first-time homebuyers and proposed weak rules for keeping foreclosed homes in the hands of families, not corporations.

Mr. Slade and Mr. Rigas have each been nominated for key roles at the EXIM Bank.

But neither of these nominees would commit to establishing basic safeguards to ensure the Bank does not become one more vehicle for corruption benefiting President Trump and his family.

Mr. Slade has an additional problem: he is currently under investigation by the Office of Special Counsel for allegedly improperly firing an EXIM employee. We still know virtually nothing about the underlying allegations—or about a separate sex discrimination claim against Mr. Slade that he said was settled when he was at EXIM during the first Trump Administration. We should have that information and the results of the ongoing investigation before voting on Mr. Slade’s nomination.

Finally, we have Mr. Wiggins, a nominee for a key trade role at Treasury, who supports President Trump’s costly and illegal tariffs and who will use his new role to push President Trump’s disastrous economic agenda.

Mr. Chairman, we should listen to the American people. We should vote to rein in corruption. We should vote to lower prices. We should vote to make life more affordable for American families. But these nominees will do the opposite, accelerating the Trump Administration’s disastrous economic policies. I urge all members of this Committee to vote no on all four nominees.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

title: At SEC, DOT, Treasury Nominations Hearing, Warren Delivers Remarks on Risks to Financial System and Held Up Transit Funds

committee.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs

text:
“Americans are sick of watching tech giants and Wall Street rip them off, and sick of the corruption in the Trump Administration that lets them get away with it.”

Watch Opening Remarks Here (YouTube)

Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, delivered opening remarks ahead of a Committee hearing on the nominations of Kristin Johnson to be a Commissioner of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Steven Levine to be a Commissioner of the SEC, Hugo Dante Jr. to be Director of the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Financial Research, Rebekah Goshorn Jurata to be Assistant Secretary for Financial Institutions at Treasury, and Mark Aesch to be Federal Transit Administrator at the Department of Transportation.

A transcript of Ranking Member Warren’s opening statement is below:

So on Election Day, Americans sent a clear message: they are fed up with President Trump’s failed economic policies. Trump’s chaotic tariffs and the illegal war with Iran have sent the cost of just about everything that Americans buy soaring.

Americans are sick of watching tech giants and Wall Street rip them off, and they are sick of the corruption of the Trump Administration that just lets them get away with it.

Right now, the red lights are flashing as a growing web of interconnected risks threaten to trigger another financial crisis.

AI companies are taking on massive amounts of debt to finance their operations and buildout. The expansion of the barely-regulated private credit market raises concerns as banks become increasingly exposed to these risks. And the growing entanglement between private credit firms, insurance companies, and Americans’ retirement accounts should raise alarms everywhere.

Meanwhile, families are struggling. Data from the New York Fed shows that unpaid credit card balances have reached a new record, and delinquencies on credit cards, car loans and student loans are all climbing.

The Trump Administration is fueling these problems.

The Securities and Exchange Commission has hobbled its enforcement division and has dropped cases against the President’s billionaire buddies when they cheat American families. Trump’s regulators are rolling back basic rules designed to prevent catastrophic bank failures and ensure that taxpayers don’t get stuck having – one again – to pay for bailouts.

I am concerned that many of the nominees before us today will only make it worse.

Mr. Levine, you’ve worked for President Trump at the Labor Department and at the White House. While you were at the White House, the Trump administration rolled out an Executive Order that shoves risky assets like private equity and private credit into Americans’ retirement accounts. How can we possibly believe that if you are confirmed as an SEC Commissioner, that you won’t be just another puppet who will put Wall Street profits over protecting American investors?

Ms. Johnson, I’m glad that you’ve been nominated to serve as an SEC commissioner. President Trump has kept Democrats off the SEC for nearly a year, and even now, he’s refusing to fill the second Democratic seat. And we know why: he’s afraid of anyone who might stand up to him. The President has shown that he is willing to fire Democratic appointees for doing their job. Even so, I trust that you will be a powerful voice for investors and fight to protect families from being cheated by Wall Street.

Ms. Jurata, you’re nominated to be the Assistant Treasury Secretary for Financial Institutions. Until recently, you served as a General Counsel for the American Investment Council, which represents the private equity industry. This looks very much like the fox guarding the henhouse. I have seen no evidence that you have any experience or any interest in watching out for families instead of for Wall Street insiders.

Mr. Dante, you’re nominated to lead the Office of Financial Research. Your job will be to identify threats to financial stability before they become full blown crises. But you’ve spent the last two years at the Council of Economic Advisers, publishing crisis management reports on the President’s failed economic agenda. Before then, you were an economist on behalf of America’s banks. We need an OFR Director who will objectively and accurately assess risks that are building in the financial system, not one who is beholden to the President and Wall Street.

And finally, Mr. Aesch, you’re nominated to lead the Federal Transit Administration. Now, I think you understand how public transportation serves both big cities and rural communities, but you would head an agency that is failing to follow the law and failing to deliver the grants that Congress has authorized. FTA and OMB have left large construction projects in limbo for more than a year, including the MBTA’s Green Line Transformation project in Boston. Transit agencies have followed every program rule, including the policies FTA put out just last year, but this Administration’s deliberate delays and proposals to change the Capital Investment Grants program now threaten to cancel at least half of all current C-I-G projects. I hope you recognize the depth of the mismanagement at the agency you would lead.

Mr. Chairman, the American people have made clear they want a reversal of the President’s failed economic policies. Every piece of evidence we have indicates that many of these nominees will make these failures even worse. We should not offer a rubber-stamp so they can simply continue the Trump Administration’s record of economic failure. Thank you.

###

title: Trump's SEC, Treasury Republican Nominees Deny Private Credit Poses Financial Risk

committee.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs

text:
Warren: “I am just stunned by these answers. We know these risks are growing. Secretary Bessent said these risks are growing. Jamie Dimon recognizes these risks growing. They are growing in the insurance market.”

“You three genuinely alarm me.”

Watch Questioning Here (YouTube)

Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, delivered a line of questioning during a Committee hearing on the nominations of Kristin Johnson to be a Commissioner of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Steven Levine to be a Commissioner of the SEC, Hugo Dante Jr. to be Director of the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Financial Research, Rebekah Goshorn Jurata to be Assistant Secretary for Financial Institutions at Treasury, and Mark Aesch to be Federal Transit Administrator at the Department of Transportation.

The Ranking Member asked the SEC and Treasury nominees if they agree that private credit could pose a serious risk to the U.S. financial system — a view shared by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and J.P. Morgan CEO Jamie Dimon. Ms. Johnson, the Democratic nominee, was the only nominee to agree that private credit could pose such a risk.

Ranking Member Warren also pressed Mr. Levine on the precipitous drop in SEC enforcement actions and Ms. Jurata on staffing cuts to critical financial regulators.

A transcript of Ranking Member Warren’s line of questioning is below:

Ranking Member Warren: Thank you, Mr. Chairman. So here we are teetering on the edge of a financial crisis that could crash markets, wipe out retirement savings, and cost millions of people their jobs. Warning lights are flashing throughout the economy. Let’s start with the lightly regulated private credit market, which has tripled since 2019 and looks a lot like a ticking time bomb. Last year, Moody’s found that banks have $300 billion of exposure, and the risk posed by these shadowy holdings is growing. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent compared the risks in the private credit market to the subprime mortgage crisis that crashed the economy back in 2008. Even J.P. Morgan CEO Jamie Dimon warned of rising private credit risks, saying, “When you see one cockroach, there are probably more.”

So I just want to go down the line here. I just need a yes or no from you with our proposed financial regulators. Do you agree that private credit could pose serious risk to the financial system? Mr. Dante?

Dr. Hugo Dante: Ranking Member, as a share of the total capital for the banks, it is a relatively small share of the $2 trillion.

Ranking Member Warren: So you are saying no? You think Bessent has this wrong? Geez. Ms. Jurata?

Ms. Rebekah Jurata: Thank you, Senator Warren. I would agree with my colleague — or future colleague, Dante — which is that I think that…

Ranking Member Warren: I need a yes or no. Do you think private credit poses a potential risk to our economy? $300 billion of exposure to our banks?

Ms. Rebekah Jurata: I believe it is a risk that is worth monitoring, but I do not believe it poses a systemic risk.

Ranking Member Warren: Okay, so you don’t think we got any risk here. Lord, I thought these were going to be the easy questions. Mr. Levine?

Mr. Steven Levine: Thank you, Ranking Member. I think any asset could potentially pose a potential risk, depending upon concentration.

Ranking Member Warren: So do you think private credit — that’s the asset I’m asking about. This was going to be the easy part.

Mr. Steven Levine: I have seen no evidence that private credit currently poses a systemic risk.

Ranking Member Warren: No evidence? Ms. Johnson?

Ms. Kristin Johnson: Thank you, Ranking Member. I am a systemic risk scholar, and I believe there is the potential for systemic risk concerns related to the market that you identified.

Ranking Member Warren: I am just stunned by these answers. We know these risks are growing. Secretary Bessent has said these risks are growing. Jamie Dimon recognizes these risks growing. They are growing in the insurance market. Insurers now have more than $1.2 trillion invested in lightly regulated private credit. They are also growing in the AI sector, where AI companies are taking out massive loans from private credit and banks, loans they may never be able to pay back. And meanwhile, banks have a smaller cushion against the panic than they have had for the past decade, and as I noted earlier, American families are struggling with $19 trillion in debt.

So maybe it’s no surprise, what is the Trump administration doing about these risks? Are they tightening rules? Are they putting more financial cops on the beat so they can watch more carefully? Collecting more data from companies about this? No. The Trump administration's response is to say, “Lalala, I can’t hear you, everything is just fine.” And it looks like at least three out of the four of you are willing to play along with that. Mr. Levine, the SEC recently released its enforcement data for fiscal year 2026. Have the SEC’s enforcement actions against giant corporations that break the law increased or decreased while Donald Trump has been president?

Mr. Steven Levine: I can’t speak to the breakdown of —

Ranking Member Warren: It’s a matter of public record.

Mr. Steven Levine: I can say I know the enforcement results that were released this year are lower in total than in previous years.

Ranking Member Warren: Yeah. Since President Trump took office, SEC enforcement has fallen off a cliff. Overall enforcement is down 40%. Actions against public companies are down 80%. Money ordered to be recovered for investors who get cheated is down almost 90%. You can spin it however you want, but this is bad for families, bad for investors, and bad news for the economy generally.

Ms. Jurata, let me just ask you — the Fed, the FDIC, the OCC are responsible for making sure our banks don’t implode. How deep have the Trump administration cuts, staff cuts, gone with the banking regulators? I’ll watch my time.

Ms. Rebekah Jurata: Senator Warren, I don't know what the underlying personal decisions that have happened thus far, but what I do believe is that this administration and the financial regulators are recognizing that a one-size-fits-all regulation in the banking system —

Ranking Member Warren: So you’re fine with the cuts. The Chairman is gonna cut me off here. You three genuinely alarm me.

###

title: Cruz, Rosen Celebrate Senate Passage of the Bipartisan Muhammad Ali American Boxing Revival Act

committee.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation

text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Today, the U.S. Senate unanimously passed the Muhammad Ali American Boxing Revival Act, legislation sponsored by Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Senator Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.). The legislation now goes back to the House of Representatives, which is expected to pass it quickly and send it to President Trump for his signature.

The bill would remove legal barriers to allow voluntary, league-style Unified Boxing Organizations (UBOs) to compete alongside traditional promoters. It would also strengthen fighter protections and safety standards and create new opportunities for organizations to compete. This will give boxers more choices and fans better matchups.

Upon Senate passage, Chairman Cruz said: “We’re going to make boxing great again with the bipartisan Muhammad Ali American Boxing Revival Act. The bill expands opportunities for fighters, strengthens safety protections, and brings back the marquee matchups fans love. I hope the House quickly sends this bill to the President’s desk and delivers a knockout win for fighters and fans.”

Senator Rosen said: “Las Vegas is the center of the boxing universe, and when boxing thrives, more visitors come to Nevada and help boost our economy. I’ve proudly worked on this bill with Chairman Cruz and numerous stakeholders – including Muhammad Ali’s grandson Nico Ali Walsh – in order to revitalize this great sport and make important reforms to protect boxers. I’m thrilled to see our bipartisan legislation pass the Senate today, and I’m hopeful that the House will quickly pass it as well.”

Background

Chairman Cruz and Senator Rosen introduced the Muhammad Ali American Boxing Revival Act in July 2026 following a Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee hearing with professional boxers, promoters, and stakeholders. At the hearing, Chairman Cruz explained that while the current system has protected professional boxers from certain abuses, it has helped create a fractured system riddled with competing interests, multiple sanctioning bodies, and persistent barriers to organizing major fights. The Muhammad Ali American Boxing Revival Act would address these longstanding challenges and help restore boxing to the pastime that Americans have cherished for generations.

The bill overwhelmingly advanced out of the Commerce Committee in September and has the support of Lonnie Ali and Nico Ali Walsh, Muhammad Ali’s widow and grandson, respectively. Nico is also a professional boxer, and both are fierce advocates for the interests of fighters.

title: Heinrich Questions Trump Interior Nominee on Unlawful Firings of Inspectors General by the Trump Administration and Trump Energy Nominee on Skyrocketing Gas Prices Due to Trump’s War with Iran

committee.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources

text:
WASHINGTON — During a U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee hearing to consider pending Trump nominees, U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, cross examined Dennis Kirk, President Trump’s nomination for Inspector General of the Department of the Interior (DOI), and Toby Deen, Trump’s nomination for Assistant Secretary of Energy for Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy, where he pressed each nominee on the President’s unlawful firings of Inspectors General and the administration’s war with Iran.

VIDEO: Ranking Member Heinrich (D-N.M.) questions Dennis Kirk, President Trump’s nominee for Inspector General of the Department of the Interior, and Toby Deen, President Trump’s nominee for Assistant Secretary of Energy for Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy, November 18, 2026.

In his opening remarks, Heinrich connected Kirk’s nomination to a pattern of partisan Inspectors General appointees from the Trump administration, “More than one year into his second term, President Trump has fired or demoted more than 20 Inspectors General (IG) across the federal government. When President Trump has opted to fill IG vacancies, he has largely appointed allies with partisan backgrounds to fill those roles. I am concerned, Mr. Kirk, that your nomination continues this trend. President Trump has opted to fill the IG vacancy at the Department of the Interior with a political appointee.”

Heinrich expressed concerns over Kirk’s partisan background and allyship to the Trump administration, due to his involvement with gutting critical federal worker protections during the first Trump administration, his connection to the Heritage Foundation as a co-author of a chapter of Project 2025, and time at the IG office in the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, which sparked concerns from intelligence community officials on whether his appointment could compromise the integrity of the IG office.

“With this context in mind, I have deep concerns Mr. Kirk will be an independent and objective IG if confirmed,” said Heinrich.

When questioned during the hearing, Heinrich asked Kirk about whether Trump’s firing of Inspectors General without Congressional notification was unlawful, “In January of 2025, the President fired more than a dozen Inspectors General. And that included Mark Greenblatt, the DOI’s Inspector General. Now, the law requires the President to notify Congress prior to the firing of an IG and also provide written reasoning for that removal. That never happened. Mr. Kirk, you’re an attorney. The facts appear to me to be pretty straightforward. Was the law violated when Mr. Greenblatt was fired without providing notice to Congress or any reasoning?”

Kirk replied, “Thank you for that question, Senator Heinrich. I don’t know, because I’m not familiar with the circumstances of what happened to him. I know that Mark Greenblatt was —”

Heinrich interjected, saying, “I’m not litigating whether there was a reason to fire him. I’m litigating whether or not the law was followed, because we were not notified, and we were also not given any written reasoning. So let me let me read the law to you. This is the 1978 IG Act as amended in 2008, and it says that ‘the President shall communicate in writing the reasons for any such removal or transfer to both houses of Congress not later than 30 days before the removal or transfer.’”

Kirk responded, “Senator Heinrich, again, I don’t know why that was done that way, and I don’t know that… because I’ve never met a living President. I don’t have a picture of a President on my wall. They don’t —”

Heinrich asked again, “Does it appear that was done in violation of the law? If it is true that there was no written reasoning nor notification?”

Kirk replied, “Well, the law is the law, Senator.”

Heinrich concluded, “That’s my point.”

Heinrich also questioned Deen on Trump’s war with Iran driving up gas and diesel prices for Americans.

Heinrich asked, “The conflict in the Middle East has had a profoundly expensive impact on the American people, and we see that everywhere from the grocery store to the gas pump, certainly in diesel prices. Do you agree that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz is the primary factor driving the currently very high and unusual prices of gasoline and diesel that the American people have had to bear?”

Deen replied, “I appreciate the question, Senator. Products like diesel, refined petroleum products, are a global commodity, and it is a complex market with multiple drivers of price. Supply demand is a fundamental driver of that, and currently across the world, we are seeing a shortage of refining capacity that is a large driver…”

Heinrich responded, “Would you agree that the conflict, the impact of the conflict actually removing refining capacity from the global market, has been one of those factors?”

Deen replied, “Global refining capacity and domestic refining capacity all play a part there, and our U.S. domestic supply acts as a buffer to global supply shocks. Global supply shocks are always going to be a risk for the United States.”

Heinrich continued, “Fair enough. Did DOE look at the potential effects of having the Strait closed on energy prices? Was there some analysis done before the decisions were made to initiate that conflict?”

Deen responded, “That’s a fair question, Senator. I was not advising the Secretary or the White House regarding that conflict. The Department of Energy Secretary Wright is the President’s principal energy advisor. I’m sure they were having those discussions.”

Heinrich’s full opening remarks as delivered are below:

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

And thank you, Mr. Kirk and Mr. Deen, for appearing before the Committee today.

Mr. Kirk, I want to start with your nomination.

The President has nominated you to serve as the Department of the Interior’s Inspector General, one of our most important government positions.

Congress created Inspector General offices as “independent and objective units.”

IG offices are often the first line of defense against wrongdoing and misconduct in government offices.

Under the IG Act, IGs are to be appointed “without regard to political affiliation and solely on the basis of integrity and demonstrated ability.”

When at their best, IGs prevent and detect fraud, waste, and abuse and promote efficiency and effectiveness in government programs and operations.

They serve as the bedrock of a functioning government.

However, under this President, we have witnessed the deliberate dismantling of independent oversight.

In his first few days of his second term, this president fired more than a dozen Inspectors General — including Mark Greenblatt, the Department of the Interior’s Inspector General at the time.

These firings occurred without notice to Congress and in clear violation of the law.

The firings continued a trend that started during President Trump’s first term — the elimination of vital oversight checks.

More than one year into his second term, President Trump has fired or demoted more than 20 Inspectors General across the federal government.

When President Trump has opted to fill IG vacancies, he has largely appointed allies with partisan backgrounds to fill those roles.

I am concerned, Mr. Kirk, that your nomination continues this trend. President Trump has opted to fill the IG vacancy at the Department of the Interior with a political appointee.

Weeks before being formally nominated, the Trump administration deployed Mr. Kirk to the IG’s office at the Department of the Interior. This was a highly unusual decision.

Mr. Kirk arrived at DOI’s IG office as a senior advisor just as the Trump administration grappled with the deeply flawed Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool project.

A project that has faced mounting scrutiny not only from myself, but from the public and from many members of Congress.

Senator Whitehouse and I wrote to DOI’s Deputy IG requesting an inquiry days before the President formally nominated Mr. Kirk.

At the Office of Personnel Management during the President’s first term, Mr. Kirk helped push along the President’s controversial personnel policies, including Schedule F, which stripped federal employees of civil service protections.

After leaving the administration, Mr. Kirk reappeared at the Heritage Foundation where he co-authored a chapter of Project 2025.

And during President Trump’s second term, Mr. Kirk served at ODNI under Director Tulsi Gabbard. After the Signal-gate controversy, Ms. Gabbard quickly deployed him to the intelligence community’s IG office.

At the time, intelligence community officials feared that Mr. Kirk’s appointment to the IG’s office could compromise the integrity of an ongoing inquiry.

With this context in mind, I have deep concerns Mr. Kirk will be an independent and objective IG if confirmed.

But you do not have to take it from me.

Listen to Mr. Greenblatt, the person who President Trump nominated in 2019 to serve as DOI IG — a position he served honorably for more than five years until President Trump fired him for doing his job.

Following Mr. Kirk’s nomination, Mr. Greenblatt stated: “President Trump’s nomination of Dennis Kirk to serve as Inspector General of the Department of the Interior raises serious concerns about the independence and credibility of one of the federal government’s most important watchdog offices.”

Mr. Greenblatt went on to say, and I believe this is particularly salient, “Mr. Kirk is not an experienced auditor, investigator, prosecutor, or oversight professional. He is a partisan operative.”

Now to Mr. Deen.

The President has nominated Mr. Deen to be Assistant Secretary of Energy for Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy.

Beyond natural gas export permitting, which the president and this administration appear to be singularly focused on, the office has other important responsibilities, such as fossil energy research and development, geothermal energy research, carbon capture and sequestration deployment, hydrogen production, and methane emissions reduction.

Following President Trump’s reckless decision to enter into a war with Iran, we have seen gas and diesel prices sharply increase.

Americans from Albuquerque to Philadelphia are struggling. Diesel prices are around $6.00 nationally and gas prices are almost a dollar more nationally than they were before the war.

Mr. Deen, I will be interested in hearing your thoughts on how your office can help bring down skyrocketing energy prices, and I look forward to your testimony today.

Thank you, Mr. Chair.

title: Heinrich: Senate Passage of Landmark Bipartisan Permitting Deal Will Lower Electricity Bills, Hold Data Centers Accountable, Create Over One Hundred Thousand Jobs, Reduce Carbon Emissions

committee.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources

text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, released the following statement after the Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), bipartisan legislation to lower energy bills, hold data centers accountable, reduce emissions, and create good-paying jobs.

“In June, SunZia — the largest clean energy infrastructure project in the Western Hemisphere — came online in New Mexico after nearly two decades. The actual construction took just two years. That’s how badly our permitting system is holding America back.

“Americans sent Congress a clear message in this historic election: lower costs. They’re tired of watching their electricity bills go up while some of the wealthiest corporations in the world get a free ride. We don’t have to wait another year to deliver relief. We can act right now.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will get more affordable energy onto the grid faster, make data centers pay their fair share of electricity and grid costs, and create more than 100,000 good-paying American jobs — all while maintaining important environmental protections and strengthening Tribal consultation.

“This was a hard-fought bipartisan agreement, and it wasn’t easy. But we proved that Democrats and Republicans can put politics aside and deliver meaningful results for the American people.

“I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished. Now let’s get this bill across the finish line and signed into law.”

Independent analyses project that the legislation will:

Lower household electricity bills: Reduce electricity prices by an estimated 3–5 percent, saving households approximately $50–$78 annually by 2040, according to Rhodium Group.

Make data centers pay their fair share: Require data centers to contribute approximately $55 billion toward transmission costs over the next decade — approximately $35 billion more than they would pay under current policy, according to Grid Strategies.

Create good-paying American jobs: Support up to 105,600 trades and manufacturing jobs through 2040, according to Employ America.

Get more clean energy onto the grid: Increase solar and wind generation to an estimated 37.4 percent of total U.S. electricity generation by 2035, compared with 19.6 percent under the current permitting regime, according to the Solar Energy Industries Association.

Reduce emissions and improve public health: Avoid as much as 1.5 gigatons of cumulative carbon emissions and $54 billion in public health damages.

Now that the legislation has passed the Senate, it must also pass the House of Representatives before heading to the President’s desk to be signed into law.

Heinrich, along with U.S. Senators Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, Shelley More Capito (R-W. Va.), Chairman of the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and Mike Lee (R-Utah), Chairman of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act in September.

Since introducing the legislation, Heinrich has led an extensive effort to build bipartisan support, engage stakeholders, and make the case for why permitting reform is essential to lowering energy costs and building America’s energy future. He has held press conferences in Washington, D.C., and New Mexico; met with labor leaders, energy developers, Tribal representatives, and community stakeholders; and secured important improvements to the legislation through negotiations and amendments.

In a recent op-ed for The Economist, Heinrich made the case that America’s permitting system has become one of the country’s most expensive economic bottlenecks — and explained how BAAJA can help the country build more energy infrastructure while protecting communities and holding data centers accountable.

Earlier this month, Heinrich released a Substitute Amendment to BAAJA. The Substitute Amendment included clarifying, conforming, and technical edits to reflect feedback received since the bill’s introduction in September.

For more information on the legislation and what it means for American families, workers, and communities, see the resources below.

title: Senate Resoundingly Passes Chairman Lee’s Landmark Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act

committee.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Mike Lee (R-Utah), Chairman of the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, celebrated Senate passage of his Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), a landmark bipartisan bill to restore Americans’ freedom to build by fixing the nation’s broken federal permitting system, lowering costs for American families, and unleashing American energy production and infrastructure development.

The bill, authored by Chairman Lee, Senate Environment and Public Works Chairman Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), ENR Ranking Member Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), and EPW Ranking Member Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), represents a major breakthrough after years of stalled attempts to enact comprehensive permitting reform.

“This is a big day for the American people,” said Chairman Lee. “BAAJA is all about giving the American people the freedom to build, the freedom to build things that the American people need.”

“Whether you’ve heard of it or not, whether you’re rooting for it or against it, you will benefit from this bill once it becomes law.”

“This is a happy occasion. We just passed a big bill. A bill that I will till my dying day be bragging to my grandkids about. Why? Well, because we’ll be able to point back, starting next year, the first year after this bill has become law, the average American family is going to save at a minimum, hundreds of dollars every year on their electric power bill.”

With Senate passage secured, BAAJA now heads to the House of Representatives. Chairman Lee urged his House colleagues to act quickly and send the legislation to President Trump’s desk.

title: Whitehouse Cheers Senate Passage of Landmark Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act

committee.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works

text:
Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Ranking Member of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee, this evening released the following statement after the Senate voted to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA):

“This bill kicks off Democrats bringing down energy costs, lowering emissions, creating well-paying jobs, and ending the free ride for data centers. Passing BAAJA in the Senate was a major step forward, and I’m grateful to my colleagues and our friends in the labor movement and the clean energy industry for their hard work to make this happen. Americans will quickly begin getting some relief on their energy bills if the House follows suit.”

BAAJA will deliver cheaper energy, more well-paying jobs, and responsible growth by accelerating the permitting and construction of critical energy and infrastructure projects while maintaining key environmental and historic preservation safeguards. The legislation provides greater certainty for projects that have already been permitted and financed, including by preventing future administrations from arbitrarily blocking entire classes of energy projects, while establishing clear timelines for environmental reviews and legal challenges. It also includes targeted reforms to expand and modernize the electric grid, speed the development of geothermal and other energy projects, and ensure that rapidly growing data centers pay the full cost of their associated transmission needs rather than passing those costs on to families and small businesses. The legislation reflects input from members of Congress on both sides of the aisle and a diverse group of stakeholders.

The legislation has been endorsed by the AFL-CIO, North America’s Building Trades Unions, Laborers’ International Union of North America (LIUNA), Evergreen Action, and Citizens’ Climate Lobby. The New York Times editorial board has urged Democrats to “take the deal” and pass the legislation, highlighting its capacity to deliver lower electricity costs and reduce emissions.

BAAJA now heads to the House of Representatives.

title: Wyden and Chu Reintroduce PROGRESS Act to Increase Capital for Women and Minority-Owned Businesses
text:
Washington, D.C. – Today, Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Rep. Judy Chu, D-Calif., reintroduced the bicameral Providing Real Opportunities for Growth to Rising Entrepreneurs for Sustained Success (PROGRESS) Act to strengthen access to capital for small businesses owned by women and people of color.

“Capital in America has a blind spot when it comes to people of color and women business owners, and as a consequence that’s holding back a lot of hardworking entrepreneurs and big economic potential,” Senator Wyden said. “This bill gives us an opportunity to drive more dollars toward a lot of dedicated entrepreneurs who are eager to grow successful businesses and create jobs.”

“Small businesses are the backbone of our communities, but too many entrepreneurs, especially women and people of color who lack longstanding relationships with financial institutions, still struggle to access the capital they need to grow,” said Rep. Chu, who serves on the House Ways and Means Committee. “That is a missed opportunity for all of us. Senator Wyden and I are reintroducing the PROGRESS Act to establish tax credits for first employees and investors, so that these promising businesses aren’t held back simply because they lack the right connections. When we level the playing field for women-owned and minority-owned businesses, we create jobs, strengthen our local economies, and unlock their full potential.”

On average, white business owners start with nearly three times the working capital of black-owned businesses. Male entrepreneurs, on average, start with nearly twice as much capital as female entrepreneurs. The numbers are even worse when considering only third-party capital. In 2025, only 1 percent of venture capital funding went to companies founded solely by women. This disparity is acutely felt by women of color who now account for 47 percent of all women-owned firms, yet received less than 1% of venture capital funding over the past decade.

Because of their size, their industry, or the way they are organized, many women-owned businesses can’t take advantage of tax benefits designed for small businesses. Simply put, minority and female entrepreneurs are underrepresented, underestimated, and undercapitalized. This lack of capital has limited the ability of these entrepreneurs to grow their businesses.

The PROGRESS Act establishes two new tax incentives to unlock the resources these businesses need to grow and reach their full potential:

First Employee Credit: A new first employee credit will stimulate business growth and job creation.

A credit equal to 25 percent of reported W-2 wages can be claimed annually, up to $10,000 in a single tax year, with a lifetime limit of $40,000.

Because many businesses do not turn a profit in their early years, the first employee credit can be claimed against the business’ payroll tax liability.

Certain businesses that have not reported full-time equivalent W-2 wages in a previous year are eligible for the credit.

Eligible businesses must be majority-owned by U.S. individuals who each earn 100,000 or less per year (200,000 in the case of joint filers).

Investor Credit:

A new investment credit will encourage third-party capital investment and help small businesses grow and thrive.

A credit of up to 50 percent of a qualified debt or equity investment can be claimed, up to $10,000 in a single tax year, with a lifetime limit of $50,000.

Investors who fund eligible businesses can use the credit to boost their rate of return.

Eligible businesses must have at least one full-time equivalent employee and be majority-owned by U.S. individuals who each earn 100,000orlessperyear(200,000 in the case of joint filers).

“We support the creation of tax incentives designed to boost the potential of all small businesses, but we’re particularly encouraged to see legislation that would help support historically underserved businesses—those owned by women and minorities,” said Alexis D’Amato Falvey, Senior Director of Federal Government Affairs for Small Business Majority. “Many types of small businesses struggle to access the capital they need to grow, but small firms owned by women and minorities are more likely to experience funding challenges. Meanwhile, our research found that the current tax code falls short for these businesses, with existing deductions instead disproportionately benefiting the largest firms. Policies like the tax credits proposed by Sen. Wyden and Rep. Chu would help address the capital gap and are critical to ensuring a level playing field that provides more entrepreneurs with a chance to succeed.”

“Small businesses are the backbone of our economy, and ensuring that women and people of color owned businesses have the resources and opportunities to grow is essential to building a stronger, more inclusive small business landscape. The reintroduction of the PROGRESS Act by Sen. Wyden and Rep. Chu represents an important step toward addressing persistent barriers to entrepreneurship by creating targeted tax credits that help small business owners navigate real economic challenges, invest in their businesses, and sustain long-term growth. At Main Street Alliance, we know that expanding access to meaningful financial support is critical not only to helping small businesses start and grow, but also to ensuring they can remain resilient, retain employees, and continue contributing to thriving local economies,” said Lauren Bealore, National Director of Policy & Programs of Main Street Alliance.

“Access to capital remains one of the greatest hurdles for Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) entrepreneurs striving to launch and scale their businesses,” said Chiling Tong, President and CEO of the National Asian Pacific Islander American Chamber of Commerce (National ACE). “The reintroduction of the PROGRESS Act is vital to breaking down systemic barriers as it leverages tax credits to increase private investment for start-ups. This legislation directly empowers our small business owners to innovate, expand, and drive job creation across the country. We deeply appreciate Senator Wyden and Congresswoman Chu for their continued leadership and commitment to championing all small businesses.”

“Angel investing, venture capital (VC), and other forms of investment can and should be viable options for women in the early stages of their businesses. Yet in 2022, women-founded startups received less than 2% of all venture capital dollars. Women, especially women of color, remain underrepresented and undercapitalized in angel investing and VC. WIPP’s Access to Capital Framework calls on congressional leaders to create tax incentives for angel investors, including incentives to invest in women- and minority-owned businesses. We are pleased to see Congresswoman Judy Chu take meaningful steps toward that goal with the PROGRESS Act,” said Angela Dingle, President and CEO of Women Impacting Public Policy. “By creating two tax credits, one for first-time employees and another for investors, the bill would pave the way for women business owners to access capital without turning to loans or dipping into their personal savings.”

“Small businesses are the backbone of our economy, yet too many entrepreneurs, particularly women and people of color, continue to face significant barriers to accessing the capital and resources they need to succeed,” said Anne Zimmerman, Co-Chair of Small Business for America’s Future. “The PROGRESS Act takes an important step toward leveling the playing field by providing targeted tax incentives that help small business owners invest in their businesses, create jobs, and build long-term economic stability. At a time when rising costs and economic uncertainty are putting increasing pressure on Main Street, we need commonsense solutions that give entrepreneurs the tools to grow and thrive. Small Business for America’s Future is proud to support this legislation and its commitment to expanding economic opportunity for small business owners across the country.”

The bill is cosponsored by Reps. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and Lateefah Simon, D-Calif.

title: Ranking Member Shaheen Opening Remarks for Nominations Hearings for Key National Security Positions
text:
WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senator Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, delivered opening remarks during a committee hearing to consider the nominations of McCoy Pitt to be U.S. Representative to the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, Austin Holmes to be Ambassador to Haiti and Elliott Hulse to be Chief Executive Officer of the Millennium Challenge Corporation. In her remarks, Ranking Member Shaheen stressed the importance of U.S. leadership to address the security and humanitarian crises in Haiti, oversee inspections and destruction of chemical weapons and engage with international partners on economic security and poverty reduction.

You can watch her opening remarks here.

Ranking Member Shaheen underscored the importance of U.S. contributions to the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons to ensure international inspections are carried out.

“Since Assad's fall, inspectors have uncovered previously undeclared chemical weapons in Syria,” said Ranking Member Shaheen. “But the Administration has failed to pay what it owes the OPCW, threatening its ability to carry out inspections in Syria. If confirmed, I hope you will help ensure that Syria's remaining chemical weapons are found and destroyed once and for all.”

Ranking Member Shaheen emphasized the severe humanitarian conditions Haiti faces, urging the nominee to be Ambassador to Haiti to address the pervasive corruption backing Haitian gangs.

“Haiti is facing a security and humanitarian crisis, as I am sure you are aware, with armed gangs controlling much of Port-au-Prince,” said Ranking Member Shaheen. “Nearly 1.5 million people have been displaced. If confirmed, I hope you will press the Administration to do more to hold the political and economic elites backing Haiti's gangs accountable. That’s the key to helping restore security and stability to the country.”

Ranking Member Shaheen urged the nominee to be CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation to restore the effectiveness of the MCC and counter expanding Chinese influence.

“The MCC has long helped reduce poverty, as the Chairman said, while advancing American economic and national security interests,” said Ranking Member Shaheen. “Unfortunately, this Administration has terminated programs and reduced the agency's capacity, even as China expands its influence in developing countries. If confirmed, I hope you will work to restore the MCC's effectiveness and make full use of the authority Congress has given it.”

The Ranking Member’s remarks, as delivered, are below.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman and welcome to our nominees, congratulations to each of you, welcome to your families and supporters who are here today.

Each of you has been nominated to an important position at a time when the Administration needs to deliver on its commitments. If confirmed, I hope you will be a voice for making sure that it follows through.

Mr. Pitt, you’ve been nominated to serve as U.S. Representative to the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons. Since Assad's fall, inspectors have uncovered previously undeclared chemical weapons in Syria. But the Administration has failed to pay what it owes the OPCW, threatening its ability to carry out inspections in Syria. If confirmed, I hope you will help ensure that Syria's remaining chemical weapons are found and destroyed once and for all.

Mr. Holmes, you have been nominated to serve as U.S. Ambassador to Haiti. Haiti is facing a security and humanitarian crisis, as I am sure you are aware, with armed gangs controlling much of Port-au-Prince. Nearly 1.5 million people have been displaced. If confirmed, I hope you will press the Administration to do more to hold the political and economic elites backing Haiti's gangs accountable. That’s the key to helping restore security and stability to the country.

Finally, Mr. Hulse, you have been nominated to serve as CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation. The MCC has long helped reduce poverty, as the Chairman said, while advancing American economic and national security interests. Unfortunately, this Administration has terminated programs and reduced the agency's capacity, even as China expands its influence in developing countries. If confirmed, I hope you will work to restore the MCC's effectiveness and make full use of the authority Congress has given it.

I look forward to hearing from you all.

Thank you very much again for your willingness to serve the country.

title: Chairman Risch Remarks at Anwar Sadat Congressional Gold Medal Ceremony
text:
WASHINGTON - U.S. Senator Jim Risch (R-Idaho), chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, today gave the following remarks at the Congressional Gold Medal Ceremony in honor of Anwar Sadat.

Chairman Risch gave the following remarks:

“Thank you all for coming here today on this important occasion.

“We are here today to honor a man, former President Anwar Sadat, who truly embodied what it means to be an ally, a partner, and a friend – something we in America cherish deeply in the Middle East.

“Sadat was a visionary—a man who could see a future of peace in the Middle East and worked to make it a reality; notably with the signing of the historic 1979 Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty, in the face of overwhelming criticism from the region.

“This treaty, which remains in place today and is the foundation of our alliance structure in the Middle East,

formally ended three decades of war and made Egypt the first Arab nation to officially recognize Israel.

“While it helped create tremendous opportunity for the region, it also sparked great opposition and ultimately led to his tragic assassination by radical extremists.

“Sadat is the first Egyptian to receive a Congressional Gold Medal, a testament to his impact and his leadership.

“I met with the foreign minister of Egypt earlier today, and we discussed the age-old subject of peacemaking in the Middle East, among other issues.

“While Sadat’s vision of a harmonious region has yet to be fully realized, I remain optimistic that we can see that goal become a reality in the not too distant future.

“Sadat once said that he hoped his tombstone would read: ‘he has lived for peace, and he has died for principles.’

“Together with allies like Israel, Egypt, and others in the region, we will honor Sadat by never giving up on peace and living out our principles each and every day.

“I’m very proud to be part of a Congress that understands the importance of Mr. Sadat’s legacy. Thank you again for having me here today and thank you to the family and the Egyptians that have traveled here today to join us in this celebration. Thank you.”

These remarks have been lightly edited for clarity.

title: JEC’s Schweikert Calls for a Tech-Neutral Approach to Rural Broadband Funding
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – A new brief from the Joint Economic Committee (JEC), titled “ReConnect: In Need of a Technologically Neutral Approach,” finds that the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) ReConnect rural broadband program could deliver significant savings to taxpayers by adopting technology-neutral requirements and allowing Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite providers, such as Starlink and Amazon LEO, to compete with traditional fiber providers.

“Our broadband policy should move with the greatest speed and efficiency to connect rural America at the fairest cost to taxpayers,” said JEC Chairman David Schweikert. “Congress can restore ReConnect to its original purpose by codifying technology-neutral requirements and ensuring federal dollars prioritize connecting communities, not subsidizing costly infrastructure that may not be the most effective solution.”

The analysis, based on JEC calculations, uses the Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program as a proxy to demonstrate the potential cost savings from technology-neutral broadband policies.

Key findings from the brief include:

Regulatory restrictions have increased costs: USDA's preference for fiber and exclusion of LEO satellite providers have limited competition and contributed to exceptionally expensive broadband deployments, including an award exceeding $1 million per person.

Technology neutrality can generate substantial savings: BEAD reforms produced nearly $853 million in actual savings across four states, or approximately $315 million after adjusting for differences in the number of locations served.

LEO satellites offer a significantly more cost-effective alternative: Average deployment costs in BEAD were $1,177 per location for LEO satellites, compared with $5,565 for fiber—nearly a fivefold difference.

Congress can institutionalize competition and fiscal accountability in ReConnect: H.R. 10288, the Rural Broadband Modernization Act, would establish technology-neutral requirements, improve transparency, and ensure federal broadband subsidies prioritize connecting rural Americans rather than favoring more expensive infrastructure.

The BEAD savings figures reflect actual and normalized savings across Louisiana, Nevada, Delaware, and West Virginia. They are not projections of potential savings from ReConnect reforms or a 10-year federal budget estimate.

Read the full brief here.

title: Durbin Calls Out Senate Republicans For Jamming Through Extreme And Unqualified Judicial Nominees
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, today delivered a speech on the Senate floor calling out Senate Republicans for jamming through the Trump Administration’s extreme and unqualified judicial nominees during the lame-duck session. In his remarks, Durbin slammed Senate Republicans for violating longstanding bipartisan Senate Judiciary Committee norms to fast-track judicial nominees because Democrats are poised to lead the Senate come January. Further, Durbin pointed to the judicial misconduct allegations against Daniel Ballou, who has been nominated to be a district court judge in the Eastern District of Kentucky and who Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD) has filed cloture on, as a dangerous example of Senate Republicans’ ploy to cram the bench with extreme judges with a history of behavior unbecoming of a lifetime appointment.

“I have been a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee for nearly 30 years and I chaired the Committee for a four year period of time. I have closely evaluated the credentials and records of more than a thousand judicial nominees appointed by Presidents of both parties. So believe me when I tell you that in the past two years, my colleagues on the other side of the aisle have largely disregarded their advice and consent duty to confirm some of the most extreme nominees in our nation’s history,” Durbin began.

“In the aftermath of this month’s Democratic landslide election, they [Senate Republicans] are shattering a number of Committee norms to jam through more inexperienced nominees before Democrats are in control of the Senate on January 3,” Durbin said.

Since the election, Senate Republicans have tried to fast-track nominees by holding nominations hearings eight days apart despite norms dictating that these hearings should be scheduled at least two weeks apart; slating nominees for hearings sooner than the standard 28 days after receiving their Senate Judiciary Questionnaires; and calling nominees for hearings even if their FBI background investigations have not yet been cleared by staff.

“What these decisions mean is that Senators of both parties will have less time to carefully consider these lifetime appointees…Republicans are setting new precedents to rush through unqualified MAGA nominees,” Durbin said. “Mark my words: Democrats will be well within our rights to rely on these precedents in the future to confirm nominees. As I have said many times, there cannot be one set of rules for Republicans and another for Democrats.”

“For as long as I can remember, every judicial nominee has been closely vetted by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and Committee staff have reviewed these investigations to determine, before a nominee’s confirmation hearing, that there are no concerning aspects of their record,” Durbin said. “As a threshold matter, Senators should feel confident that judicial nominees don’t have a criminal record, that they are not financially insolvent, and that they are well-regarded by judges and others in the legal community. This week, the Judiciary Committee will do something unprecedented: it will slate nominees for these lifetime appointments to the federal bench even if their background investigations haven’t been completed and reviewed by the Committee.”

Further, Senate Republicans have allowed blatantly unqualified nominees to seek lifetime appointments to the federal bench.

“If there is a theme among Trump nominees, it is the vast majority are blatantly inexperienced. As an example, at last week’s nominations hearing, we heard from two nominees who have been out of law school for just eight years. One of them has practiced law for just seven years. The other has only practiced for five years. That is less experience than any Biden nominee or any prior Trump nominee,” Durbin said. “Two of the nominees at last week’s hearing have never tried a case.”

Durbin then called out Majority Leader Thune for filing cloture on Daniel Ballou, nominated to be a district court judge in the Eastern District of Kentucky, despite being the subject of an outstanding judicial misconduct allegation.

“This is not the first time that Judge Ballou has been investigated while on the bench. In 2011, he was publicly reprimanded by Kentucky’s nonpartisan Judicial Conduct Commission for using his position as a judge to campaign for a political candidate. And just days ago, the same commission filed three new misconduct charges against Judge Ballou for repeatedly belittling an attorney for posting a video on social media that Judge Ballou didn’t personally like,” Durbin said.

“These allegations reveal a troubling pattern of poor judgment, which is going to be rewarded with a lifetime appointment to the federal bench by this Republican majority in the Senate. My Republican colleagues seem intent on advancing Judge Ballou regardless of his conduct. What a shame. In my time in the Senate, I cannot recall another instance where we confirmed a judge who was the subject of a pending judicial misconduct complaint,” Durbin continued.

Durbin concluded his remarks by calling on Senate Republicans to abandon their plans to jam through unqualified judicial nominees and instead honor their constitutional advice and consent responsibility.

“It is clear that to this President, experience and sound judgment do not matter when it comes to judges…His sole consideration is loyalty,” Durbin said.

“My colleagues on the other side of the aisle are opening Pandora’s box—their flouting of longstanding norms will reshape the way that we approach judicial confirmations for years to come. It is not too late to reverse course. It is not too late to honor our responsibility under the Constitution to provide advice and consent,” Durbin concluded his remarks.

title: Durbin Introduces Legislation To Repeal MLB’s 100-Year-Old Antitrust Exemption
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, introduced the Competition in Professional Baseball Act to repeal Major League Baseball’s (MLB) 100-year-old judicially-created antitrust exemption, which would place baseball on the same footing as all other professional sports. U.S. Senator Mike Lee (R-UT) is a cosponsor of the legislation.

“I have said for years that it is time to reconsider MLB’s special antitrust exemption, which allows them to act as a lawful monopoly. It is important to note that MLB is the only professional sport to benefit from a broad exemption from the antitrust laws—one that is based on a Supreme Court decision that the Court itself has said is wrong. My bill would repeal professional baseball’s judicially-created antitrust exemption and finally place baseball on the same footing as all other professional sports,” said Durbin.

As Chair of the Judiciary Committee during the Biden Administration, Durbin led efforts to improve working conditions for minor league baseball players by investigating how MLB’s antitrust exemption impacted those working conditions. In June 2022, Durbin led a letter to Advocates for Minor Leaguers asking about the impact of MLB’s antitrust exemption on competition in the labor market for Minor League players. In July 2022, Durbin sent a similar letter to Commissioner Manfred.

These letters played a role in pushing MLB to recognize the unionization of Minor League Baseball players under the umbrella of the Major League Baseball Players Association (MLBPA) in September 2022.

In November 2023, Durbin and a group of Senators pressed Rob Manfred, the Commissioner of the MLB, on its lobbying for a broad exemption from wage and hour laws at the same time it was negotiating its Minor League CBA with MLBPA. Following this, Durbin introduced the Fair Ball Act, which would have contingently repealed an exemption from federal wage and hour laws for Minor League players if they were not being compensated pursuant to the terms of a CBA.
