title: Durbin Releases GAO Report On The Wasteful Immigration Detention Spending Under The Trump Administration
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, today led the release of the Government Accountability Office’s (GAO) newly-completed report examining the cost of immigration detention under the Trump Administration’s U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) entitled, “ICE Should Determine Cost Effectiveness of New Initiatives Before Continuing”.

ICE received $45 billion in immigration detention funding in July 2025 through Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act. According to GAO’s report: “In addition to maintaining existing facilities with these funds, ICE began implementing an initiative to buy and renovate a collection of warehouses to use as new detention facilities. However, after acquiring 11 warehouses for about $1.07 billion, ICE scaled down the initiative significantly and plans to sell seven of them. In July and August 2026, ICE also bought four existing detention facilities for about $2.2 billion total. However, the scope, time frames, and estimated costs for further acquisitions remain undetermined. In addition, ICE did not update its spending plan for detention funding to reflect the shifting status of the warehouse initiative or other planned acquisitions, as required by its internal guidance. As a result, the spending plan includes an inflated estimate of planned obligations, which affects oversight efforts and ICE’s ability to assess long-term budget needs.”

“This report has uncovered more of what we’ve come to expect from the Trump Administration—rushed and wasteful spending of taxpayer dollars without any benefit to the American people. Remember when Donald Trump promised to get rid of ‘waste, fraud, and abuse’? Well, GAO continues to expose a shocking pattern of waste within the Administration’s unconscionable mass deportation campaign,” said Durbin. “The midterm elections showed that the American people are sick and tired of the Trump Administration’s cruel immigration tactics. It is time to hold DHS and ICE responsible.”

GAO’s key findings include:

Warehouses bought, then abandoned. From January to March 2026, ICE bought 11 warehouses for about $1.07 billion. It paid at least 50 percent above assessed tax value for nine of them and at least double for seven. After DHS paused the initiative, the DHS Secretary testified that the department “had not conducted appropriate due diligence and planning.” ICE now plans to sell seven of the properties, and GAO warns the sales could lose the government money.

$2.2 billion more in facility purchases, with no expected savings. In July and August 2026, ICE bought four existing detention facilities for about $2.2 billion. ICE officials told GAO they do not expect these purchases to save money because the goal is to keep operating where ICE faces pushback from state governments. ICE is considering buying up to seven more but gave GAO no timeline or cost estimates.

Paying for empty beds. ICE has committed to pay for 46,688 beds at 64 facilities whether or not they are used. From October 2025 to April 2026, an average of 9,733 of those beds sat empty each day. At just four facilities, GAO estimates ICE paid about $13 million a month for empty beds.

Guantánamo Bay at more than $110 million. ICE and the Department of Defense obligated about $111 million for immigration detention at Guantánamo Bay, where the average daily population was fewer than 30. ICE officials told GAO that cost did not factor into the decision and that conserving costs is not a goal there.

An outdated, inflated spending plan. As of June 2026, ICE’s spending plan still projected about $38 billion in fiscal year 2026 obligations. Through July, ICE had obligated $9.1 billion. GAO called it unrealistic that ICE would obligate another $29 billion in two months.

Overstretched oversight staff. The staff who validate facility invoices are short-handed, with 55 of 87 positions vacant while the number of detention facilities roughly doubled.

A copy of the GAO report can be found here.

title: Grassley Speaks on Recent DOJ Report Exposing Biden Admin’s Targeting of Parents’ First Amendment Rights

The Justice Department’s October report concerns a 2021 legal memo issued by then-Attorney General Merrick Garland.

Now, that memo absurdly accused parents of nationwide harassment and threats of violence against school boards.

The cause of this disgraceful memo was this, simply: that moms and dads were merely voicing their concerns at school board meetings in the wake of the pandemic.

So, these parents – moms and dads – [were] just stating their concerns at a school board meeting. Things you could expect would be done by any citizen [at] any time.

So, at the time, parents in Iowa and across the country had become unsettled about COVID-19 policies and transgender topics in schools, among many other issues that they wanted to talk to their school boards about.

When taxpayers think something’s wrong, they can certainly demand a change in course from government officials, and that’s especially the case when it involves the children of those families.

In recent campaigns, I heard a lot of concerns by Democrats about children, but in the case of the Garland [memo], they were radio silent...

The right to petition and express one’s political beliefs are very fundamental rights – that’s what our Constitution and the First Amendment recognize and guarantee.

Yet, that’s not how the Biden Department of Justice saw these parents, and my Democratic colleagues didn’t do any real oversight on this matter. And in a sense, by doing nothing, [Democrats] refused to hold the government accountable. And that’s the very basics of the checks and balances of government – for people in the congressional branch of government to make sure that the executive branch faithfully executes the laws.

Garland’s [memo] asserted that there’s been “a disturbing spike in harassment, intimidation and threats of violence against school administrators, board members, teachers and staff.”

Now, you might ask yourself: “What were the threats that the Biden administration had in mind?”

Bizarrely, the memo doesn’t provide a single example.

What unfolded next was government weaponization against moms and dads going to school boards to express their views.

The Garland memo authorized the use of DOJ and FBI resources to “discourage these threats, identify them when they occur and prosecute them when appropriate.”

All of this just for exercising freedom of speech.

In short, the Garland memo was a license for federal law enforcement to impose the immense power of the government on concerned parents just simply expressing a view.

According to DOJ’s report, the FBI opened 25 “Guardian assessments,” including on a mother because she belonged to a “right-wing mom’s group” and then again, a father because “he rail[ed] against the government.”

What’s more, the FBI admitted that it created an internal threat tag for its systems called E-D-U OFFICIALS in response to the Garland [memo]. E-D-U as in the word, “education.”

According to DOJ’s report, the Biden administration was lobbied to develop these weaponized policies at the request of the National School Boards Association (NSBA).

Before the now discredited Garland memo was written, the NSBA sent a letter to President Biden describing these concerned parents as participating in “domestic terrorism” – a charge which the NSBA later was forced to apologize for.

According to DOJ, the NSBA did more than smear families—they actually lobbied the Biden administration to unleash federal law enforcement on parents.

The DOJ’s report claims, in part, the Garland memo was “an outgrowth of the NSBA Letter . . . label[ing] parental speech protesting school board policies as potentially involving . . . domestic terrorism, hate crimes or conspiracies.”

The Department’s report also made clear that the Garland memo was a product of collaboration between the NSBA leadership and high-level officials in the White House. Not just at the DOJ.

So, we need to look at what the consequences of the Garland memo [were].

The DOJ’s report spells it out in very plain English.

The DOJ states that “Biden Administration actions chilled the exercise of parental and free speech rights.”

That’s something that my Republican colleagues and I condemned way back in October of 2021. Where were my Democratic colleagues? Nowhere to be found.

For example, during an oversight hearing of the Biden DOJ shortly after the Garland memo was issued, this senator reminded the Attorney General that parents have a vested interest in how schools educate their children.

I further reminded the then-Attorney General that concerned mothers and fathers exercising their First Amendment rights should never be smeared with a broad brush as national security threats.

It was fundamentally wrong to target American parents.

My Democratic colleagues couldn’t care less at that time, or maybe even now.

In fact, not one of my Democratic colleagues joined a letter my Republican colleagues and this senator wrote to Attorney General Garland three days after the Garland memo was issued.

In that letter, my Republican colleagues and I made it plain that “federal law enforcement muscle should never be used against protesting parents.”

These wrongs must be addressed – and it’s very encouraging that Attorney General Blanche is committed to righting the wrongs of the Biden administration by exposing this unconstitutional activity.

Congress, a co-[equal] branch of government, must also continue to ensure that the rights of individual Americans are safeguarded—regardless of the party in power.

And this senator will certainly do that.

title: Grassley, Wyden Introduce Crime Victims Fund Prioritization Act
text:
WASHINGTON – Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) this week introduced the Crime Victims Fund Prioritization Act to authorize the transfer of funds from the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) Working Capital Fund to the Crime Victims Fund (CVF), in the event the Crime Victims Fund’s balance drops too low. This bipartisan legislation would ensure the critical program continues to have the resources necessary to support victims and survivors of crime.

“The Crime Victims Fund is a taxpayer neutral program that supports victims and survivors of crime across the United States. By establishing new funding sources, the bipartisan Crime Victims Fund Prioritization Act will ensure the critical fund can continue assisting Americans for decades to come,” Grassley said.

“Inconsistent funding has left crime victims without the support they need for far too long,” Wyden said. “It’s past time to secure a funding fix to ensure victims of crime and their families get the help and care when they need it the most, and our bipartisan bill is the way to do it.”

Bill text is available HERE.

Background:

Congress in 1984 established the Crime Victims Fund to support victims and survivors of crime across the United States. The program was designed to be taxpayer neutral, funded entirely by fines and penalties collected through federal criminal convictions and settlements.

Despite passing the Grassley-backed VOCA Fix Act to bolster the Crime Victims Fund in 2021, Grassley’s oversight last Congress revealed that billions of dollars in fines and penalties weren’t being collected or deposited into the fund. Rather, these dollars were being directed elsewhere, including to the DOJ’s Working Capital Fund, which pays for the agency’s IT services and equipment.

title:
Blumenthal Grills Oracle CEO Over Skyrocketing Cost of VA Electronic Health Record Contract
At oversight hearing, Blumenthal raised scrutiny over the link between Oracle’s Executive Chairman Larry Ellison and President Trump
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – At a Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee oversight hearing yesterday, Ranking Member Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) pressed Oracle CEO Mike Sicilia on the ballooning cost of the VA’s Electronic Health Record Modernization (EHRM) program and close relationship between Oracle’s Executive Chairman Larry Ellison and President Trump. Oracle’s contract for the VA EHRM program was recently modified, increasing the cost ceiling of the no-bid contract from $10 billion to $27 billion.

“Veterans have waited almost 10 years for an Electronic Health Record that is still not fully deployed, and the estimated costs have nearly tripled…Oracle says this contract is about veterans. But we know the company’s chairman is reportedly a $45 million backer of the President’s political network. We also know this administration just tripled his company’s no-bid contract, told no one in Congress beforehand, and still can’t explain or justify that number,” said Blumenthal.

During his questioning, Blumenthal called out Sicilia’s “non-explanation” for why the cost of the contract dramatically increased and stated Oracle’s delivery of the EHRM project “could hardly be called satisfactory.”

Blumenthal also questioned Sicilia over the link between Ellison and Trump in light of the three-fold cost increase of Oracle’s no-bid contract: “Are you aware of ahead of the 2024 election Larry Ellison gave about $45 million to a non-profit backing Trump’s campaign as well as other funds connected to Trump’s legacy initiatives, as their called, Freedom 250, reported to be about one million dollars?”

“Are you aware of other business involvements between Larry Ellison and the Trump family?”

“Are you aware Oracle was awarded a ten year $395.8 million contract by OPM to establish a single HR system for the federal government?”

“Are you aware of stock in Oracle owned by President Trump?...The estimates are that his stock ownership is in the millions of dollars, we don’t know precisely how much. It may be at least one to five million dollars, but very likely higher, because of when and how he purchased that stock earlier this year. Would you say that those kind of links between Larry Ellison and President Trump create a reason for this Committee, and also the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations which I’m the Ranking Member now, hopefully Chairman [soon], to do further factual inquiry?”

When Sicilia answered he did not know this information, Blumenthal concluded by calling on Ellison to come before the Committee: “You’re not able to answer these questions. You’re not directly involved—Mr. Ellison is. He’s not here. I think he should be here.”

Prior to this hearing, Ellison and Sicilia have avoided fielding public questions about significant cost overruns, repeated schedule delays, and patient safety concerns. On September 2, Ellison and Sicilia failed to testify before a Congressional oversight hearing on the EHRM program, which triggered a unanimous vote in the House Committee on Veterans’ Affairs to subpoena the two Oracle officials.

Soon after, Blumenthal and Senate Committee Democratic members wrote Ellison and Sicilia demanding documents and an explanation for the cost increase. They backed the House subpoenas and called on Chairman Jerry Moran (R-KS) to hold a full-committee oversight hearing on VA EHRM programs’ cost overrun and delays.

Blumenthal and House Veterans Affairs’ Committee Ranking Member Mark Takano (D-CA) also wrote to VA Secretary Doug Collins requesting additional documents and information surrounding the cost increase and expressing their concern about VA’s lack of transparency with Congress in managing the EHRM.

title: Chairman Moran Leads Hearing to Examine VA Electronic Health Record Modernization Program
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Jerry Moran (Kan.) – chairman of the Senate Committee on Veterans’ Affairs – this week led a hearing on the status and future of the Department of Veterans Affairs’ (VA) Electronic Health Record Modernization (EHRM) program. The committee heard testimony from Dr. Neil Evans, the Program Executive Director of the EHRM Integration Office at VA; Mike Sicilia, Chief Executive Officer of Oracle Corporation, accompanied by The Honorable Seema Verma, Executive Vice President and General Manager of Oracle Health and Life Sciences; and Carol Harris, Director of Information Technology and Cybersecurity at the U.S. Government Accountability Office.

“The implementation of a modern electronic health record carries tremendous opportunity for improving the delivery of care and benefits to veterans,” said Sen. Moran. “Despite repeated requests, this committee still has no answer on what this program will cost over its full life. Veterans, VA staff members, taxpayers and lawmakers deserve to know the program’s total cost. Congress’ duty in providing oversight is to understand the cost of the program, and the committee continues to await the detailed cost assessment. That is why I am calling on VA to provide a complete, updated, independent lifecycle cost estimate of the EHRM program as soon as possible.”

Currently, the new electronic health record is live at 19 VA medical facilities, and VA is expected to deploy the record to all of its 170 facilities by the end of 2031. The record will deploy in Kansas in January 2028; during the hearing, Chairman Moran raised concerns he has heard directly from Kansas veterans and VA employees and asked how VA and Oracle will make certain that the new system will reliably serve them.

title: Kaptur & Murray Call for Independent Review of DOE’s Sweeping Rewrite of Safety and Accountability Rules
text:
Toledo, OH — Today, Congresswoman Marcy Kaptur (OH-09), Ranking Member of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Energy and Water Development, and Senator Patty Murray (D-WA), Vice Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee and Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Energy and Water Development, sent a series of letters to the Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Inspector General (OIG), the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board (DNFSB), and the Government Accountability Office (GAO) asking for each to investigate the sweeping changes that DOE is making to its operating directives. The cumulative impact of these changes risks the safety of work being done at DOE labs, plants, and sites, and they reduce transparency and oversight and risk wasting taxpayer dollars.

In September, Kaptur and Murray called on DOE to restore critical safety rules it scrapped and to justify its revisions to dozens more of the operating directives. But DOE has failed to respond—prompting the lawmakers to call for independent investigation.

In a letter to DOE’s Inspector General, Kaptur and Murray requested the OIG evaluate DOE’s decision to revise forty-six operating directives and cancel four orders, which required DOE to track safety incidents and worker injuries across its labs and sites, and let workers formally challenge technical decisions they believed put safety at risk. The lawmakers wrote: “While the Department claims Project Velocity modernizes operations by shifting from procedural compliance to performance-based accountability, we are concerned that these sweeping rollbacks weaken critical safety protections, eliminate standardized occurrence and injury reporting, and eliminate formal dispute-resolution mechanisms. Further, we are troubled by the lack of transparency around the process of determining which DOE orders were modified or cancelled, who was involved in that process, and what criteria were used to make final determinations under Project Velocity.”

In a letter to DNFSB, the primary independent Federal agency charged by Congress with providing recommendations and oversight regarding defense nuclear facilities, Kaptur and Murray also asked to investigate the changes to the critical safety and accountability measures: “We are deeply concerned over the scale and speed of these regulatory changes, particularly because the changes touch upon nuclear facility safety, quality assurance, conduct of operations, worker training, and incident reporting. We remain very concerned about these simultaneous changes weakening critical safety controls and diminishing independent Federal oversight.”

In a letter to GAO, Kaptur and Murray ask the agency to conduct a comprehensive review of the operating directives. “GAO has raised concerns over the Department’s contract management and project oversight for decades, making this recent wholesale rewrite by the Department of dozens of operating directives highly concerning,” the lawmakers wrote to GAO. “Project Velocity represents a massive expansion of regulatory rollback across dozens of orders and directives. While DOE characterizes these changes as a transition from ‘procedural compliance’ to ‘performance-based accountability,’ we are deeply concerned that the scale and speed of these alterations weaken critical safety protections, undermine independent Federal oversight, shift core responsibilities to Management and Operating (M&O) contractors without adequate safeguards, and potentially increase taxpayer liabilities and costs.”

The lawmakers requested detailed answers and in-depth reviews from all three entities within 30 days to guarantee independent safety oversight is maintained to ensure public health and worker safety are preserved across all nuclear labs, facilities, and sites.

title: THE MORE YOU KNOW: Financial Services Committee Has Long Been the First Committee for Congressional Leaders
text:
From House Speakers to Powerful Committee Chairs, Financial Services Has Helped Launch Congressional Leaders Across Generations of Congress

Before Congresswoman Maxine Waters (D-CA), the top Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, made history as its first woman and first African American chair, the Committee had already established a decades-long tradition of helping Members build influential careers and rise to leadership positions across Congress. As the only exclusive House committee that welcomes freshman Members, Financial Services provides lawmakers with opportunities to tackle consequential issues from their very first term, develop expertise, and build relationships that strengthen their leadership throughout Congress. A review of historical Committee membership records identifies at least 20 Democratic Members who went on to serve on the Ways and Means and Appropriations Committees between the 102nd and 114th Congresses, spanning multiple Committee chairmanships.

Among them are some of Congress' most recognizable leaders. Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Reps. Barbara Lee, David Price, and Debbie Wasserman Schultz went on to serve on the Appropriations Committee, while Richard Neal, Rahm Emanuel, and Joe Crowley joined Ways and Means. These transitions occurred under several Committee chairmen, including Barney Frank, demonstrating that Members pursuing opportunities across Congress is a longstanding practice that predates Ranking Member Waters' leadership. The historical record below illustrates that tradition.

Ways and Means Congress

1 Jim McDermott (WA) 102 2 Richard Neal (MA) 103 3 Jerry Kleczka (WI) 103 4 Peter Hoagland (NE) 103 5 Max Sandlin (TX) 108 6 Stephanie Tubbs Jones (OH) 108 7 Rahm Emanuel (IL) 108 8 Joe Crowley (NY) 110 9 Artur David (AL) 110

Appropriations Congress 1 Nancy Pelosi (CA) 102 2 Richard Lehman (CA) 102 3 David Price (NC) 102 4 Esteban Torres (CA) 103 5 Jim Moran (VA) 103 6 Lucille Roybal-Allard (CA) 106 7 Jesse Jackson, Jr. (IL) 106 8 Carolyn Cheeks Kilpatrick 106 9 Barbara Lee (CA) 110 10 Steve Israel (NY) 110 11 Debbie Wasserman Schultz (FL) 110

While some Members have pursued opportunities on other exclusive committees, others have made Financial Services their legislative home for decades. That includes Ranking Member Waters, who has served on the Committee for more than 30 years, alongside longtime Members Nydia Velázquez (D-NY), Brad Sherman (D-CA), Gregory Meeks (D-NY), Stephen Lynch (D-MA), Al Green (D-TX), and Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO), each of whom has served for more than 20 years. Other longtime Members include Jim Himes (D-CT), Bill Foster (D-IL), Joyce Beatty (D-OH), and Juan Vargas (D-CA), who have each served on the Committee for more than a decade. At the same time, newer Members represent another generation of lawmakers bringing fresh perspectives and priorities to the Committee. Together, they reflect the Committee's depth of experience and ability to bring together Members at different stages of their congressional careers to tackle issues ranging from housing, banking, consumer protection, and the stability of the financial system.

In closing, the Financial Services Committee has long been a place where Members are encouraged to grow, lead, and make a difference, both within the Committee and throughout Congress. Under Ranking Member Waters’ leadership, that tradition continues, with a commitment to supporting Members’ ambitions, recognizing their contributions, and ensuring that the Committee remains a powerful force for working families, economic opportunity, and a stronger, fairer financial system.

title: American Banker - Q&A: Maxine Waters talks priorities for House committee
text:
Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., who serves as ranking member of the House Financial Services Committee. Bloomberg News

When Democrats swept the 2026 midterm elections, the party regained a solid control of Congress and the gavels of committees that oversee and make rules for banks.

In the House, that means Rep. Maxine Waters is back. The tenured lawmaker has represented her California district for three and a half decades, and has been the top Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee for 13 years. While she’s a familiar, if not always a friendly, face behind the podium for the nation’s banks, she’s joined by progressive allies like Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who’s next in line to lead the Senate Banking Committee, and enjoys support from her caucus to dig into the Trump administration and its financial relationships with private companies.

Waters does face a challenge for the gavel of the powerful committee in Rep. Sean Casten of Illinois. He is, however, still viewed as an underdog in the race by K Street, and Waters has the benefit of strong support from the influential Congressional Black Caucus, as well as more senior members of the committee.

Waters, in a conversation with American Banker, talked about how she would steer the panel should she win control of it. Democrats in both the House and the Senate will focus on oversight — with legislation being difficult to pass without a filibuster or veto-proof majority — but Waters is noted for her relationship with leading banking Republicans like current committee Chair French Hill, R-Ark.

She outlined issues where she might work across the aisle, such as deposit insurance reform, and where she will turn her oversight attention toward the private sector, notably involving cybersecurity concerns among the country’s largest banks. She wants to steer the committee toward a focus on housing, and said she would work on issues ranging from artificial intelligence in the financial sector to Federal Reserve master account access.

What follows is a transcript of the conversation between American Banker and Waters, edited for length and clarity.

American Banker: One of the things our readers are most interested in hearing about is oversight and the degree to which the Trump administration, as well as private industry, will be targets of that oversight. Can you talk a little bit about that? Give us a little bit of a preview of what your agenda looks like on oversight for industry in the next Congress.

Maxine Waters: Let me just say this: Oversight is the top mission of what we have the responsibility to do in our committee. We have to make sure that we hold the hearings, that we create legislation, that we call in witnesses to talk about the top issues, and that we get something done.

There has been extraordinary deregulation. We have to correct that. We look at how we can further help our small banks to thrive and to be able to service our communities and our neighborhoods.

Are there any specific agencies or any specific industries you’re interested in overseeing?

Well, we are concerned about the banks. We are concerned about what has happened recently, where we had the banks that were basically invaded for all intents and purposes. We need to understand what is happening and how to protect our banks from cyber attack.

We’re very interested in private equity, AI and asset managers. We know that there are some issues between AI and the banks, and trying to make sure that we understand that the banks do not want this competition necessarily with stablecoins being able to give interest. It just doesn’t work right for the banks, in particular the small banks.

A lot of bankers say that the industry got out of the housing mortgage finance space after Dodd-Frank. Is that something you’re open to look at to get the banking industry more involved as opposed to nonbank financers?

No, I’m not worried about that, and I haven’t seen any proof of that. We think that the bankers are interested in mortgages but I think they want the larger mortgages, and we want rural, small towns, suburbs, urban areas, everybody to have the opportunities for home mortgages.

You had a brief mention in your Dear Colleague letter of Federal Reserve master accounts and expanding access to them. Can you elaborate a little bit more on that? Who should we be expanding access to Federal Reserve master accounts to?

We were sitting here with my staff just talking about the fact we should revisit, we think that’s very important, and certainly reforms are needed. Absolutely.

Do those reforms come in the form of legislation?

I think so. I think we want to include that. We want to make sure that we take a good look and that we’re not excluding the possibility. We think that it is so possible for us to be able to solve some of the issues that have occurred.

Tell me a little bit more about your views on community bank deregulation. It seems like that’s an area where you and current Chairman Hill worked very well together. Talk to me a little bit about what you would do as chair to help banks under that $10 billion threshold?

I want to help community banks with deposit insurance. We think that’s an important issue. We have support on both sides of the aisle. We just haven’t agreed on the amounts yet, but we do believe that is something that’s going to happen. It’s been years since we’ve increased federal deposit insurance, and we do know that there’s a good reason to do it.

Times have changed, the economy has changed, and it makes good sense for us to keep up with what is happening in the economy and to give depositors some assurance that if there’s a run on the banks, if something happens that the banks all of a sudden do what Silicon Valley Bank did, that the deposits will have some support.

We need community banks and credit unions. Period. They helped during the pandemic, and I want to help them. This is a very important time for banks and credit unions not only to receive support, but to show what they can do once they get the resources and the support that they need.

Are we going back and starting from scratch on deposit insurance, or are you open to taking up any specific bill that’s already been in the Senate?

I don’t think we’re starting from scratch. A lot of work is going on. A lot of discussion is going on. I think we have support from both sides of the aisle to do something, and there’s recommendations that maybe I’m interested in that we can increase to $10 million, and we’re going to keep working. I think we’ve come a long way, and we’re going to have something coming out of this Congress for sure.

You had in your Dear Colleague letter a mention of an AI financial services bill. In your mind, what does that look like?

Well, I don’t know, but let me just say this: that it is an issue, a very controversial one, that’s got to be dealt with. It’s real, and of course, we have a lot of rumors about what it is and what it is not, and we’ve got to make sure that we are developing the experts and utilizing the experts to make sure that we have some guardrails. We’ve got to learn a lot about the agents and what their power is and what they’re doing. We are already getting a lot of information about the possibility of job loss, and so we’ve got a lot of work to do.

We have to be very careful about all these investments that are going to AI because we could end up with a problem that we don’t want to have to deal with. We have bailout concerns. We have a bill already that basically says we’re not bailing out firms because of a bubble that is created with all these investments. And of course, the whole liability issue has just got to be dealt with. It is now on the table for discussion, but no real solutions have come yet about how to deal with liability and with the agents and what they do or don’t do, etc. AI is a big issue, and we’re going to deal with it. It’s at our agenda, top of our agenda.

###

title: Meeks, Kamlager-Dove Demand Answers from Commerce on Megaspeed
text:
Washington, DC — Yesterday, Rep. Gregory W. Meeks (NY-05), Ranking Member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (CA-37), Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on South and Central Asia with jurisdiction over export controls, wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. They are demanding answers on how the department handled its investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company suspected of helping divert advanced Nvidia AI chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls.

“The Department of Commerce has a responsibility to protect American national security, enforce export control laws, and ensure that no corporation receives preferential treatment in matters involving potential violations of federal law. The circumstances described in recent reporting raise fundamental questions about whether federal export control enforcement is being conducted independently and consistently,” wrote the lawmakers.

“The American public and Congress deserve a full accounting of what happened, whether Under Secretary Kessler permitted or encouraged Nvidia to contact BIS agents actively investigating transactions in which the company was involved, and whether the Department allowed a major American corporation that is financially and personally linked to the Trump Administration to interfere with law enforcement activity,” continued the lawmakers.

While the Trump administration announced it is now pursuing a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, there are still unresolved questions about why the original investigation was halted and transferred to the Department of Justice in the first place.

title: Ranking Member Raskin Puts DOJ, FBI, DHS, ICE, and Bureau of Prisons on Notice: Preserve All Records—Including Signal Chats
text:
Records Obtained by Judiciary Democrats Reveal FBI’s Top Lawyer Discussed a Federal Investigation in a Signal Chat Set to Auto-Delete After One Week, Likely Violating Federal Law

Washington, D.C. (November 20, 2026)—Rep. Jamie Raskin, Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee, demanded that the heads of the Department of Justice (DOJ), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and Bureau of Prisons (BOP) preserve agency records, determine whether officials improperly deleted government communications from Signal and other messaging apps, and take immediate steps to recover any such records.

In the letters, Ranking Member Raskin disclosed a Signal exchange between FBI General Counsel Samuel Ramer and Drew Lynch, an associate of Donald Trump Jr. They discussed a potential or ongoing investigation involving an individual wanted by federal authorities on health care fraud and related charges. The exchange appears to show that the participants set their messages to disappear after one week. The exchange is one of many incidents already reported to the Committee.

“The FBI’s top lawyer should be ensuring that all 35,000 FBI employees are preserving government and law enforcement records; instead, he has conducted official business on a platform specifically configured to erase communications,” wrote Ranking Member Raskin.

Federal recordkeeping requirements apply to official communications on third-party messaging apps, including those sent from personal accounts. The National Archives has warned that automatic deletion can violate those requirements when it prevents officials from identifying and preserving federal records.

Ranking Member Raskin’s preservation demands cover official records on government and personal devices used for agency business, including records sought by the Judiciary Committee’s Chair or Ranking Member since January 20, 2025. He called on each agency head to open an inquiry into improperly deleted records and begin recovering them, including any available backups and associated metadata. Ranking Member Raskin asked all five agency heads to certify compliance by December 3 and detail the steps they have taken to determine whether officials used messaging apps to evade federal recordkeeping requirements and to prevent future violations.

title: Transcript of Ranking Member Khanna’s Opening Statement from Hearing on Outproducing the CCP and Restoring American Manufacturing

committee.name: House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party

text:
WASHINGTON – Today, the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party held a hearing entitled: Outproducing the CCP and Restoring American Manufacturing. The hearing examined trends in U.S. and China manufacturing and provided an outlook of China’s manufacturing sector.

The following witnesses provided testimony:

Mr. Owen Herrnstadt, Former Member of the Board of Directors of the Export-Import Bank of the United States and Former Chief of Staff of the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers

Mr. Pat Gelsinger, General Partner, Playground Global

Mr. Mark Widmar, CEO, First Solar

Mr. Tom O'Leary, CEO, JetZero

Below is a transcript of Ranking Member Khanna’s opening statement. Footage of his opening statement can be found here.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Since this is one of our last public hearings [of the year] I just want to thank you for your leadership of this Committee, this Congress, and your bipartisan leadership. The report that we [released last week] is a testament to your hard work and bipartisan leadership, and I appreciate that.

I want to thank our witnesses for joining us today.

Over this past year, we have been on two tours of the deindustrialized communities across our Heartland and across the South. We saw the devastation brought about by deindustrialization in this country.

This country has offshored jobs to China, and we abandoned workers who held them, while others built fortunes moving production overseas and putting profits over our country.

The result is not just hollowed out towns; it is the loss of the social fabric and moral fabric in this country. An America dependent on Beijing for everything from the necessities of daily life to the technologies of the future, is not an America that will lead the world in the 21st century. Enough is enough.

Last week, this Committee released a bipartisan report entitled “Rigging the Game: How China Undermined Western Manufacturing and Hollowed Out American Industry.” It examines four industries: biomanufacturing, aerospace, semiconductor, and machine tools, and shows how the CCP has not played by the rules.

Let me give you an example. I was just in the South. We were meeting with textile manufacturers – people who spin the yarn. I said, “What about the tariffs on the 60 to 70 percent on yarn that we've put on China?”

They said, “It doesn't matter. China just eats them because they have a jobs program. They're just hiring these young people and they just eat the tariff.”

China is simply not playing fair. They are dumping and having a government compete against industry in biomanufacturing. China is subsidizing and prioritizing the sector in a race to supplant American leadership.

As a Commissioner on the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotech, I am glad this report reflects our bipartisan commitment to biomanufacturing. Our analysis should be a call to action to fund our universities, support our innovators, and attract high-skilled talent to the United States.

In aerospace, our report shows how the CCP is pouring unprecedented resources into COMAC, China's state-owned answer to Boeing and Airbus. I'm pleased that Owen Herrnstadt, a former senior leader at the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, is one of our witnesses today. Thank you, Owen.

In semiconductors, China's efforts to outcompete us are no secret. Thanks to Pat Gelsinger’s leadership and others, Congress passed the CHIPS ACT, and we made progress on shoring advanced chip production as a result.

But China is increasing its dominance in legacy chips, which power everything from cars to electronics. And China is cheating. As we saw with the recent allegations about Nvidia – circumventing our export control laws and trying to steal our chips. If we do not act fast, the CCP will have yet another chokepoint it can use against us.

And finally, our report shows how China has ramped up its machine tool industry as America's has slipped away. If American factories depend on Chinese equipment, we've only solved half the problem. We need to reindustrialize the nation and ensure it runs much deeper than just four industries.

The CCP’s Made in China initiative targeted 10 priority high-tech sectors, which aim to transfer China from a labor-intensive assembler into a global tech leader.

While America has rolled back investment in clean energy, China poured resources into the green economy. Last spring, I visited First Solar’s factory in Ohio with their CEO, who's here as one of our witnesses. I saw with the right policies, domestic manufacturing can lower prices, restore jobs, and reinvigorate American leadership. It is time for Congress to step up in a bipartisan way. If we invest in our workers and innovators like never before, American manufacturing in hollowed out communities can prosper again. We can outproduce the CCP.

Thank you and I yield back.

title: Statement of the Committee on Ethics
text:
On November 19, 2026, the Committee on Ethics (Committee) adopted changes to the Rules of the Committee with the goal of improving the speed of investigations, increasing transparency, and protecting victims of sexual misconduct.

In the 119th Congress, the Committee encountered several notable circumstances, including multiple complex matters under review by investigative subcommittees (ISCs), an unusual number of investigations involving allegations of sexual misconduct, and the first adjudicatory subcommittee (ASC) in over a decade. The Committee reviewed its rules taking into account these experiences, the views of outside stakeholders, and best practices for ethics and compliance investigations. That review identified areas for improvement while also seeking to preserve the procedures that ensure victim and witness privacy protection, fairness, due process, and bipartisanship in all investigations.

These changes improve the speed of Committee investigations in several ways. For example, the Committee delegated subpoena authority to the Chairman and Ranking Member, acting jointly, instead of requiring that the full Committee vote on subpoenas. This should significantly expedite Committee investigations. The changes also streamline the conclusion of the Committee’s ISC process by consolidating duplicative procedural steps. The rules also simplify the ASC process and make it easier to expedite the process once there is a sufficient factual record. These changes should accelerate the conclusion of investigations by several months or more while still providing for important due process protections.

To ensure transparency in sexual misconduct matters while protecting victims, the Committee codified its longstanding policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct in violation of clauses 9 or 18 of the Code of Official Conduct with explicit requirements to protect victim identities.

Finally, the Committee also made other changes to its rules, including expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered as appropriate sanctions and requiring the Committee to continually review its rules to ensure that they provide for fair, efficient, and effective investigations. Through these changes, the Committee will continue its mission to hold Members of Congress and House officers and staff to the highest ethical standards.

title: Chairman Hill Applauds Signing of Common Cents Act into Law
text:
Today, H.R. 10167, the Common Cents Act, was signed into law. The measure permanently ends the production of pennies for general circulation and gives consumers, businesses, and financial institutions greater certainty as the United States transitions away from the penny. In the House, Republican Conference Chairwoman Lisa McClain (MI-09) led this bipartisan legislation.

House Committee on Financial Services Chairman French Hill (AR-02) said, “Today, President Trump signed the Common Cents Act into law, ending the costly production of the penny and providing the U.S. Mint greater flexibility to produce coins more efficiently. For years, Members of Congress have recognized the fiscal irresponsibility of spending more producing a penny than it is worth. This legislation takes an important step toward eliminating wasteful government spending while also providing clear legislative guidance for retailers, financial institutions, and consumers. I thank Conference Chairwoman McClain, Representative Frank Lucas, and Senator Cynthia Lummis for their leadership in getting this commonsense legislation across the finish line.”

Chairwoman McClain said, “Washington has a spending problem, and it shows up in places big and small. If the federal government is spending nearly four cents to make a penny worth one cent, something is broken. House Republicans are proving that common sense still has a place in government by cutting waste and protecting taxpayer dollars.”

Task Force on Monetary Policy, Treasury Market Resilience, and Economic Prosperity Chairman Frank Lucas (OK-03) said, “I am pleased to see the Common Cents Act become law,” said Congressman Lucas. "This fiscally responsible legislation ensures taxpayer dollars are protected while providing certainty for businesses in their cash transactions with customers. I am grateful for my colleagues who helped get this critical legislation across the finish line.”

Further Background

The Common Cents Act permanently ends the production of pennies for general circulation, while existing pennies remain legal tender and the U.S. Mint may continue producing collectible coins.

A previous version of the legislation passed the House Financial Services Committee on July 23, 2025.

The bill passed the House of Representatives on September 14, 2026.

The bill passed the Senate on September 28, 2026.

title: Chairmen Garbarino, Moolenaar Release Joint Investigative Report Urging Removal of PRC Open-Weight Models From Federal Systems, High-Risk Critical Infrastructure
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. –– Today, House Committee on Homeland Security Chairman Andrew R. Garbarino (R-NY) and House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar (R-MI) released a joint investigative report detailing the national security, cybersecurity, and economic security implications of U.S. companies integrating open-weight artificial intelligence (AI) models developed by the People’s Republic of China (PRC) into consumer platforms, enterprise software, and systems with access to sensitive commercial or personal information. Read more in CNBC.

The joint investigation examined the provenance of these models, the data and techniques used to train them, whether their capabilities were advanced through unauthorized distillation from leading U.S. systems, and how they are being repackaged, deployed, or made available to companies in the United States and around the world. As part of that work, the Committees also examined whether the United States has a sufficient open-weight AI strategy to ensure American companies and cyber defenders are not forced to choose between expensive or proprietary U.S. models and cheap, capable PRC-developed alternatives.

The Committees’ investigation was launched in April 2026 and included correspondence with three U.S. companies: Airbnb, which uses Alibaba models in customer support; Anysphere, which built the flagship proprietary model in its Cursor coding platform on a Moonshot AI base model; and DoorDash, which reported that multiple PRC model families had been authorized and deployed. The Committees engaged in productive discussions with the companies regarding the technical, commercial, and security considerations surrounding their evaluation and use of PRC-developed open-weight models.

The Chairmen provide 12 policy recommendations in the report, centering on the need to build the American open-weight alternative, know which models are running in sensitive systems, share threat information and strengthen defenses, impose costs on illicit extraction, and set durable rules with allies. Building on the Department of Homeland Security’s order excluding DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems, the Chairmen call for prohibiting PRC-developed models in federal systems and federal contract work, removing them from high-risk functions of critical infrastructure, and barring the use of federal cybersecurity grant funds to buy them. The Committees have provided the findings and recommendations in this report to help lawmakers, agencies, and companies make informed decisions to protect U.S. systems, critical infrastructure, and our economic and national security. The Committees will continue their oversight of these issues.

In the Foreword of the report, Chairmen Garbarino and Moolenaar write, in part:

“The investigation uncovered risks that American businesses, policymakers, and national security officials can no longer afford to overlook or downplay. From Silicon Valley startups to Fortune 500 companies, American businesses are increasingly adopting PRC-developed open-weight models because they are inexpensive, customizable, and competitive with leading American systems. Federal investigations, however, have found that major PRC developers used proxy networks and fraudulent accounts to harvest outputs from American frontier models and replicate their capabilities. While America is investing billions and racing to build ‘Super Intelligence,’ Beijing is using stolen intelligence to close the gap.”

“Congress has too often been behind the curve on emerging technology. As one of our colleagues observed after a briefing on these issues, AI is advancing so quickly that Congress risks being ‘light years behind.’ With this investigation, we intend to narrow that gap. We should not wait five years to discover that much of the world, and much of the United States, runs on AI shaped by the CCP, leaving policymakers with little choice but another costly rip and replace effort. The time to act is now, while we still have the opportunity and leverage to do so.”

Read the full report here. Highlights of the report can be found below.

Findings:

PRC-developed open-weight models are already widely used across the American economy, but much of that use is hard to track.

Cost, customization, and near-frontier performance are driving adoption, and the United States lacks a competitive open-weight alternative at the price and performance the market demands.

Much of the PRC’s apparent progress rests on capabilities extracted from American models, and American data-labeling firms are helping supply the data that trains PRC models.

Beijing is using open-weight distribution, state support, and low prices to expand global dependence on PRC models, while the terms of that dependence are beginning to change.

The risks are increasing as PRC models become more capable, while their behavior and security properties can differ in ways ordinary evaluations may not detect.

Policy Recommendations:

Launch a national American open-weight AI initiative.

Make trusted American AI the global default.

Establish a model provenance standard and an AI bill of materials.

Extend federal restrictions beyond DeepSeek, keep PRC-developed AI models out of federal contract work and high-risk functions of critical infrastructure, and give agencies the visibility to enforce these restrictions.

Secure long-term information-sharing authorities and build a developer-level AI threat channel.

Evaluate PRC models systematically, translate the results into guidance, and give the Information Technology Sector a single accountable federal partner.

Prepare DHS and CISA to defend at machine speed and secure AI agents on federal networks.

Make CISA the single point of submission for AI-related cyber incident reports and establish an independent board to investigate significant incidents.

Hold illicit distillers accountable and close the gray market.

Examine sales of American training data to PRC AI laboratories.

Govern both closed and open models and avoid overregulation.

Work with allies and deepen understanding of PRC strategy.

Background:

Over the past seven months, the Committees conducted the investigation through document requests, company briefings, review of company productions and written responses, and classified briefings, and consulted frontier AI developers, cybersecurity executives, federal agencies, industry leaders, and academic researchers. The review also drew on an expanding body of public and government research. The House Committee on Homeland Security continues to engage with the private sector on AI through roundtables, briefings, and hearings on the future of cybersecurity and best practices for developing secure AI technology.

The new report comes as the PRC has intensified its efforts to close the AI innovation gap with leading U.S. frontier labs through model distillation, intellectual property theft, and other illicit means. In September 2026, the National Security Agency (NSA), CISA, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) released a joint advisory warning of the national security impacts of these large-scale distillation efforts against American AI companies, particularly as the PRC utilizes advanced AI models to increase the scale, scope, and speed of its intrusions into U.S. systems.

In May, Anthropic provided Committee Members with one of the first live demonstrations of Mythos given to Congress, allowing Members to see firsthand how advanced AI can find software vulnerabilities. The demonstration reinforced the urgency of ensuring that federal agencies, including our civilian cyber defenders, can responsibly use advanced U.S. models to find and patch vulnerabilities.

In June, the Subcommittee on Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Protection convened a hearing to examine how AI is transforming the cybersecurity landscape and reshaping the resilience of America’s critical infrastructure, as well as policy solutions to secure our networks, strengthen America’s domestic technology base, and ensure the United States maintains its leadership in emerging technologies.

In September 2025, Chairman Garbarino introduced the “Widespread Information Management for the Welfare of Infrastructure and Government Act,” or WIMWIG Act, which would enhance and extend the “Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015” for the next decade. The bill improves voluntary, real-time information sharing on cyber threats between federal and non-federal entities and preserves the original law’s privacy protections. Rep. Andy Ogles (R-TN), Subcommittee on Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Protection chairman, introduced the “Protecting Information by Local Leaders for Agency Resilience Act,” or PILLAR Act, to reauthorize DHS’s State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program. The program provides grants to state, local, tribal, and territorial governments to address cybersecurity risks and threats to information systems and operational technology systems, including those using artificial intelligence. The Committee on Homeland Security advanced both pieces of legislation in a bipartisan markup.

###

title: Chairman Moolenaar’s Opening Statement: Restoring American Manufacturing & Rebuilding America's Industrial Base

committee.name: House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party

text:
Today, Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar delivered his opening statement at the Select Committee’s hearing titled Outproducing the CCP: Restoring American Manufacturing.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Chinese Communist Party has spent decades executing a deliberate campaign to dominate global manufacturing in the industries that matter most to America's economy and national security. In most of those industries, China is no longer merely competing with the United States. It has surpassed us.

This did not happen by market forces. It happened by China’s design.

After World War II, the architects of the global trading system faced a basic question: should a command economy run by an authoritarian government be allowed to benefit from the open markets free nations had built for one another? Washington warned that the Soviet economic system was not compatible with the world trading body. It was one of the most prescient judgments in the history of

American trade policy.

When a new century began, America made a different choice and offered a seat at the table to the Chinese Communist Party. Since joining the World Trade Organization in 2001, China has run the same playbook again and again. Massive state subsidies. A deliberate buildup of overcapacity. Dumping products below cost, bankrupting foreign competitors, consolidating market share and weaponizing pricing power. The results have been disastrous. American workers and innovators have paid the price and our industrial base has been hollowed out.

The scale of this effort is staggering. In 2019 alone, China spent roughly $248 billion on industrial policy — 1.73 percent of its GDP. The United States spent less than a quarter of that as a share of our economy.

This Committee's new bipartisan report, Rigging the Game, documents exactly how industry after industry has been ruined.

In semiconductors, China has poured more than $100 billion into its national chip fund, and the latest phase alone could mobilize over $200 billion more. China is on track to control nearly half of the world's mature-node chip capacity by 2027 — the chips that run our cars, our power grid, and our weapons systems.

In aerospace, China has spent an estimated $49 billion dollars propping up its commercial aircraft champion — more than twice the subsidy Airbus received from Europe.

In machine tools — the machines that make the machines — China has used state funds and state-owned enterprises to push domestic control of its market from low single digits to over 30 percent in the high-end segment.

Biomanufacturing is now dominated by China, which produces 70 percent of the world's fermentation output. China's strategy is a sword and a shield. At home, it eliminates China's dependence on the rest of the world. Abroad, it makes the rest of the world dependent on China — and then uses that dependence as leverage. We have seen it with rare earths. We have seen it with solar. If we do nothing, we will see it again.

Make no mistake: this is not only an economic fight. Manufacturing capacity and military deterrence are inseparable. China today has roughly 230 times the shipbuilding capacity of the United States, and its commercial and military shipyards share the same resources. In a modern great-power conflict, the side that can replace its losses is the side that will win. Right now, that is not us.

The good news is that we can change course. Rebuilding America's industrial base is a cause that unites every American, regardless of party.

The expert witnesses before us today have built, led, and invested in American manufacturing while competing head-to-head against the Chinese state. We are going to hear what that competition looks like from the inside, and what it will take to restore American production in critical industries. Our bipartisan report is the launchpad for what Congress can do to make sure the next generation of American industry is built here at home.

Manufacturing cannot be treated as a relic of the past. Instead, we must recognize Made in America as a foundation of 21st-century power that will ensure good-paying jobs for millions of Americans, control of our nation’s destiny, and American leadership of the world for generations to come. I look forward to hearing from our witnesses.

title: Joint Investigation Report: China is Trying to Get U.S. Companies Addicted to Chinese AI Models

committee.name: House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party

text:
Today, Chairman John Moolenaar (R-MI) of the House Select Committee on China and Chairman Andrew R. Garbarino (R-NY) of the House Committee on Homeland Security released a report following their joint investigation into the integration of Chinese-developed open-weight artificial intelligence (AI) models into American companies' consumer platforms. The committees began this investigation in April 2026 with letters to Anysphere and Airbnb. As a next step in the investigation, the Chairmen sent a letter to DoorDash requesting similar information in July 2026.

In the report, Chairmen Garbarino and Moolenaar write:

“The investigation uncovered risks that American businesses, policymakers, and national security officials can no longer afford to overlook or downplay. From Silicon Valley startups to Fortune 500 companies, American businesses are increasingly adopting PRC-developed open-weight models because they are inexpensive, customizable, and competitive with leading American systems. Federal investigations, however, have found that major PRC developers used proxy networks and fraudulent accounts to harvest outputs from American frontier models and replicate their capabilities. “Congress has too often been behind the curve on emerging technology. As one of our colleagues observed after a briefing on these issues, AI is advancing so quickly that Congress risks being ‘light years behind.’ With this investigation, we intend to narrow that gap. The time to act is now, while we still have the opportunity and leverage to do so."

The Committees’ investigation found that personnel associated with the 1st Bureau of the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) Cyberspace Force, the unit responsible for cyber espionage, and attacks have been present on multiple occasions at the Beijing headquarters of Zhipu, most recently in August 2026. These visits indicate a channel between the PLA’s cyber intelligence apparatus and one of China’s leading AI developers.

The Committees’ review of PLA procurement records also found the Chinese military building these models directly into its cyber operations. A July 2026 procurement for a large PLA cyber range, a system for generating “cybersecurity professional capability,” required integrating DeepSeek to support “intelligent attack” and “intelligent penetration.” Other records show a command information system built around Alibaba’s Qwen and DeepSeek, and a 2026 project requiring models from DeepSeek, Alibaba, Moonshot, and MiniMax to run on a network cut off from the internet for military AI agent development. Documents produced to the Committees show that these same model families are running inside major American companies.

Findings

China-developed open-weight models are already widely used across the American economy, but much of that use is hard to track.

Cost, customization, and near-frontier performance are driving adoption, and the United States lacks a competitive open-weight alternative at the price and performance the market demands.

Much of China’s apparent progress rests on capabilities extracted from American models, and American data-labeling firms are helping supply the data that trains Chinese models.

China is using open-weight distribution, state support, and low prices to expand global dependence on Chinese models, while the terms of that dependence are beginning to change.

The risks are increasing as Chinese models become more capable, while their behavior and security properties can differ in ways ordinary evaluations may not detect.

Policy Recommendations

Launch a national American open-weight AI initiative.

Make trusted American AI the global default.

Establish a model provenance standard and an AI bill of materials.

Extend federal restrictions beyond DeepSeek, keep China-developed AI models out of federal contract work and high-risk functions of critical infrastructure, and give agencies the visibility to enforce these restrictions.

Secure long-term information-sharing authorities and build a developer-level AI threat channel.

Evaluate Chinese models systematically, translate the results into guidance, and give the Information Technology Sector a single accountable federal partner.

Prepare DHS and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to defend at machine speed and secure AI agents on federal networks.

Make CISA the single point of submission for AI-related cyber incident reports and establish an independent board to investigate significant incidents.

Hold illicit distillers accountable and close the gray market.

Examine sales of American training data to Chinese AI laboratories.

Govern both closed and open models and avoid overregulation.

Work with allies and deepen understanding of China’s strategy.

Background

The new report comes as China has intensified its efforts to close the AI innovation gap with leading U.S. frontier labs through model distillation, intellectual property theft, and other illicit means. In September 2026, the National Security Agency (NSA), CISA, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) released a joint advisory warning of the national security impacts of these large-scale distillation efforts against American AI companies, particularly as China utilizes advanced AI models to increase the scale, scope, and speed of its intrusions into U.S. systems.

title: Murray & Kaptur Call for Independent Review of DOE’s Sweeping Rewrite of Safety and Accountability Rules
text:
Murray & Kaptur Call for Independent Review of DOE’s Sweeping Rewrite of Safety and Accountability Rules

ICYMI: Murray, Kaptur Demand Energy Department Restore Eliminated Safety Rules, Justify Rewrite of Dozens of Critical Safety and Accountability Measures

Washington, D.C. — Senator Patty Murray (D-WA), Vice Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee and Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Energy and Water Development, and Congresswoman Marcy Kaptur (D-OH-09), Ranking Member of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Energy and Water Development, sent a series of letters to the Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Inspector General (OIG), the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board (DNFSB), and the Government Accountability Office (GAO) asking for each to investigate the sweeping changes that DOE is making to its operating directives. The cumulative impact of these changes risks the safety of work being done at DOE labs, plants, and sites, and they reduce transparency and oversight and risk wasting taxpayer dollars.

In September, Murray and Kaptur called on DOE to restore critical safety rules it scrapped and to justify its revisions to dozens more of the operating directives. But DOE has failed to respond—prompting the lawmakers to call for independent investigation.

In a letter to DOE’s Inspector General, Murray and Kaptur requested the OIG evaluate DOE’s decision to revise forty-six operating directives and cancel four orders, which required DOE to track safety incidents and worker injuries across its labs and sites, and let workers formally challenge technical decisions they believed put safety at risk. The lawmakers wrote: “While the Department claims Project Velocity modernizes operations by shifting from procedural compliance to performance-based accountability, we are concerned that these sweeping rollbacks weaken critical safety protections, eliminate standardized occurrence and injury reporting, and eliminate formal dispute-resolution mechanisms. Further, we are troubled by the lack of transparency around the process of determining which DOE orders were modified or cancelled, who was involved in that process, and what criteria were used to make final determinations under Project Velocity.”

In a letter to DNFSB, the primary independent Federal agency charged by Congress with providing recommendations and oversight regarding defense nuclear facilities, Murray and Kaptur also asked to investigate the changes to the critical safety and accountability measures: “We are deeply concerned over the scale and speed of these regulatory changes, particularly because the changes touch upon nuclear facility safety, quality assurance, conduct of operations, worker training, and incident reporting. We remain very concerned about these simultaneous changes weakening critical safety controls and diminishing independent Federal oversight.”

In a letter to GAO, Murray and Kaptur ask the agency to conduct a comprehensive review of the operating directives. “GAO has raised concerns over the Department’s contract management and project oversight for decades, making this recent wholesale rewrite by the Department of dozens of operating directives highly concerning,” the lawmakers wrote to GAO. “Project Velocity represents a massive expansion of regulatory rollback across dozens of orders and directives. While DOE characterizes these changes as a transition from ‘procedural compliance’ to ‘performance-based accountability,’ we are deeply concerned that the scale and speed of these alterations weaken critical safety protections, undermine independent Federal oversight, shift core responsibilities to Management and Operating (M&O) contractors without adequate safeguards, and potentially increase taxpayer liabilities and costs.”

The lawmakers requested detailed answers and in-depth reviews from all three entities within 30 days to guarantee independent safety oversight is maintained to ensure public health and worker safety are preserved across all nuclear labs, facilities, and sites.

The full letter to the DOE IG is available HERE.

The full letter to DNFSB is available HERE.

The full letter to GAO is available HERE.

text:

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee, delivered a speech on the Senate floor recognizing last night’s historic passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), permitting reform legislation she authored alongside U.S. Senators Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.).

In her remarks, Chairman Capito recognized the unwavering effort from her fellow negotiators to pass this legislation, thanked supporters and sponsors, and urged the House of Representatives to quickly pass BAAJA to make life more affordable for American families.

HIGHLIGHT:

“I hope our colleagues in the House will act quickly. I said last night and I believe this in the very heart of me, that people send us here to do things, to make their lives better. This is an affordability bill, this is jobs for the future, this is building America’s infrastructure quicker and faster and more efficiently. That’s what the American people want us to do. They don’t want to see us fight and bicker and not try to work out our differences. This is a great example of a difficult climb, where we were able to work out our differences because we put the principle of doing what we think is right and good for the American people first. So, I hope our House counterparts, when they return, will act quicky and send this bill to President Trump’s desk without delay.”
